Prosperity!
The *Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati*,
composed by the venerable Īśānaśivagurudevamiśra.
(The Kriyāpāda.)
Now begins the thirty-first chapter.
Maya spoke of fourteen distinct types of consecration (adhiṣṭhāna), while Parāśara and others have declared them to be of two or three kinds.
The *pratikramaṇa* with four-line stanzas (*pādabandha*) spoken by Parāśara is of two kinds; since each of these has four varieties, it is said to be eightfold.
For example:
when the height of the base (adhiṣṭhāna) is divided into three parts, one part shall be the jagatī; one part shall be the kumuda; and the remainder, having been divided into eight parts— || 3 ||
One part for the fillet (paṭṭikā), one part for the base-molding (kampa), and one part for the neck (kaṇṭha); above the neck, one should fashion the vājana with three parts.
This "foot-binding" (pādabandha) is to be known as prescribed for the primary castes and others; it is a foot-binding where the height of the base is one-fourth [of the total]. 5.
The jagatī should consist of eight parts; the kumuda should be seven parts; the padma, the paṭṭikā, and the kampa should each be one part; and the gala should be two parts.
The upper vibration (ūrdhvakampa) should be by one part, and the fillet (vājana) by three parts;
this is declared to be the *viprabandha*, and it is likewise called the *cārubandha*.
The jagatī is seven parts; the kumuda is six; the lotus (ambuja) is one; the fillet (paṭṭa) and the projection (kampa) are each one; the neck (kaṇṭha) is two parts; and the lotus is one part.

Two [parts] for the *vājana*, one lotus (*abja*) with two parts for the upper fillet (*ūrdhvapaṭṭika*), and a beautiful band (*cārubandha*); this base (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is distinguished by its various components. (9)

The Cārubandha [is formed] as previously described; however, the Jagatī [portion] is made with one part of the arrows (five), while the lotus is supported on one side by four parts, and the upward-facing lotus by four parts; the remainder is as abundant as before.
Puṣkala: here, the *jagatī* and the *kumuda* are equal; the *samāna* is half [the height]; the *aliṅga* is equal [to the *samāna*];
the *antarita* is one-third; and the *prasyuttama* part is the *padma* and the *vājana*. This is called the *pratikrama*.

It is auspicious for gods, brahmins, and kings; it is inauspicious for others. Furthermore, Parāśara states that a face shaped like a crocodile (*kakarī*), with a makara-like mouth, and adorned with predatory beasts, deer, and elephants, is indeed inauspicious for everyone.

One should visualize the makara as having become a crow, with the faces of a deer, a serpent, and an elephant; it should be made level and all-pervading in its activity, for that is what obstructs it.
The *pratibandha* [is formed];

that very same [structure] would be the *nāgabandha*, which is the binding of the serpent's mouth. That same [pattern], when placed in the position of the *jagatī* with an eightfold division, becomes the large lotus (*bṛhadambuja*).
The neck [should be] one part, the lotus one part, and the lily (kumuda) should be three parts;
then the upper lotus is one part, separated from the embrace by three [parts].
The remaining part of the *vājana* should be equal and slightly elevated;
this is called the *śrībandha*, which is suitable for gods, brahmins, and kings. 14.
The Śrībandha:
In this twenty-ninth part, at the emergence of the foundation (adhiṣṭhāna), there shall be that very lotus, the kumuda, and likewise the kampa and the vājana as before. 15.
From the upper lotus, the *kapota* (dove-cornice) should be one and a half parts; then, from each part, it extends to the end of the *āliṅga*, rising again by two parts and then by one part.
And with an increase of one and a half *vājas*, it is called the *kāpotabandhana* (dove-binding);
this is achieved by increasing [the measurement] by two, four, one-quarter, one-half, and three-quarters of a *yava*.
Alternatively, one may create beauty for each individual limb according to one's preference.
Likewise, there should be a small platform upon the main platform, adorned with lotuses and provided with a movable support. (18)
One should arrange it as a square, according to its beauty, upon the foundations.
Regarding this, Maya says:
"For the Taitilas, four cubits; for the twice-born, three and a half cubits; for kings..."
The [throne] for the king is three cubits and a half, while that for the crown prince is two cubits.
For merchants, it is two cubits; for a Śūdra, it is traditionally held to be one cubit.
Thus ends the section on the foundational supports. The pillars, the beams, as well as the pedestals, the pots, and the supporting feet;

Now, the synonyms for a pillar (stambha) are given, and then its characteristics are described: it should be four-cornered from base to top and provided with a capital and a neck (kumbha-maṇḍi). || 20 ||
A pillar made of stone or even wood may be called *brahmakānta* if it is octagonal;
one known as *viṣṇukānta* is hexagonal, while a *skandakānta* has six corners. || 21 ||
That very same [gem] called Indra becomes Bhānukānta when it has twelve facets;
Candrakānta when it has sixteen facets; and if it is circular, it is Īśakāntaka. || 22 ||

In its own high and beautiful sections, circular according to the measure of four times eight (thirty-two), and joined with the pot-base (kumbha) and other ornaments, it is declared to be "dear to Rudra. (23)
At the base, there is a lotus-seat adorned with ruddy geese;
its central portion is auspicious, beautiful, and possesses two circular bands.
That which is adorned at its base by serpents, elephants, and lions, and likewise has a desired form above, shall be known by the name Tattatkānta. || 25 ||
A *vṛtta* (circular) base, joined with its own long *śuṇḍubheda*, is a *śuṇḍupāda*;
if it is variegated with pearls, it is a *bhiṇḍipāda*.
It is four-cornered at the base and adorned above with sixteen corners and so forth.
It may be known as the "square base" (mūlacaturaśra), and it is traditionally called the "lotus-throne" (padmāsana). || 27 ||

At the base and the top, however, it has four corners, while in the middle it is adorned with eight corners; that which is beautiful with vajras and possesses pearl-like pillars is to be known as the *samauktika* [type]. (28)
Whatever gem adorns its pillars, by that gem it shall be named; at its base it has a lotus-seat, and in the middle it is adorned with sixteen facets.

The foot that is square in its upper portion is known as the Citrakhaṇḍa; that same foot, when it has eight sides in the middle and is adorned with a binding band (paṭṭabandha), is called the Śrīkhaṇḍa.
In the center is the one known as Śrīvajra, which has eight corners and is bound with a band;
that which is known by the name Paṭṭakṣepaṇa is square and bears three bands.

If it is circular, it is called *daṇḍapāda*; if it has edges shaped like a thunderbolt (*vajra*), it is *vajrapāda*. It should be broad at the base and the tip, and slender in the middle by one-quarter of its width. (32)

It may be known as Ulūkhalapāda, having its base and plinth shaped like a mortar; the projection of the wall from the pillar shall be one-quarter, one-half, or one-third [of the pillar's width]. || 33 ||
The width of the base, the ground, and the pillar should be known respectively as square, octagonal, and circular; indeed, [the measurement] is twenty-eight finger-breadths.
The width should be reduced by two finger-breadths at each successive level;
furthermore, the height of the pillar is considered to be twice the height of its base.
From eleven, nine, eight, and four parts, one part is subtracted for each successive tier;
thus is the width and height of the pillar and the wall established at both the base and the top.
In this context—
that which is as broad as a wall or the top of a pillar is called a *daṇḍa*; by that measure all the constituent parts of the celestial mansions (*vimāna*) are to be measured.
Thus says Parāśara:

"The *śikhā* (the pinnacle) should be made according to a measurement of three, four, or five parts from the base and the top of the pedestals; all [the other members] should likewise be established upon the stones."
One should fashion the altar at the base of the pillars using the very same material as the pillars;
the height of the altar should be one-ninth or one-eighth of the pillar's elevation.
And its width should be that same measure; that altar (vedī) is of four kinds: Puṣpakhaṇḍā, Citrakhaṇḍā, Śaivalā, and Citraśaivalā. || 39 ||

Trembling sleep (*kampanidrā*), accompanied by trembling and divided like a flower, with the altar for the worship of the root-feet (*mūlapādārcanāvedi*)— this is called the "flower-fragment" (*puṣpakhaṇḍa*). (40)
That very same [footprint], when decorated with lines of sleep-patterns, tremors, and lotus petals, and variegated at the foot and between the feet, is called the *citrakhaṇḍa*. 41.
It is adorned with pillars, tremors, lotuses, and bands; on the band it is variegated with moss;
it is enriched with lotus petals above and below, at the base, and even between the bases.
Indeed, the altar named Śaivalā is variegated with the leaves of men and women;
it is beautiful with a pair of cane-staffs between the lower and upper lotuses.

As before, that altar should be variegated in appearance like a bed of diverse moss; one should not cut away the altar for the sake of the lattice-work, except for the purpose of the archway (toraṇa).
Or, in this case, according to the specific instruction, cutting the altar at the doorway does not cause any fault.
A flower-section and a painting-section are recorded as the two altars for men.

A square altar (vedīcatuṣka) is prescribed for the pillars and other parts of temples; it should occupy one-third of the pillar's height, while its base should have four corners and consist of one part.
The middle section of the pillars may be octagonal, sixteen-sided, or even circular;
in some cases, the upper portion of the pillars may also be quadrangular.
When the base width is divided into five parts, two parts are reduced from the middle of the pillar;
the final part, when reduced by one-seventh, becomes the width at the base.
The *kumbhas* (vases) should serve as the pedestals (*pādaviṣkambha*); they may be increased by one-fourth, or decreased by one-fourth, or indeed become double [the size]. || 49 ||
Śrīkara, Candrakānta, Saumukhya, and Priyadarśana—these are the four types of *kumbha* (pitchers); among them, Śrīkara is the circular one.
For octagonal [pillars], the moonstone (candrakānta) is auspicious; for sixteen-sided ones, the śrīkara is desired.
For square pillars, the saumukhya pitcher is prescribed.
For the remaining very heavy [weights], Kumbha shall be Priyadarśana;
however, in the ninth part of the Kumbha division, Dhṛti is ordained by one [author].
With four [parts], it should be a pitcher (kumbha); the neck with one part, and the mouth with one part.
Having divided the remaining two parts into three, the lotus should be made with one [of those]. (53)
The circular portion [of the pillar] is formed from the remaining part; above that, at the neck, are two distinct [ornaments].
The shoulder should be of equal width, following the path of the corner at the top of the pillar.
Above that, one should fix the *vīrakāṇḍa* (heroic shaft), and upon it, the *potikā* (bud-shaped capital); its height should be three or even four times the width of the pillar.
The height of the fillet (maṇḍī) is prescribed to be equal to the tip of the foot [of the pillar], measured by a fourth part of the shaft;
the height of the fillet and the height of the vīrakāṇḍa should both be that same measure.
The width of the maṇḍī should be one daṇḍa, and its length five parts [of a hasta]. The thickness of the wooden planks should be half of that, and the protrusion of the cane should be equal to that.
Having the shape of a curl or an utpala petal,
shaped like a crest or like a lotus leaf, with a beauty equal to that of betel,
it brings happiness to the sacrificer.
That which is contrary and deformed should be avoided because it is inauspicious; or else, there may be another type, namely the expansion of the face, neck, and feet. (59)
One should place, in sequence on the top of the pillar, a section of a young cucumber, a jar, garlic, radish, and locations for garlands of lotuses. (60)
If one avoids garlic, the root [of prosperity] will become lofty and vast;
the lotus [pedestal] shall rise to half the height plus one-eighth, or three-quarters of the total height.
One should employ a pillar that is as wide and high as the Mālāsthāna and as long as a staff; its width at the base should be three or four times the thickness of the shaft.
The height of the mandyā should be equal to the top of the pillar, or five parts less;
the vīrakāṇḍa is the same, being three parts or three-quarters [of that].
The height of the wooden planks (phalaka) should be one and a half parts out of five parts of the height of the maṇḍī;
the bamboo (vetra) supporting the maṇḍī should be known to be of the same measurement.
The shape of the *pālī* should resemble a lotus, with three folds like the petals of a serpent; above that, the *potikā* should be placed, and its characteristics are now described. (65)
And that [pillar] should be three, four, or even five times the width of the pillar-base; it is recorded as being low, medium, or superior [respectively]. (66)
The *nāgavṛttā*, the *patracitrā*, and the *samudrormi*—these *potikā*s are to be known by these three names; their characteristics are now described.
The best *potikā* (pedestal) has a height equal to the width of the pillar;
the middling one is reduced by one part out of five; and the smallest is reduced by two parts.
Variegated with figures of elephants, crocodiles, tigers, and jewels, and featuring beautiful creepers as its decorative borders,
it is known as the *citrapotikā*.
A *patrapotikā* is variegated solely by leaf-like creepers; a river (*taraṅgiṇī*) is a *potikā* that is variegated merely by its waves. (70)
And here, the waves should be made equal on both sides, numbering four, six, eight, and twelve, with their centers covered by a wooden panel (paṭṭikā). || 71 ||
When the height of the *potikā* is divided into three parts, the *agrapaṭṭaka* should be one part;
below that, it should be half of that [again], and it should be provided with the *kṣemacchāyā*.
One should fashion the pinnacle-ornament (tākhāgra-maṇḍana) here from three or two parts out of half the height of that [pedestal],
or one should make it from three-quarters of its own diameter.
Regarding this, Parāśara states:

"Although they possess various forms, all types of bases (pādas) are praised by the sages for the construction of temples and pavilions; however, for the construction of halls, assembly halls, and houses, square and circular bases are recommended."
But those intent on attainment yield the opposite result, while others are likewise.
Thus:
"Columns that are both mixed and unmixed are worshipped in temples; however, for men in their homes, it is traditionally taught that only unmixed columns bestow auspiciousness. (74)
The Pillar Ornament:
One should place the *uttara* (top-piece) above; that too is considered to be of three kinds: the *khaṇḍottara*, the *patrabandha*, and then the *rūpottara*.
The *aṅghrijātika* [type] is as wide as the pillar and elevated; from this, the *khaṇḍottara* should be one-quarter less, while the *patrabandhaka* is three-quarters less.
The height of the pillar should be equal to its width, and its breadth half of that height; or conversely, it may be low with the proportions reversed—this is known as the Rūpottara type. || 77 ||
The fillet (paṭṭikā) should be made with one part, which is one-sixteenth of the height of the upper section;
above that, a lotus-fillet (padmapaṭṭikā) should be fashioned with two parts.
The characteristics of the upper part:

From this point upward, there should be a cornice (*prastara*); on this seven-part cornice, the *kapota* (dove-cot) should be formed by two parts, with its egress (*nirgama*) equal to the *upānasa*. (79)

The horizontal band (paṭṭikā) should also be one part, and the corner (karṇa) should be one part; one should make the fillet (kampaka) with two parts, and the upper band (ūrdhvapaṭṭikā) with the remainder.
One should place a cover over its top;
its length is said to be three, four, or five daṇḍas. || 81 ||
The pillar may be raised to one-quarter of its width, or to three-quarters;
above the fillet (vājana), however, one should fashion a row of beams (bhāratulāvali).
The *tulāvalī* should be as wide as one-third of the pillar's width and half as high;
above those, one should construct the *jayantikās*.

The *jayantī* arches should be as high as the span of a balance-beam (*tulāvistāra*) and as wide as possible; their path should follow the [main] route, and they should be piled up with a thickness equal to half the length of a staff (*daṇḍa*).

The height should be one and a half times [the width], and then the side-projections (pārśvānuga) should follow; likewise, the cross-beams (vājana) and those following the scales and doors should be arranged accordingly.
The *jayantī* [braces] follow the lineage [of their respective posts], while the *anumārgaka*s are like the *tulā*.
On this point, Parāśara says: "The *prastara* and the *pādaviṣkambha* are half of two *daṇḍa*s. [Kh, Ga: *ardha*]
The space between the scales should be whitened with two or three *daṇḍas*.

For the *jayantī* balances, the interval between them should be two *daṇḍas*, and for the *anumārga* balances, it should be one *daṇḍa*; above that, one should cover them with high-quality wooden planks that are as strong, wide, and thick as possible.
Alternatively, color strips should be affixed using bricks or similar materials, or on a wooden plank, like a chessboard.
In the case of a stone [temple], it should be covered with stones above the wooden framework (vājana). || 86 ||
And having covered the upper part with a *vasantaka* cloth according to one's means, there may be either a row of swans, or sleep, or a raised staff. (87)

The base (vājana) may be three-quarters [of the height], or the upper base may be above; there is also the sleep-line (nidrā), the colored band (varṇapaṭṭī), and the pillar-base (tulāpāda) situated therein. || 88 ||

Above the *vājana*, one should construct a pigeon-ledge (*kapotālī*) measuring one and a half rods; the projection of the pigeon-ledge should be two or three [rods] in height, resembling a split bamboo cane.
Above that, there is a crest-fillet (sāgrapatta) with pālikās in the middle of the ears; then, by a staff measuring two and a half parts, there is again the *kapotālambana*.
Indeed, there are nine [units] above the northern *vājana*;
the hanging of the *gopānasī* is below the northern *potikā*.

In that interval, the height should be half a staff (daṇḍa) from the measurement of the balance (tulāmāna), or it may be three times the thickness; the crossbeams (kampā) should be joined with equal spacing.
Having covered [the structure] with gold, silver, copper, or earthen clods,
the rule for the staffs (daṇḍikā) shall then be determined from half the height of the base (anīpra).
The thickness of the staff (daṇḍikā) should be half the width of the pillar;
one should construct it in a rectangular shape according to the prescribed proportions. || 94 ||
The *daṇḍikā* is thick at the door and has a lower base with a channel; it is equal to the staff in its fist-like binding, or it may be placed separately above the *vājana*. 95.
Then, from her foot, a swarm of spirits emerged, adorned with serpents, lions, elephants, and ghosts, and perched upon a dove.
The pedestal (prati) should be established with a height equal to one-fourth or three-fourths of the width of the base (pāda),
and its projection should be three or four parts of that height.
The base (vājana) should be level; it is not auspicious if it is elevated.
For the limit of the earth is indeed the boundary between the upper and lower surfaces. 98.
The crocodile face is for gods, brahmins, and kings; the svastika is for the gods, while the half-moon is for vaiśyas and śūdras. 99.
The *nāga* plan for the remaining [deities] should be inferred individually in this manner:
on each side there is a *prati* with a pinnacle, and two *pratīs* at the front and the back. (100)
The entrance and exit should be equal, with a half-daṇḍa added; in all cases, the wise man should construct the door directly above the [inner] chamber.

One should never construct a door by means of a partition; this concludes the section on the foundation stones and so forth. Regarding the height of the pillars, one should divide it sequentially into eight, nine, eight, and seven parts. (102)
One should determine the height of the door by six parts of the Nandavasu (eighteen) units; indeed, in temples, the door should have a width that is half of that [height]. 103.

Similarly, from one part of the expansion of the nālī-house, there is a half [of the width]; in the nine-part [division], it is by five parts; in the five-part [division], it is by three parts. || 104 ||
The height of the door should be such that its width is desired to be half of that;
thus are the doors of the celestial palaces (devavimāna). However, when the height has been determined, it should be divided into parts of ten, nine, eight, and seven [units]. 105.
The width of the door for the *mānuṣa* (human) type is one-sixth, one-fifth, or one-fourth [of the temple's width];
this is the *mānuṣa* door.
There are two half-ornamented pillars on both sides of the door. (106)
For the sake of ornamentation, one should place two well-decorated [pillars] on the exterior;
they should be equal in width and height to the door, excluding all finger-measurements for cutting.

Having multiplied the years by seven and divided by twelve, the remainder is the increase in fingers; the income is known to be the years increased by three and divided by fourteen, while the expenditure is recorded as the years increased by four and divided by fourteen. (108)
Having multiplied the day by three and divided by eight, the remainder shall be the *yoni*.
When thirty is reached at the end, the lunar date (*tithi*) is obtained; the day of the week (*vāra*) is found by dividing by seven. (109)
A door or a house situated in a zodiac sign favorable to one's birth star is excellent;
however, one that is pierced by a road, a tree, a pillar, or a corner is inauspicious.
The main door, however, is for the gods and especially for humans;
it should be two parts below, out of five parts remaining after the height of the doorway.
Above, there should be three parts, and here the door-panel (phalaka) should be decorated.
In the center, there should be the eight auspicious symbols (aṣṭamaṅgalāni), and on the two sides, creeper-patterns (nakravallayaḥ).
The thickness of the door-panel should be four, six, or eight parts of the length of the bolt (daṇḍa).
In all abodes, [the levels] are to be known as superior, middling, and inferior, respectively. || 113 ||
The width of the base-pillar (talpadaṇḍa) should be half of the thickness of the planks, or even a fourth part;
its thickness shall be half of that.
Indeed, there are eleven staffs (daṇḍas), equal in number to the arrows of Rāma, the sages, and the lords;
the tip of the staff is shaped like a bodhi leaf or the shoulder of a horse. 115.
Parāśara, however, states that one should make it appear like a *svastika* (crossed-lattice) here;
[it should have] a beautiful face, joints, guards, petals, short shafts, earrings, horns,
and hooves within the ankles and throat.
One should construct the parts such as the crescent moon and so forth, using a forest of *valāhaka* and *piñjarī* clusters, or with primary metals or iron, making them very firm.
Both the door-leaf and the bolt are produced from the same species of tree. || 116 ||

The other two types of marriages, however, bring about prosperity; conversely, they yield contrary results. Moreover, women would become ill-behaved [in those cases]; therefore, one should not perform a mixed marriage.
The outer portion shall be on the outside, and the inner portion indeed within; there should be four types of door-panels, both even and odd. (118)
Their withdrawal and rushing forth are said to be distinct characteristics;
[this occurs] by means of the pair of door-panels standing on the left and the right. (119)
Where a pair is prescribed by means of two horizontal bands (paṭṭikā), one door-panel situated on the left side is called "odd" (ayugma).
A secret entrance or exit, whether in a pillar or even above it, is called *saṃhāra*;
that is a door-panel (*kapāṭa*), and there is also a running passage (*dhāvana*) hidden within the wall.
When the pairs and non-pairs of gods, brahmins, and kings are worshipped, the door-panels (kavāṭas) for others indeed consist of ten thousand (ayuta) and so forth.
In the abode of the gods, the door-panel should consist of both an odd and an even number of planks;
however, for humans, it should indeed consist of an odd number alone. (123)
The joint of the door-panels at the end of the frame should be free from three or four parts; it should indeed be devoid of a middle [projection], and this is called the *skandhapaṭṭikā*.
It has a width of two times the width of the bed, is three-quarters of a *sama* in height, variegated with various forms and creepers, square, and free from blemishes. (125)
The shoulder-band (skandha-paṭṭikā), which consists of parts with eight and nine facets, should be adorned with lotuses on both sides and attached to the right at the double entrance.
One should omit either one-third or one-fourth of the height of the *yoga*;
the remainder above the door-panels and so forth should be adorned with *mañjarī* ornaments and lotuses.
One should likewise decorate it with creepers, leaves, and men, as well as women, swans, and elephants; similarly, one may adorn it with lions and other wild beasts according to one's taste. 128.
The *yogāvagāḍha* [variant: *ḍhaṃ*] should be joined above, and the *śikhā* (spike) should be placed above the *upagrati*.
In the case of an odd number [of elements], it should have the width of the bed (*talpa*) and the length of the ear (*karṇa*).
The *parighā* (crossbeam) should be [proportionate] to the *nāha* (circumference), or it may be one-quarter or even half of a quarter;
the height of the *parighā* and the *pāda* (pillar-base) should be twice their length.
The two ends of the iron bar (parigha), which are one-third of the length of the staff and have a thickness equal to its width, should be thickened at the joints according to their strength. n131.
The bolt for a single-tiered structure is four cubits long, three-quarters of a cubit wide, and square in shape; it should be thick by three or four parts.
Having left a space of half a finger-breadth from the middle of the yoga, one should bind it with an iron rod so that it becomes very firm. || 133 ||
The diameter of the staff of the water-clock (ghaṭikā) should be one-fourth less than its length; it may be square or circular, according to one's ability. (134)
It should be three or four *daṇḍas* in length, with a width and depth of half that measure; it should be provided with five faces on the outside and two necks as is appropriate.
A long iron pin, joined with a pair of rings, should be fixed; one should then attach two equal pairs of bolts to the pair of doors known as the "twin-doors. (136)
With a width equal to its height from base to top, and with a girth half that of its diameter, it should be provided with upper coverings and with staffs and staff-cushions.
Having equipped it with iron chains, pegs, and so forth, and having raised the bedstead by three finger-breadths,
one should install it against the wall at a distance of twelve parts of its width;
then, gradually, extending outward and inward to five parts and three parts respectively.
The middle of the door-panels should be the center of that, which is the middle of the wall. || 139 ||

On a wall that is seven parts or five parts [in width], starting from the fourth or third part, the yoga should be established at the fifth or seventh part respectively; it is superior when placed within the interval.
The door is prescribed in the middle between the gods and the humans;
for the remaining [deities], it should be in the intermediate space, and above the door is the eighth auspicious sign (aṣṭamaṅgala).
One should have a plank with eight auspicious marks and a central hole for the doorpost placed above the door;
this is for the purpose of a toraṇa for the castes beginning with the gods and the twice-born.
As for the two toraṇa pillars, they should be circular, equal in height, and extend three-quarters of the width, or even one-and-a-quarter times the width.
Or rather, it is held that the width of these two is equal. || 143 ||
The tip of those two [lines] should be diminished by one-sixteenth part of the length of the direction-line;
above that, the half of the northern staff should have a total height equal to three-quarters [of the base].
From both sides of the exit, the thick part should be three or four parts; the emergence of the upper plank should be one and a half, or one and a quarter, *daṇḍas* in height.
Upon that [plank], there should be eight auspicious signs (*maṅgala*), and above those, three-pointed [ornaments].
Those [faces] should have five faces, with two staffs (daṇḍas) raised from the middle.
The extent from the base of the three feet to the edge of the side petals should be equal;
the width of the petals is prescribed by tradition as two, three, or four finger-breadths, according to the requirements of the design.
The thickness of the petals is traditionally held to be eight and one-ninth parts; the stone slab should have a firm insertion-point and be adorned with side-petals.

(320) One should likewise perform here the eight auspicious rites prescribed for the depositing of the embryo (*garbhanyāsa*), individually, both for the deities and for those belonging to the [four] social orders (*varṇa*). 149.
The characteristics of the door:
for palaces, there are various types of foundations, many pillars, as well as the *kāya* and *anukāya*, various kinds of *potikā* brackets, and the lintels (*uttara*). The door [is described].
And the ornamentation of the gateway has also been described. || 150 ||

Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, concerning the rules for the doors beginning with the *adhiṣṭhāna*, in the *Kriyāpāda* of the *Uparibhāga* of the *Siddhāntasāra*, the *Śrīmad-Īśānaśivagurudeva-paddhati*.
Now begins the thirty-second chapter.
The archway (toraṇa) is to be known as threefold: [the crocodile, the variegated-leafed, and the other];
among these, the crocodile archway is recommended for gods, Brahmins, and kings.
For Vaiśyas, however, it should be known as the Citra [arch]; for Śūdras, a leaf-arch (patratoraṇa).
One should also construct a wall-arch (kuḍyatoraṇa) on both sides and at the back.
The emergence of the arch (toraṇa) is said to extend from the front to the northern boundary; its width is half of that, and within its span, there is a portion consisting of five parts.
With three [units] there should be a pair of *makaras*, and with two parts the placement of the feet; therein, according to the variation of beauty, there may also be an entrance into a cave.
The leaf-arch was adorned with leaves resembling half-moons,
and it was embellished by a central filling fixed between the mouths of two crocodiles.
The variegated archway (citratoraṇa) is prescribed for the middle and the two sides,
constructed by supporting [the structure] with uplifted jeweled garlands rising from the mouths of sea-monsters (makara).
On both sides, there should be a gateway (toraṇa) in the shape of a sea-monster (makara), from which boys mounted on spirits, vidyādharas, serpents, and lions are suspended.
In the niches of the archways, one should likewise install images of women, men, and others as appropriate, decorated with various colors according to their beauty.
In the necklaces, in the middle of the balconies, or even in the main hall, there should be arches on the walls;
that wall is said to be of five kinds.
It may be made of stone, brick, or even lattice-work; the last may be made of wooden planks, and another may be made of clay, in that order.
That wall, made of stone and consisting of rock, was as high as its width according to the proper proportions;
and that wall which was composed of lattices was constructed with various kinds of lattice-work.

The wall in the middle should be constructed of wooden planks, with its pillars arranged as appropriate and its craftsmanship made of excellent timber; it should be filled with planks and consist of wood.
A wall made of clay should be smeared with excellent earth, decoctions, water, and so forth, and then allowed to dry. On that wall,
one should fashion a lotus at the top [of the central column], with a band whose thickness is one-third of the width of the wall.
Or one should fix a square [image] upon the wall. || 14 ||
The space between two pillars may be two cubits or more, up to five cubits; in the middle of that, a wall-creeper should be made in three ways, increasing by one span [at each stage].
One should fashion a lotus seat below the width of the wall or pillar, twice that width in extent and half as high; above that, one may design it according to one's preference.
One should fashion a pitcher with its neck protruding from the side of that [base], adorned with various leaves emerging from its mouth, arranging them so as to be as beautiful as possible. (17)
Above that, one should fashion a pedestal with lotus-feet resembling walls and pillars, topped by an unbroken pitcher (akhaṇḍakalaśa) joined with lotuses, jars, and creepers.
That very same [element] known as the pitcher-creeper (kumbhalatā), when placed successively upon a section (khaṇḍa) like a crocodile-archway (nakratoraṇa),
is considered a pillar-pitcher-creeper (stambhakumbhalatā).
That same [creeper], joined with the pitcher and the lotus seat and endowed with all creepers, should indeed be known as the creeper named Padmakumbhalatā. || 20 ||
One should place the images of the various celestial chariots in the directions;
one should install Nandīśvara and Mahākāla as the presiding deities of the eastern gate.
To the south [he should worship] Dakṣiṇāmūrti, to the west Liṅgasambhava; or else Viṣṇu in the north, or Durgā, or indeed Brahmā. (22)
In the pavilion, one should worship Vināyaka on the middle petal to the south, Nṛttarūpa to the north,
and Kṣetreśa in the northeastern direction.
Furthermore, one should arrange around the foundational wall the forms consisting of stories such as the sports of Rudra’s incarnations, according to the described characteristics.
Then, on the upper level, one should place Indra or indeed Ṣaṇmukha in the east; in the south, Dakṣiṇāmūrti or likewise Vīrabhadra.

In the west, one should likewise worship Nārasiṃha, and in the north, the bestower of wealth (Arthada) according to the rule; on the second level in this same manner, and on the third level, the hosts of Maruts.
He likewise saw the immortals, the Siddhas, the Yakṣas, and the Vidyādharas;
the Gandharvas, the Apsarases, the Siddhas, the Nāgas, and the Munis.
One should likewise place the Pramathas, the Daityas and others, as well as the sixteen images;
below the neck and above the chest, one should install the bulls in each corner.
In every corner of all the deities as well, one should place their respective vehicle from the neck downwards on the lowest level, at the base of the enclosure wall and so forth.
A celestial chariot endowed with such qualities as these is the abode of all perfections;
its great nose-ornaments extend in the four directions, equal in width to half the interior.
Their emergence is said to be from half or three-quarters of that [measurement];
one should cause the small nose (kṣudranāsā) to be made from half of that or from a quarter (rāmāṃśa).
The ancient masters have described eight types of nose ornaments (*nāsikā*).
First, there is the *siṃhapañjara* (lion-cage), then the *pañjara*, and the *ardhapañjara*.
The *niryūha-pañjara* is described as having a hanging nose; likewise, there are the *siṃha-śrotra*, the *khaṇḍa-niryūha*, and the *jhaṣa-pañjara*.
It is two to four *daṇḍas* in width, provided with rice-paddies,
equipped with two needle-like footings, and surrounded by a closely joined enclosure wall.
It should be provided with the six-fold division, or with equal projections and recesses; it may also be joined with a spear and a banner, as well as a frontal panel. (35)
The lion-cage (siṃhapañjara) should be provided with a railing, lattice-work, and pillars; it is attached to the parapet (nīpra) of the palace and extends out halfway from the parapet.
It is provided with a base and feet, joined with a stone neck; likewise, it possesses a pinnacle and a front panel facing the trident-banner.
It is enriched with railings, lattices, and ears, and is known as the "half-cage"; the remainder is as previously described, with a projection equal to one-quarter of its width.
With a *niryūha* (projecting porch) measuring one-third of the width, and possessing the work of a circular *sphuṭita* (fluted) ornament, it is known as the *pañjara*;
furthermore, its summit is equal to its own [base] height.
With its corner-projections (nīpra) closely joined and its parts such as the pigeon-niches (kapota) properly combined,
this type of penthouse (niryūha) is called the "Hanging Nose" (lambanāsika).
With its ears and feet closely joined, it was adorned with nāgadaṃśa and other ornaments; it possessed a *niryūha* (turret), was complete in all its limbs, and had a hanging nose-rope.

This very same [form], however, when joined with a lion’s ear and crest at the feet, and having the portion of the ear resting on a *nīpra* [pedestal], is designated as "Siṃhaśrotra" (Lion-Ear). || 42 ||
That which is joined with a projection measuring two-fifths of its own width, and provided below the *nīḍa* with a *khaṇḍaniryūhaka* (a small turret) for pigeons and other birds; 43.
The *nīprā* should extend below and above by one and a half *daṇḍas*;
it should be provided with an arch (*toraṇa*) above the neck and joined with the pigeon-cornice (*kapota*) and other architectural members.
That which is known as the *jhaṣapañjara* follows; now the *kūṭa* and other elements are described.
The *kūṭa* is one part from six parts of the temple (*prāsāda*), while the hall (*śālā*) extends across two parts.

The height of the cage (pañjara) is greater than that of the palace, the victory-terrace (jayabhūmi), and so forth, due to its attachment above the pigeons' perch (kapota); the proportional division of this is now described. (46)
In the Pañjara style, when the height is divided into nine parts, one and a quarter parts is the height of the base;
half of that is the height of the entablature (prastara), and the height of the corner (karṇaka) is equal to that.
With the remainder, the half-ear (ardhakarṇa) should be made; above that, the head-rise (śīrṣodaya) is prescribed.
From half of that pillar comes the base (adhiṣṭhāna), and with the remaining portion, the pedestal (upapīṭhaka).
Thus has been described the height of all the enclosures here; now,
[the measurement] of the archway hall is half that of the root-base.

The base (adhiṣṭhāna) should be high, and the pillar (stambha) is traditionally held to be twice that height. The entablature (prastara) and the neck (kandharā) are each reduced by one-eighth of the height of the base. The height of the archway (toraṇa) is determined by what remains, or one may have it constructed to resemble the main hall (śālā).
The cage should be located either within the peak of the hall or in the middle of the hall. || 51 ||
One should construct the Mahānasi, the Pañjara, and the Śukanāsikā above; however, one should never construct a nāsī above a nāsikā.
All the pillars should have bases, and there should be an altar (vedikā) above each one;
one should fashion the height of the altar to be one and a half or two or three daṇḍas.
Having decorated it in four ways as before— with *puṣpakhaṇḍa*, *citrakhaṇḍa*, *śaivala*, and *citraśaivala*— one should then perform the wall-decoration beginning from the base.

Above that, there should be a neck-ornament (*galabhūṣā*), and above the altar-platform (*vedikā*) there should be a lattice-work (*jālaka*). It may consist of three, four, or five pillars, or it may be elevated toward the northern end.
The width of the lattice (jālaka) should be one-third less than its height; likewise, there are the types known as ṛju, gavākṣa, gajākṣa, and gulikā.
Cow-urine, *patraka*, and likewise *nandyāvarta* as the seventh;
the individual characteristics of these seven types of lattices are now described. (57)

That which has straight, needle-like feet and is known as having a straight lattice-work, with its length being equal to its width and possessing upward-pointing ears, is a *gavākṣaka* (a window-type pavilion). || 58 ||

The elephant-eye [window] is that which has its openings obtained from square corners and is released [from the wall], with its beads [mouldings] at the base, top, and middle, due to being set within straight walls. || 59 ||
The lattice known as *gulikā* has its openings concealed by a curtain;
that which has openings in the intermediate directions and curved passages is shaped like cow’s urine and is called *gomūtra*.
A *patrajālaka* consists of holes separated by various leaf-patterns;
that which is formed by holes between five lines arranged in a clockwise direction [is another type]. (61)
The lattice-work known as *nandyāvarta* has openings in the shape of a *nandyāvarta*.
The emergence of the neck (*galodaya*) should be twice, one-and-a-half times, or equal to the height of the pedestal (*vedikā*). (62)
The entry for the pedestal (vedikā) should be one-third of the width of the wall;
above that, the entry for the neck (grīvā) should be equal to five parts. || 63 ||
One may even perform the adornment of the neck with lotus stalks, the curved feet of cranes, or the skins of deer, or by means of stories of the dance of serpents.
Then, one should fashion the pinnacle (śikhara) evenly with a measurement equal to half the neck; the projection of the pinnacle from the neck should be two staff-lengths (dvi-daṇḍa).
From the exit, one should fashion the external molding; having turned it from the two staffs, one should construct the dome together with its pitcher, exactly in the shape of a mountain peak.
Furthermore, the configuration of the pinnacle (śikhara) is said to be of eight kinds:
square, oblong, circular, and likewise oval; || 67 ||
The needle-shaped, the hexagonal, the octagonal, and the sixteen-sided—these are the eight types of pinnacle shapes; their description is now being told. (68)

The eight types of *lupā* (pedestals), such as the Pāñcālī and others, are used for the half-crests, the *sabhāgra*, the *mukhapaṭṭikā*, the *ratnāstra*, the *śīprastara*, the *chatraśīrṣa*, the *gṛhapiṇḍi*, the *hastituṇḍaka*, and so forth; they are equal in width to the *daṇḍikā* and the *uttara*.
The [measures for] the half-rising and so forth are, in sequence: five, two, seven, three, four, eleven, six, five, thirteen, six, fifteen, seventeen, eight, and ten.
There are the Pāñcāla, Vaideha, Māgadha, Kaurava, Kausala, Śaurasena, Gāndhāra, and Āvantika [styles].
The Āvantika style possesses breadth, height, and elevation; however, by name, it is a mixture of those two. These two—
It is divided into two parts, and also into one, two, or three portions. || 69 ||
Due to an increase of four, five, six, and seven parts respectively,
there are seven names for the heights of the peaks.
They know the Kāliṅga, Kāśya, Vārāṭaka, and Ullaka varieties, as well as Śauṇḍika; and likewise the Kāśmīra and Gāṅgeya types—these are known as the distinct Śikhara varieties. (71)
These [proportions] apply to half the height of the divine shrines; for others, they are otherwise.
Furthermore, in all cases, the pillars, beams, and rafters may also be one cubit [in length].
The cupolas of the gods should also be odd in number and beautiful; for humans, an even number is praised in all dwellings. (73)
The height of the lotus-base should be one-fourth or one-fifth of the height of the spire;
it may also be one-quarter greater than that, or even one-and-a-half-quarters greater.
The construction of the stūpa and its subsequent placement will be described hereafter.
Regarding the characteristics of the spire (*śikhara*):
the making of the front staircase is of two kinds, namely *guhya* (hidden) and *aguhya* (unhidden). (75)
The triangular, the long-quadrangular, and the circular—these are the three origins; there may be four types [of shapes], while the conch-mandala consists of three sections.
Then there is the Ardhagomūtraka and also the Vallīmaṇḍala;
that which is composed of three sections in form is the Trikhaṇḍaka staircase.
The conch-mandala, which is contracted from the base to the tip in successive stages, is divided into two sections; it is a staircase known as the "half-cow's urine" (ardhagomutra).
Having the appearance of a tree with red shoots and designated as a staircase of creepers,
the various sections for reclining should indeed be raised separately by one and a half or two and a quarter *vyāsa*s.
One should fashion the steps with equal segments in due order; thereafter, the hand-hole (hastabila) should be two daṇḍas or one and a half daṇḍas.

The height of the hand-niche (hastanīpra) is prescribed as being either three-quarters or half [of the total height]; its entrance should be made according to one's strength, whether for one standing or even for one reclining.
The width at the end of the staircases should be eight, three, four, five, six, seven, and ten daṇḍas;
for the horse-shoe-shaped (aśvapādaka) stairs, it should be two, three, or four daṇḍas.
One should fashion its shape to be like a half-moon; and that [pedestal] should be one cubit in thickness, or perhaps two-thirds of a cubit above it.
Having stood upon each successive level, one should ascend by performing circumambulations to the right; even that [number of circumambulations] should be odd, whether in a temple or in a pavilion.
In halls and other such structures, the main staircase is considered to be at the front;
on both sides, one should construct a side-staircase elsewhere, encircling it.
The staircase:
For all shrines (dhāman), there are those that are accumulated (sañcita), unaccumulated (asañcita), and semi-accumulated (upasañcitaka); likewise, the linga is male, female, or neuter. 86.
That which is constructed of stone or brick, known as "accumulated" (sañcita), and is solid with the heads of pigeons and the like attached, is called a male linga (puṃliṅga). || 87 ||

Whether made of brick or wood, and constructed from the components of a pleasure ground, that celestial vehicle (vimāna) which is designated as "unaccumulated" (asañcita) and possesses feminine characteristics is thus described.
A *ṣaṇḍa* is a collection of bricks and wood, sometimes solid and sometimes not, gathered together and joined with various limbs of enjoyment and ornamentation. (89)
On both sides of the door, there should be a cave for the door-keepers; one should make an opening below and above, and employ a tube on the outside.
Starting from one finger-breadth (aṅgula) and increasing by three fingers at a time, the length of the stalk is recorded as fivefold, ending at thirty-two fingers.
Starting from eight finger-breadths and increasing by two finger-breadths each time,
he declared that the tube (*nāla*) is of five types, ending at sixteen units (*mātrā*).

One should dig a hole in the center that is equal [in depth] to three, four, or five *tanmātras*, with a width of one, one and a half, or two *tanmātras*. That [hole] is called *tāra* and is characterized by its levelness. (93)
The tip should be one-fifth of the base and provided with edges;
it is fashioned with a lion’s mouth and its tip is bent sharply from the base.
In the middle of the northern side of the temple, one should arrange a tube in this manner;
the external tube should be equal in size to the internal tube of the pedestal.
One should construct it according to its width and length and decorate it as is appropriate.
Regarding the characteristics of the stalk:
whatever foundation has been prescribed for the temple (prāsāda) shall also serve as that of the pavilion (maṇḍapa). 96.
The feet should be exactly as previously described, and the *prastara* (the base) should also be as before;
one should cause it to have a wide path at the top of the upward-pointing staff. || 97 ||
A pavilion with four square pillars is called Nandyāvarta; one with eight pillars is named Svastika, while the Vīrāsana is characterized by its fish-shaped legs.
One should know that a pavilion established for Śrī consists of sixteen pillars;
Jayabhadra consists of thirty-two, and likewise Aṅghri consists of thirty-six.
Maṇibhadra would be a pavilion with one hundred pillars, and Viśālaka [is formed] from more than that.
Those pavilions were also vast, supported by pillars. || 100 ||
One should construct a pavilion for the gods and humans that is square or oblong, measuring one and a half times, twice, or even more than the length of a foot [of the deity]. 101.
In the pavilion, one should construct pillars at intervals of two or three cubits, or four cubits,
according to the requirements and in a manner appropriate for the load and the height.
One should construct a pavilion according to the proper method, facing toward a temple, or in a grove, a sacred field, and so forth, or in the midst of a village or a house. (103)
For the purpose of initiation, consecration, and sacrifice, as well as for the site of the dance,
one should begin with a space of one and a half cubits, increasing it by six finger-breadths [at each stage].
One should measure the distance between the pillars in sequence, starting from the hand-length of an arrow up to the extent of one's knowledge;
this is done by dividing the interval into one, two, three, four, or five parts.

The increase shall be by one part; the length [of the wall] is according to its own width. Extending from its own division, it increases by three measures at each step until the end of the hand (the corner). || 106 ||
Length is said to be of eight kinds; one should apply [the measurement] by that standard.
And all that which is elongated is designated by that very name. (107)
Starting from two and a half cubits and increasing by six finger-breadths each time,
there are twenty-three measurements up to eight cubits, including the feet.
Alternatively, the height of the pillar may be increased by two or three finger-breadths;
beginning from eight finger-breadths, it may be increased by half a finger-breadth at each step.
p.
329) Up to the number of fingers in the *nandapaṅkti* sequence, the thickness is as before;
however, for the height of the pillar, when divided into eleven parts (*rudrāṃśa*), it should consist of five, nine, and eight parts [respectively]. (110)
The root-timber (mūlatāra) should be one part, and each subsequent part should be reduced by that same portion;
when the height of the pillar is divided into five parts, the base (talaka) should be two parts high.
The height of the pillar and the *masūraka* (pedestal) should be one part out of three;
the *adhiṣṭhāna* (base) may include a *pīṭha* (plinth) or consist solely of the *masūraka*.
The pillar above the base, the entablature consisting of three bands, and the pigeon-cornice—this is known as the general type of pavilion. || 113 ||
Square, with four pillars, and adorned with wealth,
it should be a pavilion known as a Brahmāsana, or else a water-shed (prapā).
It has three divisions, sixteen pillars, and is adorned with rafter-ends; it possesses eight pediments, is provided with a pinnacle, and is endowed with four gates and four archways.
They say that here a pavilion or even a water-shed is called "Siddha" by name, as it is worthy of gods, brahmins, and kings, and is honored in all rites. (116)

The Characteristics of the Maṇḍapa: Now, the characteristics of the water-sheds (prapās) are also described here in general terms. The length of the base (pāda) should be as previously stated, consisting of four, five, or eighteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
The width of the base should be one-fourth [of the length]; the legs should be made of solid wood, or they may be fashioned from bamboo, as should the upper beams and the lintels.
One should cover the front hall and the rear hall of the water-shed with coconut leaves and other foliage as may be available.
When the height of the pedestal (pādatuṅga) is divided by fifty-seven, the portion [thereof] shall be the height of the altar (vedikā);
one should likewise arrange the performance area (raṅga) in the center.
From the height of the base (pāda), the altar-slab (vedimaṣūraka) should be one-fourth of a part;
the length of the lintel (talima) should be two parts, and its projection (prastara) should be one part.
Whether in pairs or singly, it may have two or one division; its width may consist of four pillars, eight pillars, or sixteen pillars. (122)
It may consist of a mixture of materials joined together in all their parts, or it may be situated in the middle of halls, assembly halls, water-stations, or pavilions. || 123 ||

The four bases are firmly established, possessing three dimensions and designated by their colors. Thus, according to the rules, here [are described] the arches, walls, and pillars, as well as the stairs, lattices, windows, and the specific neck-pieces; and likewise, the images on each floor.
The various types of spires have been fully described, as well as the water-sheds (prapās) accompanied by specific pavilions (maṇḍapas).

Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, concerning the characteristics of the arches and other structures, in the section on ritual practice (kriyāpāda) of the latter part of the *Siddhāntasāra*, which is the *Śrīmad-Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati*.
Now begins the thirty-third chapter.
Now, the materials for palaces and other structures are said to be of six kinds: stone, wood, bricks, clods of earth, clay, and lime. (1)
In this regard, the characteristics of stone are now described hereafter; first, however, the collection of the five materials, such as wood and so forth, is stated.
However, those trees that were previously mentioned as being hollow, entwined with creepers, infested by insects, or thorny, are to be avoided. (3)

Those trees that are always rich in flowers and fruit, those inhabited by humans, gods, and spirits, those frequented by many birds and deer, and those growing at shrines, on roads, or in cremation grounds; || 4 ||

Those trees that are crooked, withered, or broken, which serve as the refuge for all manner of creatures— such as *palāśas*, *kuṭajas*, *lodhras*, *bilvas*, *pīlus*, and *śirīṣakas*— [should be avoided].
Śleṣmātaka trees, kadambas, kovidāras along with kiṃśukas, pathyās, akṣas, āmalakas, pārthas, as well as snuhi, snuṅ, and varaṇa trees.
Ambaṣṭhas, saptaparṇas, kāraskaras, vikaṅkatas, nyagrodhas, udumbaras, aśvatthas, plakṣas, śalmalis, and tindukas; || 7 ||
(331) Nandyāvarta, badara, karavīra, kapittha,
sarpamāra, arimeda, putrajīva, and ṣaḍuṇḍuka [trees]. || 8 ||
The tintriṇī, pāṭalā, aśoka, karpūra, agaru, gṛñjana,
and arka trees should be avoided in the dwellings of gods and humans.
They were straight, full of strength, firm, and long-lived; they could endure rain, wind, and heat, and were capable of traversing both water and land.
Those trees appropriate to each respective region and deemed auspicious should be accepted in sacred abodes; generally, however, milky trees are not suitable for human dwellings.
Among all the trees suitable for the abodes of the gods, the *likuca* is auspicious;
it is round in shape from root to tip, possesses many branches, and is firm and tall. (12)

A tree is male when it possesses femininity [in its form], such as having a thick base and a thin top; it is neuter when there is thinness at both the base and the top, and thickness in the middle. (13)

For the stabilization of the womb during the *muhūrta* and similar rites, one should have it performed using only male trees; for all remaining rites, however, it is recommended that they be performed with trees of all three genders.

The Dāru-niyama (the ritual for the wooden image): During the bright fortnight, under an auspicious constellation and so forth, the performer, having bathed, wearing white garments and unguents, and having performed the auspicious marriage-thread ceremony (*kautuka-maṅgala*), shall proceed together with the architect (*sthapati*). || 15 ||
Having had the Brahmins recite auspicious benedictions, and preceded by all kinds of musical instruments,
he should proceed to the designated region, which is characterized by the trees previously specified.
At the time of departure, having ascertained auspicious signs through weapons and omens,
he should smear a mandala under the shade of a specified tree.

One should worship Gaṇeśa with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, as well as with various kinds of food and edibles; likewise, one should worship the Lord of the Field (Kṣetreśa), the Lord of Herbs (Oṣadhīśa), and the deities of the forest.

Having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, with sacrificial porridge (caru), fruits, milk-rice (pāyasa), and sweetmeats (modaka), one should present the bali-offering to the spirits (bhūta) with food for beings, kṛsara, and cooked rice.
Having bathed, the master craftsman (sthapati), together with his assistant (saṭaṅkaḥ), should recite these two mantras: "May the spirits and the deities, along with the Guhyakas, depart. (20)
May you possess great strength; may Soma grant you trees. O sons of the Earth, may there always be auspiciousness for you and for us as well. (21)
"I shall accomplish this task; let the change of residence be made. Having spoken thus and having paid homage to the trees with a serene mind, [he departed]. (22)
Having drunk cow's milk at night to the east of the tree to be cut down, the master carpenter should sleep upon *darbha* grass; having risen in the morning with auspicious dreams, [he proceeds]. (23)
Having bathed and being well-adorned at an auspicious moment, the wise master craftsman,
remaining silent, should smear the edge of the axe with the five products of the cow.
Accompanied by musical instruments, auspicious sounds, and prayers, facing either east or north,
he should leave a space of one cubit at the base of the tree and cut it from above that point.

If milk flows from its incision, it brings prosperity; however, the flow of water brings happiness. But if blood flows, it leads to the destruction of the planter; therefore, one should not cut that tree.
The sounds of lions, elephants, and bulls at the time of its fall bring auspiciousness;
however, laughter, abuse, weeping, and shrieking from it are inauspicious.
Avoiding that tree, one should select another endowed with auspicious characteristics;
its top facing the directions of Indra (East), Īśa (North-East), Artha (South-East), or Dikpati (West) is recommended.

Otherwise, one who has fallen must be abandoned; such a failure is censured in all circumstances. Even becoming entangled among trees or other obstacles causes impediment and affliction, and is inauspicious. (29)
The cutting of the auspicious portion and the falling of the tip should be equal for both the root and the top of the tree;
having cut it according to the desired measurement, one should plane it into a square shape.
Having designated the pillar for the muhūrta and covered it with a white cloth, one should place it upon a cart or similar vehicle and bring it to the intended location.
For gods, brahmins, kings, and vaiśyas, the fetching of wood is desirable by means of carts or elephants; for others, it should be carried by men.
Then, having entered through the auspicious door into the area of the workshop, one should lay the wood upon a heap of sand with its head facing east.
One should not effect a reversal for eight, five, or three months; thus, by this procedure regarding wood, one should collect [the materials] for the work of the temple. (34)
The acceptance of all the wood must be performed according to the prescribed rite;
this is the acceptance of the wood.
Now, the fashioning of the bricks and the lime are described. (35)
The clay known as *cikkaṇā* and that called *pāṇḍarā* are censured, as is the *saloṇā*. The fourth, however, is the *tāmraphullā*, which is considered fit for ritual use.
It should be free from husks, charcoal, bones, stones, wood, gravel, and clods of earth;
it should consist of fine sand and be well-fitted with copper plates and bricks.
Having thrown that [earth] into the pit, one should pour water knee-deep;
having stirred it with the feet and agitated it, one should knead it again and again. (38)
Then, for exactly one month, it should be rubbed with a decoction of milk, agastya, and śirīṣa bark, along with water from the three myrobalans (triphalā), by men skilled in that work.
One should properly fashion the bricks, twelve finger-breadths in length;
one should make them half that measure in width and three parts of a Vyāsa in height.

Alternatively, they may be three-quarters less than that; one should dry them in the heat. When the moon is in a full constellation and at an auspicious moment, having prepared the hearth in accordance with the wind, || 41 ||
There, one should join those bricks with intervals, piling them up gradually;
they should be filled without gaps by means of wood, bundles of straw, and so forth.
One should properly cover them on the outside and smear them with clay;
having placed fire within their openings, one should leave them for ten days or even for a fortnight.
Having performed the funeral rites when the fire has been extinguished, he should then extract the bricks and cast them into water for eight years or six months.
One should extract those bricks which are suitable for the construction of vimānas and other structures.
Regarding bricks: the preparation of clay-bricks is traditionally taught to be done with the same clay prescribed for bricks. (45)
p.
334) Indeed, the lumps of clay for the superior and other [levels] are to be made with lengths measured by twelve, ten, and eight of their respective finger-breadths. (46)
The width (vyāsa) is traditionally said to be half of the length, or one-fifth, or even two-fifths;
and when the width is divided by four, five, or five, the height of the pedestal (loṣṭa) shall be one part.
In this manner, the procedure is prescribed for lumps of clay according to the sequence beginning with the best;
for lumps of gold, silver, and copper, the results are superior and so forth, corresponding to the quality of the material.

One obtains [the fruit] at the abodes of the gods and other such places; the lowest of the low is achieved with earthen materials. The measurement and quantity of metals should be understood according to one's wealth. (49)
All of these are likewise equal, and they are of seven types:
the two-edged, the double-pointed, the side-blunt, and the circular.
The corner-stone, the crooked stone, and the lotus-stone as the seventh;
these should be placed in their respective rows according to the proper method.
The preparation of bricks and clods:
Karāla, mudga, gulma, āsaka, and kalka-cikkaṇa—these five, when used as powders, are considered the primary materials for lime (sudhā). (52)

The *abhayā* seeds should be the size of sugar-candies (*śarkarā*) and are called *karālakā*; the *mudga* beans are known to be equal in size to *mudga* beans, while the *mudgina* are small sugar-grains (*kṣudraśarkarā*). || 53 ||
That which consists of three and a half parts of powder, twice as much of filaments (kiñjalka),
and an equal amount of sugar and oyster-shell (śukti) powder is called gulmāsa.

According to the previously stated measurement, one should prepare a paste (kalka) consisting of the powder of chickpeas mixed with sand, using the same proportions as those for the *karāla* and *mudga* beans mentioned before. (55)
The water is of two kinds: smooth and pure, and that which is bound with water. First, one should pound the previously mentioned substances three times with pure water alone.
The bark-water of milk-exuding trees, myrobalan, lac, kadamba, and abhaya, as well as the decoction of triphalā and black-gram soup, are equal [in their efficacy]. (57)
Having restrained [the sediment] from the powder of sugar and oyster shells in that water taken from a pit,
he should crush it with his hooves, and then strain it through a cloth.
One should prepare a thick paste with that; it is then called "bound water" (baddhodaka).
[This is done] with curd, milk, bean soup, molasses, ghee, and plantains. (59)
This should be well-prepared with the waters of coconut and mango fruits; it becomes "bound water" (baddhodaka), and one should employ it in equal proportions.
One hundredth part of the obtained powder should be used, while honey should be two parts; likewise, there should be ghee, ripe plantain, coconut water, and black gram soup. (61)

Then there is the decoction of the bark of the *kṣīrāgā* tree, milk, curd, jaggery, and slimy water from the *triphalā* fruit; these are used in sequence, starting with three parts [of the first] and so forth.
Having mixed mango-juice with sugar-candy according to one's capacity,
and having combined it with Karāla that has been firmly ground, one should pour it in.
After one day has passed, it should become firm; then, one should repeatedly strike it with sticks such as the branches of a coconut tree. (64)
But after ten nights have passed, when it has been well-ground and properly mixed with a paste of mudga beans and gulma,
it becomes beautiful lime through the correct application of the method.

Furthermore— first, the two parts [of the mixture] are pungent; then there is honey, ghee, plantain, coconut water, bean soup, or a decoction of tree bark, as well as breast milk, curd, jaggery, and the three myrobalans (triphalā) in water.

And thus: having ground the increased portion in due order until it is as white as the clear moon, when all is ground down to a hundredth part, it becomes excellent nectar, just like that which is bound by a diamond.

Having been dwelt upon for four, three, or two months and refined through application, the nectar used for the construction of palaces and other structures is to be known as superior, middling, or inferior.
Then, having first washed the wall and other surfaces— which are dry, without gaps, very level, and soft— with pure water, one should apply [the paste] mixed with curd, milk, and molasses.
Having smeared it with bound water and removed it for one day, one should then employ pure [water] by means of skillful methods, as may be appropriate in each case. (69)
On that wall and so forth, there should be a painting of most wonderful form,
depicting deities mentioned in one's own scriptures along with stories recounted in the Purāṇas.
(336) It is beautiful, endowed with the colors of the stage, neither deficient nor excessive in any respect;
it is permeated everywhere by appropriate forms, aesthetic sentiments, emotional states, and actions. (71)
A variegated [action] always yields diverse fruits for both the employer and the agent;
other than that, an inauspicious variegated action yields contrary results. (72)
One should not cause it to be written, nor should one write it oneself, out of a desire for happiness in both worlds.
This is the section on nectar (*sudhādhikāra*).
[This applies] even to materials such as wood, for the sake of achieving power (*bala*) and the like. (73)
The joining of those parts that are standing and those that are lying down is described; it is performed externally, internally, on the sides, below, and likewise above. (74)
And in other cases as well, one should join them as is appropriate according to one's preference; one should join all the wooden pieces with their tips pointing eastward and northward.
That which is auspicious in its beginning leads to the opposite, the highest inauspiciousness, in this world. One should not join root with root, nor should one unite tip with tip. (76)

The joining [of the parts] through the application of materials from the base to the top is the foundation of all prosperities; this applies to the center of the site, then to the door, to the portions of the deities, and also to the two corners.

One should abandon the *sandhāna* (junction) for the sake of avoiding the destruction of one's position and the ruin of the lineage; likewise, one should avoid the *meṣayuddha*, the *trikhaṇḍa*, the *saumadra*, and the *ardhapāṇika*.
The *mahāmānavṛtta* pillar type, as well as the *sandhāna*, are indeed fivefold:
namely, the *ṣaṭśikha*, the *jhaṣadanta*, and also the *sūkaraghrāṇa*. 79.
The *saṅkīrṇakīla* and the *vajra* [are placed] at the five joints when lying down;
from the width of the pillar material, the pinnacle is one-third of that measure from the center.
The *meṣayuddha* (ram-fight) mudrā resembles a *svastika*, possesses three crests, and consists of three segments;
it is called *saubhadra*, having four points reaching toward the sides.
Having cut the wood, which has been measured for its thickness and value, at both the root and the tip so that they meet without gaps,
it is said that the joint shall be "half-a-hand" (ardhapāṇika) in measure.
In the center, by means of half of its own [diameter], that which has a circular top is the *mānavṛttaka*;
one should apply it according to the stated method when producing a form that is to be completed.
Then, when the tips of those [flames] take the form of ploughs (halākāra) by means of the Arghapāṇi and Khaṇḍa [mudrās], and Kali is situated in their center, that is the six-crested [fire]. || 84 ||

(337) Jhaṣa (the letter *jha*) and danta (the letter *ta*), followed by the mother of the self (*nijāyāmātṛ*, i.e., the vowel *i*), and joined with the ten thousand-fold auspiciousness of the arms of Agni (*agnibāhuśivamayuta*); this is conjoined with the power of the crest (*yathābalaśikhāyuta*) through the union of the support and the supported (*ādhārādheyayogena*). 85.
It should be applied like the "pig's snout" (sūkaraghrāṇa) in what is called the "pig's snout" [position], joined with various kinds of pikes according to the method and as appropriate. (86)
The type known as *saṅkīrṇakīla* (mixed-stake) is like a thunderbolt (*vajra*), with a thunderbolt-shaped crest;
its length at the junction should be one and a half times its own width or its diagonal. || 87 ||

One should not join [the pillar] in the middle of the *rasa* (six) and *bha* (nine) units, for a central joint causes destruction; rather, that joint should be between the top of the pillar and the *stambha-cūḍā* (capstone) on both the right and the left.
The middle of the joint should be joined; thus it becomes a locus of prosperity.
However, one must not pierce the crest-pin (śikhākīla) when it is already pierced by a mutual joint.
A crest-line situated in the middle of the expansion of that substance destroys prosperity;
when joined at the south and north, the crest-line becomes a bringer of prosperity.
In a pillar-base that is wide, divided into seven, six, or eight parts, the width of both the pinnacle (śikhā) and the peg (kīlaka) shall be one part.
In pillars arranged in a single row, the joints should be of a uniform form;
a mixed joint leads to destruction, therefore one should avoid a mixed joint.
The joint of the pillar;
the joints [are formed] by means of short and long materials: *raghuḥ*, *bahis*, *vīhiḥ*.
That which is to be joined internally should be internal, and likewise southern and northern. || 93 ||
One should join the middle material, which is as long as [the space], to the two sides of the short materials;
or in some cases, all three may be joined equally upon the recumbent material.

One should join everything together, excluding the ornaments at the base and the tip; here, in the joints of the materials that lie flat, the base is on the inside and the outer part is on the outside.

Regarding this, Parāśara states: "The root [of the bed] should be joined with the root in the southwest (nairṛtya), and the tip with the tip toward the north (śūlin); the union of the root and the tip, however, should be in the southeast (agni) and the northwest (māruta)."
One should join new material with new, and old material with old;
one should join wood with wood, and bamboo with bamboos.
One should join things of the same kind with those of the same kind, not with those of a different kind; one should join stones with stones,
and likewise bricks with bricks.
The opposite leads to destruction, while that which has been prescribed brings happiness.
Thus it is said; and Mayu also says: "The mallakīla, the brahmarāja, the veṇuparvaka, the kramuka, the devasandhi, and the daṇḍaka is called the sixth."
Thus:
"The junction of two substances in one place would be like a peg in a bowl;
with three substances—namely Brahma, Rāja, Veṇu, Parva, Abdhi, and Bāṇaka—it is [the junction called] Brahmarāja. (96)
The *kramuka* joint is formed by six or seven materials; the *devasandhi* by nine or eight;
the *bahusandhi* by many materials; and the *daṇḍikāsandhi* is so called [for its specific construction]. || 97 ||
The svastika, the vardhamāna, and after that the nandyāvarta;
then the sarvatobhadra—these are the junctions of their respective forms.
The root should be inside and the tip outside, while the side materials should be beautiful; the opposite leads to destruction, therefore one should not act in such a way. 99.
Just as it was observed by the ancients in the scriptures of the Grandfather (Brahmā) and others, so should one perform each respective rite for the sake of increasing happiness and longevity. 100.

The specific types of wood, bricks, clay, and lime, as well as their various applications according to their defining characteristics, have been declared; likewise, the many kinds of joints for both standing and lying structures have been duly demonstrated.

Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, concerning the characteristics of wood and other materials, in the Kriyāpāda of the Upper Section of the Siddhāntasāra, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva.
Now begins the thirty-fourth chapter.
In all undertakings concerning material objects, a master architect who understands measurement, weight, and dimension, and who is proficient in the treatises on the arts, must first be sought out.
In the same way, one who knows the Śiva scriptures and is endowed with the characteristics of an Ācārya, having been chosen as the Sthāpaka (the consecrator),
the performer should carry out the ritual action regarding the material object.
Whether it be a celestial chariot or something else entirely that has been commenced by both of them,
it shall be completed by those two alone and not by others until its completion.
In their absence, that subsequent rite must indeed be performed by their sons or disciples until its completion, following the instruction of the Guru depicted in the painting.
On this point, there is the statement of Pitāmaha and others:

"Having first performed the ritual according to the prescribed rule, one should carry it out until its completion in that very manner; otherwise, if it is performed by another and completed by another, it will result in misfortune."
Of those who dwell in the lands of lords and sovereigns.
Thus, from the commencement of the material until its completion, there is a restriction on the agent.
One should place the *stūpī* and the *kumbha* in front of the constructed *vimāna*. Having consecrated four bricks according to the rule as previously described, [one should proceed]. (5)
Then, having made five pits in the middle of the summit,
one should place all kinds of jewels, medicinal herbs, seeds, metals, minerals, and essences [into them].
Then, having consecrated excellent fragrances with the root-mantra, the lord-mantra, and the weapon-mantra,
one should place them in the central pit according to the sequence of circumambulation.

One should place four bricks in the four corners beginning with the southeast, using the four principles starting with earth (pṛthivī) and the [mantras] beginning with Sadyojāta, corresponding to the heart and other limbs.
Having fashioned the pinnacle-pin (stūpikākīla) out of iron or even wood, shaped like a *liṅga*, or with a needle-pointed tip, or indeed in the form of a mountain peak; || 9 ||
Extending upward from the pillar-base, it should be long and wide according to the measurement of a foot;
it should be made gradually tapering toward the top, with a width of one finger-breadth at the front.
When the length is divided into three parts from the base, it should be square;
the middle portion should be circular, and the final portion should be like the feet of a peacock.

At the auspicious moment (lagna), accompanied by the sounds of musical instruments for a "meritorious day" (puṇyāha) and other rites, one should insert the ritual stake (kīla) into the central pit previously described,
at a distance of one-fifth of the stūpa's length.
Three parts should be invisible, while two upper parts should be visible;
one should bind it firmly all around with stones or bricks.
The covering of the top of the stūpa all around is prescribed with one, two, three, or more of those materials, or with both, or even with all of them. 14.
Then, having strengthened it with lime along with the creepers and the auspicious marks,
one should fashion an eight-petalled lotus and thereafter decorate the stūpikā.
With new garments made of linen or cotton, one should construct a great banner that extends from the base of the stūpa to the ground and is equal in length and width.
Having tied the banner to the top of the stūpa, one should release it facing north.
If the banner first touches the ground in the direction of Soma (the Moon), Īśāna (the Northeast), or Indra (the East), [it is auspicious]. (17)
If [the omen] other than that should be auspicious, one should perform oblations with sesame seeds for the sake of pacification;
likewise, one thousand oblations should be offered with clarified butter and *caru* using the *saṃhitā* mantras.
One should perform the Vāstuhoma sacrifice and offer the Vāstubali at night; likewise, one should honor the master builder and the preceptor with gold, garments, and other gifts. (19)
He should gratify the Brahmins and others, as well as the carpenters and laborers. [This concludes] the arrangement of the stūpa.
Now, the jar (kumbha) should be made of gold, silver, or even copper. (20)
Having selected either a stone or an earthen structure endowed with the proper characteristics,
the wise architect, having bathed on an auspicious day, under a favorable constellation and at a propitious moment, [should proceed].
Adorned with garments, gold, and other ornaments, facing either the east or the north, he should place gold, gems, medicinal herbs, and juices into the base of the water-pot (kumbha).
One should place a pitcher-shaped pinnacle (*stūpikā*) that has a crest in the form of a stūpa;
