it may consist of one, three, or five straight rows arranged at its tip.
Accordingly, one should install a single form or multiple forms by means of mantra; in the case of one [deity], it should be Śiva alone, while in the triad, they are Brahmā, Hari, and Īśvara.
Brahmā and the others, up to Sadeśa, should be established in the five jars;
[ensuring] that the base of each jar is firm and perfectly free of cracks on all sides. (25)
One should bind the smooth, finely pounded floor with a binding of lime, metal, and so forth; this is the arrangement of the water-pots.
Now, the procedure for the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) of the completed temple (vimāna) is described. || 26 ||
When the sun is situated in its northern course (uttarāyaṇa), at the beginning of a muhūrta endowed with auspicious qualities,
one should first perform the rite of sowing seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa) and then construct a pavilion (maṇḍapa) in the northeast.

Alternatively, one may construct a four-cornered pavilion with Nanda-rishi holding an arrow in his hand as the central figure; it should be of the highest or other classes, supported by twelve, eight, or four pillars, and adorned with canopies and other ornaments.
In the center of that, a square sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) measuring two cubits,
one span high, made of rice grains and divided into sixty-four squares, should be prepared.
Having worshipped the deities of the site (vāstudeva), beginning with Brahmā, according to the prescribed rite upon that [altar],
one should place twenty-five water-filled jars.
Having equipped them with gold, garments, and other offerings, along with the deities situated upon the pedestals,
the master builder, having bathed and adorned himself with white clothes and ornaments, should install them.

Having drunk milk on a bed of *kuśa* grass spread to the north of that [altar], he should sleep at night. In the morning, as before, he should go to the sacrificial pavilion (*vedāśrama-maṇḍapa*) to the east of the palace.
[One should construct] a pavilion adorned with canopies and the like, featuring four gates and arches,
which is equal in its width, height, and length, being one-third of the [temple's] total width.
Having constructed an altar with four corners,
one should fashion square sacrificial pits upon it in the four cardinal directions and at the intermediate points, shaped like the leaf of the *aśvattha* tree.
Having constructed an octagonal sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) between Indra and Īśa in the Śiva-fire, the preceptor,
together with the guardians of the images, [should perform the rite] in the four directions with the mantras of the deities.

One should offer oblations with the ancillary mantras (aṅga-mantras) in the corners according to the *Saṃhitā* and *astra-mantra*. The offerings should be made in the cardinal directions by the image-keepers (*mūrtipāḥ*), and in the eight-cornered [mandala] by the preceptor (*ācārya*).

One should worship Śiva, together with his limbs (the retinue), upon the sacrificial mound on the altar, and in the pitcher; and in the four directions of the temple, one should worship him with the weapons and the forms in circular fire-pits.

One should also offer oblations everywhere with sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, cooked rice, and sesame seeds; then, one should cover the temple—from its foundation to the pinnacle—with new cloths. (38)

One should encircle it with garlands of *darbha* grass and various flower wreaths, as well as with offerings of rice cooked with the four types of grains, and with *kṛsara* and milk-rice (*pāyasa*). || 39 ||
Having filled a golden vessel with curd, milk, jaggery, honey, gems, gold, fruits, and unbroken grains, one should offer the bali-oblation to the Vāstu-spirits at night.

Then, at dawn, having given [the gifts], both the master architect (sthapati) and the installer (sthāpaka), having performed the rites such as bathing and so forth, shall ascend the celestial chariot (vimāna).
Then the consecrator, together with the image-makers, having performed the consecration upon that temple with those jars in the proper sequence,
should thereafter worship it with perfumes and other offerings.
Then, having drawn mandalas on the front part of the pinnacle and on the two eyes with a golden needle, one should likewise perform the ritual release of the eyes (netramokṣa).
Having covered it with a new cloth, he should then remove it and show it to the Brahmins—a cow with her calf, a heap of grain, and gold. (44)
Then the architect, remaining composed amidst the sounds of conchs, trumpets, and other instruments,
should hoist the banner as before, with its face tied to the top-knot at the front of the stūpa.
Having ascertained the auspicious and inauspicious [signs] as previously described, one should perform a propitiatory rite (śānti) for those that are unfavorable;
then, with water from the kuśa-grass and the pitcher situated upon the altar, [one should sprinkle] everywhere.
Having sprinkled that celestial chariot with water, he should mutter the mantra of Bhuvaneśvarī;
then, descending from the chariot, the architect, surrounded by carpenters, [should proceed].
Having consecrated the sacrificial site, including the inner pavilion, with water mixed with kuśa grass and fragrant scents in due order, one should scatter eight kinds of grain all around it.
Standing at the forefront, the architect (sthapati), with hands full of flowers, perfumes, unbroken rice grains, and water,
should recite these verses while calling to mind the gods.

May the gods, asuras, and others protect this dwelling from the obstruction of rainwater, from the falling of thunderbolts, from fierce winds, from the burning of fire, from thieves and the like, and from the assault of enemy armies.
May men be free from disease, prosperous, happy, and long renowned for their glory;
may the virtuous and victorious king protect the entire earth, abounding in livestock and crops. 51.

May Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śaṅkara, the Moon and Sun, Nandin, Lakṣmī, Vāg-vadhū, Skanda, Indra, the Earth, the gods, and the sages bestow upon living beings prosperity, good fortune, health, and enjoyments. (52)
Thus, having uttered this, the master builder (sthapati) should complete his own work;
then the architect (sthāpaka) also should complete his own work. || 53 ||

Having first caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, one should sprinkle the entire temple in due order with water from a jar, water with *kuśa* grass, and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
Then, having projected the form of the temple, one should meditate upon it in its entirety;
the seed-syllable of the temple (HRĪM), enriched by the *haṃsa*, has emerged from the end of the twelve [fingers].
Having brought [the deity], one should place it within that fire-altar (dhiṣṇya) image which is of the nature of consciousness;
then, likewise, with the arghya and other offerings, as well as with perfumes and so forth, in due order.
Having offered the concluding oblation, the patron, with a serene mind, should duly worship that celestial mansion with gold, garments, ornaments, and other such gifts.
Having honored both the architect and the master-builder according to one's own capacity,
[one obtains] that which consists of the fruit of the intense hardships endured during the construction of the celestial mansion.
One should receive the entirety of the dharma from the carpenter with a stream of gold; there, however, the master-builder himself should bestow it with a stream of water.
Furthermore, the patron should satisfy him with gold, garments, and other gifts; for if he, being of deluded intellect, should not accept them from the carpenter, [the ritual would fail].
That action would indeed be fruitless; therefore, that [agent] must certainly be accepted.
Furthermore, there are others as well, such as carpenters and laborers who perform the work. (61)
One should satisfy the image-protectors (mūrtipās) and the Brahmins with appropriate offerings;
one should give everything—cows, grain, banners, garments, and so forth—to the architect (sthapati).
One should feed the Brahmins and others and satisfy them with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā). The officiating priest (sthapati) is indeed Brahmā himself, and the sacrificer (yajamāna) is Hari himself.
Whatever object has been accomplished by the three— the Teacher, the Blessed One, and Rudra—
that object shall indeed be stable, bestowing both visible and invisible fruits. (64)
The Chapter on the Installation of the Vimāna:

Now, once the divine abode has been well-established, the installation of the Heart [mantra] should be performed; having decorated the pavilion, which is provided with four doors and so forth, as previously described. 65.

Preceded by the scattering [of flowers], the throwing [of the vessel], the discharge of the water-pot weapon (kumbhāstra), the placement of fire, and so forth, one should perform the ritual actions for the mantras up to the libation (tarpaṇa) just as in the initiation (dīkṣā).
Having fashioned a golden image of the deity according to one's means, one should bathe it outside on the northern altar (uttaravedī) and clothe it with a garment.

Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) and worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, he should then lead the person— the *pralayākala*— to the pavilion and have him lie down upon the bed on the altar.
Then one should make the conscious [mantra] awakened by the vocative form of Śivājñā;
thereafter, having extracted the Haṃsa enclosed within the Tāra and Hṛdaya, one should then employ the word "ātman. (69)
Having uttered, "By the command of Śiva, you must remain within this body," he should then fill his hands with flowers up to the *dvādaśānta* while joining his palms in reverence (*añjali*).
Having projected the consciousness in the form of a star into the handful of flowers, one should join it to the heart-lotus of the Golden Person (Hiraṇyapuruṣa) by way of the channel.
Then, having mentally projected the body consisting of the Kalās and other principles upon that [deity], one should perform the ritual placement (vinyāsa).
It is as follows:
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Kalā; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Lord of Kalā; Oṃ hāṃ...
"Bring about the manifestation of the agency of the Lord of Kalā;
in this very manner, [bring about the manifestation] of Vidyā, Rāga, and the others as well. (72)
One should indeed assign the principles (tattvas), having separately enunciated the ego (ahaṅkāra); for the specific case of Vidyā and the others, a distinct procedure is recommended.
Namely:
the manifestation of knowledge for one who is dominated by learning; passion toward sense objects for one who is dominated by passion;
the performance of one's own duty for one who is dominated by nature; and awakening for one who is dominated by intellect.
One should apply the words "O you whose presiding deity is the ego (ahaṅkāra), exercise pride! at the end of every [mantra], saying "do, do.
Furthermore, there shall be separate presiding deities for the mind and for the ten sense organs.
Namely:
the Moon, the Quarters, the Wind, the Sun, Varuṇa, and the two Aśvins. || 74 ||
Agni, Indra, Viṣṇu, Mitra, and Brahmā are, respectively, the presiding deities (adhipāḥ) here over the sense organs beginning with the ear. (75)

The five presiding deities of the organs of action, such as speech and the rest, are considered [the lords]. The activity of the mind (manas) and the intellect (buddhi) consists of conceptualization and discrimination. (76)

The capacity of the ear and the other senses to grasp sound and the rest is traditionally taught as distinct from the functions of speaking, grasping, moving, excreting, and experiencing pleasure. (77)

The state of being the grasper should be stated separately for speech and the others in their respective order. Now, first, there is the pentad of sound and the rest, preceded by the seed-syllable *tāra-hṛd*. (78)
One should pronounce each [name] four times, ending with "namaḥ" once for each; then one should speak of the five [elements] beginning with space, ending with "namaḥ," as before. (79)

Those [deities] beginning with Sadāśiva and ending with Brahmā are the presiding lords over the five elements beginning with space; they should be addressed as before, with their names followed by the fourth case-ending and the word "namaḥ. (80)
Having thus assigned the principles (tattvas), one should assign the ten channels (nāḍīs) in the same manner,
preceded by the Tāra and the Hṛdaya-mantra, ending with "Namaḥ," and including the dative case suffix.
Iḍā, Piṅgalā, Suṣumṇā, Gāndhārī, Hastijihvikā, Suyaśas, Alambuṣā, Pūṣā, Kuhū, and also Śaṅkhinī. (82)
The ten names of the channels (nāḍīs) are:
likewise prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, samāna, nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya. || 83 ||
One should also place these ten vital breaths (prāṇas) as before, ending with "namaḥ," while recollecting Māyā preceded by one's own authority. 84.
Considering Time and Niyāmaka as the binders, and likewise [considering] the thumb-sized [Puruṣa] and others as the impellers through mantras; (85)
One should then install the Blessed Lord as the Person (puruṣa) by means of pervasiveness,
and subsequently cause even the three-part path (trikhaṇḍādhvan) to cease through the [mantra] Niṣṭhurā.

Having meditated [on the protection] up to Rudra, who resides within Māyā, and likewise having performed protection by means of the Weapon-mantra (astra), one should then go near the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and [meditate on] Śakti, known as the Foundation (ādhāra). (87)

As before, having placed the principles beginning with Time (Kāla), preceded by the seed-syllable of Tāra-hṛd and ending with "namaḥ," into the fire, one should then [offer] oblations of clarified butter.
Having offered oblations and performed recitations that many times, he should then proclaim the command of Śiva:
"Oṃ hāṃ! O Lord of Time, by the command of Śiva, you must remain here together with your own principle until the completion of the temple's construction."
One should thus restrain [the elements] individually, starting from Vidyā and ending with Ādhāraśakti. || 89 ||
Then, above the inner sanctum and over the *śukanāsa*,
upon a couch prepared with a bed, there should be a jar made of gold or some other precious metal.

Having placed it [the vessel], filled it with clarified butter and honey, endowed it with gems and other such items, covered it with a pair of fine garments, and worshipped it in due order with perfumes and other offerings; || 91 ||
Having placed that golden man upon it, one should worship him again;
then, having offered oblations with the Aghora mantra as an expiation, one should give the teacher’s fee.
One should give gifts to the guardians of the images and to the Brahmins according to one's capacity; then, one should bid farewell to the Blessed Lord and to the Fire as before.
The Chapter on the Installation of the Heart.

Thus, the installation of the stūpa and the pitcher, as well as the installation of the celestial palace (vimāna) which is taught in the tantras, has been explained; and herein is also taught the installation of the heart by means of those [mantras].
The temple should be well-established as Maheśa. || 94 ||

Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, concerning the characteristics of the stūpa and other structures, in the Kriyāpāda of the Upper Section of the *Siddhāntasāra*, the *Śrīmadīśānaśivagurudevapaddhati*.
Now begins the thirty-fifth chapter.
Now, the subsequent procedure should be understood according to the specific site or the ripening of time, whenever a component of the temple becomes fallen, displaced, or decayed. (1)
p.

347) Indeed, it should be restored with the respective materials such as stone and so forth, just as before; the configuration should be exactly as previously described, as well as whatever ornaments and the like there may be. || 2 ||
Neither the loss nor the increase of the breadth and height is recommended; for the measurement of the various types of *jāti* meters remains exactly as before. (3)
If the original abode of a self-manifested (svayambhū), divinely created (daivika), or rishi-made [shrine] is small, dilapidated, or fallen, its enlargement shall not bring about any fault. || 4 ||

If the gate, enclosure wall, pedestal, and so forth, or the retinue, are located in a place not previously mentioned, one should construct them in the prescribed locations according to their defining characteristics.
One should fashion the divine abode of former times— which was devoid of pride and free from blemish— endowed with auspicious marks and beautiful in its original configuration.
Whether it be of Svayambhuva or Arṣadeva, whether it be formless (niṣkala) or with form (sakala), one should not move the liṅga from its place; it deserves to remain in its original location.
If it is carried away or displaced by river water, ocean water, wind, or other such causes,
one should re-establish it within a thousand *daṇḍas* while the area remains secure.
In the absence of that very [image], however, a ninth [type] is equal to the previous linga; but when the vimāna is similar to the previous one, it follows immediately after the expiation.
The installation should be performed for the sake of prosperity, for the welfare of the king, the kingdom, and the subjects.
Therein, from the primary shrine, one should protect the directions of the Rakshasas, Yama, Agni, and Marut. (10)

Having abandoned [the image] as desired, one should install it elsewhere according to the prescribed rite in a direction other than that of Yama, the Lord King; for in those directions, there is destruction by Yama, Bhṛgu, Rākṣasa, and Agni respectively.
Therefore, having avoided that [fault], it is beneficial to establish the shifting [of the altar] from the previously mentioned asterism of the *chandās* to the east or west, or further around. 12.

An abundance of height resulting from the measures of māna, unmāna, and pramāṇa is praised; however, a site where the measurements and so forth are inferior to those of the preceding [site] is detrimental to the patron and the king. (13)
The removal of doors, walls, courtyards, and so forth causes destruction;
once the ruined material has been discarded, one should lay down the foundation (garbha) again.

One should perform the consecration (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and so forth as before, even for pillars and other such structures; provided that the house or similar structure is to be constructed using the same materials as previously used. (15)
Having first commenced with nine new substances, he then joined them with nine ancient ones; among the new ones, the new were desired through unions, and among the ancient ones, the ancient.
In a mixed configuration (miśrayoga), destruction occurs; therefore, one should not perform a mixture.
Cities, villages, dwellings, and so forth should be established in accordance with their original locations. || 17 ||

One should construct that which is beneficial and abandon anything that causes harm or leads to the destruction of one's lineage; [this includes] constructing small shrines for the Liṅga and so forth, located either inside the city wall or outside the original foundation.
Or one should act like a snake that has vomited its venom so as not to injure its own root; it is not permitted to harm a minor enemy excessively, for he is like the dwelling place of the root. (19)

Half, three-quarters, or one-third [of the total] is recommended for the portion of the arrows (five parts), extending sequentially from Indra to Vāyu; however, the temple of Śiva is measured from the base (mūla).
It destroys the established order, the dwelling place, the performer, the royal lineage, the kingdom, wealth, and the crops; therefore, one should avoid it. || 21 ||

In this same manner, for villages, cities, and so forth, as well as for one's own house, [the ritual] is the same. Therefore, from the north to the east, starting with Mukhya and ending with Parjanya.
One should indeed install a human-made Śāṅkara Liṅga, for it bestows auspiciousness; Śiva, facing either east or west, brings welfare to mankind. (23)
Except for Aghora, Nṛtteśa, Dakṣiṇeśa, and Vāma, all the deities are auspicious and bestow blessings upon men when they face [the worshipper]. (24)
Fierce [deities] are recommended when facing away from cities, villages, houses, and the like. One should not construct a human dwelling that is higher than a temple of the gods. (25)
In its vicinity, an excess of that [human element] is especially not desired; by fate, the human dwelling may be inferior to, or equal with, the auspicious divine abode. (26)
The procedure for the subsequent rite:
From the foundation up to the pinnacle of the stūpa, beauty brings auspiciousness; however, deformity and deficiency or excess in the components of the temple are censured. (27)
A hole, a wound, a cave, a depression, or anything else inauspicious [indicates] the destruction of the region, its ruler, the site, the builder, and the master. (28)
Furthermore:
In the case of *adhiṣṭhāna*, there is deformity and the destruction of one's lineage; in *pratyā*, it leads to the death of a woman; and in *stambha*, there is the defeat of the king. (29)
If it is on the ridge, there will be the destruction of the twice-born; if on the neck, the ruin of merchants;
if on the nostrils, the destruction of one's own faction; and if on the summit, the downfall of the king. (30)
Deformity in the dome or the pinnacle of a stupa brings about the destruction of that kingdom and its people;
likewise, a door or staircase in an improper location brings misfortune to everyone.

A wall built on an unsuitable site, pillars that are out of place, deformity in the unmentioned parts of the body, ornaments not prescribed by rule, and anything else of this kind brings about undesirable suffering. (32)

The interruption of ritual offerings and services, as well as the cessation of sacrificial oblations (bali), are caused by drought; therefore, one should construct a temple that is beautiful in all its parts and endowed with the proper characteristics.
The cave of the eastern direction brings about destruction, suffering, death, nourishment, the increase of one's lineage, the ruin of one's lineage, wealth, happiness, and poverty. (34)
It brings death, disease, fear of fire, loss of kinsmen, wealth, a son, the arrival of friends, prosperity, and destruction in succession. || 35 ||

The placement [of the deity] from the station of Brahmā down to Īśāna within anthills, houses, and so forth, as well as the descent of lightning and the deposition of honey, are all censured everywhere.
The arrival of wealth, the loss of wealth, the acquisition of friends, happiness, prosperity, rain, the arrival of a daughter, a son, and strife with a passionate maiden. (37)
From the station of Brahmā, however, [the deities] beginning with Śakra and ending with Īśāna are placed in due order;
elsewhere, as previously stated, at the intermediate points and at the door, Kalaha and the others are situated.
Since it brings about misfortune, one should offer clarified butter as an oblation for its pacification.
[In the case of seeing a woman with red garments: owls, vultures, hawks, and likewise wild pigeons— (39)
If *piṅgala* and *cakora* birds should appear in a house, they bring misfortune;
so too in the dwellings of gods and humans, in monasteries, cow-pens, assemblies, and the like. (40)
Now, the pacification of defects caused by anthills and other such wonders is described:
having removed them through actions such as digging and having smeared [the ground] with plaster... (41)
Having performed the *adbhuta-śāntika* rite and the *rakṣoghna-vāstuhoma* in that place which was surrounded by cows, he then offered the *vāstubali* oblation.
Having fed the Brahmins, one should again cause them to pronounce an auspicious day;
by dwelling there according to the prescribed rule, it shall bring about all prosperity.
The pacification of portents:
For the sake of achieving protection and ornamentation for palaces, mansions, and the like, one should construct ramparts in the sequence of five, three, two, and one [units]. (44)

Therein, first is the inner circle (antarmaṇḍala), and outside that is the inner necklace (antarhārā); then the middle necklace (madhyahārā) as the boundary, and beyond that the great boundary (mahāmaryādaka).
Regarding this, Maya says:

For small temples with low towers, one should construct an inner mandala measuring half the width of the sky [the temple's diameter], and its surrounding wall should be three cubits wide and equal in measure to that.
The second and the third [altars] are each five cubits more than that;
the fourth should be equal to that, measuring seven cubits.
The fifth [type] should be equal to that, measuring nine cubits.
Thus it is said:
"But for those of medium size, half of the root [measurement] shall be the inner mandala; from that, [the measurements] shall be five, seven, seven, eleven, and four cubits respectively. (46)
The width of the space between the ramparts in a city with five walls has been declared; now, first, the sages have stated that for the best [cities], it is half of the base measurement.
Indeed, the necklaces consist of nine, eleven, thirteen, and sixteen cubits;
the width of the wall of the inner circle shall be one and a half cubits.
Therefore, due to an increase of two or three finger-breadths in succession, the halls indeed come into being;
[the circumference] is threefold or fourfold according to the measurement of their respective diameters. (49)
The height of the wall (prākāra) is said to be [one unit], and the thickness of the coping (śiroghana) is one-eighth of its own high point (svocca). On this matter, Maya says:
"It may be as high as the northern edge, or as high as the elevation ending at the pitcher-molding (kumbha-maṇḍi)."
It is rich with sections such as the *masūraka* and others, and adorned with *khaṇḍa-harmya* pavilions and similar structures.
"The wall is desired to be either shaped like a bubble, a half-moon, or a crest, or straight.
Thus, for a small wall with a narrow span, starting from one cubit, it is as described before. (50)
One should gradually increase the height by two or three finger-breadths up to one and a half cubits;
the walls should be provided with lintels, cornices, and capitals like parasols.
Above all the embankments in the temple of Śiva,
one should construct a most beautiful row of bulls all around.
The root-base is the place of origin; the height from the base-trunk is one cubit, and each subsequent trunk is successively less by six mātrās. (53)

The height of the pedestal (pīṭha) should be half a cubit; from that, it may be reduced by two or three finger-breadths up to the end of the wall of the great boundary (mahāmaryādā). Alternatively, it may be diminished in this manner.
In the *kṣudra* [vīṇā], it is eighteen finger-breadths; in the *madhyama*, it is the root-pādukā. One should diminish it by four mātrās until it reaches the *pañcāntasālaka*.
The characteristics of the enclosure wall:
the station for the bull should be in front, the kitchen in the southeast, that of the Mothers near Yama (the southwest),
and that of the elephant-faced one in the northwest.
The abode of Vāsudeva is in the west, that of Skanda immediately following it;
the abodes of Umā and Durgā are recorded as being in the northwest or the northeast.

To the north of the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) should be the storehouse; for the wielder of the trident (Śiva), it should be between Īśa and Indra; for the Lord of Beings (Brahmā), it should be between Īśa and Indra, or in the northeast, or in front.
(352) Some say that the house for the bathing water is located between the fire-altar and the gatehouse; others maintain it is situated in the middle of the fire-altars and the Mothers' shrines. 59.
The monastery (maṭha) should be outside in the south, between Puṣpa, Yama, and Vighna;
the weapons should be between Rakṣas and Ambu; and the cowshed should be outside in the west (Varuṇa).
The seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha) should be located within the western side of the bed for Jyeṣṭhā, to the south of Vāyu for Mukhya, and for Kṣetrapa, it should be in the direction of Parjanya.
The [image] of Caṇḍanātha is within [the circle], while those of the Ādityas are outside the [circle] of Brahmā;
the [images] of the World-Guardians (Lokapālas) are in their own respective directions, and those of the Aśvins are between Indra and Agni.
On the second outer enclosure are those of Viśve, Yama, and Rakṣas;
and in the direction of the Rakṣas from the Teacher, as well as outside, is that of Bhadrakālī.
Between Rākṣasa and Varuṇa, the abode of the serpent Śeṣa is recorded;
[the abodes] of objects, water, and wind, as well as of sages, are between Vāyu and Soma. 64.

One should thus arrange the Rudras in order within the center of Someśa; the measurement of their retinues and celestial chariots (vimānas) shall be half the measurement of the inner sanctum (garbha).

In small [temples], one should calculate [the dimensions] from one-third or one-fourth; however, in the case of a very small [shrine], there should be a single enclosure wall as well as the eightfold retinue.
Vṛṣa, Gaṇapati, Brahmā, the Mothers, Guha, Hari, Durgā,
and Caṇḍeśvara— these eight are proclaimed as the retinue.
Moreover, there are ten world-protectors (lokeśas), as well as Caṇḍa and the Antarmātṛs; these twelve indeed reside in either the inferior or the middling abode.
These twelve—the Vighnas, Guha, Durgā, and Hari—shall be the attendants in their respective directions;
there are sixteen [deities] in the central sanctuary.
In the excellent celestial palaces, one should establish the retinues without exception,
as well as the deities of the site (vāstudeva), in order starting from Īśāna.
In the thirty-two intermediate great cities, up to their respective locations;
the arising of the images of the retinue is twice that of the arising of the portion for worship.
"According to Parāśara, the best [attendants] should be one and a half times that size, the middling equal to that, and the lowest [the same];
when the deity is standing, they should stand as his retinue, and likewise when seated; they should also be seated when [the deity] is reclining—so said Pitāmaha."
Regarding this, Maya states:
"The bull should face either east or west, or it may not face the gods; however, all other attendant deities must always face the gods."
Thus it is said:
whichever direction the deity faces, one should place the vehicle and banner in front of him; then, beginning with Indra, one should worship the world-protectors (lokeśas) in a clockwise direction.
One should arrange the bearer of the floral remains (nirmālya-dhāraka) in the northeast, the Mothers in the south, the deity everywhere,
and the water-channel (pranāla) in the north.

Outside the gopura, one should construct the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha) according to its proper characteristics; its intermediate space should be three-quarters [of the width] or even half the width of the temple (prāsāda).
The pedestal (pīṭha) should have a width of half the inner sanctum (garbha) and a height measuring three-quarters of that;
one should fashion it with heights of three, two, or one cubit for the best, middle, and lowest types respectively.
The birth-mould (janmā) is made with sixteen parts of that [height], and the jagatī with three;
the kumuda with four parts, the paṭṭikā with one part, and the gala with three parts.

The *kaṃpa* (molding) is one part, while the *vājana* and the upper fillet (*ūrdhvapaṭṭikā*) each consist of two parts. Then, regarding its width, by reducing two parts from each of ten parts [of the total width], [the proportions are established].
The upper lotus should be spread out over eight parts, or indeed one less; the emergence of the petals is said to be two parts, and the pericarp is derived from a third part of that.
The sacrificial seat (baliviṣṭara) may be of the Sabhadra, Vibhadra, or Sopapīṭha type, or it may be furnished with the ornaments described for celestial chariots (vimāna). || 79 ||
Either in the middle of the *hārā*, or at the boundary, or even outside the *balipīṭha* toward the east, one should install the flagstaff (*dhvajastambha*).
Outside the flagstaff, one should construct a bull-shrine with four doors;
it is best when equal to the door-linga, and middling when reduced by a quarter.
The bull, endowed with auspicious marks, may be half as small [as the main image] to be the smallest;
it should be one and a half times the height of the door, or twice the height plus a quarter. (82)
A bull, seated and possessing a most beautiful form, should be depicted; now the characteristics of the gate-towers (gopura) are duly described.
At every embankment (prativapra), a gatehouse (gopura) must be constructed at each gate.
Regarding this, Maya says: "For the shrines (dhiṣṇya) that are small, minor, medium, or principal, [the dimensions] should be according to their own respective measurements."
In the width of the main temple, it should be divided into seven, eight, or nine parts.
And by reducing each successive part from one-tenth and one-eleventh of the width of the door-ornaments and so forth,
that gateway (gopura) shall be formed in due order.

For small and minor temples, the measurement should be as previously stated. For medium-sized temples, however, the width of the main temple (mūladhāman) should be divided by four, five, or six; the gatehouse (gopura) shall be separately one part less than that. For large temples, the width of the main temple should be divided by four, five, or eight; the gatehouse shall be separately one part less than that.
In the case of a three-part [measurement], there should be one-third, one-sixth, one-half, and two-thirds.
In the case of the best gopuras, the width of the door-ornaments and so forth is prescribed as three parts out of four, or four parts out of five.
The height of the gate-towers (gopura) should be one part out of seven parts for a tall tower;
it should be six parts high when divided into four parts, and seven parts high when divided into five parts.

The height of the doorway and its vestibule (āyatana) is determined by dividing [the total height] into seven parts and taking four parts, or into nine parts and taking five parts, or alternatively, doubling these proportions respectively.
The width of the gopura, however, shall be one-third of [the temple's] width, or one-fourth,
or two-fifths.
The exit from the gate-towers should be outside the rampart wall; it should measure one and a half, one and three-quarter, or two and a half cubits from the base.
The width of the gateways and the towers has been briefly specified.
On this point, Parāśara states:
"By an increase of six, nine, or twelve *mātrās*, it [the width] ends at five, seven, or nine cubits."
The door has fifteen divisions; it occurs separately in the small, the middle, and the great [mandalas].
In that case, because of the width of the doors, the height is said to be fivefold. (84)
From five parts, there is a seven-part [measure]; from seven parts, a ten-part [measure].
The height is fivefold: double, increased by half, and increased by a quarter. || 85 ||
Having successively set aside thirty-one, seven, and nine finger-breadths from each of the five halls, proceeding from right to right; 86.
Having examined the fundamental materials, one should install the door there;
its height from the base of the pedestal should be measured by four, seven, or eight units.
The height of the base together with its pedestal (adhiṣṭhāna) should be one-twelfth of the total height from the root; the remainder shall be the upapīṭhaka.
One should properly fashion the foot-binding and the *masūra* [moulding]; the measurement of the beam, the member, the pedestal, and the pillar, however, should be like that of the base (*mūla*).

The height of the gate-tower (gopura) and its pillars should be less than one-eighth of the Vasunanda [measurement]; having fixed the base (nikhātapāda) up to the conclusion of the fire-offering (homānta), one should install the pedestal (adhiṣṭhānaka) after overcoming [the obstacles].

That [inner space] should be equal to the northern limit or half of it, and it should be wide; one should place the inner sanctum (garbha) on the right side of the entrance once the walls have been erected.
The height of the *miśraka* (mixed) type of door is greater than the height of the pedestal (*pādādhiṣṭhāna*). This is declared for doors in cities, villages, capitals, and so forth. (92)
One should install the Yoga [deity] joined at the top of the gateway wall and on the two door-panels; one should establish its boundary at the edge of the rampart in the middle of the temple.
Indeed, the gopuras for the small [temples] have from one to five stories; those for the medium [temples] likewise range from two stories up to six floors.
Two, three, or up to seven stories for the highest class; however, the *gopura* (gate-tower) is the most excellent.
Herein—the pedestal (*upapīṭha*), the base (*adhiṣṭhāna*), and the height of the plinth (*pāda*) extend to the end of the upper story (*uttarāntaka*). The remainder—
The measurement of that portion is prescribed as extending up to the edge of the stūpa.
Thus is Maya’s [system]: the gopura is sixfold, divided from the top of the stūpyanta down to the north. 95.

The height of the pedestal (mañca) is one and a quarter parts; the height of the entablature (prastara) is one part; the height of the neck (kandhara) is one part; and the head (śiras) is three-quarters of a part. (96)

But according to the remaining [tradition], the "tall-peaked" (śikhātuṅga) has a single-storied gopura; however, for those with two stories and more, it is determined by the division of the additional floors.
One should construct [the structure] up to twelve stories in due order;
[the height] should be one-fifth of the width of the gateway (gopura) and three parts of the inner sanctum (garbhāgāra).

In a single-storied temple, one should construct the wall-thickness using two parts; when the width of the gateway (gopura) is divided into seven parts, the inner sanctum (garbha) should be made with four parts.
One should construct the wall with the remaining three [parts] at the rising point, or in the nine-part division;
the width of the kūṭa should be one part, and the koṣṭhaka should be three parts.
Between the *kūṭa* and the *koṣṭhaka*, having adorned it with five parts such as the *pañjara* and other elements according to its beauty, the gateway (*gopura*) shall consist of two stories.
In nine parts it is three-storied; in ten parts, four-storied; in eleven parts (rudrāṃśe) it is the Śarabhauma type;
and likewise, in twelve parts (sūryāṃśe), it is six-storied.
In the thirteenth [chapter], one should construct seven stories according to the logic previously stated.
On this point, Parāśara says:
"From one story up to seven stories, it applies everywhere."

The gate-towers (gopura) should be adorned with balconies, pavilions, peaked roofs, halls, front porches, cages, lion-heads, elephant-backs, wing-halls, lentil-shaped pillars, altars, lattices, and archways.
[The height] of the main entrance should be one-fifth less than its width. (103)
One should arrange the doors of the upper stories lower than those below; however, within the inner sanctum (garbhāgāra), one should place the stairs one above the other.
A staircase with four railings is recommended for the pedestal; it should be constructed by the wise according to what is logical and what is aesthetically pleasing.

One should construct the ornamentation of the gate-towers (gopura) in accordance with the fundamental structure, providing beauty of form and so forth for the vimānas, palaces, and other edifices. 106.
It possesses a pedestal and a foundation, adorned with pillars and other ornaments; it is beautiful, endowed with two stories and more, featuring a great door and a circumambulatory path. || 107 ||
(357) It possesses stairs for mounting, is provided with intermediate floorings,
is enriched with the beauty of *ūha* and *pratyūha*, and has fourteen (two times seven) decorative bands (*paṭṭikā*). || 108 ||
The arrangement of the long-pointed form is known as the Śrīmandira; that very same [form], however, with the head and sides omitted and returning to the original base, [is another]. (109)
The abode of Śrī should be provided with six friezes at its front,
possessing a single assembly hall as its roof and endowed with six great nostrils.
It shall be named Sumaṅgala; now the Viśāla is described: it is exactly as previously stated, but with an increase of one part on all sides, including the gaṇḍī.
The glorious gateway named Viśālā is endowed with a crest-pavilion; that very same [gateway] is called Bhavya when it is appropriately surrounded by devotion.
That same [gateway], circular at the top, elongated in form, and beautiful, with a rounded peak at its summit,
is the gateway named Pauṣṭika for the corners.
That very same [structure], when provided with half a portion of the Veda at the entrance and equipped with pavilions, adorned with small towers and banners, is the gateway named Sumaṇḍa. (114)

The one joined with a pigeon-house (kapotaśālā) shall be known by the name Pārikūṭaka. These are the eight gate-towers (gopura), according to the application of pure or mixed construction methods. 115.
Then, [the temple] was endowed with three stories and so forth, possessed two sets of sixty [pillars] as its nostrils, and was equipped with a foundation,
pillars, pinnacles, halls, and archways.
From the hall, there was a gatehouse named Subhadra, provided with a cage, ascending from the secret to the most secret, worthy of the best of gods and the lords of men. 117.
It should have two stories divided on both sides of the inner chamber; it must be square, adorned with four *nāsīs* and beautiful with its various architectural members and limbs. 118.
If that very same [structure] on the summit possesses the designation "Bhadra-kalyāṇa," being enriched with eight-sided pinnacles and halls, it is designated as "Bhadra-sundara. (119)
In every opening there should be that same [structure] from which the hall-front has emerged; it is surrounded by an increase in parts and provided with seven floors.
That most beautiful gateway is called Śrīkara;
thus concludes the procedure for the gateway (gopura).
Thus has been stated the procedure for the subsequent rites; first, pacification was duly explained here, as well as portents.
The characteristics of the enclosure wall have been told, the marks of the bull have been described, and the entire rule for the gate-tower (gopura) has been declared in brief.

Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, concerning the characteristics of the subsequent rites and so forth, in the Kriyāpāda of the upper section of the *Siddhāntasāra*, which is the *Śrīmad-Īśānaśivagurudeva-paddhati*.
Now begins the thirty-sixth chapter.
Now, the *liṅga* is to be known as threefold: the partless (*niṣkala*), the with-parts (*sakala*), and the mixed (*miśra*).
Furthermore, that *liṅga* is twofold: immovable (*acala*) and movable (*cala*). (1)

The partless (niṣkala) is known as the *liṅga* alone; the whole (sakala) is remembered as the image (*pratimā*); that which is called mixed (*miśra*) is the face-liṅga (*mukhaliṅga*), characterized by mixed features.
The Niṣkala Liṅga is of six kinds, according to the sequence: made of stone, precious gems, metal, wood, clay, and again, that which is temporary. (3)
The stones for the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra [castes] should be white, reddish, yellow, and black respectively; one should fashion the liṅgas from them in that order.
Alternatively, some say that all [the stones] should be used; white and other colored stones grant liberation, victory, wealth, and grain.
Crystal, ruby, diamond, sapphire, gold, lapis lazuli,
coral, and topaz— thus the jewel-liṅga is of eight kinds.
Sphaṭika, sūryakānta, and candrakānta—these are the three types; they are all varieties of sphaṭika itself, which bestow desire, liberation, and wealth respectively.
One obtains prosperity, the fulfillment of desires, as well as health, wealth, sons, victory, and happiness,
by worshipping the lingas made of ruby and other gems in their respective order.
In this world, there are generally nine defects common to all gems: lines, spots, stains, crow’s feet, scratches, and dust. (9)
One should carefully avoid any cracks caused by fear of frost in gems made of gold,
silver, copper, brass, bell-metal, or iron. (10)
The metallic linga is of eight kinds, namely those made of lead and tin;
the golden linga bestows enjoyment and liberation, while the silver one grants nourishment.
A vessel made of leather yields sons; one of bell-metal grants happiness; one of brass bestows longevity and health; and an iron vessel is known to cause death.
Lead and tin are used for inciting enmity, expulsion, and killing; indeed, the four primary metals beginning with gold are auspicious.
One should avoid other metals such as piśāca-iron, as well as bell-metal (kāṃsya) and the like; likewise, one should avoid sandalwood, devadāru, śamī, pippala, and śiṃśapā wood.
The khadira, āsana, mālūra, madhūka, bakula, padmaka, and karṇikāra—these three each are for the Brahmins and the other castes respectively. (15)

One should know that auspicious trees are suitable for wooden liṅgas in their respective order; likewise, clay originating from sacred fords, holy fields, mountains, groves, or meritorious regions [is recommended]. (16)
Taking white, red, yellow, or black [sandalwood], one should grind it together with the powders of barley, wheat, and mung beans, as well as guggulu resin. (17)
Take equal parts of lac, śrīveṣṭaka, śyāmā, and sarja; then add one part of kundaruṣka and an amount of powdered earth equal to the total weight of all these ingredients. 18.
One should rub that earth with the five products of a tawny cow mixed with oil;
having been thus rubbed, it should be left for another month.
Having taken [the clay], one should fashion the linga together with its pedestal according to one's desired measurement; however, the clay linga, being raw, should be dried in the heat for a month.
Alternatively, one may take pure clay suitable for ritual work, which has been pulverized,
kneaded with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and likewise left to soak for exactly one month.

Having taken [the materials], one should have a liṅga fashioned together with its pedestal, endowed with the proper characteristics; it should be cooked by skilled artisans in the fire, and thus that liṅga becomes fully baked.
(360) Those made of sand, cow dung, flour, sour gruel, clay, fruit, and butter—
these seven types of lingas are indeed momentary.
Indeed, for those who worship them every day, the momentary lingas bestow liberation, health, wealth, food, nourishment, prosperity, and subjugation.

No pedestal (piṇḍikā) should be made for these; rather, one should fashion the liṅga upon their seat. For these, there is no measurement consisting of three sections, nor is there the carving of the head (śirovartana) and so forth. (25)

For these [images], there is no requirement for specific times, muhūrtas, and so forth, nor for rituals such as the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa). Having fashioned them instantly, one should invoke Śiva into their respective lingas and worship him.
Having discarded that linga without further regard, one should cast it into the water.
This is the rule for a temporary linga.
For lingas made of stone and other such materials, the pedestal (piṇḍikā) itself shall serve as its own source, provided there is no defect in it. 27.
In the absence [of these], however, it should be made of bricks, stone, gems, gold, silver, or copper, according to the sequence of superior, middling, and inferior quality. (28)
The authority for the materials of the liṅga and the pedestal (pīṭha) is as follows: they may be made of the very same metals [as the deity], or of bricks, or of wood.
This should be done when the sun is situated in its northern course (uttarāyaṇa), during the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa), and endowed with auspicious qualities. || 29 ||
The taking up of the stone and other materials is prescribed on an auspicious lunar day, weekday, and asterism;
having first fed the twice-born and caused them to pronounce blessings, one should then proceed.
Having fully worshipped the Lord of Gods along with his limbs (retinue) and having performed the ritual sacrifice of the weapon (astrayāga),
he should proceed toward the east or the north, observing the auspicious omens.
A bull with a blazing fire-lamp on its head, courtesans, and young maidens;
flowers, food, a full water-pot, clarified butter, a conch, milk, and curd. 32.
Rice, śāli grain, meat, honey, an umbrella, and a chowrie;
auspicious women, a king, a banner, a full vessel, and a bow. (33)
When a milch cow and a horse are seen facing one's direction, they serve for the traveler’s accomplishment of desired goals; it is all the more so if they move clockwise around him.
The cry of a female lizard or a crow is auspicious when heard on the left during a departure; it is likewise favorable on the right during an entry.
Indeed, a sneeze at the very beginning is inauspicious.

Except for the back, the cawing of birds is auspicious for men on the left side; however, for the currents of rivers and the like, it is auspicious on the left, while for the *bharaṭa* and others, it is auspicious on the right.
In the direction of Śāntā, the singing of two types of Piṅgalas is beneficial;
so too are the jackal, the crow, the tiger, the cakora bird, the heron, and the pigeon. (37)
Moving from left to right are auspicious, but a serpent is censured everywhere;
so too are the hare, the owl, the vulture, the hawk, the deer, and the water-snake. (38)
Moving from right to left are praised; auspicious words grant auspicious results.
The sound of a donkey or a cow on the left, and movement toward the right, are auspicious. (39)
Thunderbolts, foul weather, rain, and likewise adverse words; Venus and Mercury being retrograde, whirlwinds, and quarrels—these are considered inauspicious.
Striking the head, the limbs, and especially the right foot;
as well as [striking] the caste, the vehicle, the dress, the mind, the weapon, and the direction. (41)
Lack of clarity, as well as the burning of the quarters, halos, the howling of jackals, the appearance of a mock sun, eclipses, meteors, earthquakes, and rainbows; || 42 ||
The breaking of a tree, a banner, a weapon, an umbrella, or a vehicle is censured; so too are the sight of a potter, a naked mendicant, one who is bald, and an inauspicious woman. (43)
There were ascetics devoid of merit, Vratyas, Yatis, and those such as the Vamanas; the deformed, fishermen, butchers, heretics, and those who carried staffs in their hands. (44)

Kāpālikas, those carrying wooden staffs, those with disheveled hair, those who are miserable, those wearing wet clothes, and those who are censurable—these are inauspicious when seen coming toward one's face. (45)
Having spent a month amidst inauspicious signs, one should proceed toward the auspicious; that which is designated as "stone-producing," such as mountains, fields, forests, and so forth. (46)
The Himādri, Vindhya, Śrīśaila, and Pāriyātra; the Śuktimān, Mahendra, Sahya, Malaya, Kalaśa, and Vedaparvata. || 47 ||
Ṛkṣa and Kumāraśaila are declared to be the principal stone-forms (śilākara); likewise, the rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā and the sacred fields (kṣetra) beginning with Amareśa. (48)
Others are middling sources for the acquisition of stone and wood; the inferior ones are those obtained as they may come. One should begin the taking of stone [from the superior sources]. (49)
The fourfold [types of] stone are known as Vāruṇī, Aindrī, Āgneyī, and Vāyavī; they are produced from those [elements] and are characterized by their respective names. || 50 ||
The earth known as Vāruṇī is that which possesses clusters of very tender trees, whose forests are in full bloom by themselves, and which is everywhere endowed with reservoirs of water. || 51 ||
That land which abounds in milk-yielding trees in the north, whose water is abundant, and which has rice fields in the south,
is known as the Māhendrī region.
A ground associated with vultures, herons, boars, bears, hawks, jackals, and crows, which is devoid of water nearby, is an ignoble *āgneyī* [region]. (53)
Ground that is devoid of water and covered with *akṣa*, *snuhī*, *kuliṅgākṣa*, *pīlu*, *śleṣmātaka*, and thorny plants is known as inauspicious and characterized by the quality of air (*vāyavī*).
Stones originating from fire, wind, or earth are excluded from being used as lingas; however, those produced in the regions of Varuṇa and Mahendra grant all spiritual accomplishments.
A land defiled by Caṇḍālas, Pulkasas, hunters, Pulindas, and others, or abounding in anthills, snakes, and cremation grounds, is contemptible; so too is its stone.
Regarding the acquisition of land, the types of ground previously described by their characteristics are commendable;
however, in the case of taking stones, one should avoid those that are censured.
Having reached an auspicious site, the preceptor, accompanied by artisans, should search for a stone there and recite this mantra: || 58 ||
Oṃ, salutation to the three-eyed Rudra, the lord of all beings! O Lord of Gods, O Bull-bannered One, be gracious and show me the stone! 59.
Then, having bathed together with his disciples, the preceptor and the architect were adorned with white perfumes, garlands, and unguents, and surrounded by artisans.
Having reached the site of stone, the Guru should address the spirits: "May the spirits depart, as well as the deities together with the guhyakas. (61)
"May you have great strength; may the earth grant me a stone. I shall accomplish this task; let the change of residence be made. (62)
One should address [the deity] with the mantra *hūṃ*.
However, in the case of taking wood, the specific mantra is: "May Soma grant trees.
Then, one should worship [it] with perfumes and other offerings.

Having offered an oblation to the spirits and the forest deities with five-colored rice, curds, milk, honey, ghee, fruits, and various foods, using meat and blood as substitutes for the fierce offerings to the *bhūtas*,
and having established a water-pot within a consecrated mandala, [the practitioner] facing either east or north—
Or, having dug the ground and concealed [the image] in the earth where it is untouched by the rays of the sun,
one should consecrate it with water from a ritual pitcher, sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) while reciting the *pavamāna* verses,
worship it up to the offering of food (*naivedya*) while reciting the five Brahma-mantras, and [cover it] with a new cloth.

Having covered it even with *darbha* grass and having placed [the fire] to the north of the main fire, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations of fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge (*caru*) with the Hṛdaya, Īśāna, and Aghora mantras; then, one should perform the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering with the *vyāhṛtis* and conclude with the ritual sprinkling (*pariṣecana*).
Then, having placed eight jars in the cardinal directions with the world-protectors as their presiding deities,
and having worshipped them, he should again consecrate the stone with those waters.
Then, having offered oblations in the various directions with honey, clarified butter, sugar, and very sweet milk-rice (pāyasa),
and having covered [the site], he performs the fire-oblation in the western fire.
Having offered caru and ghee with the mantras of the weapons of Śiva, the eleven Rudras, and the guardians of the directions,
he should again offer ghee one hundred times with the Pāśupata weapon mantra.

Having consecrated the weapons suitable for cutting with the Astra-mantra, one should lay them down; having encircled [the site] with those very weapons, one should sleep there upon Darbha grass at night while reciting this mantra.
Salutations to Śambhu! Salutations to the three-eyed one, to Rudra, and to the bestower of boons;
salutations to Śiva, whose form is the universe, the sovereign lord of dreams. (67)
"Speak, O Lord of the gods! I have sought refuge at your side. Whatever tasks indeed reside within my heart, [reveal them] even in a dream. (68)
"Śūlapāṇaye hili hili svāhā"—this is the mantra known as Svapnamāṇavaka.
In a dream, one may see a blazing stone, or one's own deity, or something else auspicious; such a stone should be taken for the rite of the liṅga. (69)
If the dream is inauspicious, that [stone] should be abandoned and another stone should be taken; having bathed in the morning, the Ācārya and likewise the Sthapati should worship the Lord. (70)
First, one should cut [the cord] with a golden needle and a grain of rice using the weapon-mantra; its lower part is the mouth, while its back is above, facing eastward.
Or if the head is toward the north, or if the sound of the bell is interrupted like sparks,
that stone with a cornered top must be rejected, for it brings suffering to the master.
Having cut it to the desired measurement— square, level, and auspicious—
one should mark the front, base, head, and back, and cover it with a cloth.
Having covered it with *darbha* grass and placed it upon a chariot, one should lead it to the temple; for a stone that is soft, delicate, and worn away is censured as being like a young girl.

One with a weak voice, one who is excessively harsh, one who is old, one who is extremely decrepit, one with various colors, and one with hair-like lines— such a woman is a Caṇḍālī and is to be avoided.
A bell-sounding stone that is firm and smooth is suitable for a young woman; a male stone is fit for the linga, being circular or circular and elongated. (76)
A square or oblong stone slab is suitable for a pedestal;
likewise, a triangular or elongated triangular stone is suitable for a pillar-base.
When a linga is fashioned from a female stone, the kingdom and the king do not perish;
and likewise when it is on a male pedestal, or on a neuter pedestal. (78)

If the pedestal on the surface of the earth is made by a woman or a man, there shall be the destruction of the kingdom. Thus, there are three kinds of stones for the footstone, the pedestal, and the liṅga. (79)

Having conveyed [the image] by means of a chariot or other vehicle to the pavilion in the northern direction, one should cause it to lie upon a pair of wooden planks; thereafter, one should have the linga fashioned.

In this [treatise], the characteristics of lingas made of metal, gems, stone, and wood; the auspicious omens resulting from the softening of the stone; and the selection of stones according to whether they are female, male, or neuter, as prescribed in the scriptures of Śiva, have been demonstrated.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, on the Specific Characteristics of Liṅgas, in the Kriyāpāda of the Upper Section of the Siddhāntasāra, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva.

Now the internal cavities (garbhas) shall be described: one should discard a linga that has an internal cavity; however, one should examine the cavities, for if a linga has an internal cavity, it should be abandoned.
Having smeared the entire linga with equal parts of poison, green vitriol (kāsīsa), and red ochre (gairika) ground with milk, it should then be left overnight.

Having washed away the impurities from the womb, one should observe it there by means of mandalas; or else, having ground together the mantras of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Īśa, and Vaiṣṇavī, one should encircle it.
One should apply a plaster made of milk, ghee, and honey mixed together; where the stone is seen to have remained for three nights and become moistened.
In that case, one should say there is a snake, or a lizard, or a scorpion within;
for a stone that has been smeared with iron sulfate, copper, and mercury, ground with cow’s milk, [will appear as such].
If, after staying for three nights, she becomes red, then there is a tortoise or a frog here;
[one should treat her] with māṃsī, kuṣṭha, and hayāri, or with triphalā and the water of a rain-cloud, for one night.
Having ground it and moistened it with breast milk, one should apply it; when a transformation occurs after three nights, one should diagnose that as the poison known as Kālakūṭa affecting the fetus.
Death may occur from touching it; therefore, one should not touch it.
[This is prevented] by applying a paste of the previously mentioned poison, kāsīsa, gairika, and milk.
One should indicate the embryos according to the mandalas formed on the first, second, or third day after conception;
namely:
in a mandala with the luster of madder, there would be a frog; in a yellow one, a lizard; and in a tawny one, a tortoise.
And mice; some say that in a black [dream] it is a snake, in a white one a mouse, and in one with the hue of a pigeon a scorpion. 9.
If it is red, it becomes a chameleon; if it resembles honey, it becomes a firefly.
In a mixture [of colors], there is a *pipīlikāgarbha*; in a weapon-like [color], water; in a grey [color], stone; in a white [color], the *vimalā*; in a smoky [color], the *pataṅga*; or else, sand.
If the tortoise is blue or yellow, it indicates defects in the womb; hereafter I shall describe [the results]: there is danger from water if it is a frog, and also for the builder and the king.
If the lizard appears in the kingdom, there will be the destruction of the maker's family; if it appears among crabs, bees, or moths, there will arise disease, suffering, and the like. (13)
In the Vimalā constellations, there is always theft or fear of foreign armies; in Pipīlikā, one goes abroad; and in Vimalā, there is the destruction of one's dwelling place.
A tortoise-shaped mark brings poverty, whereas marks shaped like a jewel-filled casket bring prosperity; one should likewise observe the auspicious and inauspicious lines upon the linga.
The lines on the stone are considered to correspond to the [caste] colors in their respective order;
lines resembling a rainbow, a conch, or a lotus are praised. (16)
Lines of various colors, thin, thick, or rough are censured;
however, in this *Mañjarī*: "Those resembling the *nandyāvarta*, the earth, a mountain, a horse, the *śrīvatsa*, or a tortoise [are auspicious]."
Lines resembling a conch, a svastika, an elephant, or a bull; comparable to a wheel, the moon, or the sun;

like a parasol, a garland, a banner, a linga, an archway, a deer, a palace, or a lotus; having the luster of a diamond, resembling a fish, or like a matted lock of hair—these lines bestow auspiciousness.
The seed-syllable of Agni and the seed-syllable of Pavana, as well as the neuter vowels, should be excluded here;
all other lines, which are auspicious and bestow blessings, are praised when they resemble the forms of the letters on the linga.
Those resembling a crow, hawk, wolf, camel, or monkey; those like a cat, vulture, snake, owl, jackal, or insect;
and those like a boar or a frog—abandoning all these and any other lines situated crosswise, which bring about defects.
Having taken hold of a beautiful stone, one should fashion a linga with it.
Starting from one cubit up to nine cubits, the *liṅga* should be fashioned by humans, Daityas, and gods;
however, for a human, the *liṅga* at the beginning should range from one cubit up to five cubits according to the distinction of social classes (*varṇa*).
"The liṅga of the Daitya is six or seven cubits, while the liṅga of the gods (gīrvāṇa) is nine or eight cubits.
Thus it is said.
Starting from the height of one cubit, however, by increasing the measurement by a quarter-cubit at each step.
Liṅgas beginning with the smallest (kaniṣṭha) should measure up to three cubits on the outside;
from a liṅga four cubits in length, they should be increased by one-quarter [of the length] as before.
One should fashion nine medium-sized liṅgas up to six cubits in height;
starting from seven cubits, one may proceed as before by increasing the height by a quarter-cubit at each step.
The nine excellent liṅgas should be, in sequence, up to nine cubits in height;
between those of three and four cubits, there should be three liṅgas as previously described.
In the middle, between the six and the seven hands, three liṅgas are likewise remembered;
thus, thirty-three well-known liṅgas have been described.
Furthermore, the length of the liṅga may be made according to a division of the palace's measurement by four, five, or six parts;
or else, another method is now described.
In the sanctum, however, when divided into five parts, the liṅga should be three parts in height;
or, when the sanctum is divided into nine parts, the liṅga should be five parts in length.
The height of the pedestal (garbha) is said to be one-eighth, one-sixteenth, or half of the length of the liṅga;
that is to say, the length of the liṅga. In that regard, for a liṅga of one cubit in length, the width should be four cubits. || 24 ||
The vimāna should likewise be fivefold or sixfold [in height];
however, the nāgara style should be twice as high as its width, or even threefold.
Therefore, that which is known as Bhūmija is prescribed; when the śikhara is twice [the height], it clearly becomes the Nāgara style, and the vimāna is named Valabhī. || 26 ||

In the measurement of the *liṅga*, the expansion of the elements, the Vedas, and the fires within the portion of the modification is declared in the *Nāgara* style to be victorious, nourishing, and fulfilling all desires. (27)

In the Trisaptabhāga style, the inferior [measurement] for the Drāviḍa style is one-tenth of the inner sanctum (garbha); the principal [measurement] is one-thirteenth. In the case of an eight-part inner sanctum, it is as previously described.

In the Drāviḍa style, when the length is divided into twenty-one parts, the proportions of six, five, and four parts respectively result in a temple that bestows victory, nourishment, and all desires.
In the *abhikṛtya* portion of the womb, sixteen parts constitute the best;
thirteen parts are the lowest; and between those two, [the intermediate] is by way of eight parts.
The nine liṅgas are perfected; one should fashion them in the *vesara* style. With a length divided into five parts of five [units], they are formed by portions of eight, seven, and six [units]. (31)
One should know that for the Vistāra and Vesara styles, the [deities] Jaya and others are as previously described. Now, for fixed lingas, the presiding deities are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa.
The base, the middle, and likewise the top—square, octagonal, and circular—should be understood as consisting of three parts each; their specific distinctions are now described. || 33 ||
The *sarvatobhadraka*, the *vardhamāna*, the *śivādhika*, and the *svastika*—these are the four types [of liṅgas]; their characteristics are described separately. (34)
The *sarvatobhadra* is for Brahmins, the *vardhamānaka* for kings, the *viśāmiṣṭa* is superior to Śiva [for Vaiśyas], and the *svastika* is beneficial for Śūdras. (35)
A linga prescribed for one's own caste should be installed for the attainment of desired success;
a linga prescribed for another caste causes the destruction of one's goals both in this world and the next.
Regarding this, Maya says:
"The first is the Sarvatobhadra; the second is the Vardhamānaka; the third shall be the Śivādhika;
and the fourth is the Svastika."
Now, among the gods of the earth, the *sarvatobhadra* is desired; it bestows happiness upon kings,
increases prosperity for those who are rising, grants wealth to commoners here,
and yields even more than a share of Śambhu to others— this *svastika* brings auspiciousness in this world.
Of the Śūdras.
Since it has been stated by others as well, the meaning is that even for the *anuloma*, *pratiloma*, and so forth, the *svastika* alone is intended as the characteristic mark (*liṅga*).
In the inner sanctum (*garbhāgāra*), one part out of three is the pedestal (*pīṭha*); on the pedestal, which consists of three parts, [one] part...
The width of the linga is its circumference. || 37 ||
The height of the linga should be equal to that [of the pedestal], and the length of the linga should be divided equally into three parts;
these are considered the portions for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa in the case of a linga where all dimensions are equal.
The portion of Viṣṇu should be equal to the pedestal (piṇḍikā), while the visible portion is the portion of Śiva; this is the rule for all liṅgas. (39) [p.
In this regard, the Piṅgalāmata states:
"The altar should be level, so that it may serve as a cover for the liṅga. For example:
For here, indeed, the portion for worship is indicated by the word "liṅga";
this applies when the four Vedas are on the pedestal and the liṅga is entirely equal [in size]. || 40 ||
When the four Brahma-threads are positioned across the circumference of the talliṅga, the width should be exactly equal;
otherwise, there will be the defect of shadow. || 41 ||
Therefore, the pedestal (pīṭha) should be equal in size to the liṅga and free from defects such as shadows; it may be circular or otherwise, depending on the field of the four-cornered pedestal.
On the pedestals, the circumference and the width at the end should be equal to those of the liṅga;
likewise, for slender liṅgas, the pedestal should have a greater width.

Having understood [the proportions], one should increase [the portion] in the part of Śiva so that it becomes equal; as much as it has increased in the part of Śiva, one should decrease that same amount in the part of Brahmā.
In the same way, having recognized the deficiency in large lingas due to the width of the pedestal, one should make the worshipable portion shorter by that proportion. || 45 ||
One should increase the portion in the Brahma-portion; there is indeed no increase or decrease in the Vaiṣṇava [portion]. As it is said in the Bṛhattantra:
"In emaciated [liṅgas] one should increase Rudra, and in thick liṅgas one should decrease [it]. One should decrease...
One should increase [the portion] for some; there is neither increase nor decrease for Hari.
Thus, this investigation into the defects of shadow is prescribed for a *liṅga* that is entirely symmetrical. || 46 ||
Some say that this [rule] does not apply to the *vardhamāna* and other types of lingas; likewise, it does not apply to manifest lingas, nor to those made of gems, whether manifest or unmanifest.
There is no such restrictive rule regarding the Svayambhū, the Bāṇa, or the Ārṣa [liṅgas];
this same procedure applies to all three types of liṅgas, beginning with the Vardhamāna.

But in the Mayasūtra, the extent of the pedestal is described without the aforementioned defect regarding its shadow, starting with the words "the dimensions of the linga and the āyati," and so forth. (49)
p.
370) It should be made equal to the portion of Śiva; thus it is explained in the Saṅgraha. The width of the pedestal (pīṭha) should be equal to the length of the liṅga.
Thus;
however, in the portion concerning Saṃskṛti, [the results are determined] by seven, eight, and nine [degrees] respectively when the sign is in its exaltation. (50)

In the Vardhamānaka [type of pedestal], the portions for Brahmā, Hari, and Īśāna shall be determined by parts; when the length of the liṅga is divided into sixteen parts, they are fashioned using six, seven, and eight parts respectively.

In this manner, in the *vardhamānaka* [type of temple], the portions for Brahmā and the others may be arranged sequentially by five, six, or seven parts, or by four, five, and six parts respectively. || 52 ||
The *liṅga* should increase [in size] according to the sequence of superior, middling, and inferior;
when the length of the *liṅga* is divided into twelve parts, [the measurements] are determined by the numbers three, three, and four respectively.
In a *liṅga* where Śiva is predominant, the portions for Brahmā and the others shall be in sequence according to their shares;
however, when the height of the *liṅga* is divided into nine parts (*nandāṃśa*), the [shares] are by way of six, seven, and eight parts.
The heights (nāha) of the portions belonging to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa are proclaimed in sequence;
that which occurs when [the linga] is entirely equal is called the "trairāśika" (three-part) method. || 55 ||
That liṅga, worshipped by the hosts of gods, is known by the names Svastika, Vardhamāna, or Śivādhika; its width is half of its own length. || 56 ||
That should be known as universal, bringing benefit to all social classes; it is described here just as it was stated in the Pauṣkara and the Kāraṇa [Tantras]. (57)
For example:
four shares and so forth are for Brahmins; five shares and so forth are appropriate for kings; six parts and so forth are suitable for Vaiśyas; and seven shares and so forth are for Śūdras. (58)
Thus, the *vardhamāna* [stūpa] is beneficial when divided into four types according to the sequence of colors;
then there is the *śivādhika*.
Regarding the portion for the shape, however, in the case of the *liṅgocca*, it is divided into sevenths, sevens, and eighths.
The liṅga which is desired by the Brahmins and is superior to Śiva is located in the portions beginning with Brahmā;
in the thirteenth portion, at the height of the liṅga, it is situated at the fourteenth, forty-fourth, and fifty-fifth parts.

In the case of a *liṅga* with a sixteenfold division (*ṣoḍaśāṃśa*), however, for one suitable for a Kṣatriya, the portion exceeding that of Śiva is determined by Brahmā and the others, respectively, by five, five, and six parts. (61)

The appropriate liṅga for Vaiśyas, which is superior to that of Śiva, has been described according to the portions beginning with *kā*. When the height of the liṅga is divided into ten parts, [the base] consists of three, three, and four parts respectively.
For Śūdras, a Liṅga dedicated to Śiva that is superior [in quality] is desired for the portions beginning with Brahmā;
however, in the case of a Liṅga equal to those previously mentioned, a Dhārāliṅga may optionally be used.
One should fashion it as a square or a sixteen-sided figure at its base; and in the Vaiṣṇava and Śaiva portions, the edge is doubled.
For all castes as well, the *dhārā-liṅga* is considered to be of three types:
octagonal at the base, or sixteen-sided, or four-sided; above that, the facets (*dhārā*) should be double [the number of sides]. Thus says Maya.
In the case of the Sarvatobhadra liṅga, however, there should be twenty-five streams.
Shaped like the leaves of the saptaparṇa tree, they are all equal and have equal intervals; moreover, on each individual edge, there are forty in number.
One should fashion equal lingas; that would constitute a thousand lingas. This concludes the section on the varieties of lingas.
Regarding the accomplishment of the portions for Brahmā and the others, the square (vedāśra) shape is prescribed according to the stated method. (67)
Having fashioned the liṅga in its entirety from the portion of Brahmā upwards,
[one should mark] the center from the middle of the diagonal line extending to half the corner of the square.
By abandoning the corners, one should make it octagonal for the sake of attaining the lineage of Viṣṇu; or else, one should divide the width of the liṅga equally into seven parts.
Having established three parts in the middle and excluding two parts on each side, an equal eight-sided figure (vasvaśra) is accomplished; now the circle is described.
Having placed the thread at the center of the top of the square linga,
one should rotate it to the extent of the directions for the sake of accomplishing the circle.
Now, for all types of lingas, the fashioning of the head (śirovartana) is prescribed; it should resemble a parasol, have the shape of a cucumber, or be like a hen's egg. (72)
p. 372) Furthermore, that which resembles a half-moon is known as the fifth, the *budbuda* (bubble).
Herein [are described] the *sarvatobhadra*, *vardhamāna*, and other types of *liṅga*.
Since the fault is established by the violation of those respective measurements through the drawing of the head at a size smaller than its actual proportion in the section for worship,
therefore, in the entire [icon], the head must be drawn only above the aforementioned measurements of the limbs, eyes, and lines.

The top of the *liṅga* should be fashioned like a crown (*makuṭa*) and so forth. Regarding this, Maya says: "For all these *liṅgas*, these [measures] are common; having added one-third of the portion of the head to its own height."
Therefore, the measurement of the head for the inferior, middle, and superior liṅgas is respectively six, six, and six parts added to that [total length] of the liṅga.
It is stated that all [the deities] are successively portions of the qualities (guṇa) of Indra, Aśvinī, and so forth. For example:
"From the portion of the principle of non-existence (atattva) within the span of the portion of worship, there are respectively one, two, and three portions. (73)

Having installed [the image] upon the lower, middle, or superior linga according to its measurement, one should further place it above the eyes and above the head for the sake of spiritual perfection (siddhi).
Having placed a stone above the parts already described according to the one-third and one-ninth divisions,
one should then produce a *bindu* (mark) in its center according to the scriptures.

Then, having placed the thread upon that [surface], one should perform the turning of the head according to the sequence to be described, for the sake of achieving the parasol-shape and other forms. (76)
Having projected one, two, or three *yava* portions from sixteen parts of the width of the *liṅga*,
and having suspended [the cord] below, on both sides of the *liṅga*— || 77 ||
One should rotate [the ritual] there; for indeed, four umbrellas appear. One should apply the first and the second upon the equal-marked [liṅga]. (78)
The third [type of joint] is for the Śivādhika [style], while the fourth is for the Vardhamānaka;
one must never create a confusion of these styles, since that would be inauspicious.
"There would also be mutual confusion and impurity of the modes of conduct," so said Maya.
When the width of the liṅga is divided into six parts, by drawing [the outline] with two and a half parts, the head becomes like a cucumber;
with three parts, it becomes like a hen’s egg.
The half-moon [shape] is formed by drawing a circle with a radius equal to one-third of the width of the liṅga;
[the other shape is formed] by dividing the width of the liṅga into eight parts and drawing [a circle] with a radius of three and a half parts.
The head of the *liṅga* should be fashioned beautifully, resembling a bubble;
the general procedures for all *liṅgas*, such as the application of tin and other materials, are as follows.
The specific varieties described for the umbrella-shaped [liṅgas] are fixed separately for each type of liṅga. 82½.

In this *Mañjarī* and by me as well, the method of drawing has been stated: having marked the desired portion at the head of the *liṅgas*, and having drawn a pair of fish on both sides of that, with two threads emerging from their mouths and tails; from those—
