And where there is a union for the wise one, enriched by the three points (bindus), that very thing should be performed here in many ways with its methods, as proclaimed by the Lord.
Thus [it is said].

Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, concerning the characteristics of human-made stone liṅgas, in the Kriyāpāda of the upper section of the Siddhāntasāra, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva.
Now begins the thirty-eighth chapter.
Now, the *liṅga* is said by me to be of four kinds: thick at the base, thick in the middle, thin, and likewise the *ārṣa*, which has a thick head. || 1 ||
When the circumference of the liṅga is divided into eight parts, at the base, the middle, and the tip,
it is traditionally taught that the base and so forth are thick when they are respectively greater or less by one part.
The Vedas and the Śruti recognize Brahmā and Viṣṇu as portions (aṃśa) [of Śiva] within the archaic Liṅgas;
however, Śiva’s own portion must indeed be circular, or else there is no turning of the head.
Then there were self-manifested liṅgas that were dilapidated and emaciated,
some short and others exceedingly long, resembling wooden planks.
They have many points, resembling the ears of a cow or a citron;
they possess six, five, or three points, and are devoid of measurement by weight, dimension, and so forth.
Even the tips of their peaks were curved and of various colors and shapes; they were both with bases and without bases, and both with enclosures and without dwellings. (6)

Even those [images] located in forests, mountains, rivers, oceans, sacred fords (tīrtha), and holy fields (kṣetra) attain unsurpassed perfection through seeing, touching, and worshipping them. || 7 ||
One should know those to be self-manifested lingas (svayambhuliṅga) in which Śiva is eternally established; one must not purify their base, for such purification brings about total destruction.

They say that these [deities] are not to be questioned, but are indeed to be worshipped according to established custom; there is no distinction of form among them, nor should there be any confusion of mantras.

Among human [lingas], there is a commingling of the mantra-form, the image-form, and so forth. Regarding this, Maya says: "The installation linga should also be equal in its portion of the pedestal to its portion of the worship; it is circular."
Or else, for the sake of liberation, one should worship the portion of the offering together with the support.
Thus, one should cause every Bāṇaliṅga to be installed exactly as it was found. || 10 ||

Or else, one should install [the image] upon an auspicious pedestal made of stone or brick, possessing the proper characteristics, at half the height of its own elevation, or at one-third, one-fifth, or one-fourth of that height.
Regarding this, in the Yogaśiva:
"Three crores are situated on Liṅgādri, three on Śrīparvata,
three in Kālikāgarta, and three also in Amareśvara."
At Kanyātīrtha, Mahendra, and other sites, as well as at Kanyakāśrama in Nepal—there stands ten million [deities] at each of these; thus, there are sixteen crores in total.
Whether with a pedestal or without a pedestal, situated upon the pedestal of any temple,
and free from all defects, that [image] bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon all.
Having installed that bāṇaliṅga according to the prescribed rite, one should worship it; and one may also worship other liṅgas originating from rivers, oceans, or mountains.

Indeed, uncarved [images] are distinguished and worthy of worship, just like arrows; however, if there should be a wound upon the head of the *liṅga*, it brings destruction to both the king and the maker.
A crack in the wife, and in the conch-shell [the crack] kills the son; in the mouth, it kills the artisan. In the middle, there is suffering and famine; in the hollow, the destruction of rain.
One that is excessively long, excessively short, thin, or thick brings about the end of the king.
Now, the extraction of the defining characteristics is stated:
a liṅga whose work is complete [is one fashioned] with whetstones, sand, and so forth.
And one should rub it evenly with cords made of cowhair until it is smooth and free of blemishes.
It should be smooth like the interior of a mirror, with a visible reflection, and perfectly round;
then, [it should be filled] with pure water, cow's milk, coconut water, and sugarcane juice. || 13 ||
Having washed them with the waters of sacred fords, one should observe the aforementioned signs; even if there should be particles of dust the size of mustard seeds, they appear as drops of gold.
Whether on the liṅga or on the pedestal, these [defects] bring benefit to all castes; yet even a liṅga or pedestal possessing only slight defects should be abandoned. (15)

Having prepared another [image] free from defects, one should perform the extraction of the *lakṣaṇas* on a day endowed with auspicious qualities such as the lunar date, asterism, *karaṇa*, and *muhūrta*.
Having constructed a sacrificial pavilion (vedāśrama-maṇḍapa) to the east or north of the root [shrine], provided with a canopy, four doors, and adorned with lamps and other ornaments. || 17 ||
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in the middle of that [space] with white rice grains,
one should cause the liṅga to lie upon it, which has been covered with a pair of white cloths.
Both the preceptor and the architect, having bathed well and being fully adorned, should bow to and worship that linga with its head facing east.

Having meditated upon Śiva, the subtle, within that [heart], one should propitiate him with this: "Whatever has been poorly performed by me, whether through ignorance or through knowledge, toward you... (20)
"O Śaṅkara, O Soul of All! You ought to forgive all of that here. Having thus obtained permission from the Lord of Gods, one should extract the characteristic mark from the liṅga. || 21 ||
There, the preceptor, first recollecting the mantra of the eye, should draw the Brahma-line in the center and the two side-lines with the Śiva-weapon mantra.
Then, with a golden instrument and a light hand, the master builder should clearly apply the measuring lines using a light tool. (23)
Having scraped [the ground] with honey, clarified butter, and milk, and having covered it with a new cloth,
one should present a cow with its calf, gold, and a maiden to a twice-born man.
One should display a heap of grain and worship it with perfumes and other offerings.
Regarding this, Maya states: "In the first case, when the Nāgara-liṅga has been divided into sixteen parts, [this applies] to the length of Śiva."
Having abandoned the six elemental Vedic portions above, [one observes] the rising of the minor [signs] and so forth.
Having thus understood the height to be three units,
one should then hang two threads from the third part on both sides, facing toward the shoulders of Viṣṇu.
The sum of those two is behind [the sun] when subtracted by four, three, two, and one; it is in front when subtracted by five, eight, three, and four.
The sum of those two is behind [the sun] when subtracted by five, eight, three, and four.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, when the conjunction has arisen in the six, the elements (5), the forest (3), fire (3),
and the noose (2), one should place one part at the neck and three and two parts for the diameter of the cord respectively upon those [sections].
Up to the lower portion, one should lead the line evenly according to the prescribed height;
thus has the correct method for the Nāgara-liṅga been described by me.
Thus:
the width of the Brahma-sūtra is one-quarter, one-third, or one-half [of the total]. || 25 ||

The placement of the Brahma-sūtra (the central axis) should extend as far as the Viṣṇu-mark; half of that [distance] should be the line of the side-sūtra, which should consist of one middle barley-corn.
Likewise, in the Drāviḍa system, the exaltations (ucca) are in the third, fifth, and ninth degrees respectively;
here, the exaltations beginning with the "deficient" (hīna) and so forth are declared to be at the ninth, tenth, and eleven degrees respectively.

One should suspend [the strings] from the divisions of seven, eight, and nine respectively; in the case of the low [tone], at four, three, and two [divisions], and in the middle, at five, two, and three [divisions].

Furthermore, in the two highest types of Liṅgas, when the number of rasas (six) is multiplied by the number of śrutis (four), the resulting conjunction (twenty-four) constitutes the Drāviḍa type; in this, the expansion of the thread (sūtravyāsa) is equal to half of its own parts.
Half of that is the width and depth of the wing-line, as before.
Now, another method for the Drāviḍa style is stated:
The length of the thread for Śivāyāmā is one-tenth of the sixteenfold part. || 30 ||
The upper portion shall consist of four parts, while the lower portion shall consist of two parts;
beginning from the shape of a bud, the two side-lines [should be drawn] in sequence.
Having set aside two parts at the back, the junction of the two lines is prescribed; or else, in the sixteenth part, one part is below and four parts are above.
Having subtracted the sūtra from the Rudrāṃśas, the elevation is traditionally held to be as previously stated;
thus is the extraction of the characteristics of the Drāviḍa-liṅga remembered.
Now, for the Vesaraliṅga, when the height of Śiva is divided into fifteen parts, the length of the stalk (nāla) shall be one-tenth; from eight parts onwards, it proceeds in sequence.
One should determine the span of the two threads using the parts derived from the elements, the Vedas, and the qualities;
the sum of those two, increased by a sixteenth part, shall be the excellent Viṣkambha. || 35 ||
In the middle portion, when the sun is at its highest point (ucca), the stalk is raised by four parts;
above it are three parts, and below it, starting from the third part, are [the remaining] parts.

In the Sūtra, however, one should hang [the cord] at the third and second parts; their junction occurs there. When the portion taken is divided into three, the diameter is formed by two of those parts. (37)
Thus has the medium [type] been described for the liṅga known as vesara;
now, for the smallest vesara, when the height of Śiva is divided into twelve parts.
The lower portion shall be one part, while the upper portion shall extend for nine parts along the length of the thread;
the junction should be understood as before, when the width is indeed divided into sixteen parts. (39)
The width of the central thread (sūtra) shall be one part, and half of that for the two side threads (pakṣasūtra);
thus is the extraction of the characteristics of the smallest Vesaraprasāda remembered.
In this regard, Maya states:

"In the portion taken for the base, a line should be drawn at one-ninthth part [of the height], with a width and depth equal to one part; it is declared by Kapi and Karkka to be suitable for all types of *liṅgas*."
Taking eight barley grains, one of firm intellect should divide them equally into nine parts;
with one part, the height of a single-faced liṅga should be fashioned.
In the case of a *liṅga* up to nine cubits in length,
that line is correctly described as being eight barley-corns deep, with the depth increasing by one part for each successive cubit.
A line raised by even half a barley-corn results in an increase as before;
however, in the case of an excellent liṅga, the depression should be four and a half barley-corns.
The width of each of the two wings shall be one and a half times the width of the central hall;
for all the lines, both the width and the inclination shall be equal.

Thus, the general characteristic of the thread for the Nāgara and other styles is stated: however, in the Śiva-āyāma, one should discard four parts from above within the portion of the *dhṛti*. || 41 ||
The stalk should consist of eleven parts, while the bud is one part;
the lower portion is two parts, and likewise, the junction at the back should be joined with two parts.
Alternatively, when the height is one-sixteenth [of the total], as before, there shall be a stalk slightly exceeding [the base] at the top and bottom;
its width at the sides shall be one-eighth [of the total].
In the fifth, sixth, or seventh part, as before, there will be a conjunction at the back;
it is uninterrupted, very smooth, without jarring noise, and free from agitation.
One should perform the extraction of the characteristics and avoid the opposite;
having first struck [the ground] with a thread and with ash, one should then form the bud-shape.
Having marked the side with the tip of the *ghaṭikā*, one should then draw a line with the cord.
Now, the characteristic of the tip of the cord is stated:
on a *liṅga* that resembles an umbrella at its head, the tip of the cord should be like the eye of an elephant. (46)

When the tip of the thread on the top of the crescent-moon-shaped *liṅga* resembles a bubble, and when the tip of the thread at the front of the *liṅga*—which is shaped like a cucumber—is like a chicken's egg; || 47 ||
At the top of the liṅga, which resembles a hen’s egg, the tip of the thread is shaped like an umbrella; now, the tip of the thread for liṅgas in general is described.
It may resemble the bud of a plantain tree, or have the shape of a lotus bud; it may be like a leaf of the holy fig tree, or generally shaped like a barley grain. (49)
(379) Having divided the portion for the linga-nāha in an *atyaṣṭi* [meter] into three parts,
two parts of the middle thread-line and half of that for the two side-thread-lines; || 50 ||
The Chapter on the Extraction of the Characteristics:
Having taken the measurement of the height, it should be divided by the *mānāṅgula*;
in the case of an increase, one should again omit the division by the finger-breadth (*aṅguli*) and [adjust] the finger-breadth once more.

Having increased [the amount] by means of the Vasus (eight), one should take away [the remainder] according to the number of the lunar mansions; the asterisms beginning with Aśvinī are to be [assigned] here in their proper sequence. 52.
In that [number] increased by four, portions are subtracted by Nanda; these [portions] are the thief and so forth: the thief, food, power, wealth, the king, and the neuter. (53)
Misfortune, poison, prosperity, and also Aṃśaka—these nine are the divisions in sequence.
Taskara, vipat, ṣaṇḍha, and vipat are censurable; the others are auspicious. (54)
In the case of the *liṅga* (ascendant), divide the group of eight, nine, and three by twelve; the remainder shall be the wealth, the debt, and the *yoni*, respectively. (55)
To increase wealth and eliminate debt, one should perform acts that bring benefit to the master;
the banners, lions, bulls, and elephants are auspicious, while others are indeed inauspicious. (56)
When nine times Śivatuṅga is divided by seven, the days beginning with Sunday result; among these, the auspicious planets are beneficial, while the malefic ones are inauspicious. (57)
Likewise, for villages and the like, that which is not in conflict with the asterism of the founder, as well as for kings and countries—that has been declared to be the ground of prosperity. (58)

The signs of the sages (ṛṣis), including those of the self-born (Svayambhū), have been proclaimed according to their respective characteristics; and here, the method for extracting the characteristics of the humans mentioned previously has also been sung.

Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, on the characteristics of the *ārṣa* and other types of *liṅgas*, in the section on ritual practice (*kriyāpāda*) of the latter part of the *Siddhāntasāra*, which is the *Paddhati* of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva.
Now begins the thirty-ninth chapter.

Now the pedestals (pīṭhas) shall be described according to their various individual characteristics; for it is through union with these that the wise know the installation (pratiṣṭhā) of the liṅgas to be accomplished.

The pedestal and the *liṅga* must be of one and the same species, and not otherwise; even in the case of a wooden *liṅga* in the Śaiva tradition, if its own species cannot be obtained [for the pedestal], [it may be made of another]. (2)
The pedestal (pīṭha) may consist of bricks bound with lime and possess the proper characteristics;
the foundation stone (pādaśilā) may be made of neuter stone, while the pedestal-base (piṇḍikā) should be of female stone. || 3 ||
"One should fashion the *liṅga* with a male stone (*puṃśilā*); such is the firm conclusion of the scripture.
It should be twice the portion of the base for worship; it is inferior if less than that, and excellent when equal to the height of the *liṅga*."
These nine are the dimensions of the pedestal (pīṭha); between those two [the base and the capital], it should be divided into eight parts.
Its height should be half its width; the low type is one part, while the excellent type is two or three parts.
Alternatively, its circumference may be three times its width, or its breadth may be equal to the [width of the] *nāha*. From the diameter of the inner sanctum (*garbha*)...
Or one-third, or even a fourth part.
One should construct the pedestal (pīṭha) with a width that is either twice or three times its breadth, and it must in every respect have a height equal to one part of Viṣṇu.
For the purpose of ornamentation, one-eighth more than its own width [should be added] from that;
for all pedestals, the root-width extends to the end of the *janman*.
The width of the front of the pedestal (pīṭha) should extend as far as the great fillet (mahāpaṭṭikā). This is the general rule for the pedestal.
Now, the characteristics of the pedestal for the three types beginning with Nāgara are described. || 9 ||
In this [system], the excellent pedestal (pīṭha) should have a width equal to the length of the three-sectioned liṅga;
it may be lower by two parts, or in the space between those two, it may consist of eight parts.
The breadth of the pedestal (pīṭha) should be nine [parts];
when that breadth is divided into three parts, the excellent pedestal is two parts in height, while the inferior one is half the breadth in height.

Between those two, at the eighth part, there are indeed nine [parts] for the height of the pedestal (pīṭha). In the Drāviḍa style as well, the best [pedestal] here has a diameter equal to three parts.
When the length of the liṅga is divided into nine parts, the width at its base is seven parts;
the width of the pedestal (pīṭha) between those two is traditionally recorded as eight parts.
In the eightfold division, one should discard three, two, and one part respectively for the portions of Brahmā and Viṣṇu;
the height of the remaining parts, starting from the nadir, is considered the height of the pedestal (pīṭha) in the Drāviḍa tradition.

381) Now, for the *vesaraliṅga*, the circumference is divided into sixteen parts; the primary [circumference] is equal to that [height], while the width is likewise [divided] by parts according to the *jagatī* [meter], with the lowest [type] being similar.
That [pedestal] should be as high as Viṣṇu’s portion, or perhaps increased by a fourth part;
this remains for all liṅgas from the height of the pedestal.

The base of the *liṅga* that belongs to the Brahma-measure should extend down to the pedestal-stone (*pādaśilā*). This is determined by dividing the width of the base of the pedestal (*pīṭhamūla*) into eight, nine, or ten parts. (17)
The width of the pedestal (pīṭha) is [divided into] low, middle, and high;
this refers to the pedestals for the three [deities], beginning with Nāga.
Now, the shapes of the pedestals are described:
They are of three types: square, eight-cornered, and circular. || 18 ||
Their pedestals (pīṭhas) should be, in order: the first is Merusundara, the second should be Vardhamāna, and then Lakṣmīsundara as well. (19)
Then there is the seat named Viṣṇusammilana, followed by the one called Padmabhadra;
next is the seat named Samāṅgabhadraka, and after that, Rudrakānta.
Somakānta, the one called Sarvāṅgabhadra, Śrīkara, the one named Puṣṭivardhana, and thereafter Sarvasaumya. (21)
Thus, the characteristic of the twelve types of seats (pīṭhas) is described: the seat of the partless liṅgas (niṣkalaliṅgas) should be known as equal on all sides.

The length [of the image] should be equal to its measurement; or, in the case of a complete [image], it may be a half-moon shape. When the height of the pedestal is divided into fourteen parts, the base-plinth (mūlapaṭṭikā) shall consist of one part.

The lotus [pedestal] consists of three parts; from half a part comes the lotus [base], and then another half-lotus. Then there is a circle of two parts, followed again by a half-lotus and a half-kampa.
The neck should be two and a half parts; the upper lotus is prescribed as half [of that];
the *kampa* is half [of the lotus]; and the upper fillet (*ūrdhapaṭṭikā*) should be two parts, in that same sequence.

With half [of the height] being the support for the trembling [pedestal], it should thus be as beautiful as Mount Meru; when the height of the pedestal is divided into eighteen parts, two parts are here declared to be the birth-[portion].
One should construct the *jagatī* with four [parts], and the *kumuda* with three on one side; likewise, the *kampa* and the *kaṇṭha* with three, and the *paṭṭikā* with one.
In the *vardhamānaka* type, the base (*vājana*) is three parts and one part; in the *saṅkṛti* type, it occurs at one part, while the height of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) is one and a half parts. || 28 ||

One should cause the lotus to be made with one part, the half-kampa with half a part, the embankment (vapra) with five parts, the petal with one part from the dhṛti-portion, and the pericarp with one part.
The square [pedestal] is made with four parts; the lotus with half [a part]; the *kampaka* with three [parts];
likewise, the neck with one part, and then the *vājana* with one share.
The *nidrā* (sleep) band should be two parts, and the lotus and the vessel of clarified butter (*ājyabhṛt*) should each be half of that;
thus, the pedestal known as Lakṣmīsundara is perfected.

In the sixteen-fold division of the height of the pedestal (pīṭha), the Jagatī, the lotus (abja), the reed-band (vetra-paṭṭikā), and the lotus-band (paṅkaja-paṭṭikā) are formed by two, one, two, three, and two parts respectively. (32)
Likewise, one should fashion the *ājyadhāriṇī* (the butter-holder) in sequence during the closing of Viṣṇu;
when the pedestal is eighteen parts high, its plinth (*khura*) should be one and a half parts.
The base (jagatī) is three and a half [parts]; the lotus (abja) is one and a half; the support (dhṛk) is half; the fillet (paṭṭa) is half;
the secondary fillet (upapaṭṭa) is half; and the neck (kaṇṭha) above that is three parts.
The secondary band (upapaṭṭa) should be half [the width of the main band], and the upper band (paṭṭa) should be half of that;
the molding (vājana) is prescribed as two parts, and the half-part should be the band containing the flame-ornament (paṭṭājyabhṛt). || 35 ||
This very beautiful pedestal (pīṭha) is to be known as Padmabhadra;
it is prescribed that its height should be one part of the support (dhṛti), while half of the water-measure (vāri) is for the base.
With one half [of the height] there is the *kampa*; with two and a half parts, the *vājana* should be formed.
The *paṭṭa* and *upapaṭṭa* are each half [a part]; the *kaṇṭha* consists of two parts, and the *paṭṭa* is half [a part].
The *upapaṭṭa* is half [a part], and the *kumbha* should be eight-sided with four parts.
The jagatī should likewise consist of five parts, and the khura (hoof) should be one and a half parts. || 38 ||
This beautiful pedestal (pīṭha), known as Samāṅgabhadraka, is thus formed;
when the height of the pedestal is divided into eight parts, the plinth (khura) occupies one part and the base (vapraka) one part.
(383) With four [units] comes a petal; half of that is a tremor (kampa), and a quarter is the support (dhṛk).
A tremor is half, and half of that is the lotus; the circle is made from two halves, and the petal from half [of that].
The neck is one-and-a-half parts; the fillet (kaṃpa) is half a part, and the lotus is half a part.
The molding (vājana) is two parts, the lotus is half a part, and the projection (kṣepaṇa) is half a part. || 41 ||
This indeed is the most beautiful sacred seat (pīṭha) called Rudrakānta, which has been described.
At the height of the Dhṛti-portion of the seat, there is one part [of the plinth] resting on the ground and two portions [above it].
The embankment (vapra), the great lotus (mahābja), and the half-Dhṛti are each four parts, while the cane-work (vetra) is one part; the remaining half is [the base].
The neck and half of the lotus should be circular, and from the middle of that half, it should become elongated.
One should make the upper petal with half [of the height]; the bamboo [shaft] and the support [pedestal] are each half [a share];
the bamboo is one share, and the upper lotus should be made with three and a half shares.
The *dhṛtabhṛt* is said to be one and a half [units] high, and it is declared to be pleasing to Soma;
this is the same for all three types beginning with the *nāgara*.
However, when the height of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) is divided into sixteen parts, the base molding (*mūlapaṭṭikā*) consists of two parts. (45)
The great lotus is made with four parts, the neck with half a part,
the circular lotus with half a part, and the stalk with half a part.
The *dhṛk* (support) is half [the height] with an upper lotus, and then a fillet (*paṭṭikā*) with two parts;
that which is supported by the *dhṛta* is called "Auspicious in All Limbs" (*sarvāṅgabhadraka*). || 47 ||
This is common to all types of lingas.

On the pedestal (pīṭha), which is divided into sixteen parts, [the measurements] are two, five, three and a half, one and a half, four, two, and one; [therein] the base (jagatī) holds a lotus and a staff, and [the deity] holds a lotus.
In the Śrīkara [mandala], there should be a band and a butter-holder (ājyabhṛt) respectively; on one [side] alone, from half a part and a half, there is a projection by means of half a jagatī.

Below the band, starting from its own shoulder-measure, the *sakampā* (the shaking part) is [one part] in the *puṣṭivardhana* type; at the front of the pedestal, in the sixteen-part division, the *khura* (the hoof-base) is two parts, or alternatively half of that.
The projection (kṣepaṇa) should be four and a half parts; the lotus is half [of that], and the filaments (kampakam) are half of that again.
The vajra should be one part, and the upper lotus should be four parts.
Half [of the height] is for the projection (kṣepaṇa), two parts for the frieze (paṭṭikā), and half of that for the butter-holder (ājyabhṛt);
this is declared to be the gentle (saumya) pedestal, common to the Nāgara and other styles. (52)
There are twelve pedestals (pīṭhas).

Regarding all these pedestals, Parāśara states that one should employ three-quarters, a half, or a portion equal to the abundance of the entry and exit of the limbs, according to the requirements of beauty and strength.
The width of the base of the stalk (nāla) is one-third of the width of the pedestal (pīṭha);
its length is equal to that, from which one-third or one-fourth is subtracted.
One should fashion the tip of the stalk with its width at the apex, its top elevated and free from defects;
the excavation should be one-third of the width of the stalk, equal in depth to its width. (54)

Others, however, place the pedestal (pīṭha) in the north; one should arrange the stalk (nāla) in this manner. It should be largely composed of an upper panel (ūrdhvapaṭṭa), being either equal to or one-quarter greater [in height] than the base.

The width of the *vājībhṛt* (the neck) is one and a half [units], and the excavation at its base is equal to that; rising from the base up to the neck, it should be elevated in that same sequence. || 56 ||
The pedestal-stone (pīṭhopala) may have either one upper ornament (ūrdhvamaṇḍana) or one lower ornament (adhomaṇḍana) on a single side; it cannot have both, according to the established rule.
There, one should join the corners beautifully without [leaving] a gap in the middle;
from the top down to the end of the limbs, one should perform the upward continuation.
Maya declared that there are fourteen types of pedestals (pīṭhas): those with four, six, eight, and twelve sides, as well as the sixteen-sided and the circular.
From these, by means of six long [units] and three triangles, one forms a shape resembling a half-moon;
this constitutes fourteen [units]. Furthermore, Maya says:
"The auspicious throne (bhadrapīṭha), the lotus, the vajra-throne, the great lotus, and the glorious hand (śrīkara)."
The lotus-seat and the great vajra are gentle.
And Śrīkāmya—thus indeed the sacred seats (pīṭhas) arise in nine ways.
For example:
on the height of the pedestal (pīṭha), which is divided into eight parts, the birth [section] consists of two parts and the yoke [section] consists of four parts.
The embankment (vapra) and the lotus (padma) are each one and a half [parts]; the neck (dhṛk) is half [a part], and the pitcher (ghaṭa) is two parts;
the spout (kṣepaṇa) is half, the throat (kaṇṭha) is one and a half, and the spout again is half.
On the auspicious pedestal (*bhadrapīṭhaka*), the cloth should consist of two parts, with half of it filled with ghee;
this is common to all *liṅgas*.
The height of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) is two and eight parts; the fillet (*paṭṭa*) is made of ten, five, two, twelve, and sixteen [parts] respectively;
and the lotus is circular with beautiful petals and a fillet. Thus, supported by its base, it is the lotus-pedestal (*padmapīṭha*).
On the elevated part of the pedestal, which measures one-fourth of the mantra-portion, there should be a cavity extending halfway down from the base.
The lotus should be two and a half parts; with two halves, there should be the fillet (paṭṭa) and the recess (nimna);
one part is the thunderbolt (vajra), half is the recess, half is the filigree (kampa), and with three parts is the lotus.
The lower half [of the base] should be one and a half times that [measurement], and the portion for the ghee-holder (ājyabhṛt) should be half of a padikā;
the pedestal called Vajrapadma should be equal in size to all other liṅgas.
On the high plinth (pīṭha), which constitutes the portion for stability (dhṛti), there should be one and a half units for the base (janman) and then the lotus (paṅkaja).
The fillet (paṭṭa) should consist of four units, while the recessed part (nimna) should be half [of that], measuring one and a half units.
The lotus should be circular with a diameter of two and a half [units]; at half of that [radius], the lotus is recessed.
Above it, the upper lotus is three [units] wide; the band is half [a unit], and the lotus is one and a half [units].
The other half, filled with the resin of *śrīpaṭṭa*, shall be called Mahāpadma.
This [proportion] is the same for both human and ṛṣi-liṅgas.
When the height of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) is divided into sixteen parts, [the measurement] is by the number of moon, fire, and Vedas (14).
The birth-mound (janmavapra) is one part, the lotus (padma) is two parts, and the half-circle (ardhavṛtta) is two parts;
the half-lotus (ardhapadma) is three parts, and the fillet (paṭṭikā) is one and a half parts.
The pit should be dug with its width equal to half the height; the stalk (nālaka) should be one-third of that.
Both its width and its projection should be one-third, and its top should be known as "glory-bestowing" (śrīkara).

In the *paṅkti* division, the height of the *ucca* (pedestal) is one and a half units; in the *dvyardhaka* division, there should be three and a half units for the *khura* (base), a *padma* (lotus) in the recessed part, and a *paṭṭa* (fillet) in the recessed part of the *paṭṭa*; and in the *abjapīṭha* (lotus-base), there is a lotus in the recessed part and a *paṭṭa* in the recessed part of the *paṭṭa*.

In the third and fifth parts, however, at the height of the pedestal (pīṭhocca), [the proportions] are by one and a half, two, one and a half, and one; and by a half, a half, a half, one and a half, and one and a quarter parts; and by one and a half and a half. || 72 ||
The lotus, the downward-facing lotus, and the cloth-band; then the thunderbolt with the hand-gesture (dhṛk-vajra);
then the sling, the lotus, and the cloth-band; and finally the downward-facing [lotus]—these are in their respective order. (73)
The pedestal (pīṭha) is indeed a great vajra; it is gentle with its circular vajra.
Regarding the height of the pedestal, from one-twelfth part [of the total height], one should take half a portion of two lunar units (two and a half parts). || 74 ||

The Janmapadma and Nimnaka [measures] are formed by [the addition of] one and a half, three-quarters, two and a half, one and a quarter, one-eighth, one-sixteenth, and likewise by one-half and one-quarter. (75)
The lotus, the holder, the petal, the circle, the lotus, the holder, the water-lily, and then the band with its recessed border—these should occur in sequence for the Śrīkāmya [temple]. (76)
Even those presiding seats (adhiṣṭhānaka) which have been taught for this abode (dhāman) should also be adorned here according to reason.
Thus says Maya: One should determine the entry and exit of the seats (pīṭhas) and their constituent parts according to strength, according to beauty, and according to propriety. || 77 ||
The projection of the conduit (praṇāla) should be one-third of the width of the pedestal, or else one-fourth;
its base width shall be equal to that [projection].
The width at the tip of the water-spout should be half or one-third of its [total] base;
it should be shaped like an elephant's trunk or resemble the mouth of a cow. (79)

For liṅgas facing the desired direction, the water-channel should be wide at the base and narrow at the top, with a width equal to one-third [of the liṅga], and its depression should correspond to the depth of the pit; it should be situated in the middle of the pedestal (pīṭha).
One should place that on the left side, either with a common base or as one pleases; one should determine the width of the front panel to be equal to its height.
The excavation at the base of that cloth should be equal [in depth] to one-quarter, or half, or even three-quarters of its strength. 82.
One should fashion that [pedestal] with a gradual elevation due to its connection with the liṅga;
however, on the pedestal called Ardhacandra, the jyāmukha should face the door.
One should not construct a corner facing the door on a triangular pedestal; the piercing of the pedestal's angles by the door-line is not recommended. (84)
The portion belonging to Śiva should not hang down even slightly from the base; even a slight protrusion leads to defects, therefore one should avoid that.
The pedestal should be without a joint and highly praised when made from a single stone;
even if that is unavailable, one should fashion the upper ornamentation with just a single stone.
(387) A joint at the uppermost part of the pedestals, at the end of a structural member, in the middle of a shaft, or likewise in the center of a corner is not recommended. || 86 ||
One should join [the breath] on the right and left sides, long and short in due order;
one should skillfully make it descend below, either in three segments or not in a single segment.
The Brahma-śilā is recorded as excellent when its length and breadth are equal to those of the Liṅga;
it is inferior when they are double the portion used for worship; and that which is between these two proportions is considered eightfold.
As before, there are nine types of auspicious Brahma-stones (brahmaśilā) in sequence;
the primary ones are raised to half their own width, while the lower ones have a thickness of one-fourth [of that].
Between those two, when divided into eight parts, the Brahma-śilā should be nine [parts] from the thickness; alternatively, it should be twice the thickness of the liṅga's diameter.
The Brahmaśīlā should be somewhat lower than one and a half times its width;
the excavation in the middle of the Brahmaśīlā should be equal to one Brahmabhāga.
The portion for Brahmā should enter [the center] so that it becomes seamless;
it should be joined with the placement of jewels and connected to the base of the liṅga. 92.
One should then place four stones, shaped like the *nandyāvarta* diagram, in sequence between the pedestal (*pīṭha*) and the self of Brahmā (*brahmātman*), proceeding in a clockwise direction.
According to the division of standing and sitting postures, for each successive image,
[the duration] is one, two, three, four, five, or six mātrās, or even more than that.
The length of the seats should be one-eighth more than their own width; their height should be up to double [the width], like the decoration on the pedestals.

The height of the seat (viṣṭara) is prescribed as being equal to four, three, and two parts of the Rāma-veda (twenty-four), respectively, for the bed, the seat, and the standing posture, while its length is equal to the enemy (six).
The length and breadth of the bed for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and likewise for Gaurī and the others, are prescribed according to what is appropriate. 97.
The lion-throne situated within the cave-like foot, complete with its pedestal, is prescribed for divine, rishi-made, and self-manifested (svayambhu) lingas, as well as for those made of arrows. 98.
p. 388) A wise man should have a pedestal (pīṭha) constructed in the form of a palace or as he desires.
Now, the characteristics of the foundation stone (pādaśilā) for the three types [of temples], beginning with the Nāgara, are described:
It should be twice as wide as the width of the liṅga and extend one-quarter of the width of the altar (vedī).
In the Nāgara style, the height of the liṅga should be three-quarters of its width;
for the best elongated type, it should be one-fourth of the width of the inner ear (garbhakarṇa).

The lowest [measurement] shall be reduced by half of the half of the diameter; between those two, there are eight ways, but when divided ninefold, these are the Brahma-stones in the Drāviḍa Śiva temple.

In the style called Drāviḍa, the half-diameter of that [base] diminished by three-quarters, divided into eight parts between those two, shall be the height of the Brahma-stone, which is further divided into nine parts.

Then, [the platform] shall be half the size of the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha), with a width of three or four parts; its height shall be one-fourth of its width, and it should be divided into eight parts in the middle, as previously described.

Nine Brahma-stones are prescribed; the pit [for the pedestal] is said to be two yavas wider than the portion of the Liṅga that constitutes the Brahma-part, and its depth is remembered as one-eighth of its width.
At its base, it should resemble a hollow pit, rich with jewels, and it should extend throughout the surrounding area.

Thus, this ritual for the sacred seat (pīṭha), which is of many kinds according to its characteristics, has been described here as a source of delight for those who know the eightfold [arts] through its ornaments. (105)

Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, concerning the characteristics of the ritual for the sacred seats (*pīṭha-vidhi-lakṣaṇa-paṭala*), in the *Kriyāpāda* of the *Uparibhāga* of the *Siddhāntasāra*, the *Śrīmadīśānaśivagurudevapaddhati*.
Now begins the fortieth chapter.
Now, regarding the unmanifest mark (avyaktaliṅga) which consists of ten parts and represents a portion of Śiva:
the shoulders, the neck, and likewise the face shall consist of two, two, and three parts respectively. || 1 ||
The *uṣṇīṣa* (crown protuberance) is one part, while the *makuṭa* (crown) is two parts above that;
the width of the face is one part, and its height is like that of the *liṅga*.
The forehead, ears, eyebrows, eyes, nose, scent, mouth, and so forth—all these are traditionally held to be complete in their dimensions of measure, weight, and size. (3)
(389) Like those of the Ṛṣis, the portions of Brahmā and Viṣṇu are mixed with the four Vedas;
now, however, the characteristics of the faces beginning with that of Puruṣa are described.
Resembling saffron in hue, with wide eyes and three eyes, wearing crocodile-shaped earrings,
with his mass of matted hair marked by the moon— this is the face of Tatpuruṣa in the east.
Resembling crushed collyrium, with three eyes like a lion's, and a nose like a lion's;
formidable with fangs, biting his lips, and radiant as he licks his tongue.
With a tawny beard and a mass of matted locks, adorned with a garland of serpents entwined around his head,
and having eyebrows like a swan and a crescent moon, Aghora should be placed on the right.
Lovely as the red bandhujīva flower, adorned with the graceful charms of women, possessing a pair of elegant eyebrows, a beautiful tilaka mark, and jeweled earrings; (8)
One should fashion the beautiful northern face, known as Vāmadeva, adorned with a crown bound by braided hair and embellished with dark locks.
In the west, one should meditate upon Sadyojāta, white as the full moon or the kunda flower, serene, adorned with jeweled earrings,
and with a mass of matted hair marked by the crescent moon.
In a temple of Śiva with a single entrance, there may be either one face or three faces;
if it has three faces, they should be oriented toward the door and the two sides.
One should not make a two-faced liṅga; that is prescribed for rites of sorcery (abhicāra). However, in a four-gated temple, one should make a four-faced liṅga.
A king should install a five-faced or two-faced *liṅga* on a mountain within his kingdom for the destruction of enemies and for victory. (13)
On this point, Parāśara says:
"Now, one should place a four-faced [image] in a single location within villages and the like; a two-faced [image] on a mountain, in a forest, or even near a foreign kingdom."
One should establish it; it effects the destruction of poverty and provides self-protection.
Thus, it is stated in the *Yogaśivapaddhati* as well: (p. 390) — [text follows] —.

The faces and lingas are, respectively, five, three, two, one, and one; for prosperity, [one should use] those with four, three, and one faces, while for malevolent rites, a five-faced [linga] is used.
For the destruction of moving [enemies], he should be installed with two faces in places such as mountains and forests— white, lying on his back,
three-eyed, and adorned with a crown and earrings.
The Īśāna [face] should be at the top of the liṅga, and it should indeed face upwards.
Thus:
one should fashion a pedestal and so forth that are uniform for the unmanifest linga itself;
a linga made of clay, wood, or stone always bestows all accomplishments.
Having placed gold, gems, and other materials within an earthen [liṅga], one should have it fashioned; for all face-liṅgas, the protrusion [of the face] should be made separately for each.
The neck should be fashioned so that it enters above the Viṣṇu-portion;
one should fashion the face-liṅga extending from the first hand to the end of the five hands.
Henceforth, one should not fashion a mixed-liṅga with the desire for auspiciousness. This concludes the procedure for the face-liṅga (mukhaliṅga).
Now, the crystal liṅga is described:
Starting from one finger-breadth and increasing by one finger-breadth in succession, || 17 ||
In this context, a set of six crystal liṅgas measuring up to six finger-breadths is considered inferior;
those starting from seven finger-breadths up to twelve finger-breadths are middling. (18)
This refers to the six types of lingas.
Lingas measuring from thirteen finger-breadths up to eighteen finger-breadths are considered the best; among these, the measurement is indeed according to the *mātrā-aṅgula*.
Regarding this, Maya says:
"By increasing eleven units by half a unit at each stage— namely, for the superior,
middling, and inferior lingas— the total height is thirty-three [units]."
The crystal [pedestal] is considered to be firm, measuring half, one-third, or one-fourth of the pūjāṃśa;
its width is equal to, three-quarters, or half of the height of the pūjāṃśa.
The auspicious liṅga should be made of crystal, either with a base (sadhāra) or cylindrical (vṛtta). The head-molding (śirovartanaka) is as before; there may or may not be a brahmasūtra.
"Even without the Brahma-thread (brahmasūtra), this fiery substance bestows boons.
[Thus it is said.
Then, [the measurement] is double its own width, or one and a half times, or triple; [this is] the lower [measure].
The middle and the principal [parts of] the pedestal-shaft (pīṭhanāla) are indeed as previously described.
The height of the pedestal (paiṇḍika) should be equal to, or half of, or three-quarters of the portion for worship.
Indeed, the ornamentation on the pedestals, even those made of crystal, is as prescribed for the formless (niṣkala) [icon].
A linga made of a single crystal slab with its own natural base is the best; a linga made of other crystals with its own natural base is middling. (22)
In the absence of its own material, the pedestal (pīṭha) may be made of gold, silver, or copper;
among these, the gold and other materials are considered superior, while the others are inferior.
A wise person should avoid the defects of gems such as crystal and the like; since a gem with defects causes total ruin, one should not worship it.
Twelve defects are traditionally recorded in crystals and the like, as follows:
a line, a dot, a stain, a crack, a crow's foot, and a scratch; || 25 ||
Fireflies, the shadow of a fly, a fracture, a joint, a husk-like appearance, and a depressed head—these are the defects of gems that should be avoided. (26)
One should avoid these defects in rubies and other gems;
for lingas made of rubies and the like, a pedestal of the same material is best.
In the absence of that [stone], there should be a pedestal made of gold and so forth, of the highest quality and so on,
measuring from one finger-breadth up to six finger-breadths, increasing by two barley-corns at each step.
One should fashion nine lingas made of jewels here with middling dimensions,
starting from seven finger-breadths and increasing by two barley-corns up to nine finger-breadths.
Indeed, there are nine excellent lingas made of jewels;
the inferior and middling lingas may also be made of gems or crystal.
p.
392) Indeed, among mobile [images], those that are fixed are the most excellent for worship; having installed those fixed liṅgas in a temple, one should worship them. || 31 ||

The Chapter on Liṅgas Made of Precious Stones: A liṅga made of metal, starting from one finger-breadth (rāmāṅgula) up to sixteen finger-breadths, is known as a movable liṅga; indeed, those above that size are fixed.
Starting from eight finger-breadths and increasing by eight finger-breadths at each step, one should fashion nine metal liṅgas, ending at three cubits in length.
Likewise, beginning from eight finger-breadths and increasing by two finger-breadths at each step, there are indeed thirty-three types of liṅgas up to the limit of three cubits.
There are lingas made of metal.
Starting from sixteen finger-breadths, wooden lingas increase successively by sixteen finger-breadths; there are nine such types, ending at six cubits.
Starting from sixteen finger-breadths and increasing by four finger-breadths each time,
there are thirty-three wooden liṅgas up to one aratni (handspan) in length.
Whatever devotion one may have for whomsoever, and whatever kind of manifestation that [deity] possesses, one should always take refuge in that very form of the Liṅga in accordance with it. || 37 ||

Thus ends the procedure for liṅgas made of gold and other metals, as well as those with mixed or single gendered characteristics. Herein, the procedure for wooden liṅgas is also declared, according to the definitive determination of the Śiva Tantras. (38)
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, on the rules for the Miśraliṅga and Ratnaliṅga, in the Kriyāpāda of the upper section of the Siddhāntasāra, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva.
Now begins the forty-first chapter.
Next, the characteristics of all types of liṅgas are correctly described. They are of three kinds: immovable (acala), movable (cala), and both movable and immovable (calācala).
A palace made of stone or brick is considered stable; those made of gems, wood, or iron—these three are considered mobile. || 2 ||

(393) All that is to be painted, beginning with the elements and colors, is of two kinds: moving and stationary. Furthermore, every painting is of three types: complete, half-complete, and merely appearing as a painting.
A painting in which all parts are visible is called *citra*; one where only half is seen is called *citrārdha*.
That which is painted on a cloth, a wall, or similar surfaces is known by the name *citrābhāsa* (semblance of a painting).

The fruits of images such as paintings are classified as superior, middling, or inferior according to the measurements of the linga, the sanctum, the door, the pillars, the base, and the cubit (kiṣku). || 5 ||
Furthermore, measurement may be by *tāla*, *mūla*, and *aṅgula*, as well as by *mānāṅgula*; measurement according to the height of the patron (*yajamāna*) is thus recorded as being elevenfold.
For example:
"I do not [state] the height of the worship [area], but having divided the width into sixteen parts,"

The measurement of the image (bera) relative to the linga is said to be ninefold, categorized by three types of divisions— each consisting of five, five, and seven units— or alternatively by parts of four, eleven, and eleven; whether it is less than, greater than, or equal to the linga, that measurement is established within the sanctum (garbhageha) in its nine divisions.
The height of the doorposts and the base should be equal to, or one-quarter greater than, the height of the pillars;
alternatively, these may be one-quarter less, provided there is a space of two units between them consisting of four parts.
Having then separated those parts, the measurement shall be distinct in nine ways;
that measurement is recorded as being ninefold, from one cubit up to nine cubits.

The measurement of the *tāla* is proclaimed as beginning from one *tāla* and ending at nine *tālas*; and in the case of a hundredfold division, when the portion for worship is elevated, it is twenty-four [units].
One part shall be one *aṅgula* of the original image; by that [unit], one should calculate the height of the image.
For a statue made with the *aṅgulas* of the original image, [the proportions] are according to those *aṅgulas*. || 11 ||
One should count the first part as the "womb" (yoni) and so forth; otherwise, it causes destruction.
[The measurements are] six, seven, and eight barley-corn widths (yavodara) respectively across the horizontal.
The *mānāṅgula* (measurement finger) is traditionally defined as being of three distinct types: the smallest, the middle, and the best;
it is measured by three lengths of rice grains, namely three, three and a half, and four [grains] respectively.
In this same manner, one should calculate the finger-measures (mānāṅgula) starting from the little finger;
[the measurement] is taken from the middle joint of the middle finger of the right hand of that patron.

In length, it is best when measured by the *mātrāṅgula*; it is recorded as being shorter in width. It should be equal to the sacrificer, and its eyes, mouth, jaw, and arms should be proportionate. (15)
The measurement from the nipples to the end of the heart is known to be sevenfold; this applies to the human, the partless (niṣkala), and the linga, excluding the head in the portion for worship.
One should determine the height of the faces according to that which is high; for when the measurement of the head is not obtained in a self-manifested (svāyambhuva) liṅga. || 17 ||
Its height should extend up to its head, and its circumference should be measured from the broadest part;
the same applies to the *ārṣa* and other types, except for the width of the head.

The height, the circumference, and the width [of the image] should be established; by means of these, one should determine the height of the image. In the measurement of the image in finger-breadths (aṅgula), it should proceed sequentially starting from seven finger-breadths.
The heights of the various images should each increase by two finger-breadths (aṅgula),
up to one hundred and twenty-four finger-breadths as specified here.
In this context, for domestic images (gṛhārcā), the measurement should indeed be by means of the units called "mātrās" and not otherwise;
even there, the rule is stated to be according to the fingers of the patron (yajamāna). || 21 ||
One should not exceed the natural proportion of the three types of finger-measures;
among those images, one should apply the womb and other parts according to their respective own finger-measures.
In the case of measurements specified by the *liṅga* and other standards, it is held that there is an imposition of the generic portion upon the measurement;
this applies when the measurement is eighty-four parts and the height is sixty-two parts.

In the case of the *saṅkṛti* portion and the *vikāra* portion, for the Brahmins and the other [castes] respectively, because of the imposition of a single part, that is indeed called the "imposition of the caste-portion" (*jātyaṃśāropaṇa*). || 24 ||

When the aforementioned measures for the Brahmins and other castes are divided by eight, seven, six, five, and eleven [respectively], one should know that the remainder is the asterism (*ṛkṣa*) of the Brahmin and other castes in their respective order. (25)
When counting the lunar mansions starting from the asterism of the sacrificer,
those with nine, eight, six, four, or an even number of stars are auspicious, but others are not.

The pride (māna) is divided by Rāma (3), Vasu (8), Nanda (9), Bhujaṅga (8), Nanda (9), the Vedas (4), Vṛddhi (1), Mahita (2), Araka (3), Dhātu (9), Sūrya (12), the Directions (10), and Nandaka (9); the remainders obtained in succession here shall be the signs, asterisms, days of the week, houses, and navāṃśas. (27)
The birth-omens known as the banner, lion, bull, and elephant are considered auspicious;
likewise, those that are inauspicious—the smoke, horse, donkey, and crow—should be avoided. (28)
The lunar mansions beginning with Āśvinī from the day of the sacrificer’s birth are: Birth, Prosperity, Misfortune, Security, Adversary, Accomplisher, and Death. (29)
Maitra, paramamaitra, and janma, and so forth, again and again;
the maitras that accomplish prosperity, and kṣema, which is paramamaitraka. (30)
The rite called Janma (the birth-rite) should be performed on auspicious days, while other rites are inauspicious;
however, the days of the Moon, Mercury, Jupiter, and Venus are recommended, but not others.
When wealth is greater and debt is less, it is excellent; when they are equal, it is middling.
If debt is greater, it should be avoided, for calamities, thieves, and eunuchs [will arise]. (32)
All others besides these are censurable; the remaining *aṃśakas* should be accepted as excellent.
The thief, the power of enjoyment (*bhukti*), the power of action (*śakti*), the dharma, the king, and the neuter [are among those to be avoided]. (33)
And fearlessness, as well as offspring and prosperity—these nine [results] follow in sequence for the village, the site, the king and others, and also for the patron. (34)

Having stated the classification according to the [three] measures, one should apply the construction of the womb and so forth; the height of the image under discussion [should be divided] sequentially starting from thirty parts.
The wise one, having divided these [measures] into parts ending in hundreds,
should arrange the construction of the womb, the stars, and so forth, in whatever way is auspicious.
Likewise, for the gods and others, the measurement of the image (bera) is distinct for each; furthermore, there are the measures known as māna, pramāṇa, unmāna, and parimāṇa.
Upamāna is that which hangs down; however, measurement (māna) is of six kinds. Māna refers to the vertical length of the image, while pramāṇa is the measurement applied horizontally.
Unmāna is the repetition of that [measurement]; however, āha is not a measure of quantity. Nimnonnata is comparison (upamāna), while lambamāna is that which is suspended. || 39 ||
The images of Śiva, Keśava, and Brahmā are considered to be ten *tāla*s in height for the superior type; those of Gaurī, Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī are considered to be ten *tāla*s for the medium type.
One should likewise fashion [the images] of Durgā and the Mothers with a middle measurement; or one may fashion the three forms (Trimūrti) with ten tālas as the middle measurement. || 41 ||
Then, the measurement for the goddesses is ten *tālas* less than that;
this applies to Sūrya, Indra, Skanda, Candra, Caṇḍa, Kṣetrapati, and Nandin. (42)
And for the sages, the Aśvins, and the Teacher (Buddha), it is from ten *tāla*s less than the smallest;
likewise for the world-protectors, the eight forms of Śiva, the lords of knowledge, the Vasus, and the serpents. (43)
The measurement for the Rudras should be nine superior tālas;
likewise for the hosts of Maruts, the Apsarases, those whose forms are weapons, and the Guhyakas.
One should represent the Vidyādharas and Pitṛs with a height of nine tālas;
the Siddhas, Asuras, and Gandharvas should be made with a minimum of nine tālas.
Then Gaṇeśa and Vāmana should be made according to the measurement of five tālas; the Bhūtas with four tālas, and the Yakṣas and Kinnaras with three tālas.
The Kuśmāṇḍa is two tālas; from that [measurement], one should fashion Hari in the form of a tortoise.
The making of the images, however, is according to the finger-breadths obtained from the specific body [of the deity].
It is said that it would be accomplished there; first, the supreme [measurement] is ten tālakas. In its height, when divided into one hundred and twenty-four parts— 48.
One part of that [measure] is called a *dehabala*; that finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) is then divided eightfold.
One should know that one part is a barley-corn (*yava*), and the same applies to the subsequent units.
In the medium ten-tāla measurement, [the increment] is one part out of two hundred and twenty;
in the smallest ten-tāla measurement, it is one part out of one hundred and twenty-five.
In the best nine-tāla measurement, one part out of one hundred and eight parts is one aṅgula;
in the middle nine-tāla measurement, however, one part out of one hundred and four parts is one aṅgula.
In the case of the smallest [image] with ninety-two *tālakas*, one part out of a hundred is to be known as an *aṅgula*;
however, in the case of the best [image] with sixty-four *tālakas*, one part out of ninety-six shall be an *aṅgula*.

By decreasing [the measurement] by one finger-breadth for each subsequent Veda, these are remembered as the medium and inferior [sizes]; according to the division of their respective *tālas*, this applies in sequence to the seven *tāla* measures and so forth.
One should know that the space between two single tālas is equal to a finger-measure (aṅgula) obtained from the body; the moon, the sky, a fraction,
a mātrā, and a finger-measure are likewise recorded as being equal.
The *kolaka* shall be one-sixteenth part [of the measurement], measuring two, three, or four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*);
however, the term "eye-ball portion" (*akṣigolakapakṣa*) denotes a measure of two finger-breadths.
A *mukha*, a *tāla*, and a *vitasti* are synonyms denoting twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
Now, the measurement of the image according to the excellent *paṅktitāla* is described. (56)
The uṣṇīṣa (crown protuberance) is three parts; the hair-limit (keśānta) is then three parts;
from there, the eye-line is four parts plus three yavas; and from there, [the nose-line is] likewise. || 57 ||
The measurement up to the nostrils is that same amount, and up to the chin it is likewise;
from there, the throat is four finger-breadths (yavas), and the neck is seven [finger-breadths].
From this [point], the heart is thirteen finger-breadths away, including three barley-corns;
from that, the navel is by that same number of finger-breadths.

From the navel to the genitals is that same measure; from there, the measurement of the thighs shall be equal to the number of lunar mansions (twenty-seven) finger-breadths; and from that, the knees shall be one part.
Therefore, the shanks are equal to the thighs; the foot, according to its measurement, consists of seven parts. Furthermore, from the big toe to the heel, the sole measures seventeen finger-breadths.

Below the *hikkā-sūtra*, the two arms [are measured] by twenty-seven units; the elbow (*korpara*) is two finger-breadths from that, and the forearm (*prakoṣṭha*) is three-sevenths of a unit from there.
The floor from the middle to the edge is recorded as being thirteen and a half measures;
the horizontal width of the face, extending to the ears, is twelve finger-breadths.
The width at the base and the top of the neck is one and a half times nine *vyaṅgula*s;
the width between the arms is eighty-one and a half *mātrā*s.
One should calculate the distance from the armpits to the base of the arms and the knees as one and a half *nandas*;
the distance between the two armpits is considered to be twenty-two finger-breadths.
The width between the breasts is twenty-five mātras;
the width extending down to the heart is eighteen and a half mātras.
The middle width is eighteen finger-breadths with a half [finger], that is, sixteen parts;
the width of the hips and the width of the waist are measured at twenty finger-breadths. (67)
The width at the base of the thigh should be thirteen and a half parts;
at the middle of the thigh it is twelve parts, and at the base of the shank it is eight measures.
The middle of the shank is six and a half [units], and the bone (nalakā) is one and a half parts in width;
from the eye to the ankle, it is extended by a barley-corn (yava) and one part in width.
The heels are one and a half finger-breadths in width and likewise in height;
the breadth of the forefoot is one-sixth [of the foot], and that of the tip of the sole is six barley-corns more.
The length of the big toe is said to be two and one-quarter parts;
its width is half of that, and the width of the nail is half of that again. (71)
The length of the nail is three-quarters of that [width], adorned with a rounded and elevated tip;
it measures four, three, three, and two mātrās, along with six, four, and four yavas respectively.

The length of the fingers, starting from the index finger (tarjanī) and ending with the little finger (kaniṣṭhā), is thus described; their respective widths should also be known in order as nine and seven-and-a-half [aṅgulas]. (73)

The nails extend six times seven barley-corns beyond half of their own breadth; the measurement from the middle of the forearm to the elbow is [half the breadth] plus one-quarter, one-eighth, and one-seventh [of the breadth]. (74)
The forearm and the wrist are each three and a half finger-breadths [in width];
the palm is seven finger-breadths in length, and the middle finger is six and a half finger-breadths long.
The [measurement] up to the little finger is one-fourth more than three-quarters of a finger-breadth.
The measurement of the fingers, from the thumb to the little finger, shall consist of six barley grains, each being the size of one and a quarter parts of a barley grain. (77)
In each respective base, the portion of the modification (vikāra) is to be subtracted from its respective tip;
at the tip of the finger, when the extent is one part of fire (three units), the nails have a width of two parts separately.
The nails should each have a length equal to one-fourth of their respective widths; the tip-joint of each nail should individually be twice the length of its own nail. (79)
The thumb should be two and a quarter units; the index finger, two units;
the middle finger, two and three-quarters units; and [the ring finger] by five barley-corns. (80)
The length of the little finger is said to be from its root-joint; and that which remains between the middle joint and the joints at the middle and the tip [is the length of the ring finger]. (81)
The thumb has two joints, while the remaining fingers have three;
the breadth of the palm, however, measures one and a half, one and a half, one and a half, and five digits respectively.
It should be at the base, the middle, and likewise the tip; then from the base of the thumb up to the base of the forefinger, by fire-parts (three units), and likewise from the base of the thumb.
The part called Śukodara extends to the wrist with four-fifths of a unit;
its thickness is two and a half units, and the thickness of the Śākaraparṣṇī is one-sixteenth.
The tip of that [foot] is reduced by a sixteenth part, as is the tip of the sole;
the fleshy part [of the heel] should be one and a half *kola*s, and here the heel is one part in width.
The breadth of the "parrot-belly" is two parts, and from the remainder, the depression in the sole is prescribed.
The surface [of the mandala] possesses the marks of the wheel, conch, lotus, makara, svastika, and so forth. (86)
The circumference at the top of the ear should be thirty-eight finger-breadths (aṅgulas),
and the circumference at the middle of the two ears is traditionally recorded as twenty-two finger-breadths.
The back of the head is [measured] by twelve parts (sūryāṃśa), and the two ears are separately [measured] from the nape;
from the middle of the head to the end of the hair, the measurement is said to be nine finger-breadths (aṅgula). || 88 ||
The two sides should be exactly the same; then, on the hairline and the eye-line, one should fashion the pair of eyebrows in the middle, auspiciously curved like a bow with an arrow.
The vertical line from the ear is equal to the eyebrows; from that measure, there is a depression between the eyebrows.
The distance between the two eyebrows is one-half part, and the length of the eyebrows is five parts.
The pupil in the middle of the eyebrows should be two barley-corns wide and tapered at its tip; the iris should be one-sixteenth of a part in width, and its diameter should then be six barley-corns.
The white portion has a black disc, and at the end, the white portion is equal to that;
the width of the eye is six barley-corns, and the corner of the eye is half a barley-corn and reddish.
The black line [of the eye] is like a louse; the circle of light is a barleycorn (*yava*).
The width of the upper and lower eyelids should be one barleycorn and half a barleycorn, respectively. || 93 ||
The distance between the two eyes should be exactly one *yugma* (two units), plus two *viyavas*. The width at the boundary of the nostril openings should be one-fourth of that [distance]. || 94 ||
The middle width is half of that; above that, it is half again. From the base of the *gojī* [the nose-bridge], the tip of the nose is two finger-breadths high, rising above the nostrils.
The two nostril apertures are known to be one barley-corn thick and stretched across;
the height and width of the nasal gateway are considered to be five and seven barley-corns respectively.
The two nostril cavities are like sesame flowers and resemble parched grain;
their width is said to be half a barleycorn, equal to one part of the height of the middle wall.
The tip of the nose should extend one and a half *yava*s from the line of the nostrils;
the *gojī* [muscle] has a length of four and a half *yava*s, and its width is half of that.

The upper lip (uttaroṣṭha) should be one and a quarter parts in length, while the *pālikā* [the upper lip's width] is one barley-corn (*yava*) in breadth; its [the *pālikā*'s] width is said to be three and a half barley-corns. || 99 ||
The corners of the mouth extend far, the teeth become sharp and gradually tapering, the lips are triple-curved and slightly drooping; such is the length of the face. || 100 ||
The lower lip should be eighteen yavas in width and one and a half yavas in height;
its border (pālī) below that should be one and a half yavas.
The lower lip, however, is eight and a half barley-corns in measurement; likewise, the depression below the lip is three barley-corns high, being the jaw.
The jaw (hanu) is half a rāma [one and a half] aṅgulas in circumference and one and a half rāmas [three] aṅgulas in width;
from the ear-attachment to the middle of the jaw, it is declared to be ten aṅgulas.

The placement of the neck is one-quarter of a foot from the jaw; from the neck, it is double that distance [to the shoulders]. The placement of the ears is from the outer corners of the eyes, and the distance between the ears is seven parts.

The width of the ear should be equal to the length of the eye; likewise, its upward elevation from the line of the eyes [should be one unit]. Below that, the ear-attachment (karṇabandha) should be two units and a half in length.
The two ear-paths, one in front and one behind, should be three and a half units in length;
they should be half a unit and half a unit in width respectively, and their thickness should be one and a half units.

The hollow of the stalk should be six barley-corns [in diameter], and its length is traditionally held to be one part of a long pepper; or else, the *piñcūṣī* should have half that width and be one *kalā* in length. (107)
Below that, from the corner of the eye-line, there should be an opening four *yavas* wide;
the ear-lobe (*karṇapālī*) is four *yavas* in length and one and a half *yavas* in thickness.

Then, the back of the ear and the curve of the nape measure one and a half units; subsequently, the kṛkāṭikā (the hollow at the base of the neck) is half a unit deep, extending from the upper part of the throat to the end of the hair.
In the region of the nape of the neck, the width of the throat is eight *mātrās*;
below that, at the boundary of the shoulders, it is eight and a half *mātrās* and ten finger-breadths (*aṅgulas*).
Afterwards, the length of the neck is three parts of a *veda* (four) and three *yava*s;
above the line of the *hikkā*, the joint of the shoulder is elevated by one part of a *veda*.
The two shoulders are lower than the line of the hiccups by seven parts and thick; behind, the hump is one part below the throat, and from that, it extends downward by finger-breadths.
The spinal column consists of twenty-seven [vertebrae] starting from the sacroiliac joint;
leaving four [vertebrae] below the region of the hump, it is situated at the two armpits.
The width between the armpits at the back should be twelve finger-breadths;
from the armpit upwards, the height of the two arms should be six finger-breadths and one barley-corn.

The shoulder-blade (aṃsapīṭha) at the junction of the aggregates (skandhasandhi) should be one and a half arrow-parts (iṣvaṃśa). Subsequently, up to the end of the breast-line (āstanasūtra), there are twelve parts (arkāṃśa) on the shoulder-blades. The width of the hump (kakuda) below the middle of the shoulder-blade is ten finger-breadths (daśāṅgula).
The bamboo staff below that should have a width of three finger-breadths and be hollowed out to a depth of two finger-breadths.
From the side of the *vaṃśa* to the shoulder-base is the *bṛhatī*; [it consists of] seven *mātṛkā*s.
Between the two *bṛhatī*s is the breast, which is solid and measures sixteen *mātrā*s.
Below the *bṛhatī*, the height down to the hip is seven *mātrās*;
from there, it is thickened by portions of the *vikāra* for eight *mātrās* below that.
The interval between the sections of the waist should consist of thirteen and a half parts;
the width of the waistband should be one and a half units.
The two buttocks are perfectly round, with a width of one and a half parts of Nanda;
from the root of the thighs, the protrusion of the buttocks extends for four and a half parts. (120)
The two buttocks hang down from below the root of the penis by four and a half parts; the neck is circular, and its circumference is provided with two parallel lines. 121.
The space between the breasts and the armpit-junction is likewise;
from the armpit, the line of the shoulder-blade (kakṣadhara) extends for thirteen and a half parts.
The elevation of the breast-plate from the depth of the heart is two and a quarter parts and one and a half measures;
the roundness of the breasts is two parts plus a barley-corn.

The nipple of the breast should be beautiful and round, measuring two *yavas* in height; the *hikkā* (the space between the breasts) should be two *yavas* lower, and the pair of knees should measure two *mātrās*.

The navel should be six barley-corns in width and depth, beautiful and spiraling to the right; the hips should be one part of five barley-corns [in width] from the navel, and the sides [of the hips] should be six parts.
The hip region of the buttocks is three and a half parts; the remainder is the circle of the penis.
It is two and five parts (five and two) long, including two *yava*s, and its circumference is likewise [two and five] parts, including two *yava*s.

The *liṅga* is supported by the seed-vessel (*bījāvalamba*), and it possesses two parts, each having a portion of the *seda*. Its width should be equal to that [length], extending from the penis upward to the junction of the thighs.

The knee-joint (jānu) is three fingers wide and three barley-corns high; it is rounded according to its proportion. Its thickness is one and a half kalās, while the side-binding (pārśvabandha) is one part.
The height of the rear part of the *jānu* is two and a half parts according to the measurement;
its width and its depth, etc., are to be inferred from this point onward.
One should fashion a beautiful image with all its limbs perfectly complete and symmetrical in terms of measurement and proportion, using the superior ten-tāla system.

Thus, according to the characteristics, the measurement for the primary [image] consisting of ten tālas has indeed been fully stated here, beginning with the dimensions of the body suitable for the image. (131)
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Rule for the Proportions of the Human Form in Ten Tall Tālas," in the *Kriyāpāda* of the *Siddhāntasāra*, the *Śrīmadīśānaśivagurudevapaddhati*.
Now begins the forty-second chapter.

The measurement of a woman is now described by means of ten *tāla*s. From the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*) to the hairline is one part; from there, [the forehead] is one part plus six barleycorns (*yava*). || 1 ||
From the corner of the eye to the end of the nostril, there should be a part measuring four *yavas*; then from there to the end of the jaw, it should be three parts with six *yavas*.
The portion from the chin to the end of the throat, and then the heart, the navel, and the pubic region, each should be thirteen parts; the thighs should be twenty-six finger-breadths.

From that [navel], the knees should be one part; from there, the shanks should be twenty-six finger-breadths. One should fashion the feet and their soles with one part each, having a length of one part.
Both the thumb and the index finger are recorded as being separately one and a half finger-breadths in length;
the remaining fingers are each separately one finger-breadth in width.
The thumb has a width of two finger-breadths (aṅgulas); the forefinger is one finger-breadth wide;
the middle finger is seven and a half barley-corns (yavas) [wide]; and the ring finger is then seven barley-corns [wide].
The little toes are six barley-corns in width; the nails are as wide as half their own [toes'] width, with their tips slightly curved upward; and the breadth of the heels is one part.
The height of the heel should be five finger-breadths (śara), and its width across the surface should also be five finger-breadths.
The tip of the forefoot should be six finger-breadths (rasa), and the distance between the ankle and the axle [of the foot] should be five finger-breadths.
The width of the shanks at the ankles is six finger-breadths; the width of the shanks is seven mātras; the width of the knees is one tāla;
and the width of the thighs is one tāla.
The waist is two tālas in width; from above the hips, it is seven parts, while its width below is four mātras, and it has the shape of an aśvattha leaf.
That [region] should be plump and beautiful; the hip (śroṇi) should be extended by eight finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
The navel should have a diameter and depth of six barley-corns (yavas), being thin in the middle and at its edges.
Adorned with broad lines of hair by the Rudra-measures alone,
there should be [a space] below the breasts measuring eight Jagatī-parts, and for each breast, there should be six Nandā-parts.
The expanse of the nipples is one part of Rāma (four parts); the breasts are raised by one and a half parts.
The diameter of the nipple is half a mātrā, and its elevation is two yavas. || 13 ||
The internal width between the armpits should be seventeen finger-breadths (aṅgulas),
and the width including the limits of the arms should be thirty-one finger-breadths. (14)
The length of the upper arm (bhuja) should be nine parts; the elbow (kūrpara) should be equal to one kalā.
The forearm (prakoṣṭha) should be sixteen parts, and the palm (tala) should be seven finger-breadths in length.
The fingers are extended in sequence according to the Vedic measures of Ṛtu, Śara, and Āmnāya;
they are spread out with nine, seven, eight, and six finger-breadths respectively.
When the width at the front edge is divided into six parts, the width of the nails is four parts;
the length of the nails is one *yava* more than that, and the width of the palm is six finger-breadths.
The wrist, the elbow, the middle of the arm, and the base [of the forearm] should be progressively wider by six, seven, and six finger-breadths respectively. || 18 ||
The neck has a width of seven aṅgulas; the width of the face is by the portions of the Rudras (eleven); the mouth should be circular and elongated, with the eyebrows occupying one and a half parts.
The length from the hairline to the end of the face is established as six and one-quarter kalās;
the mouth is one-quarter of that, and the length of the forehead is half of that.

The lip-border (oṣṭhapālī) shall be as wide as a barley-corn; with the remainder, the width of the lip is formed. Its length shall be one part, and the triple-layered rim (trivargottarapālikā) shall be one part more.

The length of the mouth is said to be [one] finger-breadth; the lower lip is one finger-breadth plus a barley-corn (yava). Its edge is one barley-corn wide, and from that, it extends by two parts of a barley-corn.
Its length is six barley-corns, and its height from that is one and a half parts;
the jaw (hanu) is two barley-corns, and there, below the jaw, is the opening of the throat.
The width of the ear is said to be three and a half mātrās;
its length is six and four-sevenths of a kalā, and the projection of the stalk is five-sevenths.

And one should fashion those two arms, beautiful like the tail-hair of a cow, adorned with ornaments; the thighs should be shaped like the trunks of elephants, and the entire body should be most beautiful.
Whatever has not been stated should be inferred by the wise according to the previous rule; the measurement for women is ten tālas in the middle [chest].
Now, the measurement for men is described as being ten tālas in the middle.
p.
