405) With two parts of a barley-corn [each], there should be the height at the head, throat, feet, and knees;
furthermore, from the hairline to the corner of the eye, and from the corner of the eye to the edge of the eyelid. (27)

The jaw is said to be according to the aforementioned measurement; the throat and the neck are half an aṅgula each. From the base of the throat to the heart should be six jagatī parts plus six barleycorns.
From that [navel], the navel [itself] is located; from there, the penis is twelve finger-breadths away.
Including six barley-corns and the additional portions, the length of the thighs is thus declared.
The length of the shanks is equal to that [of the thighs], and the length of the soles is by eight-sixteenths (one-eighth);
the length of the arms is by nine-sixteenths, while the elbow is one-sixteenth [of the total height].

The forearm should be one-twentieth [of the total height]; the length of the palm from the base to the tip is thirteen finger-breadths; and the width of the space between the arms is likewise thirteen finger-breadths. || 31 ||
The face should be thirty-five and a half finger-breadths, including three parts of a *nanda*;
the bases of the neck and the arms, as well as the two middle portions of the knees, should likewise be below that measure.
From the *Hikkāsūtra*, the space from each armpit to the end is nine units;
the region below the armpits is one *kalā*, while the measurement of the chest is by parts of *prakṛti*.

The space between the breasts is [measured] from the breast to the *dhikkā* [mark]; the distance from the *dhikkā* to the armpit is thirteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), and the middle of the abdomen is fifteen and a half finger-breadths.
Therefore, the width at the hips should be greater by one *kalā*; likewise, the width at the waist and at the base of the thighs should be greater by thirteen degrees (*aṃśa*). (35)
Between those two, the measurement of the shanks is seven parts consisting of portions of Rudra; the width of the ankles is four parts, plus five and a quarter finger-breadths.
The width of the two ankles and the width and height of the heels are then [determined] by four parts plus two barleycorns,
and then by four and a quarter finger-breadths.
The middle of the foot and the tip of the foot are each extended by six and a half finger-breadths (aṅgulas);
the thumb is four and a quarter parts, while the index finger is one barley-corn (yava) longer than that.
The middle finger is three and a half parts in length; the ring finger is three parts long;
and the little finger is two and a half parts; and they are likewise in this same order in terms of width. (39)
The breadth of the nail is measured by one-sixteenth part (kalā), or by seven barley-corns (yava), or by six barley-corns, corresponding respectively to eight,
five, and four [finger-breadths].
With barley grains numbering three, four, and five, its length shall be half of its own width;
then, respectively, with eight, seven, five, and four-and-a-half finger-breadths [the widths are determined]. (41)

The distance between the upper arm and the elbow, and between the forearm and the wrist, as well as the length from the wrist to the palm, should be seven parts, which is six finger-breadths (aṅgulas). || 42 ||
The middle finger, however, is just over one iṣu [five aṅgulas] long; the ring finger and the little finger are four and a quarter aṅgulas in length respectively.
The width of the base shall be two and a half parts, and the thickness of the base shall be two and a half parts;
the thumbs and the other fingers, however, shall measure twelve, eight, and nine [parts] respectively.
The width of these [mandalas] is considered to be, respectively, one barley-corn and one *vasu* (eight) parts of their own diagonal.
When the diagonal is divided into three parts, the width of the nails (*nakha*) shall be two parts. || 45 ||

The length of the penis is praised as being equal to one's own span plus two barley grains; its length is said to be five parts [of a finger], and its circumference is traditionally held to be two fingers.
The scrotum and the penis together occupy two parts; the forehead is one part and nine parts in length; and the distance between the ears at the back should be thirteen mātrās.
The length of the eye and its internal width are indeed two and one-quarter parts; the width of the eye is six barley-corns, and the black pupil (kṛṣṇamaṇḍala) should be of that same measure.
On the white side-mandala, there should be two [spots] five barley-corns in length; the light within the center of the black mandala should be the measure of one barley-corn.
The vision (dṛṣṭi) should be one *yūkā* in measure, the pupil (*kanīnikā*) one *yava*;
at the outer corner (*apāṅga*) there should be half a *yava* which is red, and the upper eyelid (*ūrdhvavarma*) two *yavas*.

The distance from the lower edge of the armor (the chin) to the midpoint of the eyebrows, measured along the line of the eyes, should be one and a quarter kalās; the height of the ears should be equal to that.
The length of the two eyebrows should be five finger-breadths (śarāṅgula); their middle should be extended by two barley-corns (yava).
The space between them should be half a part (of a finger), and their curvature should be one finger-breadth.

The two eyebrows should be long and curved like a bow; the ears should be two *yava*s in width, and the *nālālambo* (the earlobe) should be of the same measure, with an additional portion when adorned.
The arrangement of the front stalk is one *mātrā*, while the rear stalk is half of that; their thickness,
however, from the root of the ear to the outer corner of the eye, is half a *mātrā*.

The height from the base of the nostril to the tip of the nose should be seven aṅgulas; it should be made with a reduction of one yava and one kalā, while the height of the *puṣkara* (the nasal opening) should be six yavas.

Its width should be one *yava* less; the nostrils, extending from the upper part of the nose, should be equal to half a finger-breadth (*ardhāṅgula*), and they should both have a thickness of one *yava*.
The length of the lower lip (gojyā) should be half a mātrā, and its width is recorded as two yavas;
the row of teeth above should be half a mātrā, and the row of teeth below one yava.
The length of that [channel] is one part including a *yava*; the width below it is one part including a *yava*. Its height is twice that; from that, the rim (*pālī*) is measured as one *yava*. (58)
That [distance] above should be six barley-corns; the remainder shall be the jaw, and the throat from the jaw should be one and a half barley-corns. From there, it should be two and a half units.
The remainder, up to the neck, should be understood by the wise as before;
this is the measurement for a person of ten middle-sized tālas.
Now, the measurement for a woman according to ten smallest (kaniṣṭha) tālas is described.
The length of the face is one and a half parts; the width from the hairline to the eye is one part; from there, the distance to the edge of the nostrils is four parts plus a yava.
Then, the distance from the chin to the throat is likewise that same [measure];
from the throat to the heart, and from the heart to the navel, the interval is one and a half *sūrya*-aṅgulas (twelve and a half finger-breadths).
When this [area] is divided into sixteen hundred equal parts, the height of the crown, the armpits, the knees, and the soles of the feet is measured by four [parts] each.
The length of the face from the hairline to the eye-line should be one and a half parts; from there, it should be three and a quarter cubits, including a portion of a barley-corn.
From the end of the *puṭa* to the jaw, then from the throat to the heart, and from the heart to the navel, and from there to the *yoni*, each is separately one and a half *sūryāṅgula*s. (65)
The thighs should be made with six parts, and the shanks and the two knees are considered equal. The length of the feet is sixteen parts, and the two arms are considered equal to the thighs.

The two elbows (korpara) are one kalā in length; the forearms (prakoṣṭha) are eighteen aṅgulas; the length of the palm (tala) is two and a half aṃśas; and the length of the middle finger (madhyamā) is six aṃśas. (67)
The thumb and the ring finger should be [measured] by nine parts;

the index and the little finger should be [measured] by eight, seven, and six barleycorns respectively. The expansion of the fingers starting from the index finger is [calculated] by nine, seven, and six barleycorns.
When the width at the tip is divided by three, two parts constitute the width of the nails;
the length is greater than that by one barleycorn, and the width of the palm is one-sixth [of the length].
The palm is thickened by a digit (kala), while the wrist, the forearm, the middle of the arm, and the upper arm are each increased by three digits. (70)
The width of the face is eleven parts (rudra), and the neck is extended by seven aṅgulas; the width of the base of the arms and the knees is seven parts, and their length is likewise.
The width of the breasts is determined by eight parts of the space between the armpits and nine parts [of that same interval];
their height is half of that, while the nipples are three mātrās in size.
The nipple should be half a part; its elevation is said to be two barley-corns.
Below the nipple, the space is measured by the parts of the Atijagatī metre, and the width at the middle is eleven digits (rudrāṅgula).
The buttocks have a width of eleven parts, and the hips are extended by five parts;
the width of the thighs is twelve parts, while at the middle of the shanks it is six parts.
The ankle-bone (nalaka) is one part in width; the skin and the ankle-joint (gulpha) are five finger-breadths [in thickness];
and the elevation of the heel's breadth, as well as that of the middle and the tip of the sole, is one part each.
Vyāsa should be six finger-breadths; Jyeṣṭhoccā should be [calculated] by degrees. Tarjanī and Madhyā should be equal to that, measuring four and a half finger-breadths in length.
The ring finger shall be three mātrās long, and the little finger two and a half aṅgulas; they are respectively expanded by six, seven, seven and a half, eight, and one and a half yavas.
The toes, beginning with the little toe, are spread out to half the width of their respective feet; the nails are three-quarters of that length, rounded, elevated at the tips, and slightly curved.
From the hairline to the eyebrows, the thread is extended by one-quarter of a kalā;
from one finger-breadth below the nostrils, the mouth extends by the sine of the arc (gojyā), and its width is half of that.
The width of the mouth is one-fourth [of the total height],
while the lip above the three-fold division is one-sixteenth;
the lower lip should be one-eighth [of the total] in height and half of that in width.

The rim (pālī) of that [eye] should be one barley-corn (yava) in measure; the remainder should have the shape of a bimba fruit. The length of the eye should be two and a half barley-corns, while its width is six barley-corns.
The placement of the neck from the jaw is recorded as being three and a half finger-breadths;
the height of the nose from the base of the chin should be six barley-corns.
The length of the ear should be one part, and the width one part plus a quarter-kalā; the projection of the stalk should be one part, and the remainder should be inferred as before.

The measurement for women is by means of the medium ten-tāla [system], and by that same [system] is the measurement for men; however, the characteristic of the female measurement here is said to be from the smallest ten-tāla [system]. (84)
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, concerning the characteristics of women, men, and others, in the Kriyāpāda of the *Siddhāntasāra*, the *Śrīmad-Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati*.
Now begins the forty-third chapter.
Now, the forms and other characteristics of the sixteen mūrtis are being declared; therein, the iconographic description of Śambhu accompanied by Umā and Skanda is stated.
Having assumed a straight posture with the dust-like state [of the mind], one should sit in the half-lotus position; one should rest the left foot on the seat while letting the right hang down.
From the end of the seat to the end of the hair, it should be level up to the knees;
and from the outer side of the knees, it should extend to the sides of the arms.
One should likewise align the middle of both the other two hands at the wrists with the upper body;
all of this should be done in due order.
One should let the middle thread hang from the tip of the crown down to the middle of the ankles; the right knee should enter [the circle] two or three finger-breadths beyond the thread.
The distance between the ankle and the tip of the big toe is measured by the degrees of the middle sūtra and so forth;
the distance from the sūtra to the middle of the hand on the right side is measured by the degrees of the fourteen (manu).

(410) According to fifteen parts of the sūtra, the distance from the left palm [to the center] should likewise be [the same]; the middle and tip of the right hand should be raised level with the breast-sūtra.

The distance between the left thigh and the left hand is two or three mātrās; the tips of the two hands in the kartarī gesture are said to be level with the line of the *hik-kā* (the supraclavicular notch).
The distance between the hips and the elbows is five parts or six parts;
likewise, the line of the nose reaches the side of the abdomen, extending from the penis to the armpit.
From the middle line, the base and the tip [of the blade] should be fourteen *jagatī* units and twelve *arka* units respectively;
the two faces should be either inside or outside the span of the hand.
One should depict a battle-axe and a deer in the right and left [hands] respectively; the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya) in the right hand, and a bracelet on the wrist in the left.
On the left and right [sides] are the mandalas called Śaṅkhapattraka and Kanaka;
from the crown of the head to the hairline, it is two tālas and three-quarters high.
One should fashion it at two and a half or two *tālas* in height, endowed with all the proper characteristics; and on the left side, one should depict Pārvatī seated together with the God.
She should extend her left leg and slightly bend her right one; resting upon a divine seat, with a slightly downcast face and fully adorned. (14)
Her left and right hands are joined with a boon-granting gesture and a blue lotus; or alternatively, her left hand may rest upon the seat on the outer side of her left thigh.
Skanda should be placed in the middle between these two, with his limbs made white by the excellence of the Vedic portions;
having divided his own height into five tālas, one should fashion the individual parts.

The measurement of the head is by means of a finger-breadth (aṅgula); from the hairline (keśānta) to the eye-line is three and a half of those same units; from there, the distance to the edge of the nostrils and then to the jaw (hanu) is likewise measured.
Likewise, the throat should be three *mātras* long; the heart from the navel is measured by nine, eight, and four *mātras* respectively; and the penis is equal in measure to the navel.
The thigh should be eleven digits long, measured by the rays of the sun; the knee should be one digit, and the shank likewise.
The foot should be eleven digits long, measured by the Rudras, and its sole should be ten digits in length.
The two arms are fourteen finger-breadths in length, and the forearm is also ten finger-breadths;
the span of the palm should be four parts (of a finger), and the middle finger is four finger-breadths long.
The index finger and the ring finger should be one and a half *rāma* (three) finger-breadths in length;
the little finger and the thumb should each be three parts [of that], and with these two hands joined, it should form a blue lotus (*utpala*).
One should stand with the two feet contracted, possessing the proper characteristics;
then, marked by the moon-crested [Śiva], one should stand with the feet even.

One should suspend [the thread] upon the crown of the head, the forehead, the tip of the nose, the middle of the jaw, the throat, the heart, the private parts, the chest, and the middle of the feet. (23)

In the case of the *kartarī* [mudrā], one should form it with the tips [of the fingers] reaching to the end of the *hikkā*, the tips of the breasts, the tips of the *abhaya* [mudrā], or alternatively, extending to the limit of the navel or even to the hips. || 24 ||

The *abhaya* [mudrā] is derived from the *sūtra*; it is free from the middle and ends, five finger-breadths wide, extending to one *hasta* by twelve parts (*arkāṃśaiḥ*), or otherwise ten finger-breadths. || 25 ||
Or, according to the Sūtra, the middle of the forearm is [measured] by eight or nine units;
the base of the thigh is one unit [from there], and the middle of the knee is one part [further].
The distance between the heels from the middle of the shanks shall be five parts;
the two upper hands, however, hold an axe and a deer.
Candraśekhara should be depicted with matted locks and a crescent moon resting upon his left side, adorned with serpents, upright in posture, and possessing the luster of a coral gem. 28.
The bull-vehicled deity may be in a balanced stance (samabhaṅga) or a triple-bent stance (tribhaṅga);
he stands upright with his right leg straight and his left foot drawn up. (29)
Or it is said that the foot and the shank are positioned transversely; [the measurement] from the crown of the head (uṣṇīṣa) to the left forehead, to the left eye, and to the corner of the eye. 30.

When there is a hanging down of the left breast and the middle of the region between the navel and the heel, this is the *tiraścīnajaṅgha* [stance]; it occurs only when there is extreme bending, and not otherwise.
From the navel to the left thigh and to the right ankle, one should drop the thread; as above the navel was done previously, so it should be done here as well.
The natimāna should be [calculated] by means of the arrow-parts (śarāṃśa) on the head of the bull of the god;
the left elbow should be placed eighteen finger-breadths (aṅgula) from the hikkā.
Likewise, from below the elbow up to the height of the bull's hump, the right hand should hang down to the region of the waist. (34)
Everything, such as the hand of another and so forth, should be like that of Candraśekhara. The Goddess should stand with an even posture, her left hand hanging down. (35)
The right arm of the Lord extends down to the breast, holding a blue lotus;
it bears the marks of Soma, Skanda, and Śiva.
Naṭeśvara has four arms, three eyes, and the moon as his crest-jewel. (36)
Having grasped the shoulder-measure from the half-measurement, the degree of inclination is ten finger-breadths, or else twelve finger-breadths; now the sagging of the cord is described.
One should cause [the drops] to fall from the crown of the head onto the left forehead, into its cavity, into the middle of the jaw,
into the middle of the two hiccups (or breasts), and onto the left ankle.
Then, with the tips of the outstretched arms extended for a portion of the width,
the tip of the forearms [from that point] measures fifty-eight finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
From the sūtra, the tip of the *sāgnikara* should be established; from there, the tip of the *ḍamaruka*.
With forty-eight parts, the width should be equal to the limit of the ear.
To the right side of the thread, at a distance of twelve finger-breadths, there should be the space for the girdle;
his mass of matted hair is spread out, and his face is slightly smiling. (41)
He should be depicted wearing a tiger-skin garment and standing upon Apasmāra,
surrounded by hosts of Gaṇas, celestial sages, Yakṣas, and others, as well as Vighneśa, Skanda, and the Mothers.
Accompanied by Bhṛṅgīśa, Mahākālī, Pārvatī, and the bull, the four-armed Nandin sat down comfortably while sounding his mṛdaṅga drum.
The hand should have its fingers slightly bent like a sprout and be joined with the *vandana* [mudrā]. This is the characteristic of the *bhujaṅgatrāsana* dance.
One should stand on the right foot, while the other lotus-foot is bent. (44)

From the crown of the head to the right side of the forehead, then to the right nostril, then to the middle of the *hikkā*, and then two finger-breadths to the right of the region of the navel. || 45 ||
One should suspend a string from the root of the penis to the middle of the two heels;
the body should be slightly bent, with the left shoulder lowered and stretched. (46)
On the right, he is the Bestower of Boons; with his lower right hand holding a knife, he bears the Gaṅgā, and with his upper left hand, he holds a deer. (47)
Embracing Umā with his left hand while she leans equally toward him, he should be saluted by Bhagīratha,
the gods, and the sages.
In this manner, one should fashion Gaṅgādhara; the remainder should be inferred as before.
This is the definition of Gaṅgādhara.
Tripurāntaka-dava should be provided with the Vaiśākha stance. (49)
It may be formed by slight bending, equal bending, or even extreme bending;
it possesses three bends, each measuring three, four, and five units respectively.

The left hand, together with the Pināka bow, reaches up to the armpit; the other [right] hand, through its parts consisting of transformation, support, and action, gradually extends to the space between the big toes.
Holding two arrows and two young deer with antlers in her two right hands, the Goddess should likewise stand on the left side as she was before. (52)
The characteristics of Tripurāntaka:
they should be on the crown of Kalyāṇasundara, on the left forehead, in the left eye, at the corner of the eye, and in the middle of the right side of the diaphragm. 53.
The cord, measuring three or four finger-breadths from the navel down to the middle of the ankles, is placed clockwise around the deity who is desirous of going toward the fire.

The hand other than the left [of the deity] should likewise be resting upon the hand of the Goddess; the left hand should be in the boon-granting (varada) gesture, while the remaining hands remain as before.
The goddess should have a blue lotus in her hand, her body in the *tribhaṅga* posture, and be adorned;
she is accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi, is fair-complexioned, and is followed by the gods. (56)
The Hotṛ priest shall be Brahmā, and Viṣṇu, together with the clouds, shall be the donor;
he shall be worshipped by all the gods, ṛṣis, gandharvas, yakṣas, and others. || 57 ||

Possessing auspicious and beautiful characteristics, the image of Ardhanārīśvara may also have an even distribution of limbs; it may have either four arms or two arms, and its right leg should be standing. 58.
The left foot should be contracted; Pārvatī is his left half. Beyond this, everything else should be conceived through inference as previously described. (59)
The characteristics of Ardhanārīśvara:
Now, the form of Pāśupati is also like that of Candraśekhara; he is three-eyed, four-armed, fierce, with hair standing erect and a massive body. (60)
With a rosary and trident in his upper hands, and granting boons and fearlessness;
this is the characteristic of Pāśupata.
Kaṅkāla is intent on departing, treading upon jeweled sandals. (61)
With his face half-turned, his two hands raised to strike the ḍhakka drum, he touches the face of the young deer with his right rear hand.
Carrying a skull-staff with a protruding skeleton of a corpse in his left hand, and bearing an alms-bowl upon his head, he proceeded at the forefront of a host of spirits.
In that way, the wives of the sages, as well as the attendants holding their parasols and chowries in their hands, should be made utterly infatuated by passion. (64)

The characteristics of the Kaṅkāla [mudrā]: the left half of the body should be straight, standing with both feet even; the left hand should rest upon the thigh, and the right hand should be in the *abhaya* (fear-dispelling) gesture. || 65 ||
In the same way, his two other hands are adorned with an axe and a conch;
there should be half a crown on the left and half a matted lock on the right.
The left half [of the body] should be like that of Hari, and the right half like that of Hara;
thus, a single form of both Hari and Īśa should be fashioned so as to be beautiful. (67)
The characteristics of Hari-Hara are as follows:
his thread for wandering for alms should be exactly like that of Samabhaṅga;
he has a mass of matted hair scattered about, is naked, and is intent on departing.
The right hand is extended, as if in contact with the face of a deer; the left hand holds a skull-cup, and likewise, there are two hands raised upward.
In his right [hand] there should be a ḍamaru drum, and likewise a peacock-feather garland in the other;
he is adorned with a necklace of serpents, a sacred thread, and a waist-string. (70)
One should assemble all the remaining [details] here as well, just as in the case of Kaṅkāla.
This is the characteristic of wandering for alms.
And one should perform the supreme act of bestowing grace upon Caṇḍa, just as in the case of Umāsahita. 71.
The right hand is in the boon-granting gesture (varada), while the other [left hand] rests upon the head of Caṇḍeśa;
and Caṇḍa, with palms joined in reverence (kṛtāñjalipuṭa), sits below, seated upon Śivāsana.
The characteristics of Caṇḍeśa’s grace are as follows: likewise, Dakṣiṇāmūrti is seated upon the throne of Śiva;
his face is half-turned, and he is adorned with a beautiful mass of matted hair. (73)
He has the crescent moon, the Ganges, the skull, and the serpent as his crest-ornaments;
and he holds a rosary and fire in his lower right and left hands respectively.
He should have the seal of radiant consciousness, with one hand placed upon the knee;
his left foot should rest upon the right thigh, while the other lotus-foot hangs down.
The Lord, who has overcome epilepsy and is served by hosts of sages, should be depicted beneath a banyan tree,
engaged in the act of exposition.

The characteristics of Dakṣiṇāmūrti: By the power of yoga, he who is the time of time (the destroyer of death) should be engaged in the dramatic representation of a dance. His right arm, holding a trident, should be raised up to the ear. (77)
Therein, another [deity] is the Giver of Wealth (Savarada), with the needle-gesture (sūcīmudrā) on the left;
and another there within [the enclosure] is joined with a plough and sprouts.
The right foot should be firm, reaching from the crown of the head to the hairline;
the left leg should have its knee raised above the navel and reach the heart of Kāla.
She should be depicted with three eyes, wearing a crescent moon in her matted hair, clad in a fierce attire, draped in a tiger skin, and adorned with ornaments of serpents. (80)
Kāla, too, shall be blue in color, lying prostrate, cast upon the ground;
with noose in hand, rolling eyes, mouth wide open, he is terrifying.
He should have fangs and tawny hair standing erect, and he should be pressing down with his foot and big toe upon the earth;
this is the characteristic of Kālakāla.
Born from the *liṅga*, he stands within the *liṅga* like Candraśekhara.
The pair of feet [of the deity] should be hidden below the ankle, at the base of the *liṅga*; the Grandfather (Brahmā), in the form of a swan, should be placed ascending upwards to the right.
The Varāha [image], however, should have Hari with palms joined in añjali and facing downwards on the left.
This is the characteristic of the Liṅgodbhava [form].
Regarding the height of the door-liṅga: the best is when it is as high as the door; the middling is by a reduction of one-fourth. (84)
The lowest [type] should be half as much less; it should be a bull endowed with auspicious marks, one and a half times as high as the door, or perhaps double that with a quarter added.

From one cubit up to nine cubits, there are three grades—low, medium, and high. In the case of the height of a bull, it is traditionally held that one part in fifty equals one finger-breadth (aṅgula).
The length of the bull, however, is five-fifths of its height; from the top of the head to the base of the neck it is long by six parts, and the neck is eight mātrās in length.
The area from the throat to the chest consists of six parts;
the length of the two thighs is six finger-breadths (aṅgulas); the knee is two mātras; the shank is six mātras; and the hoof is elevated by two parts.
The interval between the peaks (śṛṅga) should be eight parts; the height of the peak is four aṅgulas.
The forehead is nine parts wide, and the width of the face is five aṅgulas. (89)
The height of the face shall be five parts (bāṇa), while the length of the eyes shall be two parts starting from the *kolaka*.
Its width shall be one and a half *mātrās*, and its height shall be four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
The distance between the eyes and the ears is the length of the ear, measured by five parts;
the nose is one and a half mātrās long, and its width is less than one aṅgula.

The lower lip should be two or three parts [in height], while the tongue is three, two, or one mātrā long; the palate is long and elevated, and the hump of the back is six or four parts of the body, slightly curved.
The width of the two thighs (ūru) should be ten, eight, and four finger-breadths respectively;
their length should be five parts (pañcāṃśa), while the knees (jānu) and the two shanks (jaṅghā) should each be two parts.

The length [of the body] is three *rāma*s (twenty-seven units) by parts; the height of the hoof is three *mātrā*s; the length of the tail up to the hock is three parts; and its width at the base is greater than that.
The tip of the tail should be one and a half parts; the width of the scrotum should be three *mātrās*. Its length should be two *mātrās*, and the length of the penis should be three *mātrās*. (95)
The remainder should be determined by reasoning through inference, whether it be lying down or standing.
This concludes the section on the characteristics of the bull.
Now, the trident (triśūla) is prescribed to be equal in height to the door or equal in height to the pillar. 96.

When two parts are subtracted from the portion of the higher bliss, there are the middle and lower [measures]; or, by the number of cubits equal to four, three, and two, there are the three types, beginning with the best.
The height of the trident's shafts shall be ten parts, and the elevation of their blades shall be three parts;
the central blade shall be half a part in height and shaped like a three-jointed thunderbolt.
In the height of the petal, there should be eight parts; from one part comes the width of the petal.
In the middle petal, the central joint should be greater by two barley-corns (yava). || 99 ||
In the upper part of the petals, the length of the stalk is one-eighth [of the total];
the stalk is like an upturned lotus, and above the stalk are the lateral petals.

Having positioned [the instrument] at two and a half parts on the middle petal, one should rotate it from both sides until reaching the tip of the lotus, and then draw [the lines] from the tip of the trident onto the side petals.
Then, standing upon the middle petal, one should draw a line evenly from the ends of the side petals to the boundary on both right and left sides. || 102 ||
The base of the middle petal, however, should be as wide as half the width of the petal;
its tip should be three-quarters of the petal's width, or its thickness should be two-thirds of that.
One should have the leaves made with a hundred edges and sharp blades; in the center of the middle leaf there should be a lotus, and elsewhere, other petals.
The tip of the middle petal should be prominent, resembling a bud by one-quarter of its measure;
the side petals at their tips should have the shape of bamboo leaves, while the middle petal [is positioned] there.
One should fashion the circular base (vṛtta) between those two at half a part;
from its own length, the width of the shaft (daṇḍa) shall be five-fifths of a part.
It should be well-rounded, free from blemishes, beautiful, and provided with a base plate beneath the neck; below that, it should be adorned with pedestals such as a maṇḍika or a water-pot.
The base of the staff (daṇḍamūla) should be lotus-shaped and three times its own width;
one should apply beauty everywhere through reasoning, by means of *ūha* and *pratyūha*. || 108 ||
It may be made of gold, silver, copper, or iron, according to one's capacity;
it should have the characteristics of a circular trident.
On this point, the Svāyambhuva states:

The *vṛtta*, the *tribhaṅgi*, and the *vetāla*—thus the trident (*śūla*) is said to be threefold; it is, respectively, for pacification (*śāntika*), for nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), and for malevolent rites (*abhicāraka*).
Thus it is said;
therein the conduct has been fully explained, and that is the same across all three [stages]. || 109 ||
But that which is distinguished by the three bends (tribhaṅga) consists of two side-leaves;
its middle part should be bent inward from the midpoint of the circle.

The trident has three bends. The leaves of the vetāla [staff] also have straight tips, measuring one-eighth [of the total length]; the vetāla is fixed at the base of its shaft, which measures one-fifth [of the total length].
It is provided with four bells at the four corners of its blade;
this is the characteristic of the Vetāla-spear.
One should fashion everything for the khaṭvāṅga in the same manner as the Vetāla-spear. 112.
With a skull at the center of the petals and so forth, joined with a Vetāla as before, it should be enriched with a circle of peacock feathers; the blade should be at the base.
It is provided with eight or four bells and faces facing the east;
like a bedstead (khaṭvā), it has four corners, and its staff is shaped like a board.
The decoration of creepers, leaves, and so forth may be executed through the application of *ūha* (adaptation) and *pratyūha* (counter-adaptation).
This concludes the section on the *khaṭvāṅga*.
Gaṇeśa should be five *tālas* in height, and he may be either seated or standing. (115)
Below the uṣṇīṣa is the face, one tāla in height; the arms are one and a half tālas long.
The neck is curved and hidden; he has the face of an elephant and three eyes. (116)
The measurement from the neck down to the line of the hips is two and a half *tālas*;
the feet should be one and a half *tālas* long, and the body should be robust throughout. (117)
Thus, the measurement of all [deities] has been clearly explained in its entirety and in due order;
here, the characteristics of the sixteen forms have been stated individually and collectively in brief.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Sixteen Forms," in the Kriyāpāda of the Siddhāntasāra, which is the Śrīmad-Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati.
Now begins the forty-fourth chapter.
When the temple has been completed, and likewise when the linga is ready for installation,
one should take hold of the temple from the hand of the carpenter, encircled by three threads made of kusha grass.
Having completely encircled [the area] with a garland and having scattered unbroken grains of rice everywhere, one should place a full water-jar and a lamp in the center. || 1 ||
Then, one should recite the hymn beginning with "kṛṇuṣva" here, verse by half-verse;

at the end, however, one should join the first half of the verse "dahāśasādyam" and recite the remainder in its entirety. In this manner, it shall be effective for the destruction of demons during recitations and other rites.
Having again prepared a sacrificial mound in the direction of the fire and having established the fire there according to the prescribed rule,
he should first offer oblations to the mouth of the fire, and then sacrifice with both [mantras] beginning with "rakṣohaṇaṃ vājinam."
Furthermore, having offered oblations with clarified butter (ājya) in due order using the mantras beginning with *kṛṇuṣva*,
one should likewise offer with the five distinct mantras beginning with *ye devāḥ*, and with four [mantras] beginning with *iṣe tvā*,
and similarly with those beginning with *agnim īle*, and with *agna āyāhi* preceded by [the previous].
And [the hymn] "śanno devīr abhiṣṭaye. || 5 ||
Then, one should offer oblations with the five Durgā mantras declared in the Vedas; the first Durgā mantra shall be the Ṛg verse beginning with "jātavedase."
The second [verse] beginning with "tām agnivarṇām" has been proclaimed; "agne tvaṃ pārayā navyo asmān" is the third.
"May he deliver us from all distress"—this is declared as the fourth mantra;
"the conqueror of armies," and so forth, is called the fifth mantra. (8)
One should offer oblations separately with clarified butter using these five Durgā mantras;
then likewise with the Vyāhṛtis, and again with the Aghora-weapon mantra.
Thereafter, he should offer one hundred oblations with *apāmārga* fuel-sticks and clarified butter, using this same clarified butter;
then, after performing the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering one hundred and eight times, he should take the remaining clarified butter.
Likewise, [he should consume] the remainder of the water. || 10 ||
Having taken that ash and mixed it with the juice of *apāmārga* in a vessel,
one should sprinkle the entire house, its precincts, and so forth with it, while surrounding the area with *darbha* grass. Then,
taking that fire and placing it in the northeast corner, or alternatively at a crossroads;
Having offered oblations of blood, water, and rice-balls, and having thus completed the offerings to the quarters,

one should perform the pacification of the site (vāstūpaśama) right there, in the north-eastern direction of the pavilion. Having placed the fire in the center of the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), one should spread the sacrificial grass.
Having instructed [them] with *darbha* grass according to the rule, || 13 ||
In the eastern direction, on ground upon which a mandala has been drawn and which is evenly strewn with śāli rice, one should place rice covered with a cloth,
and that too should be completely covered with a cloth.
Having scattered there items such as the śamya-plant sprouts and having placed upon it jars filled with unbroken rice (akṣata), he likewise filled another jar with water,
along with gold, cloth, unbroken rice, perfumes, and flowers.
Having recollected the peace [brought about] by the mantra "śanno devī," one should recite it;
then, having established the fire there according to the procedure prescribed in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra* and having performed the "mouth of the fire" (*agnimukha*) rite,
one should offer oblations in sequence with these mantras— a sacrificial porridge (*caru*) prepared with cow's milk and sprinkled with clarified butter.

Having recited the *puronuvākyā* beginning with "O Lord of the Dwelling (*vāstoṣpati*), acknowledge us," one should offer the oblation after pronouncing the *yājyā* beginning with "O Lord of the Dwelling, [protect] us together with the assembly," and then recite "O Lord of the Dwelling, may the pillar be firm" for the sake of domestic prosperity and the removal of fear.
And by means of [the recitation of] "akṣispandādinā," as well as "duḥsvapnetyādinā," and also by "vāstoṣpate prataraṇo na edhītyādinā. || 19 ||
He indeed offers oblations with the mantra beginning "amīvahā vāstoṣpate," and he also offers oblations of clarified butter with the five Brahmans and the Śaṃnu sections.
Then he offers sacrificial pegs, fuel sticks, clarified butter, and cooked rice;
furthermore, he offers one hundred and eight blades of dūrvā grass that have been purified with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Then, one should offer oblations of Jaya and the others with the mantra "śaṃ no devī"; after that, having performed the Sviṣṭakṛt offering, one should smear the ground.

There, having spread darbha grass in front of the fire, one should cast the remnants of the oblation with the mantra beginning "Obeisance to Rudra, the Lord of the Dwelling" (namo rudrāya vāstoṣpate).

Having washed the cooking pot with this very mantra, one should pour that water into some vessel after washing it; then, [one should place] the remaining clarified butter and the remaining water [therein]. (24)
Having unified [the elements] with the mantra, one should do so either with a branch of the udumbara tree, or with a branch of the palāśa tree,
or again with a handful of darbha grass.
In the case of temples, pavilions, and so forth, one should circumambulate three times everywhere while sprinkling water;
then, having honored the twice-born, one proceeds around.

One should feed [the guest] with this mantra: "You are a brahmin, you are a sage. Having first caused [the guest] to pronounce blessings, one should cause him to say, "May there be auspiciousness. (27)

For the sake of pacifying the palace and for purification here, the *rakṣoghnahoma* and the *vāstuhoma* must also be performed prior to the ritual of the installation of the *liṅga*; this has been stated here according to the rules.
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, on the *rakṣoghnahoma* and *vāstuhoma*, in the *Kriyāpāda* of the *Siddhāntasāra* within the *Śrīmadīśānaśivagurudevapaddhati*.
Now begins the forty-fifth chapter.
The installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) of *liṅgas* such as the *niṣkala* and others is recorded as being fivefold:
*pratiṣṭhā*, *sthāpana*, and likewise *sthitasthāpana*.
The distinct characteristics of raising up [the image] and establishing it are now written;
wherein, having first placed that linga upon the Brahma-stone (brahmaśilā), || 2 ||
The application of the *piṇḍikā* (pedestal) is performed; they call that *pratiṣṭhā* (consecration).
The installation of *bāṇaliṅgas*, those of the sages (*ārṣa*), and self-manifested (*svayambhu*) [liṅgas] is likewise [performed]. (3)
If there is a single pedestal for liṅgas made of jewels, gold, and so forth, then it is designated as *sthitasthāpana*; and when [the pedestal] has decayed, it becomes *utthāpana*.
The installation should likewise be performed for manifest [deities] such as Viṣṇu and others;
then, during the northern solstice, in the bright fortnight, at an auspicious moment endowed with excellent qualities.

On a day and so forth characterized by an auspicious lunar date, asterism, weekday, yoga, and other factors— devoid of the previously mentioned defects and endowed with the aforementioned virtues— and which is highly esteemed.
The rite of consecration (pratiṣṭhā) is commended when it is favorable to the patron; one should construct a square pavilion in front of the temple.
(422) With excellent timber, bamboo, and other materials, it should be made very beautiful with new [components];
for the first triad of liṅgas, ranging from one hasta up to nine hastas.
In the third [case], it should be with eight, ten, ten, and twelve [fingers],
and with those equal to nine and twenty-one.
It is joined to the boundary walls and adorned with doors on the four sides;
it consists of eighty-one square sections, with the center [occupied] by a group of nine.
One should construct a beautiful altar (vedi) elevated by one-sixteenth of the height of the mercury (rasa),
and one should fashion eight sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) in the directions starting from the east in due order.
The first is based on the Vedas, the second is a crescent moon, the third is a triangle, the fourth is a circle, the fifth is a hexagon,
the sixth is lotus-shaped, the seventh is an octagon, and the ninth is a square.
That [image] is prescribed to face the east in the space between Indra and Īśāna;
the Liṅga should face the west in the space between Rakṣas and Varuṇa.
Some say that all [the mandalas] are either square or circular;
however, for those possessing the three characteristics beginning with the "youngest" (kaniṣṭha), they consist of cubits (ratni) and the measure of a forearm (aratni).
The sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) should be of the smallest size and so forth, according to the number of oblations (āhuti) offered at night;
however, in the case of the fivefold form (pañcamūrti), there should likewise be five such pits.
There should be four square fire-pits in the cardinal directions, five in the middle between Īśa and Śakra, and one in the direction of Vāyu;
or, in case of inability, there may be a single smallest pit.
To the northeast or to the north of the consecration pavilion,
one should likewise construct a bathing pavilion measuring half its size.
Then, having left one row of squares on all sides outside of that, one should construct the bathing altar (snānavedi),
six parts high, surrounded by six parts [in width].
One should construct a beautiful raised platform (vitardikā) equal in width to the height; and the water-overflow channel should be auspiciously situated to the north.
One should prepare the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and other implements individually, equal in number to the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*).
One should also prepare the sleep-pitcher (*nidrākumbha*), the peace-pitchers (*śāntikumbha*), the Śiva-pitcher, and the *vardhanī* for the weapon-mantra.

One should likewise place the pitchers of the Lords of Knowledge and the World-Protectors, or those attached to the arches, as well as the vessel for the oil massage, the garments, and the eight auspicious symbols.
Rice grains, sacrificial pots, water jars, the five products of the cow, the nine gems, gold, and abundant quantities of honey and clarified butter. (22)
Clays originating from mountain peaks, riverbanks, crabs' dwellings, lake shores, sacred fords (tīrtha), the horns of bulls and elephants, anthills, and the edges of ponds. (23)
Then [he offered] the waters of the eight oceans and rivers, as well as the waters of sacred fords (tīrtha),
along with the barks and young sprouts of the milk-tree (kṣīra-āga), the rose-apple (jambu), and the mango (āmra).
Two silver vessels, two golden rods, an auspicious seat,
all medicinal herbs, minerals, seeds, metals, a pestle, and so forth.
One should also bring whatever household utensils have not been mentioned, as well as water-vessels, mechanical contrivances, supports, sugar-candy,
and guggulu resin.
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, saffron, a yoga-band, betel,
areca nut, oil, or a new bed or plank.
All items suitable for the bed, such as new woolen blankets and fine silk cloths from the celestial realm, should be placed upon the Uttaravedī within the Maṇḍapa of the Lakṣaṇoddhāra.

One should arrange [the syllables] in nine squares, beginning with the square of Śiva, in sequence; the square of Śiva shall be in the center, and likewise in the eight directions starting from the east.

The principles ending with the final category (tattva) consist of the individual soul (puruṣa), primordial nature (prakṛti), and the limiting factors known as space, lordship, knowledge, illusion (māyā), time, and necessity; these are the compartments.

The five products of the cow (pañcagavya), beginning with milk, [should be placed] in the center and in the intermediate squares; likewise water, the implements for the fire-oblation (homa), clothing, and whatever is required for incense.
Then, in the southeast and southwest, one should perform the rites of illumination, waving of lights (nīrājana), and so forth;
in the northwest, [one uses] bark, decoctions, and the like; and in the northeast, sandalwood and such.
Furthermore, one should station the multitude of ritual officiants according to their respective designations;
moreover, the archways (toraṇas) should be made of Plakṣa, Udumbara, Aśvattha, and Nyagrodha wood.

The names Śānti, Bhūti, Bala, and Ārogya are assigned in order starting from Indra (the east) to the three genders beginning with the little finger (the neuter), measured by five, six, seven, and eight *kiṣkus* respectively.
The auspicious spikes (śūla) should be as high as the [respective] sections, with their widths being half of that height;
they are, in order, nine, eleven, and thirteen units in height.
The width between the prongs is composed of parts of the *vasu-paṅkti* and *jagatī* meters;
the prongs are [presided over by] Aryaman, Mitra, Tvaṣṭṛ, Bhaga, and Purandara. (36)
Parjanya, Viṣṇu, Savitṛ, Dhātṛ, Īśa, Varuṇa, and Pūṣan are declared to be the deities; three in each triad, beginning with the east. (37)
One should place two banana trunks at a time, rooted, adorned with fruits and sprouts, provided with water-basins and *sāla* trees, as supports for the archways.
Then, having decorated the upper consecration pavilion as beautifully as possible with new materials such as dukūla, devāṅga, and paṭṭa cloth, [one should proceed].
Having covered the pillars with unwashed white cloths that have been washed,
it should be adorned with hanging strings of pearls, garlands, betel nuts, flowers, and other ornaments.
Having wound a garland of *darbha* grass all around while recollecting the weapon-mantra,
[he should perform the rite] with a broom made of *darbha* bundles and *palāśa* leaves.

Having cleansed [the area] from the east (Indra) to the northeast (Īśāna) in a clockwise direction, one should smear it inside with cow-dung mixed with water strained through a cloth, while reciting the Gāyatrī mantra.
One should sprinkle [the site] with fragrant water while reciting "āpaḥ punantu" and so forth, and with *darbha* grass, unbroken grains, and white flowers while reciting "iṣetva" and so forth. (43)
Or, having scattered white mustard seeds (siddhārtha) on the ground around the weapon-mantra,
the preceptor, together with the image-bearers (mūrtipas), should then perform the consecration (adhivāsana).

Those who have completed their Vedic studies and vows, who are of noble birth and possess auspicious marks, who are neither too young nor too old, and who are adorned with learning, good conduct, and other virtues. (45)
Having chosen those eight with the previously mentioned mantras and having worshipped them, or in the case of five,
having chosen those five with those same five mantras.
One should also adorn [the image] with garments, rings, and bracelets according to one's ability; having first performed the rite of offering sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) on the fifth or seventh day.
The preceptor, having been requested and honored by the sacrificer as before, and having performed his daily rites and bathed, remains near the pavilion with speech restrained.
Having washed his hands and feet and sipped water for purification, with a serene mind, he should properly worship Gaṇeśa upon a sacrificial mound outside the pavilion. (49)
Having obtained permission, the Guru should then pray for the rite to be free from obstacles, using garlands, perfumes, incense, lamps, and so forth, as well as fruits, sweetmeats, and laḍḍukas.

With the mantra "yoge yoge" or "yogaḥ," one should join the arches (toraṇas) in sequence starting from the base; or with the mantra "devasya tvā," one may also join them with the spikes (śūlas) along with one's own limbs.
Having covered it with new garments and even with leaves of the mango and *aśvattha* trees,
one should first arrange the mantras beginning with "uttiṣṭha brahmaṇo" at the front and the ends.

Having filled the pits and pounded them down, and having smeared the roots with cow dung, one should place banners marked with the weapons of the world-protectors (lokapālas) in the cardinal directions as well as in the center.
[He beheld] those who were white, red like Indra’s bow (the rainbow), black, dark-blue, and smoky;
those yellow, lotus-red, pale-white, and possessing the luster of peacock feathers.
In the center, one should cause it to fall with the Pāśupata weapon or the Aghora weapon;
all the banners, adorned with flags, should rise higher than the half-torana.
Then there are Bhṛṅgin and Mahāsena, the lords of the banners, as well as Vṛṣa, Nandīśa, Mahākāla, Kumbhodara, and Mahodara.
Vīrabhadra, as well as Brahmā and Vāstvīśa, are thus proclaimed. Then, by the Brahmins assuming their respective forms, [the offerings were made] in the center of the altar.
The preceptor should first cause the auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be performed according to the injunctions of his own Veda;
[he should select those] who are endowed with noble lineage, good character, learning, and conduct, and possessed of auspicious marks.
Thirty-two, sixteen, or eight Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas, who are purified by vows such as the Kṛcchra, who have been invited beforehand, and honored. || 59 ||
Seated in the east, south, north, and west, those of firm vows should,
at the beginning of their study, perform the rite prescribed by their own Vedic school in each respective direction.
Having designated the *puṇyāha* (auspicious day) and so forth as an ancillary part of the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), the Guru,
with waters of the *puṇyāha*, [sprinkles] inside the pavilion while circumambulating it to the right.
One should sprinkle the outer archways and other structures with a bunch of darbha grass;
at that very time, O brahmins, the students should begin their recitation according to the prescribed directions.

Then, having prepared the general offering (sāmānyārghya) with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and so forth, one should first worship the banners with the mantra consisting of the *tāra* (oṃ), one's own name, and the word *namaḥ*. (63)
Having worshipped the arches of Peace and the others with their respective names, and having placed the suns upon the spikes,
one should then worship them in the pitchers at the bases of the arch-branches.
Mahodara and Mahākāya, Mahākaṇṭha and Mahodara, Agninetra and Agnijihva, and then Virūpākṣa in the north. 65.
And [he should worship] Viśālākṣa and the eight lords of the Gaṇas in order starting from the east,
as well as Sahasravīcī, Vimalā, Śatadhārā, and Pramodinī.
One should worship the deities of the doors within the gentle jars at the entrances by their names: Kumbhakarṇa, Bhadrakarṇa, and Śvetakarṇa.
One should also [worship] Gokarṇa and those situated at the eastern and other doors and in the southern pitcher;
then, by means of three claps, a snap of the fingers, a strike with the heel, and a glance, [one performs the purification].
One should swiftly remove the obstacles situated in the celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial realms;
then, having reached the western door, one should employ the iron-arrow weapon (nārācāstra).
Without touching the threshold, one should enter leaning against the left doorpost; having placed the Astra-mantra on the threshold, one should circumambulate it clockwise.
Facing east and standing in the southwest (nairṛta), one should worship Vāstveśa upon the ground;
likewise, one should worship Brahmā, the presiding deity of the site, in the center, along with his own seat.
Therefore, having sat down facing the northern direction with a serene mind, one should first perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and then the ritual of empowerment (sakalīkaraṇa).
Having constructed a rampart outside the pavilion with the *astra* mantra using the index finger,
he should wear a turban and upper garment consecrated with the root mantra.
Having prepared the special *arghya* offering and having sprinkled his head with it, he should place the hand of Śiva— smeared with sandalwood paste— upon his right side.

Having uttered the Śiva-mantra, which consists of light and ends with the syllable of peace (Śānti), and while recollecting it, one should place it upon the crown of one's own head, contemplating, "I am Śiva. (75)

But having beheld the entire pavilion and so forth from the perspective of ultimate reality, holding the sword of knowledge in his hand as before, he should [proceed] according to rule in the five compartments.

Having prepared the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), he stands in the pavilion in the southwest; having scattered the offerings (vikira) in the northeast, he places the Śiva-vase, the weapon-vase, and the vardhanī-vessel.
Having fully occupied the moving seat presided over by the two Śivas, one should worship [the deity] whose vehicle is the bull and the lion with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Then, at the gates, he should place in pairs the deities named Praśānta, Śiśira, Parjanya, Aśoka, Sañjīvana, Amṛta, Artha, Īśa, and Kusuma.
Having placed them on both sides, one should worship the gatekeepers beginning with Nandin: Nandīśa, Mahākāla, Bhṛṅgīśa, and Gajānana.
One should worship Vṛṣabha, the six-faced Kārttikeya, and the goddess Caṇḍī in order, starting from the east;
likewise, one should worship the ten guardians of the directions, beginning with Śakra, in the pitchers placed in their respective directions.
Having invoked and worshipped [the deity], one should circumambulate the jar clockwise with the *vardhanī* as before,
and having placed the jar down, [one should sprinkle] with water gathered by means of *darbha* grass.
Having prepared a seat with scattered offerings, one should place the *vardhanī* vessel upon it;
then, one should announce the command of Śiva to Indra and the other world-protectors in due order.
Oṃ!
Ho, Śakra! By the command of Śiva, you must remain vigilant in your own quarter for the pacification of obstacles until our return. 84.
With these and other [mantras], one should cause [the deities] from Brahmā down to Ananta to be heard by their respective names.

Then, having properly worshipped the jar (kumbha) and the vardhanī vessel with perfumes and other offerings, one should present the sword of knowledge (jñānakhaḍga) to him after the concluding offering (nivedya). || 85 ||
And with this [mantra], one should also pray:
"O Śambhu! You, together with your attendants and your sons, must remain here until the end of the sacrifice."
Śaṅkara, together with Ambā, was the presiding priest of the sacrifice! || 86 ||
Having been told "So be it" by Śiva,
he placed the *arghya* offering before the water-pot and [took] the scattered offerings from the sacrificial pavilion.

One should visualize the obstacles as having been cast far away by means of blazing weapons; then, having sat down before the central sacrificial pit according to the prescribed rule, [one should proceed].
Having properly established the Śiva-fire in a consecrated vessel and having purified it with the five sacraments ending with the [disciple's] name, the Guru worships it. (89)
Situated in the directions from the center to the east and so forth, or divided fivefold,
one should place the fire-angles for each respective direction into their corresponding fire-pits (kuṇḍa).

Then, having invoked Śiva into the fire of the central sacrificial pit, the preceptor should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) for the mantras; that [libation] begins with the root mantra and ends with "to Śiva."
The fourth [mantra] should end with "agnipriyā"; having offered one hundred and eight oblations with that, he offers a tenth part of those as oblations for the Brahma-mantras and the limb-mantras.
Having established the peace-pitchers (śāntikumbha) for each individual fire-pit (kuṇḍa) with the Śiva-weapon mantra,
and having performed the oblations with the residual drops (saṃpāta), the Guru, together with the bearers of the [deity] forms (mūrtidhara), [proceeds].
Having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), he should proceed to the pavilion for the removal of marks (lakṣaṇoddhāra-maṇḍapa),
which is located either to the north or the northeast of the consecration pavilion (adhivāsana-maṇḍapa).
One should construct a pavilion for the extraction of the characteristics, endowed with the three altars;
therein, upon the southern altar, one should place the *liṅga* on a pedestal.
And one should prepare a pedestal to its south for the purification of the form, using the eight types of earth previously mentioned and the decoctions prescribed in their proper order.
Having bathed [the deity] with cow urine and cow dung, and with flowers, incense, and water,
on the second day, one should perform the rite upon an altar or a prepared sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
Having placed the liṅga upon that [altar] with śāli rice and grains, one should perform the extraction of the marks according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Then eight or four women possessing auspicious marks should touch that image with *darbha* grass and likewise perform the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*).
Having struck [the object] with the Astra-mantra and having enveloped it with the Kavaca-mantra using the water for the Arghya offering,
one should then perform the worship either with its own specific mantra or with the general one.

One should consecrate [the image] individually with cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and honey; then with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), water infused with kuśa grass, and scented water.

Then, having worshipped with garments, perfumes, garlands, incense, lamps, and offerings, he mounted him upon a chariot and so forth, accompanied by the sounds of kettledrums, drums, and ḍiṇḍima cymbals.

With the sounds of jhallarī cymbals, timila drums, conchs, tāla-clappers, mṛdaṅga drums, and kāhala trumpets, and with the auspicious resonance of flutes, ḍamaru drums, lutes, and other musical instruments; (103)

With songs, dances, cries of victory, and blessings; with lamps, umbrellas, and chowries; and with spectacles, banners, and other such items, one should perform the circumambulation of the village and so forth.

Having approached a river, sacred ford, lake, or similar body of water for the purpose of the preliminary consecration with water (jalādhivāsa), and having reached its bank, one should establish the deity upon a well-smeared surface and worship him.
Even more so, having constructed a four-legged water-shed in the middle of the water reaching up to the navel,
one should cause Śiva to lie down upon a pedestal or similar surface within it.
Wrapped with garments and darbha grass, with its head toward the east and the thread positioned above,
one should place a seat beside it, adorned with darbha grass, cloth, and other materials.

Having placed eight water-pots for protection, with the world-protectors (lokapālas) as their presiding deities, and having worshipped them in the various directions as well as the guardians stationed all around; || 108 ||
Having passed five, three, two, or one night, or even half a day or a single watch,
he should rescue the liṅga and, having placed it on the bank, worship it.

Having bathed [the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and so forth, as well as with the nine jars, and having anointed it with a series of fragrant pastes and a garment of red silk; || 110 ||
Having covered him with golden garlands, adorned him, and honored him, he placed him upon a vehicle such as a chariot amidst the auspicious sounds of dance, song, and other festivities. || 111 ||
With hymns and the chanting of the Vedas, one should perform a circumambulation of the village and other such places;
there, one should cause a linga to be made from gold, cloth, and other materials.
The sacrificers and others scattered small shells, betel nuts, silver, parched grain, unbroken rice, and so forth,
as well as abundant showers of flowers.
The Guru should walk in front, and the patron (yajamāna) behind;
the bearers of the [deity’s] forms should sprinkle the path with the common arghya water. (114)
Having reached the bathing pavilion and circumambulated it clockwise, one should bring the deity down at the western door of the pavilion.
Having offered the arghya water at his feet, one should lead him inside the pavilion; there, in the center, one should establish Śiva upon the opening of the auspicious throne (bhadrapīṭha).
430) One should also worship the pedestal on the southern side with perfumes and other offerings.
Thus [ends] the procedure for consecration, including the pavilion and so forth, along with the instruments and the purification of the vessel.
Likewise, having reflected upon the ritual consecration of water as it has been correctly described in the various manuals of the Śiva-tantras; || 117½ ||
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, concerning the characteristics of the ritual for installation, in the Kriyāpāda of the Siddhāntasāra, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva.
Now begins the forty-sixth chapter.
Then the preceptor, with a serene mind, having bathed together with the bearers of the [divine] forms,
washed his feet, sipped water for purification (ācamana), and entered the bathing pavilion.

Having first caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, one should worship Gaṇeśa in the front and [the deities] in the south; then, having performed the scattering of the *vikira* offerings, one should set out the Śiva-pitcher (*śivakumbha*) and the *vardhanī* vessel.
Having placed [the deity] and worshipped it, and having performed the protection rite in the pavilion by mistake for that [deity],
one should sequentially arrange forty-nine water-pots in the eastern direction.
With ten threads each running eastward and northward,
there shall be nine squares in the center, and two rows and three [squares] in each of the directions.
Having established [the layout], one should cleanse it so that there is a row like four paths;
six squares separately in each direction, and four squares in each corner.
But for the nine [vessels], one should fill the eastern and subsequent jars in sequence with astringent decoction,
cow urine, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and likewise milk.
Then one should remember prosperity, curd, soft earth, and kusha-grass water; one should remember the seven oceans and the jar as the eighth, containing the cosmic waters.
In the center, one should fill the Brahma-pitcher with fragrant substances; in the second enclosure, however, [one places] clarified butter, cow dung, honey, and sugarcane juice.
Nutmeg-water, coconut, citron, pomegranate, plantain fruit, lime, jackfruit, and bilva fruit; || 9 ||
The waters of sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and saffron—these sixteen; and the jars situated in the third enclosure, numbering eighteen. (10)
Having recollected the sacred fords (tīrthas) such as the Gaṅgā and others, one should fill [the vessel] completely: the Gaṅgā, Śatadru, Yamunā, Narmadā, and Sarasvatī. (11)
The Gomatī, Sarayū, Sindhu, Śoṇā, Tāpī, Paruṣṇikā, Godāvarī, Kṛṣṇaveṇī, Nandā, and also the Bhīmarathī. || 12 ||
The Tuṅgabhadrā, the Vegavatī, the Kāverī, and the Tāmraparṇikā; as well as Prabhāsa, Naimiṣa, Gokarṇa, and Tripuṣkara.

One should likewise visualize Kedāra in the eastern and subsequent pitchers in due order; having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) with the Brahma-mantras and the ancillary mantras (aṅgas) in their respective directions, one should worship the group of nine.
In the second enclosure, one should place the jars with the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas) and the eight forms (Mūrtis);
in the third enclosure, with the Tattvas beginning with Śakti and ending with Dharā.

One should worship the pitchers, together with their grass-brooms and wrapped with threads, by placing upon them the syllables *tāra* (oṃ), *svākhyāta* (samyak-saṃbuddhāya), and *namaḥ*, excluding the ten sense organs and the mind.
[He saw] those [vessels] clothed in gold and jewels, adorned with sandalwood and garlands, containing mango and pipal leaves, along with lids, fruits, and unbroken grains of rice. || 17 ||
Having filled the jars according to the rules, one should worship them with perfumes and other offerings. Then, having prepared nine squares in the western part, || 18 ||
The preceptor, having filled and worshipped a set of nine jars— consisting of eight jars associated with the Lords of the [eight] forms and one in the center associated with Śiva— [should proceed].
Then, in the five compartments, one should worship five jars filled with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) in sequence starting from the northeast,
using the five Brahmā-mantras, and provided with golden wicks.

Having established the fire upon an altar in the east according to the prescribed rite, and having invoked Śiva along with his limbs (attendants), [one should offer] sacrificial wood, clarified butter, sesame seeds, and cooked rice.

Having offered oblations with the mantra-saṃhitā and eight hundred oblations with the root-mantra, and having offered oblations with the Brahma-mantras and their limbs in a tenth part [of that number], one should collect the residual clarified butter (saṃpātita-ghṛta).

Having poured [the water] from the Brahma-pitcher with the tip of a blade of kuśa grass, one should then perform the bath; having offered the arghya with the heart-mantra upon the head, one should remove the flowers and other offerings.

First, with the immortal Vedic hymns beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," and then with flowers, he should ensure that the head [of the deity] is not empty, with incense placed between the water and the flowers.
Having thus performed the consecration, offered the *pūrṇāhuti*, and worshipped Śaṅkara,
one should then proceed with the sequence of installation using forty-nine jars. (25)
One should [purify] with the ash of cow-dung decoction and earth, with the *vyomavidyā* mantra, with cow-urine using the *gāyatrī*, and with milk using the mantra "cāpyāyasva. (26)
With the mantra "dadhikrāvṇo" he should offer curds, and with "devasya tvā" he should offer kuśa-water; likewise, in the second enclosure, he should offer ghee with the mantra "tejo 'si."
With the mantra "madhu vātā" [he sprinkles] with honey; with "gandhadvārām" [he sprinkles] with cow-dung; with the root-mantra of sugarcane [he sprinkles];
and with "ākṛṣṇena" [he sprinkles] from the gem-vessel.
Having worshipped with Brahma-mantras, water from fruits, the Śrīsūkta, sandalwood paste, and so forth, followed by water and incense, one should worship with the jars in the third enclosure.
With the eleven Anuvākas, one should bathe Śiva with Rudra;
having worshipped him with offerings beginning with perfumes and ending with oblations, accompanied by the sounds of musical instruments and the like.
Having performed the *ārātrika* ceremony, one should then consecrate the Lord of Gods with the water from the Brahma-pitcher while reciting the root mantra ending with the five-syllabled mantra.

Having worshipped again with perfumes and other offerings by means of the latter nine [verses], one should bathe [the deity] with the *pāvamānī* verses, and again with the *brahma* verses in the middle.
Having again worshipped Śaṅkara with offerings beginning with perfumes and ending with oblations, he was granted permission by Śiva and Śivā residing within the water-pot.

Having sprinkled the pedestal (piṇḍikā) in the Vardhanī vessel with its own mantra, encapsulated by the seed-syllable of Gaurī and preceded by the syllable Om, one should then [sprinkle] it with the Śiva-pitcher.
One should bathe Śiva with the collection of mantras ending with the Vyomavidyā; and with the Aghora mantra, one should smear the liṅga and the pedestal with fragrant unguents.

Having adorned [the deity] with garments and other items on the left, one should worship with flowers; however, one should cause incense, lamps, and food offerings to be presented with the Puruṣa-sūkta.
With the hand of Sagandhaśiva, one should touch the four directions of the Liṅga with the Gāyatrī mantra,
touching each of its three sections while recollecting the respective [deities].

Having performed the lustration ceremony with white, fragrant flowers, as well as garlands, incense, and lamps, and with flour-lamps and other offerings, one should then cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited.
Having covered the linga with two silken cloths, the twice-born should raise it up with auspicious musical instruments and the mantra beginning with "Arise, O Brahmaṇaspati. (39)
Having led the Lord to the consecration pavilion with songs and dances, one should bring him down through the western door and worship him according to one's desire.
First, upon a bed-platform prepared with a svastika drawn from rice grains on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila),
one should place either a tooth-stool or a firm, new plank.
Having spread it with blankets made of wool and silk fabrics such as *kauśeya*, one should prepare a beautiful bed provided with pillows and an upper coverlet.
One should then install the eight auspicious symbols—the conch, the discus, the banner, the mirror, the bull, the goad, the fly-whisk, and the pair of fish—in the various directions. (43)
Then, having caused the liṅga to enter [the sanctum], the preceptor, together with the guardians of the images (mūrtipās),
should lay it down upon the couch with its head [toward the east], using the Śikhā-mantra as its pillow.
Having offered [the weapon] and covered [the deity] with armor, one should worship until the end of the food offering (*naivedya*).
Regarding this, the *Mañjarī* states:
"Having placed [the deity] upon the bed facing the temple, one should [transfer] that consciousness by means of the left-hand mantra."

Having duly enshrined the Supreme [Deity] within that [liṅga], which is endowed with the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan) and resplendent with the five Brahmans, and having conceived it as the manifest (sakala) form of the Vyomavyāpin mantra according to the sequence of emanation, one should divide it into three principles (tattvas).
Thus, having brought all the household utensils and set them down. || 45 ||
One should offer a silver vessel filled with honey and ghee at the [deity's] feet,
and worship with the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra together with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya), as well as with the verse "āpo hi ṣṭhā."
One should fill the pitcher called Nidrā near the head with the Astra-mantra;
having filled both the Śiva-pitcher and the Vardhanī there as well, one should worship them.

(434) One should demarcate the boundaries with garlands around the pitchers of the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśa) at the Linga, each in its own respective domain, for the purpose of making known the principles (tattva) beginning with the Self (ātman). || 48 ||
At the doors, one should place two small jars each, and at the corners, rows of sprouts; at the archways, one should set two shallow bowls with auspicious sprouts.
Outside the jars of Nidrā, Vidyeśa, and Kumbha, having constructed three ramparts with ashes, *kuśa* grass, and sesame seeds, one should install the lords of the worlds within them.

At that time, the students should also recite the Astra-mantras; furthermore, they should recite the Vedas while positioned in the cardinal directions starting from the east, and likewise Rudra, Kadrudra, Bhāruṇḍa, and the Camakas in the intermediate corners.
Then the preceptor, facing either east or north, having sat upon his seat with the [deities] bearing forms, should thereafter contemplate the three parts within the liṅga.

In the portions belonging to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa, one should install the principles beginning with the end of the Tattvas and the Self (Ātman), along with the Lords of the Principles (Tattveśvaras) and the Mūrtiśvaras together with their forms.

One should place the principle of the self (ātmatattva), ending with Māyā, within the portion of Brahman; therein [one places] the Tāra, the seed-syllable of the heart, and the principle of the self, ending with "namaḥ. (54)
Likewise, one should also place [the mantra] "Obeisance to Brahman, the Lord of the Reality of the Self," and then place the *tāra* (om) joined with the head-mantra (*śiras*). 55.

Having performed the placement (vinyāsa) of the *vidyātattva* up to the end of the region (*sadeśānta*), ending with the dative case and the word "namas," one should place the *tāra* (the syllable Om) upon the head and [the mantra] "to the Lord of the *vidyātattva*. (56)

Having said "Salutation to Viṣṇu," one should place [the mantra] upon the portion belonging to Viṣṇu; however, from the topknot upwards, the Śiva-tattva ending with Śiva should be placed with the Praṇava (Oṃ).

Likewise, one should place the word "I" (ahaṃ) ending in the dative case, followed by "to the Lord of the Śiva-principle" (śivatattvādhipāya) and ending with "obeisance to Rudra" (rudrāya namaḥ), in the portion belonging to Rudra. || 58 ||
One should separately assign the eight forms— designated as Earth, Fire, Sacrificer, Sun, Water, Wind, Moon, and Ether— to the three parts [of the body] individually.
Śarva, Paśupati, Ugra, Rudra, Bhava, Īśāna,
Mahādeva, and Bhīma— these are the guardians of the eight forms.

Preceded by the seed-syllable *tāra* (oṃ) at the heart, one should place [the syllables] in sequence from the east to the northeast within the eight petals, using the mantras of their respective names ending with *namaḥ*. (61)
One should suppress [the breath] with force and worship with perfumes and other offerings; indeed, in the installation of Śiva alone, there are five forms according to the five-fold system.
The lords of those [elements] known as earth, water, fire, air, and space are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva. (63)
When the installation for one desiring liberation is performed according to the five-fold system, there are the five digits beginning with Nivṛtti,
as well as the [five] forms and the guardians of the forms.
The five [faces], beginning with Sadyojāta, are situated in their respective directions starting from the west;
then, when the pedestal (liṅga) located to the north has been bathed, it is treated in the same manner as the [central] liṅga.
When the Bhagāṅkā has been worshipped according to the rules in the middle of the cavity,
and likewise when the Brahmaśilā is established at the base of the Liṅga.

One should also install the respective lords of the principles (tattveśvaras), as well as the embodied and unembodied lords; therein, one should likewise install the mistress of the principles beginning with the Self (ātmatattva), together with action, knowledge, and will.
Having placed the forms beginning with Earth (Kṣmā), one should place the presiding deities of those forms, beginning with Dhārikā:
namely, Dhārikā, Dīptimatī, Ugrā, Jyotsnā, and likewise Cetanā. (68)
Balotkaṭā, Dhātrī, and Vibhu—these are the eight guardians of the forms (mūrtipās).
They are for the practitioner who desires enjoyment during the consecration on the pure path.
From Śuddhavidyā up to the end of Śakti, the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas) are remembered as the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās).
On his very throne, the Lords of the Forms (Mūrtīśvarīs), beginning with Ananta, are situated in sequence.
Similarly, in the fivefold system as well, the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās) are designated with feminine endings; these six are known as Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Kriyā, Jñānā, Īcchā, and [the sixth]. 71.
Those deities who reside on the path of the pure and impure, beginning with Puruṣa and ending with Māyā—for their installation, the guardians of the form (mūrtipāḥ) [are required]. || 72 ||
The Lord of the World (Bhuvaneśa) shall be the size of a thumb, and Bhava shall be the one-eyed (Ekapiṅgekṣaṇa) Īśa;
both Bhava and Mahādeva of great splendor shall serve as the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās) in rites for desired objects and for consecration.

Those deities who reside on the impure path, beginning with earth and ending with primordial nature (prakṛti), are the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās) such as Kapālīśa and others during their installation.
Kapālīśa, Agnirudra, Yama, Nirṛti, Bala, Śīghra, Nidhīśa, and Vidyādhipati as the eighth. (75)
