Indra and the others are traditionally known as the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās) during the consecration of the deities Vasu, Āditya, and Rudra, as well as the Yakṣas, the lords of the Bhogins, the Rākṣasas, and human beings.

That is to say, the eight world-protectors beginning with Indra. When the consecration is performed for the purpose of minor malevolent rites and the like, there should be eight image-guardians (mūrtipās), namely the Bhairavas beginning with Asitāṅga. || 77 ||
Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodhana, Unmatta, Bhairava, Kapālī, and Bhīṣaṇa; the eighth is known as Saṃhāra. || 78 ||
In the consecrations of the fierce *pratimās*, the presiding deities are Tamā, Ādikā, Mūrtīśvarī, Tamā, Mohā, Kṣayā, Niṣṭhā, and Mṛtyunā; likewise,
Mayā and Jvarā are the presiding deities for the fierce ones, corresponding to the elements beginning with Earth.
But in the fifth fortnight, she was seized by Tamas and by terrible Moha.
Arati and Jvara are the presiding deities (mūrtīśvarīs) declared in sequence; this same procedure is considered applicable for the consecrations (pratiṣṭhā) of all images. || 81 ||
In the consecrations of female deities (strībera), the visualization of the three parts extends up to the knees, the throat, and the head;
however, the power of action (kriyāśakti) resides in the pedestal.

Having performed the placement (nyāsa) upon the body for the Knower (jñānin), one should perform the remainder as in the case of the sacred seats (pīṭha). This concludes the section on the placement of the principles (tattva), the lords of the principles (tattveśvara), the forms (mūrti), and the lords of the forms (mūrtīśvara).
Having thus placed the principles, their lords, the forms, and the guardians of the forms... [83]
One should worship [the deities] with their respective names, beginning with "Tārā" and ending with "namaḥ.
One should then meditate upon the presence of the principles (tattvas) and so forth within the liṅga and other such objects. || 84 ||

Then, having gone to the vicinity of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), they should sequentially invoke the principles (tattvas) beginning with the Lord of Principles (Tattveśvara) and others into the pits, and offer oblations separately with clarified butter.
p.
437) That is to say—
having first placed the *ādhāra-śakti* in the heart of *Tāra*, and having worshipped it in the fire;
Having offered three oblations, one should then deposit the principle of the self (ātmatattva).

At the end of the mantra for the Lord of the Reality of the Self, one should add "namas" (salutation) to Brahmā; then, having invoked and worshipped the forms beginning with Earth, as well as the presiding deities of those forms.
Having invoked them in sequence and worshipped them, he performs oblations of ghee— one hundred and eight, or half of that,
or half of that again— for the principles (tattvas) and the other elements.
Thus, they should offer oblations to those who bear distinct forms by means of their respective forms.
Then, the preceptor and all the others, having gone together to the vicinity of the Liṅga— 89.
Having touched the respective locations of the forms with the roots of *kuśa* grass,
they should recite the mantras of the forms and their presiding deities as many times as there are oblations.
One should separately address Brahmā, the presiding deity of the *ātmatattva*, with the command of Śiva:
"Oṃ!
O Brahmā, presiding deity of the *ātmatattva*! As long as this *liṅga* remains on earth... (91)
"By the command of Śiva, you must remain faultless and well-established for now.
Saying "Oṃ, obeisance to Brahman," they touch the images with the root mantra using the roots of *kuśa* grass. (92)
They should sprinkle the base of the *liṅga* separately with the waters from the *śānti*-vessel.
Then, having gone back to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), [they should recite]:
"Oṃ, obeisance to the *ātmatattva* and the *vidyātattva*."
Having thus contemplated the reality, || 93 ||
Having joined the pure and the impure, one should deposit the Vidyātattva;
preceded by the Tāra and the Hṛt, as before, ending with "Namaḥ" for the Vidyātattva. (94)

Having worshipped and offered oblations with clarified butter (ājya) to Viṣṇu with the mantra "Salutation to Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Principle of Knowledge," as well as to the forms (mūrtis) and the lords of the forms (mūrtīśvaras).

Having invoked [the deities], one should offer oblations as before; those standing near the linga should likewise recite [mantras] while touching the middle [part] of the linga with the middle of the kuśa grass.
One should separately proclaim the command of Śiva to the mantras of the embodied and the formless:
"O Viṣṇu, Lord of the Vidya-tattva! As long as this Linga remains upon the earth... (97)
p.
438) "By the command of Śiva, you must remain faultless and well-established for now.
Oṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu.
And they should sprinkle [the area] with the water from the peace-pitcher (śāntikumbha) as before, starting from the root mantra. || 98 ||
Having gone to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit as before, and having contemplated the pure and the impure,
one should join [the two] within the principles (tattva) called Vidyā and Śiva, ending with the word "namaḥ."

Having established the Śiva-tattva and having worshipped it as before, he should offer oblations; and having assigned the forms (mūrtis) and the lords of the forms (mūrtīśas), they should offer oblations separately as previously described.

Having likewise gone to the vicinity of the *liṅga*, they should then mutter the root mantras at the tips of the *kuśa* grass, touching the portion belonging to Rudra, according to the number of oblations offered.
Having sprinkled [the area] with water from the *śānti*-vessel, they should cause [the officiants] to hear the command of Śiva:
"O Rudra, Lord of the Śiva-tattva! As long as this liṅga remains upon the earth... (102)
"By the command of Śiva, you must remain faultless and well-established for now.
*Oṃ rudrāya namaḥ*.
In this manner, one should [worship] upon the pedestal and in the Śivā [liṅga], beginning with the Tattvas and so forth, along with their respective forms. (103)
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) and touched [the disciple], one should purify him and also cause him to hear the command of Śiva.

Then, one should offer oblations of clarified butter (ājya) by means of the Sadyojāta and other [faces of Śiva] along with their limbs (aṅgas), each in its own respective direction, a thousand times, half that number, or a hundred times, as well as with the Vyāhṛtis.
On this point, it is said in the Mañjarī:

One should offer oblations individually with the *vyāhṛtis* using fuel-sticks (*samidh*) of *palāśa*, *udumbara*, and *pippala* wood, each soaked in milk, clarified butter, and honey, a thousand times at a time; or likewise, one may offer oblations with sesame seeds using the mantras of the eight forms (*aṣṭamūrti*).

The Guru should reverently perform oblations there with clarified butter, in due order, using the mantras of the Mūrtis, Gaṇanāthas, and the Lords of the Directions, as well as the mantras of the weapons such as the Vajra.

One should offer oblations of *caru*, parched grain (*lāja*), barley meal (*saktu*), white mustard seeds (*siddhārtha*), sesame seeds (*tila*), and barley (*yava*), as well as rice (*vrīhi*), into their respective directions with the appropriate mantras as before. Then, having offered a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with all these substances combined, one should do so from the root mantra of oneself.

Then, having arisen, the Guru [should worship] the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti), consisting of sound, within the right ear of the God, preceded by the syllable *tāra* (oṃ) and the heart-mantra (*hṛt*). || 106 ||
Having said, "Salutation to Śiva," one should dedicate the performed action. Oṃ.
O Blessed One! In all three parts, the ritual action has been performed by me.
"O Lord! By your grace, may all that be fulfilled!"—thus one should offer [the gift].
Having thus restrained her with harsh words and worshipped her with perfumes and other offerings... (108)
Having offered some *bali* at the conclusion of the oblation according to the prescribed rite in all directions,
one should spend the night without sleep, diverting oneself with dance, song, and other entertainments.
Thus, concerning the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) of Śambhu, beginning with the initial bathing and so forth,
the entire procedure for the placement of the principles (*tattva*) and other elements has been described, by which the rite of the preliminary dwelling (*adhivāsa*) is accomplished.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Kriyāpāda* of the *Siddhāntasāra*, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva.
The forty-sixth chapter: On Acceptance.
Now begins the forty-seventh chapter.

Then, at dawn, the preceptor, having bathed together with the image-bearers, as well as the patron along with his sons and others, [should perform the rites] prior to the auspicious moment for installation.
Having reached the temple while reciting the Śivāstra mantra, the preceptor should dispel the obstacles by looking at them and then enter the temple of the deity.
Having determined the center of the Śiva [mandala], one should place the Brahma-stone (brahmaśilā) there;
as follows:
having determined the portion of the door in the four directions within the womb-chamber (garbhabhavana). || 3 ||
One should divide that area with twenty-two threads running eastward and northward;
therein, the central square is known as Brahmā.
And having divided that [space] into six parts by means of lines running eastward and northward, there shall be thirty-six squares; and from the center of those squares—
p.

440) That which lies between the two lines in the northeast and northwest directions is the abode of Brahmā; indeed, that must be avoided in the consecrations of Śiva and the other deities, who are situated in the center.
If, out of delusion or negligence, one should install a linga or other object in the middle of a Brahma [image],
then it will cause the destruction of the king who rules the kingdom.
When the square located to the northeast of the Brahma-square has its thread-junction situated in the northeast corner,
it shall be positioned in the middle of the *liṅga* during the consecration ceremony.
Having thus understood the center to be Śiva, one should establish Śiva in that very place;
one should then divide the inner sanctum (garbhāgāra) into forty-nine compartments (seven times seven).
The central square should be the Brahma-square; outside of that, there are eight squares which constitute the divine (daivika) region; and outside that enclosure, there are sixteen squares.
Then, outside the enclosure, there is the one called Mānuṣa with its constructed compartments; therein is the field named Paiśāca, and the installation of these is now described.

The installation of Śiva is performed in the Brāhma rite; for Viṣṇu, it is prescribed in the Daiva rite; for all the gods, it is in the Mānuṣa rite; and for the Mothers and Rākṣasas, it is in the Paiśāca rite.
It is recommended for the Daivas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Nāgas, and others; herein Maya says:
in the inner sanctum (garbhāgāra), which is divided into seven parts, the central portion is for Brahmā and the divine deities.
The human [realm] is one-eighth of that; however, the external piśāca realm is one-sixteenth, which is twenty-four parts.
The Śaiva, Brāhma, Vaiṣṇava, and all divine deities are to be established in the divine portion; in the demonic portion, the Mothers, Asuras and others,
Rākṣasas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Nāgas are to be established.
Thus,
from the center of Śiva, to the south of the Brahma-thread, and likewise to the north.
Having stretched the eastern thread straight through the center of the squares,
one should install Viṣṇu and the other deities in order within their respective central positions upon it.
One should place the deities facing west in the eastern plots, facing east in the western plots, and facing north in the southern plots. (15)
One should [place] Viṣṇu and the others in due order and by proper method in the northern and southern portions; this is the section concerning Śiva as the central deity.
Now, for the successful installation of the gems and other items upon the Brahma-stone (brahmaśilā): || 16 ||
p.

441) One should fashion pits in those respective directions as well as in the center according to the proper method; just as it was previously stated regarding the center of the Śiva[-stone], so too regarding the center of the stone. || 17 ||
The preceptor, facing either north or east, together with the image-bearers, should establish [the deity] amidst the sounds of musical instruments and the abundant chanting of the Vedas. (18)

Having uttered "Oṃ namaḥ vyāpini," [one should address] the firm, immovable, and constant [goddess]; then the seed-syllable of the earth (laṃ) ending with the nasal drop (bindu), and likewise the syllable hṛllekhā (hrīṃ) with the wife of fire (svāhā). || 19 ||
The seed-syllable of the heart preceded by *tāram* (oṃ), followed by "to Ādhāraśakti" and ending with *namaḥ*;
likewise, having uttered "Anantaśakti," one should similarly append *namaḥ*.
Having established the Brahma-śilā, one should touch it and consecrate it with this mantra:
"Oṃ!
You alone are the supreme power; you alone are the sustainer of the seat. (21)
"O Goddess! By the command of Śiva, you must remain here forever;
for, having visualized the entire path ending with Śuddhavidyā within her. (22)
One should arrange the five groups of jewels and so forth in their proper order: the diamond, the sun-gem (sūryakānta), the sapphire, the great sapphire, and the pearl. (23)
Puṣyarāga is for the head, vaiḍūrya and padmarāga [are for the other parts],
while māṇikya is prescribed for the center, extending from Indra to Īśāna.
Copper, tin, lead, silver, brass, bell-metal, iron, and gold—these, starting from the east and ending in the center, [are the nine metals]. (25)
Tāla, śilā, torikā, mākṣika, hemamākṣika, gairika,
gandhaka, abhra, and pārada is remembered as the ninth.
Uśīra, harikrāntā, red sandalwood, agallochum, śāri, utpala, māleya, ruk, and the one called śaṅkhakusuma; || 27 ||

Then one should place medicinal herbs, and likewise rice, wheat, sesame seeds, black gram, mung beans, barley, śyāmāka, and śāli rice; these should be placed starting from the direction of Indra (the east).
When the condensed foundations are established and gems and such are unavailable, [one may take] vajra, gold, and mercury from among the five groups beginning with gems. (29)

One should place *yava* grains in the shape of a lion’s stride (*harikrāntā*) within the central pit; one should then separately deposit the various groups of jewels and other substances with the *kalās* beginning with Sadyojāta. (30)

In the center of the pit, one should place either a golden tortoise or a bull, surrounded by the [mantras] beginning with *sadyojāta* and ending with *brahma*, or else by those known as the *lokeśas*.
Having established [the deities] with the Ananta-mantra in the eastern, southern, western, and northern directions, one should place the bull,
the axe, the rosary, and the golden trident.
Having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa) with the kalās beginning with Nivṛtti and having indeed smeared the stone,
one should cover it with milk-rice (pāyasa) and with a clean, unwashed cloth while reciting the Varma-mantra.

Having worshipped with offerings beginning with perfumes and ending with the presentation of food, one should offer the oblation to the quarters (diśābali) consisting of kṛsara, cakes, parched grain, water, dhānā, turmeric, and barley flour.
Having sequentially offered [oblations] of sugarcane juice and food with the names of the lords of the directions, [one should say]:
"Oṃ!
Having placed the god Rudra at the forefront, may they accept this bali. (35)
"We worship all beings here, ending with the Piśācas. Homage to all beings dwelling in every direction.
Having thus offered [oblations] in each direction, having bathed and sipped water (ācamana), one whose mind is serene— (36)

One should offer a hundred oblations with the Astra-mantra to destroy defects such as flaws in the stone; then, having raised the Liṅga from the heart and offered Arghya with the Siraḥ-mantra, [one should proceed].

And having praised him with words of auspiciousness such as cries of "Victory!", along with the sounds of songs and musical instruments, and with gifts of gold, jewels, garments, and the like. || 38 ||
Having led the deity clockwise around the sacrificer and others who were scattering [flowers], the preceptor,
together with the guardians of the images (mūrttipas), should then bring it down at the doorway.

Having established [the deity] upon the auspicious seat (bhadrapīṭha), one should say, "May you be firm. This applies even to a door, its lintel, and so forth, where no sacrificial grass (prastara) has been laid.
Without making physical contact, one should cause that linga and pedestal to enter within,
either at the threshold, the door-posts, the wall, or above the udumbara beam.

If one touches the *liṅga* or the pedestal (*pīṭha*), then even a great fault occurs; for its pacification, one should perform oblations with the Brahma-mantra, the root-mantra, and the limb-mantras, and give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). || 42 ||
Without touching the branches and other parts, one should insert the internal liṅga; this is when the wall has not yet been commenced and the door has likewise not been constructed. (43)
Then one should cause the deity to enter by way of the region designated as the door; thereafter, having worshipped the Brahma-stone (brahmaśilā), one should cover the sky with weapons (hetis).
When, having removed it from the hollow of the rock, one enters the linga, it is rendered straight by means of an appropriate machine without effort. (45)
Likewise, when the auspicious moment had arrived and the preceptor was present together with those bearing the [divine] forms, he meditated, "I am Śiva," at that well-determined instant. (46)
Meditating on that unity of Śiva and Śakti, while perceiving Śakti as a stone,
one transcends the heart, throat, palate, the space between the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahmā.

Having abandoned the causal deities beginning with Brahmā, and while reciting his own mantra up to the Niṣkala [level], he of serene intellect, having installed the Liṅga, should meditate upon it. 48.

Having meditated upon the path of the principles (tattvādhvan), beginning with Śakti and following the order of Īśāna, Puruṣa, and so forth, according to the path of emanation, within the form of the Liṅga; || 49 ||
One should fill the cavity of the stone with pure sand; then, having repeatedly ground it down, one should fill the cavity with a golden probe.
Having led the pedestal near the top of the liṅga by means of suspension ropes, one should then slowly lower the liṅga once the auspicious moment has been well determined.

Then, recollecting the mantra in the order of emanation: the syllable *tāra* (om), the seed-syllable of Śakti (*hrīṃ*), followed by the word for the power of action (*kriyāśaktyai*), and ending with *umāyai namaḥ*.
While reciting [the mantra], one should join the pedestal with the liṅga; when the liṅga or the pedestal being installed happens to move, [one should perform the rite]. (53)
Whichever direction it has entered, one should perform a rite of pacification (śānti) for that respective guardian of the quarter (dikpāla) by means of its mantra,
having first stabilized it in its own place with threads.
Having offered two hundred or three hundred oblations of clarified butter and sesame seeds,
one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consisting of an elephant or one fashioned of gold for the deities beginning with Indra.
A golden buffalo, a goat, a pearl necklace, brass, a milch cow,
and silver should be given in sequence to the *sthāpaka*. (56)

Then, having prostrated to the *liṅga* and the *pīṭha* which have attained oneness, the preceptor (*ācārya*) should offer a hundred oblations of clarified butter with the *brahma-mantras*, the *mūla-mantra*, and others.
Having returned and bowed to the Lord of Gods, the Guru should petition: "Be gracious regarding his faultlessness; O Lord, forgive this transgression."
Having said this, one should fill any small cavity with sand and make it completely seamless by means of the eightfold binding.
Lac, resin of the Sarja tree, conch-shell, sand, the juice of the three myrobalans (triphalā), and kunduruṣka— these, when ground together, are declared to be this "adamantine ointment" (vajralepa).

This means "it is indeed raw. Alternatively, lac, resin of the *sarja* tree, beeswax, powdered sugar, *guggulu*, red ochre, molasses, and oil are declared to be the eightfold binding (*aṣṭabandha*). (61)

There should be an increase in the proportion of the final ingredient, and the cooking process should be like that of a viscous substance. Furthermore, [this is done] with equal parts of lac, resin, and bdellium. (62)
The powder of sarja should be equal [in weight] to that, and half as much as the gairika;
one should apply oil at the proper time with a measure equal to half of all these ingredients. (63)

Having combined [the ingredients], one should cook them in an iron vessel over a gentle fire using a ladle; for even here, the cooking must be known by the skilled practitioner as being until it becomes smooth and glossy (cikkaṇī).
Having applied these eight types of binding, one should bring about firmness so that the liṅga and the pedestal are without any gaps, such that water cannot enter.
Alternatively, the making [of the image] seamless with lead plates is prescribed;
then, having washed the linga with skillful application according to the method of removal and replacement, one should proceed.
Having consecrated [the deity] with the jar of sleep and also with a little water for rinsing the mouth,
one should proceed in order with the *arghya*, the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), and the offerings of water and incense.
Having rubbed [the image] with barley, wheat flour, and other substances, one should perform the consecration;
then, one should [consecrate] the Śiva-pitcher and the Vardhanī vessel situated upon the bed-altar.

Then, having brought [the deity] together, one should consecrate the Lord with the jars of the Vidyeśvaras; thus, having consecrated [him] in due order beneath the pedestal in its respective directions. (69)
Furthermore, one should place the *śāntikumbhas* in their respective locations; then, having offered the *arghya* and performed worship, [one should present] the *bali*... || 70 ||
Touching the pedestal with his fist and Śiva with the tip of his thumb,
he should meditate on the Liṅga as Śiva and remember Pārvatī as the Piṇḍikā.

The mantra for Śiva consists of the syllable *tāram* at the beginning, followed by "to Śiva" at the end, and the word *namaḥ*. For Śakti, it is likewise *tāram*, followed by "to Kriyāśakti" and "to Umā," ending with *namaḥ*.
One should join the two mantras for the sake of liberation for one desiring enjoyment; however, they should be joined in reverse order in the third part beginning with *ka*.
One should install the principles beginning with the Self (Ātman) and the lords of those principles in sequence as before;
one should also install the supports (Ādhāra), Ananta, Dharma, and so forth, as well as Vāma and the others, situated upon the sacred seats (pīṭha).

One should [install] the Mūrti-vidyā-tanu-mantras in the liṅga, beginning with the Tāra and Hṛdaya; likewise, one should [install] the Mūrti and Vidyātanu with the five kalās and the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan).

Having contemplated everything through the relationship of the pervaded and the pervader, one should join them; the form [of the deity] consists of the principles ending with Śakti, and possesses a circle of arms extending in the ten directions.
The divine one has five streams as her faces and the five mantras as her body;
she has Nivṛtti as her feet, shanks, and thighs, and Pratiṣṭhā as her hips and other parts.
Her heart is knowledge, her chest is speech, and her lotus-face is peace;
the kalā beyond peace is her head, and the path of the worlds is her body hair.
She is known as consisting of the path of phonemes, mantras, and sacrifices, as well as blood; she consists of the path of the principles (tattvas), marrow, semen, bones, and all the remaining paths.
Having recollected the root mantra, together with Śiva at the *dvādaśānta*, as a mass of consciousness, the supreme, stainless light, from the lotus of one's own heart; 80.

Therefore, having brought [the deity] from the handful of flowers in due order to the head of the Lord, [one should place him] within the lotus of the heart by means of the form, through the path of the channels, as far as the linga.
Having established [the deity] in every part of the form, one should place the limbs upon the form:
the letter *ṣa* (ṣa), joined with the sixth vowel (*ū*), with the nasal dot (*bindu*), followed by "to the Power of Consciousness, salutation" (*cicchaktaye namaḥ*). || 82 ||

Having uttered this [mantra] beginning with *tārā* and so forth, one should deposit the pervasive *liṅga*. Then, having restrained it as before, [one should perform the rite] with [images] fashioned from flour and other materials. (83)

One should anoint Śiva with the respective weapons of the world-protectors while reciting their respective mantras, using designs such as the nandyāvarta, utpala, ambhoja, śrīvatsa, svastika, and lotus. 84.
Having rubbed [the image] with flour-paste and scented water consecrated by the Aghora-weapon mantra, one should bathe Śiva properly with a mirror and a fly-whisk.

One should worship the deity with the aforementioned services, beginning with garments, ornaments, and perfumes, up to the offering of food (naivedya); then one should perform the recitation of the mantra one hundred and eight times.
Having first uttered the name of the sacrificer, ending with a word denoting sovereignty, one should pray: "Be ever present in this [image]. (87)
Saying "So be it," and being authorized by the gods, the Guru went to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit and offered ghee and milk-rice with the root mantra and the Umā-mantra.
Having installed Vṛṣa in the east and Lakulīśvara in the south, one should install Gaṇeśa in the southwest and the world-protectors (Lokapatis) in their respective directions as well. (89)
Having established Mātṛs to the west of Yama, the Teacher (Śāstṛ) in Mṛga, and Guha in Bhallāṭa,
one should place them in the eight directions starting from the east in due order.

Having established fires upon the sacrificial altars, the guardians of the images (mūrtipās) should each offer oblations separately: with the verse "indrakratuṃ naḥ" for the fire dedicated to Indra, and likewise with "agniṃ dūtam" for the fire dedicated to Agni.

In the *nāka* [direction] is *suparṇa*; in the southern direction is *yāmya*; in the south-western direction is *moṣuṇaḥ parā*; in the western direction is *yaṃ rakṣanti*; and in the north-western direction is *vāyav āyāhi mārute*.
One should place King Soma in the north and Tryambaka in the northeast;
[the sacrificial posts] are made from Palāśa, Khadira, Aśvattha, Plakṣa, Nyagrodha, and Bilva wood.
And eight fuel-sticks of *Audumbara* and *Kāṣmarya* wood, in due order;
he offers oblations with all the substances, but in the middle with the limbs, the *Brahma*, and the root-mantras.

With those very same materials and the mantras of Lokeśa, one should offer oblations into the various directions; and at night, one should present a bali-offering to the Gaṇas, starting from the east in due order.
The First Day. (p. 447) Then, on the second day, the Guru, together with those bearing the [divine] forms, having bathed according to the daily ritual procedure, [proceeds].
Having worshipped Śiva according to the prescribed rite. || 96 ||

To make [the ritual] free from defects, one should first offer clarified butter into the sacrificial pits located in the south, west, north, and southeast, using the mantras of Śiva, Aghora, and Astra.
Likewise, by means of the Pāśupata weapon and the Mūla-mantra in due order,
and from the Āgneya weapon up to the Aghora weapon, and with the Sāvitrī mantra, [he acts] by the command of Śiva.
Having worshipped the Lord three times a day with a thousand recitations of the Gāyatrī and likewise the Gaurīgāyatrī, and having offered the bali-oblation to the spirits at night; || 99 ||

On the third day as well, having worshipped the deity according to the prescribed rite as before, he offers oblations with clarified butter into the fire-pits of Indra and the other deities for the pacification of the quarters.

With the limbs of Brahmā and their respective mantras, one should offer a thousand oblations into each fire-pit, as well as the sacrificial porridge (caru) and the ritual offering (bali) in the tenth part of that amount, according to the previous procedure.
Then, on the fourth day, one should worship Śiva with special care, duly using water-pots numbering one hundred and eight.
Or rather, by means of [the mantras] numbering forty-nine, eighty-one, twenty-five, or nine, according to one's capacity and in accordance with the respective *liṅga*. || 103 ||

One should perform the bathing according to the procedure that will be explained hereafter in the chapter on bathing; and there should be a great food offering (mahānaivedya) appropriate to the ritual bathing.
Having offered ghee one thousand times into each pit for Vāgīśvarī,
one should offer oblations with the Brahmā-mantras and their limbs as before, and cook the sacrificial porridge (caru) in the Śiva-fire.

Having offered the *argha* to the deity, the preceptor and the image-protectors (*mūrtipāḥ*) should offer the remaining portion, divided into nine parts, into each fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) according to their capacity.
Having offered ghee according to his capacity with the eight mantras beginning with *Śivāstra*, which were prescribed for the second day, he offers a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) separately.

Then, having removed the withered offerings (nirmālya), having bathed [the deity], and having offered eight flowers, one should perform the directional oblation (digbali) and then recite one's own mantra with full devotion.
Having relaxed the fierce [form] in the image, one should worship [the deity] in the linga as blue-colored, four-faced, and three-eyed in each face. (109)
Four-armed, with a blazing face, his crest adorned with matted locks and the moon,
he bears a rosary, a trident, a chisel, and a water-pot. (110)
Adorned with a sacred thread, bracelets, and red garments— having meditated thus,
one should extract that [deity] from the liṅga and place it within the lotus of one's own heart.
Having established the fierce form (caṇḍabera) in its own place within the temple of Śiva,
one should install it upon the lotus-throne of the foundational power (ādhāraśakti) in its heart.

Having brought Caṇḍa residing in one's own heart, one should place him within the channel-path and worship him with the primary offerings in the sequence beginning with the seat and the water for honor (arghya).
It is as follows:
the Caṇḍāsana mantra should end with "namaḥ," and the form of Caṇḍa should be likewise; then there is the root mantra beginning with "dhunya" and so forth, followed by the word "Caṇḍeśvara. (114)
The seed-syllable of the crest (śikhā) ending in the dative case, followed by the syllable *phaṭ* and joined with *namaḥ*, constitutes [the mantra].
The limbs, beginning with the word *caṇḍa*, are the heart and so forth, in their proper sequence. (115)

Having worshipped [the deities] with the five [offerings], beginning with the seat, by means of the [mantras] ending in the fourth case, followed by *hūṃ phaṭ* and ending in *namaḥ*, and by means of the services such as bathing and so forth; || 116 ||
One should worship him with flowers and other offerings that have been presented as *nirmālya* to Śiva; then, having bathed the Liṅga and invoked the mantras as before, [one should proceed].
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and having presented the food offering (naivedya), the preceptor should offer seven oblations into the central fire-pit (kuṇḍa).
Namely:
stable, pervasive, and likewise immeasurable; beyond that, it is the beginningless Buddha, eternal, and consequently indestructible. (119)
"May you be eternally satisfied at the end of the seven," thus joined with "svāhā," these are the mantras;
having offered clarified butter with these, one should touch Śiva with these very same [mantras]. || 120 ||
One should offer a thousand, or half of that, or a hundred oblations of clarified butter with the Aghora-weapon mantra and the Vyāhṛtis; and then one should again offer a full oblation.

Having dismissed the fires of the individual mantras from the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) into the lotus of one's own heart, one should likewise [dismiss] Śiva, the water-pot, the weapon, the world-protectors, and the deities of the gates.
One should dismiss the deities residing in the arches, banners, and vases; having offered the *bhūtabali* at night and bathed together with those who bear the [divine] forms. (123)
Having circumambulated Śiva and paid obeisance, one should seek his grace; then, with gold, garments, fields, ornaments, and vehicles, || 124 ||
Having first satisfied the preceptor without any stinginess regarding wealth, one should [satisfy] the lords of the forms with a tenth part of that, and the students with half of that.

He should give half of that to the reciters, and half of that to those who desire to serve; likewise to Brāhmaṇas, to those bearing sectarian marks, to devotees, and to the poor, the blind, and others who seek assistance.
One should also satisfy others according to one's ability with gold and other gifts, or even with one's entire property, or half of it,
or a third part of one's own wealth.
The sacrificer should perform the consecration of the liṅga with devotion;
for he who, though possessing the means, performs the consecration with stinginess regarding his wealth, [incurs sin]. (128)
One whose mind is overcome by greed does not obtain that fruit; therefore, the offering of the respective fruits of their own actions is made to the patron.
Then the preceptor and others should perform [the rite] with hands holding water and flowers; thereafter, the patron, surrounded by his sons and other kinsmen, [should proceed]. (130)

One should provide the necessary resources there for the sake of accomplishing daily worship and other rites; whoever performs such acts with devotion, beginning with the construction of a temple, according to their own capacity. (131)
Having obtained his desired objects of enjoyment in that world through the installation of a *liṅga*, he shall,
at the end, attain the worlds he desires along with his sons, friends, and others.
He attains divine palaces and the like; for as many thousands of years as there are atoms within them, he enjoys pleasures and shall go to Śiva. || 133 ||
Thus has been duly described the consecration of the Lingas of Jyeṣṭha and the others belonging to the Moon-crested Lord,
after having examined in many ways the excellent Tantras proclaimed by Śiva up to their very limit. 134.
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, on Consecration, in the Kriyāpāda of the Siddhāntasārasaṃgraha, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva.
p. 450) Now begins the forty-eighth chapter.
Now, one should perform the daily festival (nityotsava) of Śambhu, which brings about his presence (sāṃnidhya).
By which misfortunes are pacified and virtues attain fulfillment. || 1 ||

Having worshipped the Lord at the three junctions of the day with offerings ending in the presentation of food and oblations, one should duly offer the bali-oblation to the attendants of Rudra according to the prescribed rite.
In this *Mañjarī*:
"One should perform the daily offering (*nityabali*) at the three junctions of the day as prescribed; for that purpose, one should cook the sacrificial rice (*caru*):
having washed the rice grains with water using the heart-mantra (*hṛnmantreṇa*), one should cook them in the fire."

Therefore, having sprinkled clarified butter over it at the time of cooking with the root mantra, and having removed it from the fire with that same mantra, one should fashion an auspicious emblem out of that sacrificial oblation.
Thus it is said:
"Just as in a golden vessel, so too in one made of silver or even copper;
sixteen finger-breadths in width, washed clean, and sprinkled with clarified butter. (3)

Having offered that consecrated oblation (havis) and sprinkled it with clarified butter while reciting the Heart-mantra, the Linga becomes elevated by twelve finger-breadths when measured by the root-mantra.
Having smeared that [image], beginning with the most excellent one, all over with clarified butter and curd,
he should invoke it into that [image] upon the head, together with a gold flower, by means of the root mantra.
One should worship Śiva, seated upon a moving throne, in due order with perfumes and other offerings,
accompanied by the sounds of kettledrums, small drums, the go-mukha, the ḍhakkā, the jhallarī, and cymbals.
With timila drums, madduka drums, ambhoja drums, tāla cymbals, kāhala trumpets, and mardala drums, as well as with flutes, lutes, and gongs— all proclaiming the procession for the offering— (7)
The musicians should play the middle [note] for sixty measures. Then, [he should initiate] the twice-born disciple who has bathed, is desirous of service, restrained in speech, and pure.

Having sprinkled that bull, which is adorned with a white turban, an upper garment, and ornaments such as bracelets, and having meditated upon it as possessing those [divine] marks situated within the vessel; 9.
Having placed [the vessel] upon his head, the Guru should offer flowers; likewise, O twice-born one, another may offer the entire linga made of gold or other materials.
Having first invoked Śiva, he should proceed while carrying [the image] upon his head, or on a chariot,
or in a palanquin, or on an elephant mounted by twice-born men. (11)
In the same manner, all the pure Brahmins, having bathed and restrained their speech, [prepared] umbrellas,
a canopy, a bell, flowers, and chowries.
With concentrated minds, they should hold garlands, perfumes, flowers, and incense; likewise, others should hold lamps, water-pots, mirrors, and golden sandals.
The Guru, carrying the general offering (arghya), proceeds. || 14 ||
Having worshipped the Gaṇas with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should cast the bali-oblation there;
in front of the deity, women of beautiful form should be well-adorned.
Others likewise performed singing and dancing, while others went before them bowing and offering hymns of praise.
Those who dance or sing are liberated from all sins;
[one should worship] the guardians of the eastern and other doors in the four directions of the celestial chariot.
And Nandin, Mahākāla, Bhṛṅgīśa, Gaṇanāyaka, Vṛṣabha, Ṣaṇmukha, and the Goddess... [18]
There, at the southern gate, [one should worship] Dakṣiṇāmūrti... [and] the world-protectors, Indra and the others, in their respective directions by their own names, such as Tārā and so forth. (19)
Having honored them with the salutation "namo 'ntam," one should offer the bali-oblation to them: to Indra in the east;
to Satyakāya, his son, and to Prabhā to his left; to Skanda in the east of Vāyu; and to Durgā to the east of Skanda. || 21 ||
To the east of Soma, to Kubera, and to Caṇḍeśa in his own domain, one should scatter the offering with the principal [mantras] in the sacred field.
Then, at the gate of the inner city-gate, one should scatter an offering for Tīkṣṇanetra as the gatekeeper on the south,
and likewise for Mṛgāsya on the north.
Then, having emerged from the gatehouse (gopura), one should proceed by way of circumambulation (pradakṣiṇya). At the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha),
those who pervade the entire world and abide there desiring the offering (bali)— they [should be honored].
May all the attendants of Rudra accept this supreme offering. || 25 ||
Having thus caused the assembly to hear [the teachings] of Śambhu, the Guru,
proceeding through the middle of the hall, should then cast the bali offering.
The eight Gaṇeśas, beginning with Nandin, along with ten million times ten million lords of the Gaṇas—namely Nandīśa, Mahākāla, Bhūtanātha, and Mahīdhara. (27)
One should scatter the bali offering to these [deities] starting from the east in sequence, using their respective names: Parvateśa, Guheśa, Kāla, Pāśaka, and Kapālī. (28)

Then, having worshipped those beginning with Bhūtidā who reside on the secondary pedestals (upapīṭha) all around the main pedestal (balipīṭha), starting from the east, one should scatter the sacrificial offering (bali).
Bestowing prosperity, difficult to behold, of terrifying form, yet possessing beautiful eyes; with a lovely face, three-pronged, triangular, and likewise having three heads.
Piṅgala, Harasena, and these ten leaders of the bhūtas— Piṅgala in that Kumudaka and Harasena likewise above.
In the center of the lotus of the seat, one should worship Harasena by his own name, ending with "namaḥ," and also with his Gāyatrī mantra.
"Oṃ, let us know Harasena; let us meditate upon Mahābala; may that Daśamūrti inspire us.
Having thus recited this, one should offer a *bali* with all kinds of food, along with flowers and other offerings, without exception, and having cast it [away].
Having paid homage, the preceptor should enter the temple of the deity.
Then, accompanied by the ornaments of music, dance, and the *tāṇḍava* performance, one should perform the second circumambulation, moving at a slow pace.
Having quickly led [the deity] around three times to the accompaniment of the sounds of song and musical instruments,
and having performed the circumambulation, one should cause the deity to enter the interior of the temple.
Having circumambulated the inner circle clockwise as before, and having washed his feet,
he should enter the pavilion or the half-pavilion.
Having seated [the deity] upon the pedestal, worshipped, prostrated, and propitiated him,
one should unite the Lord residing in the food-liṅga with the root-liṅga. || 37 ||
But in the case of a food-liṅga, having invoked Caṇḍeśa, worshipped him, and then dismissed him,
one should cast that temporary food-liṅga into deep water.

Or one should constantly give [offerings] to the cows; therefore, this is known as the "Eternal Festival" (*nityotsava*). This concludes the section on the Eternal Festival. Now, the procedure for the Great Festival (*mahotsava*) of Śambhu is described, by which [the gods] are gratified. (39)
The Gaṇas, together with their lords, shall bestow all peace upon men,
whether performed every year or even every six months.

One should properly perform the festival of the Śiva-procession for the sake of accomplishing all goals; therein, the procession should take place by means of a chariot or else by means of a palanquin and so forth. (41)

By way of metaphorical designation as a universal monarch (cakravartin), he is described by those very marks; [this includes] palanquins and the like, chariots and the like, as well as whatever vehicles such as couches there may be.
The designation "bed and seat" (śayanāsana) shall apply; its characteristics are stated separately.
The palanquin (śibikā) may be of three kinds: the *paiṭhī*, the *śaikharī*, and the *mauṇḍī*. (43)
The *paiṭhī* type ends with a wall; the *śaikharī* is provided with a pinnacle; the *mauṇḍī* ends above the pillars and is joined with a roof covering for the hall. || 44 ||
Their width and other dimensions are the same, and that is now described:
they are three vitastis in width and five vitastis in length. || 45 ||

The smallest, medium, and largest [measures] exceed [the standard] by three, six, and nine finger-breadths respectively; or they may be one and a half times longer in width, or even equal to the length of one's own ear.

The height of the wall should be half the [total] width; it is classified as excellent, middling, or inferior according to whether its height is reduced by one, two, or three *mūrti*-aṅgulas respectively. (47)
The width of the shaft (iṣikā) is traditionally held to be one-fourth of the combined length of the arrow and its shaft;
it should be as high as half of its own width, and may be constructed from ivory, wood, or other materials.
The depressions for the lotuses and the kumuda should be made with a gentle slope; if there is a small fillet here, it should be adorned with *īṣikā* [moldings]. || 49 ||
p.
454) Above the base (bhitti), the width of the hand (hasta) is one and a half aṅgulas for the lowest [type];
two and a half mātras plus a third part for the middle and the highest [types], respectively. 50.

The hand [of the image], made of ivory or other materials, should extend one and a half, one and a quarter, or half a cubit above [the head], like a sphere or like the half of a cane; it should resemble an umbrella. || 51 ||
When the space between the two *iṣikā* hands is divided into three parts,
the *vedakampa*s should be placed in the middle and at the end of the lower and upper portions, as well as at the beginning.

The movements of the best [type of dancer] and others are performed with two and a half, two, and one and a half mātrās respectively. Likewise, in the middle section, the remaining two movements—upward and downward—are also performed.
One should then appropriately adorn [the performance] with men, women, dance dramas, and so forth. 54.

Between the two hands of the *iṣikā*, there should be serpents (*vyāla*) situated at the outer corners. The emergence from the fist-binding occurs by means of the diagonal (*karṇa*) of its own diameter (*vyāsa*), or the emergence may be like the mouth of a crocodile (*makarāsya*) according to the division of the diameter and length.
The pillars should be made equal to nine or eleven [parts], or they may be equal to five or seven;
the thickness and the diameter of the pillars are traditionally held to be the same as those of the brackets (kampa).
[They are] three or four mātras in width and six, seven, or eight aṅgulas in height. || 58 ||
The jars with their necks covered by a cloth should have their bases joined together; they should be made secure on all sides through skillful means using copper, iron, pegs, and bands. (59)
Regarding the sages (*ṛṣis*), however, [the procedure is as follows]...
[omitted]. Thus has the *śibikā* been described according to Paiṭhīnasi, as well as for the *śikhara* and *mauṇḍika* types.
One should perform it by this path; now the specific distinction is being stated. (61)
With its feet raised upward to a height equal to its own width, it was covered by a wall of lattice-work. || 62 ||
It should be provided with a peaked roof and doors according to the rules; the measurement for palanquins is prescribed from the center of the pillars. (63)
p.
455) Madhuka, śāka, timiśa, and panasa... [etc. | The section on palanquins (śibikādhikāra).
The chariot, however, should be made with six, seven, or eight vitastis. || 64 ||
The width of the axle is the same as that of the nave; the length of the rear axle is one unit greater than that.
The length of the chariot floor is declared to be one and a half times its own width. (65)
The chariot—whether nine, seven, or five [spokes]—is skillfully bound with axles fixed above and below. (66)
That which is made firm by as many iron spikes extending horizontally,
with its weight centered at the middle rather than at the front axle, is desired as the *iṣā-daṇḍa*.
Above that, the curved piece of wood [is called] the *kūbara*;
its length should measure three cubits.
The front part, however, should have a straight axle-box and resemble a lotus bud; above that, it should be joined with planks made of *bhāradāru* wood according to the proper rules. (69)

The platform (prastara) should be made very firm with wooden planks, pegs, and so forth, and perfectly level; its projection at the front of the chariot-base (rathopastha) shall be one-fourth of its own length.
It should be prepared for the purpose of seating the charioteer and others;
the width of the wheels is recorded as being equal to the length of the axle.
Situated in the middle of that, they are ten finger-breadths high,
and their circumference is likewise remembered to be that same measure.
In all the wheels of the lords, there should be thirty-two spokes or half of that;
they may be either "ant-shaped" (tapering from the hub to the rim) or "barley-corn-shaped" (thickest at the center).
Shaped like the petals of a blue lotus or resembling a citron fruit, their length from the navel onwards should extend to the limit of the rim of the nave. (74)
The diameter of the hub (nemi) in the Vedas is six units from the end of the innermost to the outermost [circle];
its decoration consists of flowers, svastikas, segments, crescents, fish-patterns, and so forth.
Indeed, there should be exactly four pillars, each as long as half the diameter of the wheel;
at their bases and tops, they should have an expansion of four and three finger-breadths respectively, increased by a sixteenth part.
And those bodies shall also be very firm, endowed with the characteristics of pillars;
the height of the wall shall be one part less than the upper portion of the pillar. (77)
One should adorn it with trembling lotuses and other ornaments extending from the pole to the hand-staff,
and embellish it with representations of spirits, serpents, elephants, and dramatic performances.
Having made it very firm everywhere with stakes and bindings of copper and iron bands,
one should proceed step by step upon the pillars in a well-considered manner.
Joined with the *potikotta-rasa* style and adorned with features such as the *kapota*,
it should be a beautiful structure in the form of a temple (*prāsāda*) or pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), complete with a spire (*śikhara*).

In this very manner, one should construct the chariot known as Raṅga, but without a pinnacle (śikhara). The battle-chariot should have two wheels and be devoid of both a pinnacle and pillars. || 81 ||
A cart (śakaṭa) may also have two wheels, be joined with a wall [of wood] measuring one vitasti, possess a pole and a yoke-pole (kūbara), and be devoid of walls, pillars, and the like. || 82 ||

The width and length of the couch (paryaṅka), however, should be equal to that of the palanquin (śibikā). The supporting beams (iṣikā) should be of the same shape and adorned with lotuses and other designs for trembling. || 83 ||
The feet, including the heels, are best when eighteen finger-breadths in height;
they are middling at fifteen finger-breadths, and smallest at twelve finger-breadths. (84)

The width of the feet is one-quarter of the height from the navel to the top of the head; these feet are classified as excellent, middling, or inferior, resembling respectively a serpent, a lion, or a tiger. (85)

The feet should be straight, complete, made of a single substance, equal, and auspicious; the reed-pieces should be equal to one another, auspicious, and fashioned from wood or similar materials. (86)
The pedestals are made of gold, ivory, or wood, being respectively the best and so forth;
the two mats are made of linen and cotton, being respectively the best and the middling.
The lowest [type of bed] should be made of wooden planks; it is prescribed as being made of cane or wood.
The lion-leg and snake-leg couches are prescribed for Brahmins and Kṣatriyas respectively. (88)
For others, the feet may be straight, or all [the limbs] may be straight;
[this applies] to those with nine, seven, or five [tattvas], respectively, by means of the subsequent [limbs] measuring twenty units each.
The first and best seat is square, equal in height to Vyāsa; its legs, like those of a couch, are of three types beginning with the serpent (vyāla), in due order.
By increasing the length by one-eighth of Vyāsa and so forth, up to double that amount, there are seven types of seats: those with the feet of an elephant, a being, a lion, and a bull. (91)
The height of the base (pāda) should be twelve aṅgulas, which is appropriate for gods, brahmins, and kings;
it should be provided with an upper lotus and a *kapota* cornice, along with the *āliṅga*, *antarikā*, and other features.
It is joined with upapīṭhas and ucitas, and adorned with lion feet; above that, on its rear half, it is variegated with gold and jewels.

One should construct a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa) joined with a gateway featuring crocodiles; the lion-throne for the gods and kings should have its height increased by one-eighth [of the total].
The worship-altar for the gods is first six mātras in width;
from there, it extends tenfold by an increase of two fingers at each step until it reaches one cubit.
The pedestal (pīṭha) should be square, circular, or oblong according to the requirements; its height should be one-third, one-fifth, one-sixth, or one-eighth [of the total height]. || 96 ||

A pedestal (pīṭha) in the shape of a lotus-base (piṇḍikā), fashioned from gold, silver, or other materials, adorned with various designs and rich in both primary and secondary motifs, is prescribed for the worship of the deity in the home and so forth. (97)
A wooden auspicious pedestal (bhadrapīṭha) is prescribed for household deities and the like; that same pedestal, when provided with a stalk (nāla), is suitable for the ceremonial bathing (snāna).

That very [measure], enriched with a central depression, one should employ for installation and other rites; the width of the tortoise-seat (kūrmāsana), however, should be one cubit, or three-quarters, or half [of that]. 99.
The heights of the best and other types [of temples] are traditionally taught to be respectively five, four, and three *śaras* (five hundred), four hundred, and three hundred cubits;
however, the best and other types may also be one less than those measures by a *rasa* (six) or a *nanda* (nine) in proportion to their own width.

The width of the staff (*daṇḍa*) shall be one-sixth of the length of the handle (*nāla*). Indeed, the staff should be circular, extending from the bottom to the middle, and there should be a mark such as a lotus and so forth; its tip, however, should be cut evenly. 102.
That tortoise-seat (kūrmāsana) is commended whether it be circular or square;
the plank-seat (phalakāsana) should have a thickness equal to one part of its own height.
The wall of this [mandala] enters below by means of its own inherent portion, [forming] the trembling lotus. 104.
At its base it should be solid throughout, and at the top it should consist of a single unit of measurement;
it should be three parts of the seat's height in elevation, circular in shape, and beautiful. (105)
For those observing vows and those who have been initiated, during worship, recitation, burnt offerings, and so forth,
as well as for kings, the tortoise posture (kūrmāsana) is appropriate.
The seat should be square only at the time of worship and not otherwise;
here, the "eternal festival" (nityotsava) is described, as well as the vehicles and other items for the sake of the "great festival" (mahotsava) of the Supreme Lord.
Where [the Blessed One] dwelt... [the monks]... ||

Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, concerning the daily festivals, processions, the laying to rest, and so forth, in the Kriyāpāda of the *Siddhāntasāra*, which is the *Śrīmad-Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati*.
Now begins the forty-ninth chapter.

The great festival (*mahotsava*) should be performed after three, four, or six months. In the months beginning with Caitra, during the bright fortnights (*sitaparvan*), the concluding purificatory bath (*utsavāvabhṛthasnāna*) [of the festival] shall take place.
But having already formed this intention prior to this [moment]. || 2 ||
One should undertake the pilgrimage of Śambhu, distribute the bali offering to the Gaṇas,
and perform a special worship for the eight [deities].
The festivals for Śreṣṭha and the others are performed with the number of Rudras, Nandas, and Ṛṣis.
It has been stated that there are three minor festivals occurring every five, three, and one day respectively;
however, one should perform [the rites] preceded by the hoisting of the flag (*dhvajāropaṇa*). || 5 ||
The raising of the banner is not recommended here on the three [types of] five-day periods and so forth;
however, for festivals of the highest and other grades, it should be performed after three, two, or one virtuous day respectively.

One should perform the hoisting of the flag at an auspicious moment (lagna) on a previous day; it is prescribed that on that very same day, at night, there shall be the sounding of kettledrums (bherī).
For each of the great festivals, there should be three offerings of ritual sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa). The first is the flag-sprout (dhvajāṅkura), and the second is the festival-sprout (utsavāṅkura).
The third [offering] would be for the purpose of the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha); all [the materials] should have been previously offered.
The flagstaff may be a tree, a betel-nut palm, bamboo, or even a leafy vegetable.
A *sāla*, *campaka*, *raktasara*, or *asan* tree is recommended; it should be without hollows, free from wounds, straight, and devoid of knots and the like. (10)
Two were bamboo and betel-nut trees with bark, while all the others were without bark; they were cut level at the roots and tips, well-rounded, and beautiful.
The height of the flagstaff should be understood from the height of the door;
five times [the door-height] is excellent, while eight times is considered middling. (12)

The smallest [stūpa] should be ten times [the height of the base], and its height should be equal to that of the dome (stūpi). The primary [height] is measured by the neck (kaṇṭha), while the medium and low [sizes] are raised by the measure of a bull's hoof-print (vṛṣatala).
Some maintain that it may be three, two, or one time the height of the vimāna; specifically, forty, thirty-six, or thirty finger-breadths.
The circumferences of the flagstaffs for the *śreṣṭha* (excellent) and other types should be threefold in sequence;
the tree used for the stūpa staff should be of the same species as the flagstaff.
The height of the subsidiary staff (upadaṇḍa) should be one-fourth, one-fifth, or one-sixth of the main flagstaff;
its circumference, however, shall be twelve finger-breadths.
The three trunks are long and wide by half their length, with rays following their modifications;
they have perforated tips, and their stalks are provided with holes and protrusions.
They should be fixed at the tip of the flagpole with proper technique, spaced equidistantly from one another.
The secondary staff (upadaṇḍa) should extend beyond the main flagpole by a length of one tāla.
At a distance of only one *tala* below its top,
there should be an iron ring so that the rope for fastening the banner may pass through it.
A cotton rope for the machine, thick and equal to the middle [finger], twice as long as the height of the flagstaff, washed and thoroughly purified. || 20 ||
One should establish the flagstaff at the front of the bull, or in front of the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha),
or within the central row of pillars, or in the middle of the boundary line.
Having left a space from the front door equal to twelve times the height of the door,
one should prepare pits at the navel, waist, and thigh levels, which are then to be plastered in sequence.
Having placed a golden tortoise and performed the sacrifice during an auspicious moment and so forth, but specifically during the day, one should erect the flagstaff,
adorned with a garland of *darbha* grass and other ornaments. (23)
Filled with joy, they should install [the image] amidst the sounds of conchs, trumpets, and other instruments;
one should then construct a pedestal for it, measuring two or one cubit in height.

The altars (vedikā), beginning with the best, are prescribed as having a width of two parts and a height of one part out of three parts of the door's height; they are constructed respectively from stone, brick, and earth.
Likewise, the length of the banner (patākā) is nine, eight, or seven cubits (kiṣku), or one-fifth of that [length].
From that width, the peak should be half the width. || 26 ||
There should be three or two tails, which are longer than the body and gradually taper;
one-fifth of its own length from the middle, one should draw a bull.
A white bull with red hooves, red ears and horns, large white and black eyes, a beautiful neck, and a handsome face. || 28 ||
He should have a beautiful tail, beautiful feet and thighs, and a full, prominent hump; whether lying down or standing, he should possess the aforementioned characteristics of an excellent bull. (29)
On the day preceding the raising of the banner, during the first watch of the night, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) and offer special worship to Śiva and the Bull.
Having offered mung-bean rice to the bull and having bowed down to him, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) before the bull using śāli rice and husked grains.
Having laid out a diagram of nine squares upon that [altar], one should place nine water-pots,
filled with pure water and provided with bundles of *kūrca* grass, gold, and fine cloth.

Having adorned the bull in the center and the eight guardians of the directions around it, one should duly invoke them and worship them properly with perfumes and other offerings according to the prescribed rite.
One should worship the bull with the Tārādi-Vṛṣa mantra and one’s own Gāyatrī: "Oṃ, salutation to the Bull; Oṃ, salutation to the One of Great Strength; Oṃ, salutation to the Vehicle of Hara;
Oṃ, salutation to the Son of Surabhi; Oṃ, let us meditate upon the One with Sharp Horns."
"Let us meditate upon the one whose feet are the Vedas; may that Bull inspire us.
Then, with their own respective mantras, he should again worship the eight lords of the worlds upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in front of him.
One should place a banner upon it and worship it with the Vṛṣamantra.
Then, having prepared a square mandala within a space of two cubits, [one should proceed]. (35)
There, having properly established the fire and performed the rite in the auspicious fire, the preceptor should offer fuel-sticks of *palāśa* with the *vṛṣamantra*.

Having offered sesame seeds, clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge (caru) separately one hundred and eight times each, as well as the full oblation and the sviṣṭakṛt offering, one should dismiss the fire.
When the night has clearly dawned, the Guru, having performed his daily obligatory rites, [should act] either in the forenoon,
at midday, or during the auspicious lagna of the early night.
With pure brahmins who are desirous of service, wearing turbans and upper garments,
one should raise the banner by means of a machine or carry it on the head.

Having performed a circumambulation of the village accompanied by the sounds of conchs, drums, and other instruments, he should enter within and place [the banner] in the designated location for the flagpole.
Then, having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), one should wash the banner with those waters—
at the base, middle, and tip of the staff— representing Vṛṣa, Ṣaṇmukha, and Māruta respectively.
Having worshipped it with its respective mantra accompanied by auspicious songs, instrumental music, and other rites, one should bring the bull-pitcher and place it near the flagpole.
One should place the pitchers containing the mantras of the Bull (Vṛṣabha) upon the banner at the heart of the Bull,
having adorned them according to the prescribed rite with auspicious sprouts, lamps, and other offerings.
One should properly hoist the banner of the bull with a rope attached to a flag, using the Gāyatrī mantra;
and one should wrap the staff with the rope.

One should consecrate [the deity] at the base of the banner with jars placed by the world-protectors (lokapālas); having worshipped the banner at its base according to the prescribed rite, ending with the offering of food (naivedya). (45)
Oṃ, salutations be to you, the three-eyed one; salutations to the Lord of the Banner! Salutations be to you, Nandin, for the successful accomplishment of the festival. (46)
Then, on a sacrificial mound prepared with rice grains in front of the banner, one should place a drum adorned with cloth.
Having worshipped Rudra to the south of the drum, Janārdana to the left, and Brahmā in the center, one should worship Guha on the corner staff.
Having drawn a lotus with an auspicious pericarp upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in front of that [image], one should install the trident there and worship it according to the prescribed rules.
Then, first with the mantra beginning with "Tryambaka," the Guru should strike the drum at a corner,
and thereafter with the mantra beginning with "Idam Viṣṇu."
One should strike the third [drum] with the mantra "brahmajajñānam"; then, the musician, having bathed and being adorned with white garments and other ornaments, [should proceed].

Having summoned [the deity], one should cause it to play [the instrument] by means of that; then, having raised the food-liṅga with the sounds of conchs, kettledrums, and other instruments, [one should proceed]. (52)
Accompanied by the sounds of song and dance, as well as umbrellas, chowries, and auspicious rites, he performed a circumambulation of the village,
honoring Brahmā, Indra, and the other lords of the directions.

Having worshipped in the cardinal directions and the intermediate junctions with mantras, his own verses, and hymns; having invoked [the deities], praised them, and offered pure food, he should cast the bali offering.
"O, O Brahmins! By these words and others, he should also proclaim the command of Śiva.
Then, having gone to the temple, he stands before the banner. (55)
The Rudras, Ādityas, Vasus, Soma, the two Aśvins, the hosts of Maruts, the Pitṛs, the Ṛṣis, and the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Vidyādharas, and Asuras; || 56 ||
The nāgas, kinnaras, and rākṣasas; the piśācas and the lords of bhūtas; the oceans, apsarases, and siddhas; the rivers, mountains, and great trees. || 57 ||
Having invoked them for the purpose of serving the festival, one should say, "May they come," each by their respective names such as Tārā and so forth,
and should cause them to hear the command of Śiva.
Oṃ!
O hosts of Rudra, together with your respective retinues and attendants, this festival of Śambhu must be honored by you, being well-pleased, at the command of Śiva. (59)

One should cause the gods and others to hear [the mantra] beginning with "Oṃ" using their respective names; and at night, one should scatter the bali offering accompanied by the sounds of conch shells, kettledrums, and other instruments.
Having adorned [the flagstaff] daily and offered the oblation, one should worship the banner until its conclusion.
This concludes the section on the raising of the banner (*dhvajocchrayādhikāra*).
Then, when the day of the festival has arrived, one should have the streets thoroughly cleaned.
In all places— such as temples of Śiva, villages, cities,
and towns— one should, according to this *Mañjarī*, sweep the village streets on every side and in every direction and sprinkle them with fragrant water.
One should further strew those [altars] with fresh flowers of divine fragrance that are in full bloom;
and one should construct seats according to the scriptures for the purpose of offering oblations at the outskirts of the village,
in the center of the village, at crossroads, at every abode of the gods, at the doorways, and at the bases of sacred trees (caityas).
And also everywhere at the gates, the gate-towers, the ramparts, and within the streets. || 62 ||
One should plant coconut trees, sugarcane, banana, betel-nut palms, and even flowering trees well in advance, or at least on the very day [of the rite], according to the circumstances.
One should decorate [the area] with banana and betel-nut trees together with their roots, which do not wither, and with variegated arches and banners from which flower garlands hang.

Having decorated it according to the prescribed ritual with lamps, pavilions, trees, and other items arranged in their proper places, as well as swings, canopies, mechanical devices, and so forth; 65.
On festival days, one should perform the occasional worship of Śambhu according to the extent of one's wealth,
avoiding any stinginess regarding expenditure.
One should duly sprinkle Maheśvara with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), with water, and with cool scented water.
While conchs, kettledrums, timilas, paṇavas, ānakas, and flutes resound,
one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) with flour-lamps and other offerings according to the prescribed rite.
Having bathed [the deity] in due order with the Brahma-mantras, the Pāvamānī verses, the Kadrudrādya hymns, and likewise the Rudra, Śrī, and Puruṣa Sūktas; || 69 ||
With very fine white garments and silk cloths of various colors, and with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and saffron finely ground into a paste; || 70 ||
Having smeared the pedestal of the *liṅga* with golden flowers and the like, as well as loose flowers,
garlands, golden bands, and ornaments; (71)
Having also adorned the temple with variegated pavilions of flowers,
one should fill it with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, flowers, and incense.
With ten lamps filled with fragrant oil and containing camphor,
one should worship Śiva both inside and outside the temple, up until the offering of the final oblation.

Every day, one should offer the daily oblation (naivedya), starting from the best quality and so forth according to one's capacity, increasing it fourfold, threefold, or twofold compared to the previous day. 74.
Following the path described in the ritual manuals, that pure food of six kinds— consisting of soup, side dishes, cakes, sweets, and fruits— is prepared.

In the morning he should eat milk-rice (pāyasa) and rice mixed with sesame (kṛsara); at midday, rice with jaggery and sugar-cane; and at the onset of night, pure food and curd-rice mixed with turmeric.

At midnight, one should offer mudga-rice with honey and ghee as the principal ingredients; or else, at all the junctions of time (saṃdhyās), one may offer milk-rice and other foods in their proper sequence.
Furthermore, one should offer pure cooked rice into the faces beginning with Īśāna, as well as at night, using yantras,
liṅgas, and the like, and likewise with leaf-cuttings and other such works.
One should worship Śiva with various offerings such as fuel-sticks (*indhana*) that are worthy of being beheld;
this ritual journey (*yātrā*) is recommended in the forenoon, midday, and afternoon, as well as at night. (79)

During the preeminent festival, [the deity] should be carried four times a day; likewise, three or two times for the other two [festivals], respectively, by means of a chariot, a platform, and palanquins.
The procession should be of the superior type and so forth, using all available vehicles; it should be adorned and covered with gold bands, cloths, and other such materials.
It was beautified by garlands of golden jewels and banners,
strewn with variegated cloths, and adorned with heaps of flowers.

Having placed the deity made of gold or other materials upon the vehicle according to the sequence beginning with the "excellent" [grade], one should ensure it is very firmly secured therein and perform the protection of the pedestal.
In this *Saṃhitāṭīkā*,
for the processions of the daily festivals and so forth, an image made of gold and other materials has been prescribed for the form of Candraśekhara.
And she should always be well-honored.
Thus;

or else, [I shall worship] the form of the sixteen-fold Mūrtis, excluding the form of the mendicant wandering for alms, and likewise excluding Umā from half of Hara’s body, as well as the skeleton. || 84 ||
Or, there may be a great festival with those twelve forms that have been described;
having properly adorned the form with garlands, garments, and ornaments. (85)
Having invoked Śiva and worshipped him with perfumes and other offerings, with a mind bowed in devotion,
one should commence the procession accompanied by auspicious sounds of musical instruments, song, dance, and the like.
In this *Mañjarī*:
"Having taken up these eight auspicious objects well-fashioned from fine metal— a drum, a bull, a fly-whisk, a lion, a pitcher, banners, and likewise lamps— one should then proceed."
Then the Brahmins learned in the Vedas, who recite the Svasti-sūktas and other hymns, having first caused the benedictions to be pronounced, should recite a prayer for well-being.
May Viṣṇu ever be for our well-being; may the four-faced Brahmā be for our well-being; may Rudra ever be for our well-being; and may Śatakratu be for our well-being. || 88 ||
May Agni be for your well-being always; may Yama be here for your well-being; may Nirṛti be for your well-being, and may Varuṇa be here for your well-being. (89)
May Vāyu ever be for our well-being; may Dhaneśvara be for our well-being; may Īśāna ever be for our well-being;
may the host of Maruts be for our well-being. (90)
May the Vasus be for our well-being, and may the Rudras likewise be for our well-being; may the Ādityas be for our well-being, and may the Kinnaras be for our well-being. (91)
May the Nāgas be for our well-being; may the Pannagas be for our well-being; may the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas) be for our well-being, and may the Apsarases here be for our well-being.
May the rivers, the Gandharvas, and likewise the streams, be for our well-being; may the oceans be for our well-being, and likewise the mountains for our well-being. (93)
May the mothers be for our well-being, and the fathers always for our well-being; may all the attendants of the gods always be for our well-being. 94.

May there be well-being for the king and for his subjects; may there always be well-being for the kingdom. May there be well-being for cows and Brahmins; may there be well-being and prosperity for the Vaiśyas. (95)
May there be well-being even for women and Śūdras; may there be well-being for all beings and may they prosper.
May there be well-being for all that moves and likewise for all that is stationary. (96)
May there be well-being from the mantras; may well-being increase for the ritual action. May there be well-being from all the gods; may there always be well-being for the ancestors. (97)

May there be well-being for the sages; may there be well-being and prosperity for those dwelling on earth; may there be well-being for the inhabitants of the netherworld; and may there be well-being forever for the celestial beings. 98.
May there be well-being from all the intermediate spaces; may prosperity increase.
In this festival of Maheśa, may well-being increase through the offerings of the devotees. 99.
Thus [it is said].
Now, for the door-keepers, the world-protectors, and the bulls, in their respective order—for Vighna, Vīrabhadra, the Mothers, and the Teacher (Śāstṛ) as well—[the procedure follows]. (100)
And [the worship] of Ṣaṇmukha and Durgā, of Kubera and Hariṇāṅka, as well as of Caṇḍa and Kṣetreśa, and of Tīkṣṇanetra and Mṛgāsya. || 101 ||
In the outer middle enclosure, starting from Nandīśa and so forth, there are likewise the seats of the lords of the Gaṇas and the Bhūtas. || 102 ||
The offering mantras for the twenty Gaṇeśas located in the various directions are now written down individually for their propitiation here. (103)
Oṃ sphura sphoṭaya hūṃ, svāhā to the three-eyed one! Oṃ hīṃ proṃ, obeisance to Kapālin haṃ! Oṃ.
Salutations to you, the wise Nandīśa, stationed at the gate with trident in hand; salutations again and again to him who has struck down the Daityas with his very glance. || 104 ||
Oṃ, salutations to you who are stationed at the gateway, whose hand is occupied with an axe; salutations to you, Mahākāla, who has struck down the Daityas with a mere glance. 105.
With these two [mantras], one should worship Nandin and Mahākāla: Oṃ bhīṃ, obeisance to Bhṛṅgīśa. Oṃ gaṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati.

Oṃ, salutations to you who are stationed at the gateway, to Bhṛṅgīśa, whose nature is emaciated; salutations again and again to the son of Śaṅkara, who destroyed the Daityas with his very glance. || 106 ||
Oṃ,
salutations to you who are joined at the gate, whose face is that of an elephant, whose self is the void; salutations again and again to the son of Śaṅkara, who has slain the Daityas with his glance.

With these two [mantras], one should worship Bhṛṅgīśa and Vināyaka. In this same manner, one should perform worship everywhere with the appropriate worship-mantras: *Oṃ vṛṃ, obeisance to Vṛṣabha*; *Oṃ suṃ, obeisance to Subrahmaṇya*.
Oṃ, salutations to you who are joined at the gate; salutations to Dharma, whose self is the bull, who has struck down the Daityas with his gaze, and who is the son of Surabhi. || 108 ||
Oṃ,
salutations to you who are joined with the gatekeepers, the six-faced one whose self is Śiva; salutations again and again to the son of Śaṅkara, by whose glance the Daityas were destroyed.
Oṃ duṃ, obeisance to Durgā. Oṃ dhuṃ, obeisance to Caṇḍeśvara.
Oṃ, obeisance to you, Durgā, who are stationed at the door in the abode of Śaṅkara; [protect us] with your glance.
Salutations again and again to you, the Goddess who has slain the Daityas. || 110 ||
Oṃ,
salutations to you who are joined with the gatekeepers, to Caṇḍeśa, the Great Soul; salutations again and again to the son of Śaṅkara, by whose glance the Daityas were destroyed.
Homage to Indra, the sovereign lord of the gods, together with his weapons, vehicle, retinue, and the attendants of Rudra; homage to those attendants. Oṃ.
Salutations to you, O Śatakratu! Salutations to the wise one with a thousand eyes, who destroys the pride of the Daityas and holds the thunderbolt in his hand. 112.
Oṃ, homage to the beings who cause misfortune, to those who exist and those who do not, to all the hosts;
homage, homage, svāhā! Oṃ, in the eastern direction, those hosts of the Blessed Śiva who have thunderbolts in their hands, who are white, white-eyed, and white-red—
To those who dwell in the heavens, the atmosphere, the earth, and the netherworld— to them and to those [goddesses],
salutations again and again, svāhā!

Oṃ! To those beings who dwell in front, the night-walkers, the fierce ones, those who are existent and non-existent, the deformed, the universal-formed, the great-formed, the terrible-formed, those with the faces of beasts and the faces of birds,
the nourishers and the non-nourishers, the givers of desires— to them, who desire the offering, [I give] this offering.
I take away. Homage, homage to all those great Rudraka-s; svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to Agni, the lord of splendor, together with his weapons, vehicle, retinue, and the assembly of Rudras.
Oṃ!
Salutation to that consumer of oblations, who is the mouth of all the gods, by whom the sacrificial offering is conveyed, and by whom everything is set in motion. 113.

Oṃ!
