To those hosts of the Blessed Lord Śiva in the southeastern direction, who hold spears in their hands, who are red, with red eyes, and crimson-hued; who dwell in the divine, the atmosphere, the earth, and the depths of the netherworld—to them, to those [goddesses], salutations again and again, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to Yama, the lord of pretas, together with his weapons, vehicle, and retinue of Rudras;
homage to his attendants.
Oṃ.
O Lord of the Pretas! Homage be to you, by whom everything is withdrawn, by whom everything is protected, and from whom this world is afraid.
And with the mantra beginning: "Oṃ, obeisance to the spirits who cause misfortune," and so forth.
"Oṃ, in the southern direction, those hosts of the Blessed Lord Śiva who hold staffs in their hands, who are black, black-eyed, and dark-red, [those] celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial..."
Salutations again and again, svāhā, to those who dwell in the netherworld; and with the mantra beginning "Those beings who sit on the right," and so forth:
Oṃ, to Nirṛti, lord of the Rākṣasas, together with his weapons, vehicle, and retinue.
Salutation to the attendants of Rudra. Salutation to his attendants.
Oṃ, salutation to him who is the lord of the *rakṣasas*, the *yātudhānas*, and the *piśācas*.
Constant salutation to Nirṛti, the lord of the Rākṣasas. || 115 ||
And with the mantra beginning: "Oṃ, obeisance to the spirits who cause misfortune," and so forth:

"Oṃ, in the southwestern direction, those hosts of the Blessed Lord Śiva who have swords in their hands, who are dark-complexioned, dark-eyed, and dark-red, belonging to the celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial realms."
Homage, homage, svāhā! To those who dwell in the netherworld (pātāla), to them and to them.
Oṃ, to Varuṇa, lord of the waters, together with his weapons, vehicle, retinue, and the attendants of Rudra.
Homage! Homage to his attendants!
Oṃ, homage to Varuṇa, by whom everything is produced and in whom everything is dissolved.
Salutations to you, the lord of the waters, who holds a noose in your hand. || 116 ||
And with the mantra beginning "Oṃ, obeisance to the spirits who cause misfortune," and so forth:

"Oṃ, in the western direction, those hosts of the Blessed Lord Śiva who hold nooses in their hands— speckled, speckled-eyed, and speckled-red— who dwell in the divine, the atmospheric, and the earthly realms."
Salutations again and again, Svāhā, to those who dwell in the netherworld (pātāla), and with the mantra beginning "Oṃ,
those beings who sit in the west," and so forth;
Oṃ, to Vāyu, the lord of the vital breaths, together with his weapons, vehicle, retinue, and the attendants of Rudra.
Homage! Homage to his attendants!
Oṃ!
That by which the vital breaths and other winds are filled and set in motion here among living beings...
Salutations to that Wind, who belongs to all. || 117 ||
And with the mantra beginning: "Oṃ, obeisance to the spirits who cause misfortune," and so forth:

"Oṃ, in the northwestern direction, those hosts of the Blessed Lord Śiva who have goads in their hands, who are yellow, yellow-eyed, and yellowish-red, belonging to the celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial realms..."
Salutations again and again, Svāhā, to those who dwell in the netherworld!
Oṃ, salutation to Kubera, the lord of the Yakṣas, together with his weapons, vehicle, retinue, and the attendants of Rudra; salutation to his attendants!
Oṃ!
Homage be to you, the Lord of the Guhyakas, the Master of Wealth, by whose grace the entire world is filled with riches. 118.
Oṃ, homage to Soma, lord of the lunar mansions, together with his weapons, vehicles, and retinue, and to the attendants of Rudra; homage to those attendants. Oṃ.
O Lord of the Moonlight! Salutations to you; salutations to you, O Lord of the luminaries! Salutations to you, O Beloved of Rohiṇī! O Jar of Nectar! Let there be salutations to you. || 119 ||
p.
470) Also with [the mantra] beginning: "Oṃ, obeisance to the spirits who cause misfortune," and so forth.
"Oṃ, in the northern direction, those hosts of the Blessed Śiva who hold staffs in their hands..."
To those who are white, white-eyed, and white-red; to those dwelling in the heavens, the atmosphere, the earth, and the netherworld—to them and to those [goddesses], salutations, salutations, svāhā!
Also with the mantra beginning: "Oṃ, those beings who dwell in the north," and so forth.
Oṃ, homage to Īśāna, the Lord of Knowledge, together with his weapons, vehicle, retinue, and the attendants of Rudra; homage to those attendants. Oṃ.
Salutations to you who hold the trident in hand; salutations again and again to you, the Lord Īśāna, the protector of the worlds and the master of the sciences.
And with the mantra beginning "Oṃ, obeisance to the spirits who cause misfortune," and so forth:
"Oṃ, in the northeastern direction, those hosts of the Blessed Lord Śiva who carry tridents,
who are tawny, tawny-eyed, and tawny-red, belonging to the celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial realms."

And to those who dwell in the netherworld (pātāla), to them and to those [goddesses], salutations, salutations, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to Brahmā, the sovereign lord of all worlds, together with his weapons, vehicles, retinue, and the attendants of Rudra; salutation to his attendants.
Oṃ, salutations to you, Brahmā, the lord of all worlds, the cause of creation, the presiding deity of sacrifice, the ordainer, and the four-faced one. || 121 ||
Oṃ, we know that Tatpuruṣa; we meditate upon Pitāmaha; may that Brahmā inspire us.
And also with [the mantra] beginning: "Oṃ, salutations to the spirits who bring about misfortune," and so forth.

Oṃ! To those hosts of the Blessed Śiva in the upward direction, who hold lotuses in their hands, who are subtle, with subtle eyes, and with subtle red [complexions], who dwell in the divine realms, the atmosphere, the earth,
and the netherworld— to them, to all of them, obeisance, obeisance, svāhā!

And with the mantra beginning "Oṃ, those beings who grant security... and so forth: "Oṃ, obeisance to Ananta, the lord of Pātāla, together with his weapons, vehicle, retinue, and the attendants of Rudra;
obeisance to his attendants."
Oṃ, salutations to the one with a thousand heads, who bears the earth upon his head; salutations be to you, Ananta, the lord of the netherworlds. 122.
p.
471) Also with [the mantra] beginning: "Oṃ, obeisance to the spirits who cause misfortune," and so forth; and:
"Oṃ, those hosts of the blessed Śiva in the downward direction who have discs in their hands and are smoke-colored..."

Salutations again and again, Svāhā! To Dhūmrākṣas, Dhūmralohitas, those of the divine, atmospheric, and terrestrial realms, and those dwelling in the netherworld—to them and to them, salutations again and again, Svāhā!
And with the mantra beginning "Oṃ, those beings who dwell below," etc., and: Oṃ, salutation to Vṛṣabha. Oṃ.
Salutation to the one whose vehicle is Hara. Oṃ, salutation to the one of great strength. Oṃ, salutation to the son of Surabhi.
Oṃ.
Salutations to the vehicle of Śambhu, you whose roar is like that of the agitated ocean! Salutations to you, the Bull, for the increase of this festival here. (123)
Oṃ vīṃ, obeisance to Vīrabhadra. Oṃ, may we know Vīrabhadra;
may we meditate upon Gaṇeśvara; may that Peaceful One inspire us. Oṃ gaṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati.
Oṃ, may we know the one with a single tusk; may we meditate upon the son of Bhava; may that Dantī inspire us. Oṃ Vyoṃ, obeisance to Brahmāṇī.
Oṃ, may we know her whose essence is Brahman; may we meditate upon her who holds kusha grass in her hand; may that Brahmāṇī inspire us.
May she impel us. Om, salutation to Māheśvarī. Om, let us know her who is of the nature of Rudra;
let us meditate on her who holds a trident in her hand; may that Māheśvarī impel us.

Oṃ māṃ, obeisance to Kaumārī. Oṃ, we know her who is of the nature of Skanda; we meditate upon her who holds a spear in her hand; may that Kaumārī inspire us. Oṃ haiṃ, obeisance to Vaiṣṇavī. Oṃ, we know her who is of the nature of Viṣṇu.

We meditate upon her who holds the discus in her hand; may that Vaiṣṇavī inspire us. Oṃ haiṃ, obeisance to Vārāhī. We know her who belongs to Prajāpati; we meditate upon her who holds the mace in her hand; may that Vārāhī inspire us.

Oṃ hoṃ, salutation to Indrāṇī. Oṃ, may we know her who is the very self of Indra; may we meditate upon her who holds the thunderbolt in her hand; may that Indrāṇī inspire us. Oṃ hauṃ, salutation to Mahākālī. Oṃ, may we know her who is the very self of Rudra.
Let us meditate upon her who holds a trident in her hand; may that Cāmuṇḍī inspire us.
Or else:

The seed-syllables of the eight Mothers are established here, distinguished by long vowels in sequence, ending with *sa* and beginning with *svā*. However, in the sevenfold system, there are indeed seven.
Thus it is stated in the Svacchanda Tantra:
Oṃ, salutation to the Mothers; Oṃ, salutation to the Mothers of all worlds; Oṃ, salutation to the hosts of Mothers of all worlds.

Oṃ! May the Mothers of manifold forms, stationed in every direction—those of the heavens, the atmosphere, and the earth, as well as those dwelling in the netherworlds—come here by the command of Śiva;
may they favor us (or accept us) and receive this worship.
Salutations again and again, Svāhā, to those Mothers who bear gentle forms. Oṃ śāṃ, salutations to Śāstṛ. Oṃ, salutations to Praśāstṛ. Oṃ, salutations to Mahāśāstṛ.
Oṃ śāṃ huṃ, salutations to Kumāra. Oṃ, salutations to him whose vehicle is elephants and horses.

Namaḥ! Oṃ, homage to the son of Rudra! Oṃ, may we know the Lord of Beings (the son of Bhava); may we meditate upon him; may that Teacher inspire us! Oṃ, homage to Prabhā! Thus, to the left of the Teacher, [homage] to his Goddess.
"Oṃ, homage to Satyakāya," [recite] thus to the Teacher’s son to the right.
"Oṃ, may all those hosts of Śāmba and the others, who are the lords of millions upon millions of hosts, be present."
Salutations again and again to those who are well-pleased with them. || 124 ||

To the west of the Teacher, one should offer an oblation (bali) to Śambhu and the others with this [mantra]. The word for speech begins with *tāra* (oṃ) and ends with *namaḥ*, and the word for the earth likewise. (125)
For the two powerful mantras of Skanda, when recited as japa, the homa must indeed end with "svāhā.
"Oṃ kārttikeyāya namaḥ | Oṃ devasenāyai namaḥ |" [These are for the deity] to his left. "Oṃ ṣaṇmukhāya vidmahe mahāsenāya dhīmahi | tannaḥ... [The rest follows].
May Skanda impel [this].
Then follows the word "Caṇḍa," preceded by the syllables "Dhanau," "Śara," "Agni," and "Svara. (126)
This mantra of Caṇḍeśvara is remembered as beginning with *tārā* (oṃ) and ending with *huṃ phaṭ*.
Oṃ caṇḍāya namaḥ | Oṃ caṇḍeśvarāya namaḥ | Oṃ caṇḍeśvarāya vidmahe mahāsenāya dhīmahi | tannaścaṇḍaḥ |
May it impel us. Oṃ kṣāṃ kṣīṃ kṣūṃ, salutation to Kṣetrapāla. Oṃ, salutation to Vaṭukanātha.
Oṃ.
To the sovereign lord of the field of the universe, the bestower of all accomplishments. || 127 ||
"Salutation to you, the protector of the field (Kṣetrapāla), whose nature is the protection of the universe.
Then, at the gate of the inner gopura, [he worshipped] Tīkṣṇanetra and Mṛgāsya.
Oṃ, homage to Tīkṣṇanetra. Oṃ, homage to Mṛgāsya.
Having gone out from the gate, standing outside to the east of the *balipīṭha*.
One should address all the attendants with this very same mantra. || 129 ||
Oṃ!
Those attendants of Rudra who abide pervading the entire world, desiring the bali offering—may they all accept this supreme bali. 130.
Having spoken thus and addressed the Gaṇas, one should offer an oblation (bali) to Nandin and the others: to Nandīśa, Mahākāla, Bhūtanātha, and Mahīdhara. (131)
Having worshipped Parvateśa, Guheśa, Kālapāśa, and Kapālin, one should scatter an offering (bali) to them with their respective names followed by "namaḥ."
Then, there are twenty lords of ten million Gaṇas;
they reside separately in each direction, and one should offer them oblations with their respective names.
Namely:
Mahākāla, Vidhātṛ, Vajrapāṇi, Kratu, Prabhu, Dakṣa, Śatakratu-tanu, Aprameya, and Vīryavān. || 134 ||
He is eternal, possessing the luster of lightning, holding a trident in his hand, and three-eyed;
he is the lamp of his own body, the destroyer of darkness, the creator of the universe, and one of immense prowess. || 135 ||
Māndhātṛ, Mahāvīrya, Nityayoga, and Prasādana—these are the lords of the Gaṇas in the east. Agni, Agnisamāna, Jvālāmālī, and Viśvabhuk [are the lords in the southeast]. (136)
The Fire-god is embodied, all-pervading, tawny, with red eyes; he is fierce, smoke-colored, with a red body, possessing seven flames, and the universal medicine. 137.
Sutapa, Vegavān, Bhasmacchanna, Marutsakha, Yogapriya,
and Dāruka— these are the leaders of the crores in the south-eastern quarter.
Yama Vaivasvata, Dhātṛ, the slayer of Daityas, the ender of creatures, Death, Lord of the Pretas, Dharma, Kṛṣṇa, and Kṛṣṇākṣa. (139)
He is the eternally united one, time itself, the swift-acting destroyer of the departed; he is the end-maker who assumes illusory forms, and he is the friend who delights in both truth and falsehood.
Pitṛnātha and Kīnāśa—these twenty [deities] are in the southern direction;
likewise Rākṣasa, Asura, Kravyād, Vīrahā, and Nirṛti. (141)
Sharp-eyed, the slayer of travelers, the destroyer of sacrifices, a night-stalker; possessed of a massive form, the son of Kaikasī, cruel, and likewise of cruel appearance. (142)
Rakṣas, Kauṇapaka, Dhūmra, Dhūmrākṣa, Bhīṣaṇa, Vīrūpākṣa, and Bhasmāṅga—these twenty are in the southwest (nairṛtya). || 143 ||
Varuṇa, Śabala, Ambhodhi, Pracetas, Nimnagāpati, Yādonātha, Pāśapāṇi, Ānanda, Ambupati, and Śiva. (144)

The one with matted hair, the giver of life, the white one, the dark-eyed, the eternal, whose dwelling is turned inward, the cloud-bearer, the life-sustainer, and the one whose vehicle is the crocodile. || 145 ||
And he who has his abode in the ocean—these constitute twenty times ten million [names]. Vāyu, Gandhavaha, Sūkṣma, Sparśana, and Prabhañjana; || 146 ||
Prāṇa, apāna, as well as vyāna, udāna, and samāna; nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya. || 147 ||
Dhvajapāṇi, Pavana, Śvasana, Māruta, and Marut—
these lords of twenty crores are the Gaṇeśvaras in the northwestern quarter.
Rakṣeśa, Rayimān, Soma, Māṇibhadra, Guhyaka, Celamālin, Kubera, Jambhala, and Śibikuṇḍalin. || 149 ||

The lord of the Kiṃnaras is Cailibilin, and the giver of wealth is Dhanada, the sovereign of riches; likewise, the king of kings is Śrīda, the eldest, the wearer of garlands, and the possessor of wealth.
And then there is Ekakuṇḍala, whose residence is in the northern quarter; these lords of twenty crores have taken refuge in the direction of Kubera. (151)
Īśāna, Īśvara, Śambhu, the trident-handed, the three-eyed, the one without beginning or end, the Yogi, Kapila, the tawny-eyed. || 152 ||
Rudra, the lord of the fierce hosts, the sustainer of the universe, sky-clad, blue-throated, the lord with matted hair, whose vehicle is the bull, and whose banner is the bull. || 153 ||
Hara, Śarva, and Viśvabhuj—these twenty are in the northeast; then Mahābala, Mahānāda, Brahmamūrti, and Caturmukha. (154)
The creator of emanation, Vijaya, Dhātṛ, Aghora and indeed Aghora; Aghora, Lāṅgalin, Manyu, Aṅgāra, and Śikhibhūṣaṇa. || 154 ||
Jīmūta, Mūrtibhṛt, Kuṇḍī, Mantrīśa, and Tripurāntaka—these twenty lords of the Pramathas, including Koṭīśa, are situated in the upward direction. || 155 ||
Buddhi, Pramardana, Śuddha, Kālarūpa, Ugradaṃṣṭrin, Dīrghabāhu, Prakāma, Bhartṛ, Hantṛ, and Vicakṣaṇa. || 156 ||
Kālāgni, Raurava, Aghora, Naraka, Śarva, the one named Nāga, Ghora, Kimpuru, Danuja, and Kṣamī; || 157 ||
It is said that there are twenty [lords] of ten million in the downward direction.
Regarding this, it is stated in the Mañjarī:
"Each of these has a hundred groups of servants, and furthermore, for each of those [groups], there is one [servant]."

There are servants by the thousands and even tens of thousands, and for each of them there is a retinue said to number one hundred thousand; likewise, their attendants are known to be in the millions, so numerous that they cannot possibly be described individually.
Thus, with their respective names preceded by "Tārā" and ending in "namaḥ," [one should worship] each of these individually. || 158 ||
In due order, one should scatter the *bali* offering in the various directions with fragrant flowers, water, and food appropriate for each respective night, or at night with the *bhūtakrūra* mantra.

One should offer [the water] with the general arghya-water and the kūrca-grass at the beginning and end of the bali-offering; then, having approached the bali-pīṭha, one should worship Bhūtidā and the others in their proper order.
Having worshipped them, one should scatter the bali offering to them as in the daily festival; however, there is a special rule here:
after bathing and giving the bali offering. (161)
The preceptor, accompanied by his disciples, having entered inside as previously described,
should then cause [the deity] to descend from the vehicle and other such conveyances, and place the deity upon the pedestal.
Having worshipped as before, one should again worship [the deity] stationed in its own place;
herein, the nights of the festival days are to be understood in their proper sequence. (163)
Just as the hosts of deities, including their presiding lords—the Brahmas, Bhūtas, Indras, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Rātris—are worshipped along with the crows. || 164 ||
Then, in the seventh fortnight, the Piśācarātra occurs in due order; in the ninth fortnight, they declare the eighth to be the Viṣṇurātra. (165)
Among those, one should offer the respective oblation during the ninth [period], the Prājeśarātra;
in the Brahmarātra, the oblation is prescribed as pure food together with flowers and kuśa grass.
Food mixed with curd, powdered turmeric, parched rice, roasted flour, and water is known as *bhūtakrūra*; one should cause this to be given during the *bhūtarātri* ceremony.
On the third night of Indra, the preceptor should offer a bali-oblation consisting of food mixed with *indravallī* and garlic, along with parched grain flour (*saktu*), milk, and curd.

In the fourth [period], that of Gāndharva, the offering consists of bamboo-food mixed with milk; in the fifth, known as Yakṣarātra, the bali-offering is made with flowers, food, clarified butter, and water. (169)
In the sixth [day], for the Rākṣasa, there is red rice with husks mixed with clay; but in the seventh, for the Paiśāca, there is black gram porridge, rice with sesame, and honey.
One should scatter an offering enriched with turmeric powder and oil along with black gram; on the eighth day, one should scatter milk-rice with clarified butter, and again on the ninth day.
Kṛsara mixed with ghee and milk is prescribed as the offering for Prajāpati;
however, some teachers have stated that there are seven such groups of offerings.
Those Bhūtas, Pitṛs, and Yakṣas, as well as the Nāgas, Brahmans, Īśvaras, and Vaiṣṇavas— these Gaṇas,
together with Skanda and the Mothers, reside in the nine sectors.
On the first night of the spirits, one should cause [the offering] to be given with fierce spirits;
on the second night of the ancestors, with sesame seeds mixed with rice.
On the third night, one should offer coconut water with boiled rice; on the night of the Yakṣas, flour mixed with milk; and on the fourth night, that of the Nāgas, flour mixed with water.
In the fifth Brahma-watch, one should offer food with lotus seeds, rice, and clarified butter;
in the sixth, which belongs to Śiva, one should cause food with cakes, rice, and clarified butter to be given.
On the seventh day, dedicated to Viṣṇu, one should offer an oblation of rice cooked with jaggery and ghee; on the night of Skanda, rice with jaggery;
and on the night of the Mothers, rice with curd.
Mixed with clarified butter and coconut water, it becomes reddish from the powder of *drākṣā* (grapes) and *niśā* (turmeric);
thereafter, for more than these [specified] days, it is used in the best and other festivals according to the sequence.

By means of the application of three, two, and one [of these] qualities, these groups of crows are formed; even by Śivas, they are reckoned as twenty-one in number, measured by āḍhakas and prasthas. (179)
Then follows the *bhūtabali*, which is respectively superior, middling, or inferior;
it consists of an oblation prepared from any one of the white grains, such as *śāli* rice and others. (180)
It should be pure and fit for the offering; otherwise, it would bring about a fault. The twice-born should have their teeth cleansed, be bathed, and wear white garments and the like. (181)
They should prepare food for the army and carry it with great care; or else, throughout all nights, [they should offer] food with ghee and plantain fruits.
Food mixed with curd and milk is prescribed for the *bhūtabali* offering.
Having thus passed the days of the festival as they have been described according to the rules, [one should proceed]. (183)

On the night before the previous day, after the ritual bath (avabhṛtha), one should perform the tying of the auspicious thread (kautuka-bandhana); having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) and having worshipped Gaṇanāyaka at a favorable moment (sulagna).
One should also worship the festival image and the trident,
as well as a ninefold silken cord, a golden one, and one with pearls.
Having placed that [consecrated water] twelve finger-breadths long upon unbroken grains,
one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and [purify] the ashes with the Astra-mantra.

Then, having consecrated it with mantras, one should tie the protective amulet (kautuka) on the right hand of the deity, using the *traiyyambaka* mantra, the *hṛdaya* mantra, and the *śūlāstra* mantra.
One should bind it there with both hands using the thumb and ring finger; having placed protection upon the forehead, one should perform the lustration ceremony with the waving of lights.

One should pass the night keeping vigil with songs, instrumental music, and other such performances; then, having bathed in the morning and completed the daily worship as before, [one should proceed].
One should place the festival image in the outer pavilion; having fixed a trident in front of it, either to the east or to the north. (190)
Having smeared a circular mandala in the shape of a square with cow-dung and water,
[one should adorn it] with canopies, umbrellas, jars, lamps, mirrors, and chowries.
Having likewise adorned them all around with small bowls and conch shells, and having clothed the mortar and pestle in washed garments; 192.
Having covered it with *darbha* grass and worshipped it, one should prepare the powder there; meanwhile, maidens, having bathed and being well-adorned, sing with sweet voices. (193)
There, they should prepare that auspicious powder with turmeric;
[the six ingredients are] curd, unbroken rice, clarified butter, tips of dūrvā grass, fragrant seeds, and sprouts.
They should place those maidens upon the pestle and the mortar; then that prepared powder, contained in a golden vessel or similar receptacle, [should be offered]. (195)
Then, having consecrated with the heart-mantra the six auspicious substances beginning with curd,
one should place them upon the head of the deity while reciting the root-mantra.
Having anointed [the image] with scented oil and rubbed it with powders of barley, black gram, and other grains,
one should then wipe the deity and the weapon with a cloth.
Having wiped the deity and the weapon with that auspicious powder mixed with gold dust, he should apply the remainder to the heads of his devotees.

One should deposit [the image] for the sake of auspiciousness, which purifies all impurities. Then, having bathed the deity with a cloth and adorned him with ornaments, perfumes, flowers, and so forth,
one should [worship] the limbs of the Vidyā, the Mūrti-mantras, and the limbs of Śiva upon the form of Śiva.
One should perform the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa. || 199 ||
Then, having established the sacred fire upon a sacrificial mound for the purpose of a pilgrimage to that holy site, || 200 ||

Having invoked Śiva and offered clarified butter with the collection of mantras, one should then offer cooked oblations of Palāśa wood-samits, clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge (caru) into his mouth.

Having offered one hundred and eight oblations for each [deity] with black sesame, and one hundred and eight with sesame and clarified butter, he should perform the expiation by offering the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) from the root mantra.
One should offer clarified butter with the six verses beginning with "kanikradat," and having offered clarified butter with the Svasti-sūkta, one should then offer it with the Jayā and other mantras.
Then, having offered the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation and dismissed the fire into the lotus of his heart, he should place the Lord upon a chariot or similar vehicle and proceed to the sacred bathing site.

Accompanied by the sounds of conchs, kettledrums, and other instruments, and with auspicious performances such as song and dance, one should place the trident weapon at the forefront along with the requisites for the ritual bath.
With various banners, parasols, chowries, fans, and so forth, and with lamps, incense, and vases, the eight auspicious symbols were held aloft. (206)
One should proceed by circumambulation from the temple and other sites for a distance of up to a yojana,
toward distinguished rivers, streams, oceans, sacred fords, and the like, which abound with water.
One should proceed with a moderate gait, neither too fast nor too slow; there, one should recite the auspicious *svasti-stuti* and the *svasti-sūkta*.
Likewise, O best of the twice-born, they should recite the Śakunasūkta and the Camaka hymn at the beginning of the singing and instrumental music, and when the sound of "Victory! swells forth. (209)
Having reached the bank of that sacred ford, which is adorned with archways and waterfalls and decorated with canopies and other ornaments, one should place the deity upon a pedestal.
Then, having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, one should consecrate that sacred water (tīrtha) with the mantra "imaṃ me gaṅge yamune sarasvatī" and others as well.
Having worshipped [the deity] with flowers and other offerings while reciting the mantra-saṃhitā, one should then slowly immerse the weapon and the deity three times.
Having bathed together with his disciples, the Guru should worship the deity situated on the bank;
then, having offered the final oblation, he should establish the fire of Śiva upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).

Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the root mantra, and then one-tenth of that amount with the Brahma-mantras, and having offered the cooked oblation and the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should invoke and worship the sacred fords (tīrthas).

He should offer into the fire the oblation for one who is ineligible to sacrifice, beginning with the verses "imaṃ me gaṅge yamune... and so forth; then, having performed the Jaya and other offerings up to the Sviṣṭakṛt, he should worship Jaleśvara at the sacred bathing place.

Having invoked and worshipped the sacred fords (tīrthas), one should also worship the Gaṅgā and others; then, having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha), one should cause the deity to enter the sacred ford.
Having seated the deity upon that pedestal, one should immerse it in the sacred water (tīrtha) with perfumes, myrobalan, turmeric, sandalwood, agallochum, and saffron.
One should gradually perform the ritual of anointing (udvartana) with water, flowers, and incense, each separately,
while sounding conchs, drums, and other instruments, and with the chanting of the Vedas in the four directions.
Having led the Lord to that seat, one should cause the Aghamarṣaṇa rite to be performed;
one should also recite the hymn beginning with "hiraṇyaśṛṅgam" until its conclusion.
Whosoever— whether women or men, or even animals— bathe at that sacred ford at that time, they are all liberated from all sins. (220)
Having removed the ritual curtain and abandoned [all hesitation], one should lift the deity out of the water;
then, having adorned the deity seated upon the pedestal in the water-shed with garments and other ornaments, [one should proceed].

Having worshipped with offerings beginning with perfumes and ending with the presentation of food, and having greeted him with music and auspicious rites as before, one should slowly place him upon the vehicle.
Having gone and reached the temple, having circumambulated it clockwise,
having placed the Lord within the pavilion and worshipped Him, one should then worship the Astra-mantra.
Having installed the festival image and the weapon in their respective places,
one should then worship Śambhu, who resides in the primary liṅga, with special rites.
Having offered the four kinds of food and completed the nightly rites regularly,
one should worship the banner with perfumes and other offerings, and then lower that banner.
As previously described, one should dismiss the hosts of deities and others who were summoned in due order, saying: "May they return to their own abodes as they please. (226)
Then, having worshipped the banner-bull with its own mantras,
one should join it to the primary bull and worship it with special rites.
Having offered the bali-oblation to the great elements, the preceptor, remaining silent and surrounded by people,
should go outside without making a sound, accompanied by all musical instruments except for lamps.
Having worshipped the world-protectors beginning with Brahmā who reside at the joints, one should then dismiss those world-protectors beginning with Brahmā who occupy the joints.

Then, having bathed and entered within, one should worship the Lord of the Field (Kṣetreśa). This concludes the section on the concluding ceremonial bath (avabhṛtha) of the festival. Now, in the morning, one should perform the daily worship as before. || 230 ||

Then, preceded by the scattering [of flowers], the waving of the yak-tail fan, and the whirling of the water-pot weapon (*kumbhāstra*), [the consecration is performed] with jars numbering from nine up to a thousand, according to the prescribed rite.
Having bathed [the image] especially, one should perform a great worship; and to the preceptor together with his disciples, one should give gold and garments.
Having given him ornaments and such, one should give the gifts according to one's ability, as well as to the ascetics, the attendants, the Brahmins, and those observing vows. (233)

Likewise, he [should provide for] the servants of the gods, female slaves, as well as actors and dancers; other servants and laborers, and likewise the poor, the helpless, and those seeking wealth. || 234 ||
One should satisfy [the deity] with food, gold, clothing, and other such items, beginning from the raising of the banner and continuing through the days ending with the ceremonial bathing. (235)

To those who seek, such as Brahmins and others, and even to those bearing religious marks, he should appropriately give food, drink, and so forth, accompanied by excellent side dishes and superior flavors. (236)
Thus, those who cause the festival of Śambhu to be performed, those who perform it themselves, or those who witness it—
all of them become leaders of the Gaṇas.

Thus has been described the ritual for the festival of Śiva, beginning with the raising of the banner and categorized according to the distinctions of the "excellent" and other classes, concluding with the ceremonial bath; by means of this, the Moon-crested Lord, together with the Daughter of the Mountain King and the lords of his Gaṇas, attains supreme grace.
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, the section on the rules for the Great Festival, in the Kriyāpāda of the Siddhāntasāra, which is the *Śrīmadīśānaśivagurudevapaddhati*.
Now begins the fiftieth chapter.
Now, first there is the minor ablution for the triad of the youngest [deities], then the three medium ablutions,
and finally the three superior ablutions.
With nine, twenty-five, and thereafter with seven, seven, eighty-one,
one hundred and eight, and two hundred [verses].
Then, following that, there were fifty-two [kalaśas], as well as three hundred,
one hundred arrows, and seven hundred more.
Then, with jars numbering more than a thousand, or even with one thousand jars plus eight more, he [performed the rite]. || 4 ||
The bath performed with [substances] filled according to the prescribed rules is said to be the most excellent of the excellent;
it is superior to [baths performed with] one hundred and eight [verses] and so forth.
In the center, however, the Brahma-vase should be presided over by Śiva.
First, the ablution known as *alpa* (minor) is prescribed with nine vases. (6)
The three minor ablutions are performed with the jars of Abhikṛtyā and the others,
using [mantras] one hundred and eight times and so forth.
For it is indeed separate from the pavilion.
The Rudra and Atijagatī meters consist of [twenty-seven and twenty-nine] syllables, respectively;
the Atiśakvarī and Atyaṣṭikara meters consist of [thirty-one and thirty-three] syllables, measured by the [number of] Atidhṛti.
The bathing pavilions for the thousand-pitcher rite are tenfold, measuring twenty-one cubits; these are the lowest [grade]. * * * * * 10.
It should be twenty-five cubits; then, with twenty-nine cubits it would be medium, and with thirty-three cubits it would be the best.
The pillars should be equal in number to the hands (fingers) of each respective pavilion plus one, in sequence; all of them should be perfectly uniform and made from wood of a single species.
In the case of minor ablutions, as well as for those of inferior status and so forth, [the height] is nine tālas;
[the mantras are] measured by the numbers of the Rudras (eleven), Atijagatī (forty-eight), and Atiśakvarī (sixty-four).
From the high platform above that paved floor, pillars arise in sequence with their bases [measured] by twelve finger-breadths;
in smaller structures, they are then two, three, or four times that measure.
The supports for the pillars should be measured in finger-breadths (aṅgula) across the three [fingers] beginning with the little finger;
likewise, there should be the lintel (lupā), the cross-beam (vaṃśa), the secondary beam (anuvaṃśa), and so forth, as well as the upper covering.
The pavilions should be constructed with excellent trees such as the pūga and others, as well as with coconut leaves and so forth, according to the requirements and available means. || 16 ||
All pavilions should be constructed in sequence as quadrangular, with four doors, devoid of a central pillar, and possessing auspicious foundations.
The site for the pavilion should be at least as large as the sun’s diameter and be of the highest quality;
its floor should be paved all around with bricks, wood, or clay.
There, having offered the *vāstu-bali* and having dismissed the carpenters, one should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be made and perform the *vāstu-homa*. || 19 ||
One should feed there as many Brahmins as there are jars; or, in case of inability, half that number, or even half of that, according to the prescribed rule.
It was surrounded by a garland of *darbha* grass, provided with a canopy and arched gateways; its pillars were draped in fine cloths and hung with strings of pearls.

Its floor was beautifully smeared, it was delightful, perfumed with incense, and sprinkled with sandalwood paste; it possessed excellent doorways and water-jars, and its pillars were draped with various kinds of fruits.
Having decorated the bathing pavilion according to its beauty and according to one's capacity, [one should do so] on the seventh or fifth day prior to the day of the ritual bath.

Having properly performed the offering of the ritual sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa), one should then recite the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāhavācana). Then, having smeared these [spots] with the products of the cow (gavya) and having sprinkled them with water and other substances, [one should proceed]. || 24 ||

Having performed the consecration with the rites of fortitude (*dhṛti-saṃskāra*) preceded by the scattering and throwing [of flowers], and following that, having worshipped the *kumbha*, the weapon (*astra*), and the *vardhanī* vessel, and performed the circumambulation and further offerings; || 25 ||
Having performed the protection of the weapons with threads smeared with flour-paste,
one should perform the laying out of the lines, extending equally toward the east and the north.
One should fashion the squares for the lowest [grade] and so forth, measuring twelve finger-breadths, as well as those of modified measurement, into four-sided shapes.
For example:
having made it two cubits square by means of threads divided into nine squares, one should place [the deity] in the central square; by that, the "minor ablution" (alpasnapana) is prescribed.
The section on the rite of the minor ablution:
In a field consisting of seven times seven squares, having set aside nine squares in the center, one should erase one square from each row surrounding it in all directions. (29)
For the sake of the pathways (vīthi), there should be three squares each in the middle of the two pathways;
in the corners, there is one [square] each... || 30 ||
The Chapter on the Thirty-five Vases.
(p. 484) In the field consisting of eleven compartments, there shall be nine squares in the center. || 31 ||
In the central square of that [grid], there should be a lotus; outside of the ninefold [group], one should erase [the lines] all around.
And one should cleanse the stomach. || 33 ||
Then, one should erase the four syllables at the end in the four directions and the corners,
so that the corners have their points clearly manifest with seven syllables each.
There should be four paths clearly visible all around due to the omission of rows;
there should be eight groups of nine in the eight directions, and in the central group of nine, there is a lotus.
One should draw [the design] thus in the central square; there shall be a lotus in the middle section of the field, in the central square of the *nanda*.
The four outer rows, extending toward the east and north, are to be erased; having established a row on the outside of the pathways in all four directions. (38)
Or [alternatively], within the nine positions, by omitting one word from each corner. || 39 ||
There are one hundred and eight squares, with a lotus in the center; having laid out rows in the four directions, there is a single outer row.
By omitting one word from each corner on all sides, there arise one hundred and eight squares, with a lotus in the center. || 41 ||
Of the one hundred and eight [deities]. Furthermore, in a field consisting of three times five squares (*puṭaka*), having established four paths as before, one should eliminate one row on all sides.
In the middle of the two rows, one should sweep out nine squares in the four directions.
Then, for the sake of the doors, there should be twenty-one squares in the corners;
and again, for the hundred [squares], it is the same.
As before, in the grid of three times five squares, there are seven squares for each of the seven [sections].
Having placed [the central element] in the middle, one should smear the four paths all around; having established the group of nine in the center, one proceeds by omitting rows all around.
* * * * * * * * * * * * * * * | Thus, indeed, there come to be * * * * * compartments as before. || 46 ||
In the cardinal directions, one should erase the four squares equally within the two inner corners of the primary squares, and one should also eliminate the central square.
Thus, twelve compartments [are formed].
This concludes the section on the three kinds of one-hundred-and-eight pitchers.
In a field consisting of twenty-one squares, there is a lotus in the center, upon the square called Nanda.
Then, there should be four paths extending completely around it;
outside of that, eight groups of nine [squares], and outside of that, [further groups].
Clearly, there are two hundred and fifty-two words.
This is the section on the two hundred and fifty-two jars;
outside that [circle], there are three hundred jars due to the skipping of rows. || 51 ||
A row in the cardinal directions should be omitted; therefore, outside of those three cells, there should be six surrounding paths extending according to their own length.
Within the sixteen corner squares, there are four inner corners. * * * * * * * * * * Thus, three hundred squares are prescribed for the three hundred pitchers.
And in the central lotus-square of Brahmā, there is also the pitcher named Śiva.
The Chapter on the Three Hundred Vases (Triśatakalaśādhikāra).
486) In the thirty-one compartments, [the deities are placed] all around for the sake of the path (vīthi).
Crush it completely.
And outside that outer row, one should likewise erase a row;
then, from the three cells, beyond the three squares on all sides.
The paths [extend] in every direction; indeed, there are eight paths. (58)
In this [mandala], there are altogether eight groups of forty-nine, and indeed twenty-eight groups of three as well. (59)
There is a group of four squares in a single enclosure, and in the center is a beautiful lotus. * * * * * * * * * Among those [vessels], the Śiva-vessel in the middle is the most prominent. (61)
Thus, there would indeed be five hundred and four squares;
this is the section on the five hundred and four jars.
One should mark out the rows one by one, extending eastward and northward. Thus.
Indeed, there are eight streets in each direction there. || 63 ||
In the center and likewise in the eight directions, there are indeed eighty-one squares; thus there shall be nine distinct arrays, with one in the very center of the central array.
One should cleanse that [area] and draw an eight-petaled lotus within it;
thus, indeed, seven hundred and twenty squares are traditionally taught.
In the center of the lotus, there is one additional pitcher designated as Śiva.
This concludes the section on the seven hundred and twenty pitchers.
When the field is divided equally into forty-five squares: (66)

In the center, within a lotus formed by five sets of five syllables each, there shall be the Śiva-pitcher; one should erase the surrounding outer row for the sake of the pathway, and that which is outside of it.
Having laid down one row and three rows, and two [rows] in the middle of these,
one should gradually erase the rows on all sides within the three pathways.
Outside of that, having left aside the rows of the Vedas, one should erase a row all around for the sake of the pathway,
as before, outside of the two rows.
There should be a pathway (vīthī) all around in rows; then, from the lotus, one should remove two squares in each row extending toward its own direction for the sake of the doors.
The junction of the four great avenues, even among the sixteen [squares], should be preserved;
however, one must protect the central squares for the purpose of placing the *vikārakumbha* (the transformative pitcher).
The door-decorations and sub-decorations, as well as the corners, should be arranged in due order; one should sweep three squares on the inside and five squares on the outside at the doorway.
One should erase three outer *śobhās* and one outer *upaśobhā*; thereafter, one should also erase the *upaśobhās* in the reverse order. (73)
Thus, there are four gates and thirty-two ornaments; likewise, there are as many secondary ornaments in that which is designated as the five enclosures.
The thousand-pitcher [consecration] should be understood according to its proper enumeration.
This is the section on the thousand pitchers within the five-fold enclosure.
However, in the field consisting of forty-nine squares, by means of the central squares— || 75 ||
Having drawn a lotus with nine squares, there should be a pathway on all sides by means of two rows; in the outer row, there shall be one square in each of the cardinal directions.

Having wiped the interior and brought about the unification of the paths, one should erase the three internal squares located at the corners of that [grid], and then those situated outside the central lotus.
In a row extending from east to north, one should erase [the lines] entirely for the sake of the path;
and outside that, all around, at an interval of three squares each.
Twelve separate rows, extending eastward and northward, should be marked out;
here, in the central array, there shall be five [units] in sequence.
Outside of that, there should be twelve groups of nine; likewise in all four [directions], and in each of the four corners, there is a separate group of nine modifications.
In this way, there would indeed be one hundred and twelve *navakas*; then, one should eliminate one external *navaka* in each of the four directions. (81)
For the sake of the doors, one should erase a single square in the final corner;
in this way, one thousand squares situated in the middle of the boundary are removed.
Indeed, there are one hundred and eight lotuses in the center, and one lotus in the middle; then, outside the pathway, there are the remaining two rows.
For the sake of adorning the doors and their ornaments, there are indeed pitchers with various forms within those compartments. (84)
Indeed, there is one thousand and eight [deities] in the lotus, as well as the Śiva-pitcher;
this is the section on the one thousand and eight pitchers.
In the field consisting of fifty-three squares, there is a lotus in the central group of nine.
Outside that, [one should draw] a row all around;
then, in order to establish the doors, one should omit one square in each direction within that outer row.
In each of the four corners as well, there should be a separate group of five squares; outside of that, one should clear away a row all around for the sake of the pathway.
For the sake of accomplishing the beauty of the doors and so forth, one should place two [lines]; between them, a single row is to be erased all around for the sake of the walkway (vīthī).
Starting from the inner path (antarvīthī), one should erase three rows in each of the directions for the sake of the door-paths, and likewise join them to the outer path.
Then, immediately after the six rows situated within the outer path,
one should clear away the great paths (mahāvīthī) surrounding the three inner rows.
There, in the middle row among the eight directions, one should protect the eight central squares; in those, one should place the pitchers at the junctions.
Having established the squares of the principles (tattva-koṣṭha) from the middle of the six rows between the outer path and the great path, one should successively erase two rows.
When this has been done, there will be thirty-six squares all around;
one should then eliminate the "Nanda" squares within those numbered by the [square of the] Kṛti [number].
"In the corners" means up to that point.
Now, for the sake of accomplishing the internal array within the array of the four inner corners, having abandoned—
One should erase one row from among the three outer rows. || 94 ||
Within that, in the corners of the inner altar (antarvedi), there shall be one hundred and eight squares; starting from the third path (vīthi), a single row [of squares] proceeds in due order.
In the middle, the great path (mahāvīthi) should be erased as far as it has extended; from that point, there are indeed twelve squares for the principles (tattva). 96.
And in their inner corners, one should clear out the Nanda-chambers;
in the inner enclosure (*antarvyūha*), there are one hundred and eight pitchers in the second [section].
In the third [section], there are three hundred and seven jars;
in the joints, there are eight; and in the fourth, there are forty-one jars and so forth.
Five hundred jars, and thus a thousand jars in total, are to be known for the four enclosures;
in the center, the jar of Śiva is additional.
In the two outer rows, as before, there are four gates in the cardinal directions; there should be forty-two *śobhās*, and the *ubha-śobhās* are equal in number to them.
The corners should consist of human-sized squares; one should erase them as before, but in every arrangement, one should fashion the corners in the shape of ploughs.
In the *Caturāvaraṇa*, this is the section on the thousand-pitcher rite:
When the field has been measured out as a level area of fifty-five squares, one should establish eighty-one central squares and nine nested compartments. (102)
Six separate paths, extending eastward and northward, are to be deleted;
thus, there shall be twenty-five arrays consisting of eighty-one squares each. (103)
The boundary path consists of two outer rows as before; there are four doors in the cardinal directions, along with the *śobhās* and *upaśobhās*. (104)
The forty corners should be drawn separately with squares for the mantras;
in the center of the central array, one should draw a lotus with nine squares.
One should also remove two rows on all sides for the sake of the pathway (vīthī). Outside of that,
in the four directions, there should be three squares each for the purpose of the doors.

One should wipe [the area] at the corners of the doors so that there may be five separate footprints; outside the central array, one should arrange a single array separately in each of the directions.

One should wipe them completely and perform the fire-oblation (homa) upon them according to the prescribed rule. Outside of that, however, are the arrays of the Kṛtis; in their center is a single square.
Having laid out two rows on all sides, one should remove them for the sake of the path; then, outside of that, there shall be one square each in the four directions between the two rows.
One should likewise smear [the area] for the sake of the doors, extending to each respective outer path;
thus, there are indeed forty-nine squares in the *kṛtivyūha*.
In the central array, however, there are twenty jars upon the lotus;
thus, in the twenty-onefold array, one thousand jars are prescribed.
In the Brahma-position, however, there is a pitcher known as Śiva, which is superior in the lotus;
this is the section concerning the twenty-one thousand pitchers of the Vyūha.
Having thus laid out the squares and having smeared them all around— || 112 ||
Having covered the footprints continuously with white powder, one should place one *āḍhaka*, half an *āḍhaka*, or a *prastha* of *śāli* rice at every step.
Having placed half that amount of rice, sesame seeds, and parched grains into them in sequence,
one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), or perhaps with rice alone.

Having placed darbha grass upon each of them for the purpose of a seat (viṣṭara), he should place upon them the aforementioned jars, which are wrapped with thread and provided with their respective implements.
One should set aside separately the brushes that have been washed and fumigated.
Then the preceptor, together with his disciples, having bathed and dressed in white garments and the like, [should proceed]. (116)
Adorned with rings and other ornaments, having washed both his hands and feet,
and having sipped water for purification, he sits comfortably and performs the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
Having properly worshipped Vighneśa to the south of the pavilion, one should, as before, perform the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa upon the body of the preceptor.
As previously stated, one should worship the gates, beginning with Śāntikalā, with flowers and other offerings. (119)
Having sacrificed and discharged the iron arrow (nārāca), he should enter as before; having placed the weapon at the threshold, [he worships] the guardian of the site (*vāstupā*).
Having honored his own seat, facing either eastward or northward, he should sprinkle the jars as previously specified with the arghya waters in due order.

Having turned himself toward the north and removed the sacrificial grass-bunches (*utkūrca*), he himself, being the very body of Sadāśiva, [worships] the Support-Energy (*ādhāraśakti*) and the jar (*kalaśa*). || 122 ||
Meditating upon that nectar arising from the moon in the lotus at the *dvādaśānta*, consisting of water and the other elements,
one should gradually recite the *praṇava* according to the order of emanation.
Having filled the jars with the prescribed substances, together with gold, perfumes, and flowers, each one should be wrapped separately in white cloth.
[He should offer] bilva and aśvattha leaves adorned with garlands and strings, along with barley,
rice grains, and vessels filled with fruits according to the prescribed ritual.

Having sprinkled water over them, having placed the respective mantra and deity upon them, and having worshipped them with the fivefold offerings (pañcopacāra), one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) as prescribed.
For ablutions beginning with the minimum and ending with one hundred and eight, the oblation should be offered in a single fire,
either in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
Then, it is prescribed that oblations be offered in the four directions for those [rites] ending with seven hundred;
likewise for the rite of one thousand and eight, and also for the rite of a thousand jars.
Having established the Śivāgni in the fire-pits (kuṇḍa) prescribed for the eight directions as before, one should then divide it from the central fire according to the rule.
The preceptor and the guardians of the images should offer oblations with the Brahma-mantras and the ancillary mantras in their respective directions;
in this rite involving a thousand jars, twenty-one ritual arrays (vyūhas) are prescribed.
There, in the eight sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) in the directions, and likewise within the four directions in the cleared arrays (vyūhas),
one should offer oblations into the fire with the Brahma-mantras in sequence.
One should offer sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, white mustard seeds, sesame seeds, and barley—
either half or even a quarter of the quantity corresponding to the number of those respective jars.
Having offered oblations with the root mantra, they should offer with the mantras of the forms and limbs in one-tenth of that quantity.
Then, having combined all that clarified butter from the residue with the tips of *kuśa* grass, [they should proceed]. (133)
One should pour a little [of the water] into the jars and worship again at the conclusion of the offering; "all rites" is declared to be the common procedure for all ablutions.
The section on common ritual duties:
The substances, deities, and mantras for the various ablutions (snapana), as prescribed in the Śaiva Tantras, are now written down in their proper order, beginning with the ninefold [ablution]. (135)
Māṇikya, pearl, diamond, coral, emerald, topaz, lapis lazuli, sapphire, and hessonite, in that order. (136)
One should place the jars in the directions of the center, Indra (East), Yama (South), Varuṇa (West), Soma (North), Agni (Southeast), Rakṣas (Southwest), and Vāyu (Northwest),
filling them with the aforementioned gems, perfumes, flowers, kuśa grass, and water.

One should fill [the vessel] with the limbs beginning with Īśa and the Brahmās, and then perform the consecration by sprinkling. However, for the filling starting from the center, the sequence for the bathing from the center to the end involves those beginning with Indra.
And one should worship the weapon (astra) in the vessel for increasing the weapons, near the Śiva-pitcher,
separated by flowers, water, and incense, according to the sequence of the four squares.

Or one may begin with the King of Waters (āporāja) using the *vyomavidyā* mantra in the middle; this applies to both the group of nine and the group of twenty-five. Furthermore, for the twenty-five, one should place the water of the five jewels in the center.

One should fill the Brahma-pitcher presided over by Śiva; then, in the various directions, one should offer water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), the respectful offering (arghya), and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
In the locations beginning with Āgneya, one should offer clarified butter, honey, milk, and likewise curd; and in the first triad, sugarcane juice, decoction water, and fruit water.
A decoction prepared with the bark of the four milky trees and bilva, as well as water from parched grain,
fragrant water, and flower-water, should be placed on the right side.
In the western triad are water with gold, water with rubies, and water with pearls;
in the northern triad are water with barley, water with coral, and water with sesame seeds.
In the fires and other elements, one should place dūrvā grass, blue lotuses, kuśa grass, and rice-water; in the center, the root-mantra, the Brahmā-mantras, the limb-mantras (aṅgas), and the deity.

In the vases situated at the corners of the three [triads] starting from the east and in the center, one should place the eight forms beginning with Earth (Kṣmā), the deity, and the mantras, ending with the word "namaḥ. (146)
To the east and on the other sides of the pitchers, the divine [deities] are each the size of a thumb:
Bhuvaneśāna, Īśāna, and likewise Ekapiṅgekṣaṇa.
Udbhava, Bhava, and Mahādeva of great luster—this triad [is used] in the filling and other rites, beginning with the central jar (madhyaghaṭa) and the water-pitcher (āpyakumbha). || 148 ||
For the water for the feet, one should use "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ" and immediately after "āpo hi ṣṭhā"; for the arghya water, "āpaḥ punantu," and for the cow-products, "agnim īle."
With the mantra "iṣe tvā," he should offer ghee; then with honey, using "madhu vātā"; with milk, using "āpyāyasva";
and with curd, using "dadhi krāvṇa. (150)
Then, for the first triad,
[one should bathe] with the *ikṣu* plants used in the hymn beginning "Upatvāgne," with the water from the fruit of the *mānastoka* plant,
and with the decoction of the *aśvāvatī* plant.
Then, in the southern triad,
[he should offer] flowers with fragrant water using the verse "agne āyāhi," and also [offer] flowers with the verse "puṣpavatī" and "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ" as well as "brahmajajñānam. 152.
Then, with the three mantras beginning with "samudrajyeṣṭhā," followed by "rakṣohaṇam," "vāstoṣpate," and "śanno devīr," [he should perform the ritual]. || 153 ||

With water containing barley, with water containing coral, and likewise with water containing sesame seeds in the subsequent [rites], one should perform the eye-opening; and with water containing *dūrvā* grass, one should perform it for the sake of prosperity and for the sake of the birth of a lotus.
Then, with *triṣṭubh* verses and water from *kuśa* grass, and again with rice-water, one should bathe the Lord of Pārvatī while reciting the hymn beginning with "āśuḥ śiśānaḥ. (155)
With the central nine-pitcher vessel and the great *vyomavidyā*,
or else with the *brahma-mantras*, the *aṅga-mantras*, and the *gāyatrī* known as *śiva*.
One should perform the ablution with the Sāvitrī, the Mūrti-mantras, and the Vyomavidyā; [this is done] twenty-five times. Then, however, from the midst of forty-nine jars— || 157 ||
One should fill the central jar with gold, jewels, and perfumes,
as well as water for washing the feet, water for sipping, the *arghya* offering, the products of the cow (*gavya*), clarified butter, honey, milk, and curd. (158)

Now, for the fulfillment of the middle group of eight and then for the five dedicated to Indra, [the offerings] are made with water mixed with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, saffron, and ushira root. (159)
In the southeast, it is recommended with the five [offerings] and with the five grains;
in the southwest, likewise with flowers such as the utpala, kalhāra, padma, and white utpala.
Then, in the five [vases] of Vāyu and Īśa, one should fill them in sequence with the five [flowers]: Mallikā, Jāti, Campaka, Pāṭala, and Karavīra. || 161 ||

The group of nine, beginning with Śiva, Brahmā, Aṅga, and Mantreśa, is traditionally taught; these are the forms [of the deities] situated in the eight directions starting from the east, as well as in the center.
From the center, to the south of the eight [cells], the powers (śaktis) beginning with Vāmā are placed;
from the center, to the north of the cells, is the group of eight guardians of the forms (mūrtipās) beginning with Śarva.
In the squares immediately following those, there is the group of eight beginning with Vāma and Bhīma;
for the remaining eight squares, the Vidyeśas are the presiding deities in successive order.
One should consecrate him with those mantras, including the Tāra and the Hṛdaya, by means of the eight Brahma-aṅgas situated in the center. || 165 ||
One should bathe Śiva with the five *camaka* hymns in the directions starting from the east,
and with the five [mantras] beginning with *pāvamānī* and *hiraṇya* located in the four corners.

In the center, one should also bathe [the deity] with the Śiva-pitcher using the Vyomavidyā mantra. [This applies to] forty-nine [pitchers]. Now, in the case of eighty-one [pitchers], there are five jewels in the central pitcher.
Gold and water from a sacred bathing place are prescribed for those eight external jars;
likewise, water for the feet, water for sipping, the arghya offering, cow-products, clarified butter, honey, milk, and curd are also [to be placed].
In the eastern group of nine, in the center, are sandalwood, yellow pigment (rocanā), and amarū; as well as camphor, saffron, kuṣṭha, māṃsī, granthi, and ura.
To the south, [he should place] earth from a bull's horn, an elephant's tusk, a sacred field, a river, a pond, a mountain, an anthill, a crab's hole, and a lake. (170)

The four—Kṣīra, Āgava, Bilva, and Āmra—as well as Madhūka, Aśoka, and Jambu, are known to be auspicious when their bark is present in the nine [trees] in the west (Vāruṇī) in successive order. || 171 ||
Plantains, jackfruit, mangoes, citron, pomegranate, lime, wood-apple, coconut, and rose-apple. (172)
In the nine northern regions, fruits are used; in the south-eastern direction, water born of the ocean, as well as water from rivers, lakes, ponds, and auspicious wells. (173)
Turmeric, parched grain, sacred ash, safflower, and water—these are indeed the nine; likewise, wild rice, mudga beans, mung beans, white mustard, barley, and śāli rice. (174)
Sesame, priyaṅgu, and śyāmāka are recorded as the nine [plants] in the southwest; likewise, the goddess Lakṣmī, harikrāntā, musalī, and bhṛṅgarāja. || 175 ||
Sadābhadra, Śakravallī, Bhītā, and Ekadala-ambuja— these are the substances that should be used in the nine squares of the northwest, in their respective order.
One should cast two lotuses, two water-lilies, three blue lotuses, one night-blooming lily, and one white water-lily into the northeast among the nine [offerings]. (177)
With the Brahmā-aṅgas beginning with the water for the feet (pādya), and likewise with the mantras beginning with "idaṃ viṣṇu" and "āpo hi ṣṭhā," as follows:
"idaṃ viṣṇurvicakrame" and "āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ. || 178 ||
Likewise, [he should worship] with "agnim īḷe purohitam" and so forth, as well as with "iṣe tvā" and so on, and with "ghṛtam mimikṣe" and so forth, and "madhu vātā ṛtāyate. (179)
From the hymns beginning with "āpyāyasva," "same tu te," "dadhikrāvṇo akāriṣam," "prācyena navakena," and "āpo rājānam," [he should perform the rites]. || 180 ||
In the south, [he should worship] with the Puruṣasūkta; in the west, with the Kadrudrādya hymn; and in the north, with the nine verses beginning with "imāṃ rudrāya tapase."
With the nine verses beginning with "āgneya," [he offers] to these Rudras who possess firm bows; and from the section beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ," [he offers] to Agni. || 182 ||
Then, in the southwest with nine [verses], and in the northwest with nine,
one should proceed in order from the beginning of the section starting with "hiraṇyaśṛṅgam" until the end of the anuvāka.
Having consecrated [the disciple] in the northeast with the nine [mantras] beginning with *śann indra*, using the central Śiva-pitcher and the great *vyomavidyā* mantra; 184.
Of the eighty-one [deities],
within the one hundred and eight [vessels], the Śiva-kumbha [is filled] with jewels, gold, kuśa grass, and water.
Having filled that [space], one should also fill the outer triads.
With *nyagrodha*, *udumbara*, and *aśvattha*; with those born from *plakṣa*, *jambu*, and *palāśa*; and with *śirīṣa*, *bilva*, *madhuka*, *saptaparṇa*, *asana*, and *arjuna* [trees]. || 186 ||
In the [mandala] beginning with Agni, there are five substances: sugarcane juice, honey, sesame, and the products of the cow;
in the nine [sections] starting from the center, there are the roots of kuśa grass and eight types of earth.
Śāka, priyaṅgu, māṣa, yava, godhūma, sarṣapa, mudga, tila, and niṣpāva—these nine [grains] are situated in the southern direction, starting from the center. 188.
One should fill the western [section] with nine [vessels] containing Campaka, Unmattaka, Droṇa, Aśoka, Kumuda, Utpala, Karavīra, Abja, and Jāti flowers. 189.
One should fill the nine [vessels] in the north with bilva, mango, badarī, pūga, coconut, pomegranate, plantain, jackfruit, and jambū fruits. (190)
River water, lake water, tank water, ocean water, water from an auspicious well, saffron, moon-powder (camphor),
rice-flour, and ashes— these are for the eight fires.
Lakṣmī, Devī, Harikrāntā, Sahā, Ekadala, Ambuja, Śakravallī, Sadābhadra, and Musalī are in the eight directions starting from the southwest (Nairṛta). 192.
Two types of *tulasī*, *ayapāmārga*, *bhṛṅgarāja*, *aparājitā*, *bhītā*, *damanaka*, and *dūrvā*— these are said to constitute the group of eight winds (*mārutāṣṭaka*).
One should fill the eight directions with eight scents, beginning with sandalwood and so forth. Then, in the three [triads], there are the Śrīparṇī, the Śamī, and the Khadira.
The *saptacchada*, the *kakubha*, the *asana*, and the *kadambaka*; the *raktacandana* and the *alaghu*, as well as the *sarala* and the *sarja*. (195)
The Bakula, Karṇikāra, Pāṭala, Aravatha, Tamāla, Bilva, Dhātrī, and the trees of the four milks as well. (196)
One should fill the three corners with rudrākṣa and putrajīva beads respectively; in the center of the four sets of three, however, according to the sequence starting from the east.
The roots are the Brahmans, the limbs are the mantras, and these are the deities;
in the four corner compartments are the four forms beginning with Kṣmā.
The deities and their names are the mantras ending with "namaḥ.
From the beginning up to the King of Waters (Āporāja), and prior to the Puruṣasūkta in the southern direction. (199)

With the hymn beginning with "kadrudrāya," [he should worship] Varuṇī; and for Rudra, [he should worship] in the north. The mantras for the nine groups should be those of Āpaḥ and Viṣṇu for the two preceding [deities].
The deity of the two hymns is Rudra; it is also for the remaining two.
For the eight verses of the Āgneya [hymn], the mantra is: "imā rudrāya sthiradhanvane. (201)

With the hymn beginning "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ," one should perform the rite for the eight jars of the southwest (Nairṛta), and with the hymn beginning "hiraṇyaśṛṅgam," for the eight jars of the northwest (Vāyavya). || 202 ||
The hymn beginning with "śanna indra" is for the northeast; however, for the group of eight, Rudra, the Waters, Varuṇa, Indra, and Agni are the deities in sequence. (203)
One should consecrate the deity with these [mantras], so it is said.
Then, starting from the three groups and the eight [groups] between Indra and Agni, there is the one the size of a thumb known as Bhuvaneśvara. (204)
Īśāna, Ekapiṅgākṣa, Udbhava, Bhava, and Mahādeva of great splendor—these are the mantras and their respective deities. (205)

The mantras consist of the respective names preceded by "Tārā" and ending with "namaḥ"; furthermore, there is this [mantra] beginning with "idaṃ viṣṇu" and the triad beginning with "dadhikrāvṇo". (206)
The first verse is "Agnimīle," and likewise "Iṣetva" and so forth; also "Ghṛtaṃ mimikṣe" and so on, as well as "Madhuvātā ṛtāyate. (207)
The mantras shall be their deities; for the first [offering], Viṣṇu is said to be the deity.
For the triad beginning with curd, the deity is Apas; for the Ṛgveda and the others, however, it is Pāvaka.
For the [mantra] beginning with "iṣe tvā," the deity is Savitṛ; for that beginning with "ghṛta," it is Agni; for that beginning with "madhu," it is the Pitṛs;
and for the [mantra] beginning with "āpyāyasva," the deity is the Moon.
Space, the sun, the moon, and the sacrificer are the deities; the mantras are as before:
the six-syllable [mantra] pervading the sky and the one consisting of the letters of the Paṅkti meter.

The Aghora weapon, as well as the [other] weapons, their mantras, and Śiva as their deity—by means of these, one should perform the consecration in due order; that is to say, with the central Śiva-pitcher and the great Vyomavidyā mantra. (211)
One should consecrate Mahādeva; Śiva himself is the deity for this rite of one hundred and eight [offerings].
But for the bathing ceremony consisting of two hundred and fifty-two [verses], however, || 212 ||
One should fill the central pitcher as before with gold, gems, and water from the *kuśa* grass; then, one should likewise fill eight or nine pitchers in the directions outside of that.
There are also nine squares situated at the four corners; thus, there are one hundred and eight.
One should fill them with the very same substances prescribed for the one hundred and eight [offerings].
Then, with those very same deity-mantras, one should fill twelve [vessels] in the four directions in sequence with these substances and with water.
Nandyāvarta, dhurdhūra, kapittha, kadambaka, mālyaṅga, bhadrā, as well as drāvaṇa and bilvaka. || 216 ||
Maruka, padma, tulasī, muṇḍī, kuravaka, and arjaka [are used] in the middle twelve;
in the east, soma, karpūra, and vallikā.
The kubjaka, the śatapatra, the karṇikāra, and likewise the baka;
the white arka, the flower of the red agasti, and the kāñcanāra. || 218 ||
A pair of *mallikā* flowers and a red *karavīra* on the right; a *tamāla*, a *mādhavī*, a white *mandāra*, and two *pāṭala* flowers. (219)
Gokṣura, bhūkadamba, the sprouts of adhyaṅkola, the flower of bījapūra, and the sprouts of lavaṅga. || 220 ||
Rājārka, svarṇayūthī, and two [plants] with white sprouts and flowers, as well as śvetadūrvā and mahāmarī, constitute the twelve [deities] of the western direction.
Kaccora, uśīra, mustā, and palāśa flowers; then white and black unmatta flowers, śephālī, and likewise bṛhatī. || 222 ||
In the northern central group of twelve, there should be substances in due order;
having filled eight of the twelve side-vessels with clear water. (223)
One should also place sandalwood, gold, and flowers upon these,
using those nine weapons recited one hundred and eight times in their respective order.
Having bathed Śiva with the eleven Anuvākas and the twelve Raudra hymns, as well as those beginning with the Aindra hymns, he should then [bathe him] with the remaining twelve.
The Brahmans [should fill] the central pitcher with the great *vyomavidyā* mantra; likewise, they should fill two hundred and fifty-two pitchers,
as well as three hundred pitchers, with gold, gems, *kuśa* grass, and water.
Having filled the central pitcher, one should fill the eight pitchers outside it with water from sacred fords (tīrtha) and the eight jewels.
Having likewise filled it with one hundred and eight substances according to the mantra, one should then place four footprints within the nine squares at its corner.
Therefore, one should fill [the vessel] with pure water from the outer corner of the plow,
using fifty-two hundred substances, mantras, and deities.
Having filled those nine central squares and the groups of three numbering twelve and eight, one should fill them with golden water.
For three hundred [villages], there are five hundred and eight; the central jar, however, is as before, having been filled according to the ritual with gold, water, and the five jewels. (231)
Outside, there are the jars of transformation;
outside of that, in the group of nine, and also in the central group of eight, there are twelve hundred jars.
One should fill [the vessel] with one hundred and eight substances and four others; outside of that, all around, in the two sets of nine coverings.
There are indeed forty-nine groups of nine;
one should place the corresponding substances within their central jars.
One should fill the corner jars with the four remaining substances,
and all the other remaining jars should be filled with pure water.
One should perform the consecration with Rudra himself, using the root-mantra according to the prescribed rite and with jars from the middle enclosure containing flowers with golden fragrance.
Outside of that, having consecrated [the deity] in sequence with all the nine [mantras] proclaimed by Nārāyaṇa,
and then with the creepers, one should perform the consecration in due order.
One should bathe [the deity] with the central ninth jar using the Vyomavidyā mantra; or else, one may do so with all the jars in sequence,
using the Saṃhitā mantras.
The Guru should consecrate the deity with the Brahma-mantras, the Śiva-gāyatrī, the Sāvitrī, and the Vyomavidyā, reciting the respective Sūktas in their proper order.
Eight Brahmins, assuming the forms [of the eight deities], should stand around and mutter prayers,
while touching the jars with bundles of *kuśa* grass and likewise touching Śiva.
For five hundred and eight [recitations];
then, for seven hundred and twenty, one should fill the middle jar with gold, jewels, and pure water while reciting the *Saṃhitā*. (241)
Outside of that, in nine groups of eight, there are seventy-two jars; these should be filled with the prescribed substances in sequence, using the mantras declared as one hundred and eight.
Externally, there are seventy-two arrays in the three enclosures in sequence; in their center is a group of nine, and there are indeed as many vases as those.
Into those [squares], one should sequentially place that many substances, one by one;
the remaining twelve substances are to be placed in the three enclosures within the corners.
One should sequentially deposit [the substances] into twelve jars, ending with the direction of Śarva;
likewise, in the arrays beginning with the center, according to the application of the eighty-one-fold [division].

One should sequentially place as many words from the *vyomavyāpin* mantra upon these [six paths] as there are; furthermore, one should apply the sixfold path specifically designated for each of them. (246)
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite with the great Vyoman-vidyā, the Guru should consecrate the deity with the Rudra-mantras as well as the Brahma-mantras.
Then, assuming their physical forms as before, the Brahmins, holding *kūrca* grass in their hands, should recite the *Kadrudra*, the *Puruṣasūkta*, the *Śrīsūkta*, and the *Pavamāna*.
Of the seven hundred and twenty [deities],
and of the thousand-pitcher [offering] endowed with the five coverings, one should fill the jar with fragrant substances, gold, jewels, and water from auspicious bathing-places (tīrtha). 249.
One should fill the central vessel called Śiva, and then the twenty vessels outside of it;

as for the jars in the corners starting from the southeast, they should be filled with water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), the respectful offering (arghya), and products of the cow (gavyaka).
The remaining [deities] [should be worshipped] with milk, ghee, honey, curd, sugarcane juice, fruit, and water;
with decoction-water, cow-urine, flowers, cow-dung, and gold. || 251 ||

One should fill [the vessels] separately with water and the five parts (*pañcāṅga*) of the *bilva* tree for the first enclosure (*prathamāvaraṇa*). Then, for the second enclosure, [one should fill them] with water containing *dūrvā* grass, barley, and sesame seeds. || 252 ||
With rice, the three types of blue lotuses, water, the four milks, mountain sprouts, and [leaves from] the Jambu, Śirīṣa, Pālāśa, Saptaparṇa, Asana, and Arjuna trees; || 253 ||
With *priyaṅgu*, mung beans, wheat, mung beans, mustard, and bamboo seeds;
with *niṣpāva*, great rice (*mahāvrīhi*), *śyāmāka*, and *aṇugavīthuka* [254].
One should fill [the vessels] according to the prescribed rule with masūraka, kulattha, āḍhakī, jartila, siddhārtha, and also nīvāra grains.

Then, [one should take] earth from a pure location, from a river, an anthill, or a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), as well as from the horns of a bull or an elephant, and from the two sites of a lineage (kula) and a field (kṣetra). || 256 ||
One should take earth from the roots of the palāśa, kuśa, bilva, and kṣīrāga trees,
as well as earth from a sacrificial altar (vedi), from ground ploughed by a boar, and from a temple.
One should take separately the earth from the roots of the kumuda, utpala, and padma; likewise, two types of campaka, three types of unmatta, pāṭala, and barley.
The four—Aśoka, Droṇa, Kusuma, and Karavīra; two Padmas, two Kumudas, and indeed two Tuladīs. || 259 ||
The *śatapatra*, the *kubjaka*, the two kinds of *mādhavī* and *mallikā*, the *saptakāla*, and the flowers of the *punnāga* and *nāga* trees [are recommended]. (260)
Rājārka, dhavalārka, as well as kalhāra and indīvara; the white and red mandāra, karṇikāra, and mahāmarī. || 261 ||
The kusumbha flower causes distress; the white and black aparājitā, the palāśa flower, the bakula, the nandyāvarta, and the kadamba [are likewise used]. (262)
Damanaka, lotus, tulasī, muṇḍī, kuravaka, as well as hīribera, maruvaka, mustā, granthi, and uśīraka; || 263 ||
Bṛhatī, āragvadha, jambū sprouts, mango sprouts, aruṇa, agasti flowers, mango blossoms, and coraka; || 264 ||
Śephālī flower, Lakṣmī, Sahadevī, Kṛtāñjali, Bhītendravallī, Musalī, Bhadrā, and likewise the two kinds of Dūrvā grass. || 265 ||
Harikrāntā, the two types of Bhṛṅgarāja, Ekadala-ambuja, and Bhūkadamba—these constitute one hundred and thirty-two [plants]. || 266 ||
This is for the second enclosure.
And in the third as well, there are the *mālyaṅga*, the *śamī* flower and its petal, the *apāmārga*, the *śaṅkhapuṣpa*, the *tāpiñcha*, and the *tamālaka*.
Brāhmī, rudrajaṭā, sūryavartinī, and suvarcalā; likewise vanamālā, śyāmā, paṭṭī, and rāvaṇabilvaka. || 268 ||
Karpūravallikā, somavallī, the sprouts of dhātrī, as well as two types of dūrvā grass, two kinds of asana flowers, bakapuṣpa, and likewise arjaka. || 269 ||
Kuṭaja, sarala, kuṣṭha, sandalwood, red sandalwood, saffron, murā, bālaka, camphor, and the two types of agaru. || 270 ||
Jātīphala, mañjiṣṭhā, devadāru, and rocanā; khaṣa, caṣāla, padmākṣa, gandha, āmalaka, and gandhaka. || 271 ||
Cardamom, cloves, black pepper, yellow orpiment, realgar, red ochre, honey, borax, vermilion, cinnabar, and saffron. (272)
Iron, steel, magnetite, copper, tin, brass, lead, silver, gold, vaikrānta, and the three types of mica; || 273 ||
Sun-crystal, moon-crystal, rock-crystal, iron, blue vitriol, and bell-metal; coconut, mango, jackfruit, plantain, breadfruit, and pomegranate. (274)
Mātuluṅga, jambīra, bilva, ātuṇḍikā fruit, pūga, badara, grapes, nāraṅga, and āmalakī fruit. || 275 ||
