Madhūka and brahmavṛkṣa, as well as śrīparṇī and khadira; padmaka, sarja, and lodhra, along with rohitaka and vikaṅkata. || 276 ||
The leaves of the *bilva* and *āragvadha*, as well as the *dhātrī* and *harītakī*, the *jambū*, and the heartwoods (*sāra*) of these— these are the nine distinct jewels. (277)
Then, the ten weapons, beginning with the vajra, are made of gold in sequence;
as well as turmeric, barley, wheat, rice flour, and ashes. (278)
The flours of mung beans, black gram, and horse gram, as well as roasted grain flour (saktu), parched grains (dhānā), karamba, uḍumba, balā, and likewise atibalā. || 279 ||

The water from the ocean, rivers, and sacred fords (tīrtha), as well as that produced from ponds, wells, and tanks, and the water from lakes and mountain springs, along with the rudrākṣa beads, [should be used] in their respective order.
Thus, in the third enclosure, one should fill four jars with a hundred and forty of the aforementioned substances. (281)
This refers to the third enclosure.
Now, in the fourth enclosure, there are four hundred and more jars; indeed, these four hundred jars [are filled] with gold, camphor, and saffron. (282)
One should fill [the vessel] with water from a river using the Gāyatrī mantra known as Śiva;
this is for the fourth enclosure.
Likewise, in the fifth enclosure, there are two hundred and seventy-two [deities].

There should be water-pots; one should fill them with water mixed with camphor, sandalwood, and agallochum, while reciting the Śiva-Sāvitrī mantra, proceeding clockwise according to the prescribed rite.
Then, one should fill the jars situated at the junction with water from a sacred bathing place; and with the *triyambaka* mantra, one should deposit fragrant paste and gold.
In the filling and likewise the worship of the vases free from all obstructions, as well as in the ritual bathing, this sequence begins from the east and ends with the northeast (Īśāna). || 283 ||

One should fill and also bathe the arrays of nine and so forth, starting from the east and ending with the south, west, and north; and likewise from the southeast, southwest, northwest, and northeast. 287.
The lords of the middle and other enclosures are Īśāna and the others ending with Sadyojāta;
likewise, there are Sadāśiva and the others, as well as the kalās beginning with Śāntyatītā.
Furthermore, the paths (adhvan) are situated within these [vessels] in sequence; they reside in the central Śiva-vessel as well as in all the other jars. (289)
The six pathways (ṣaḍadhvan) should be meditated upon according to the methods of both the collective and the individual;
furthermore, one should place a gold piece weighing one māṣa into all the ritual jars (kumbha).
Or half of that, or even half of that, according to the sequence of superior, middling, and inferior;
one should pour three, two, or one *niṣka* of gold into the *śivaghaṭa* for the superior and other categories respectively.
The common rule for all pitchers is that they should be filled with pure water, excluding milk, honey, and molasses; [each should also have] a cloth, a tuft of grass, and a golden [ring].
The sprouts and the covering of the products of the cow and so forth are likewise equal.
This concludes the section on the five coverings and the thousand jars.
For the one thousand and eight [jars], the jar of Śiva is filled with water as previously described.
Having filled [the vessels] according to the ritual rule with gems, gold, and perfumes, one should proceed in sequence with twenty substances in the five directions beginning with the east.
As before, one should fill the five [vessels] beginning with fire with mantras; one should fill them with pure water mixed with camphor and flowers.
In the second array on the exterior of the Madhyamavyūha, one should fill the nine transformational sections with Mālyāṅga and the others mentioned in the description of the third enclosure.
[This concludes] the second array.

Now, regarding the third array: there are nine [deities] in each of the four directions, consisting of those mentioned in the second enclosure, beginning with *dūrvā* grass and ending with wild rice (*nīvāra*). || 297 ||
One should fill [the vessels] with lotus seeds and rudrākṣas, using substances corresponding to the principles (tattvas),
for the nine groups of eighty-one remaining [units], in due order.
One should fill the central pitchers with the same substances mentioned for the second enclosure, such as river-clay and so forth, while reciting the Vyoma-vidyā mantra.
Then, with the remaining eight substances, one should fill the door-pitchers as before,
using exactly the eight *mūrti-śamana* mantras. (300)
Regarding the one thousand and eight pitchers:

even in the case of the fourfold arrangement (caturvyūha), one should fill the central pitcher as previously described; thereafter, for the three arrangements, one should fill those situated in the cardinal directions up to the intermediate corners.
In the arrays shaped like ploughs, one should fill the jars in sequence as before, and also fill those situated at the junctions with the previously mentioned substances and mantras. || 302 ||
Everything, beginning with the path of the deities, is traditionally taught as having five enclosures.
This is the section on the thousand-pitcher [mandala] with four enclosures.
In the twenty-one-fold array, there is the central pitcher and those outside it. (303)
One should fill the twenty [vases] in the middle array with substances as before;
then, one should [fill] the vases situated in the middle of the twenty arrays outside of that.
One should fill [the vessels] with twenty substances beginning with dūrvā grass and ending with wheat;
then, one should place the jars belonging to the outer enclosure of the arrays in the eight directions.
One should fill each individual array in sequence with twenty-eight items,
using the aforementioned substances such as mung beans and so forth.
Having filled the jars situated within the four inner enclosures with saffron water along with forest products,
[he should fill] the eight outer lateral enclosures.
One should fill [the vessels] in due order with cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, sugarcane juice, honey, and coconut water.
Then, in the intermediate directions between the arrays in the eight quarters, one should fill the square-shaped jars with the remaining substances. || 309 ||
Now, for the twenty-one-fold arrangement, the deities and the mantras of the thousand pitchers are described in sequence according to their respective order of enclosure. (310)
Furthermore, the obscurations of the ninefold array and so forth are to be understood as five distinct types, corresponding respectively to the five obscurations. (311)
The presiding deity of the central Śiva-pitcher is indeed Sadāśiva; the limbs of Brahmā and the root-mantras are formed by means of the Vyomavidyā.
Now, the deities of the womb-enclosure (garbhāvaraṇa) are the eight forms (aṣṭamūrti);
those of the second enclosure are known as the powers (śaktis), beginning with Vāmā.
The presiding deities of the third form are remembered as Śarva and the others;
then, for the fourth enclosure, the deity is the size of a thumb.
Bhuvaneśāna, Īśāna, and likewise Ekapiṅgekṣaṇa; Udbhava, Bhava, and then Mahādeva of great splendor. (315)
Now, regarding the fifth enclosure, there are those situated in the ten directions, including the hundred Rudras:
Kapālīśa, Agnirudra, the one belonging to Yama (Yāmya), and the one named Nirṛti. || 316 ||
Bala, Śīghra, Nidhīśa, and Vidyādhipati as the eighth—
these are traditionally taught as the presiding deities (adhidevas) of the arrays situated in the eight directions, respectively.
The Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas) stand as guardians at the primary and secondary gate-decorations and so forth;
[the rites proceed] with the *pādya* water, beginning with "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ" and following immediately with "āpo hi ṣṭhā".
One should offer water with the mantra "āpaḥ punantu," arghya with "agnim īle," milk products with "gavyam," clarified butter with "iṣe tvā," and honey with "madhu vātā. (319)

One should offer milk with the mantra "āpyāyasva," curd with the mantra beginning "dadhi krāvṇaḥ," sugarcane juice with the mantra "upa tvāgne," and parched grain flour (karambhaka) with the mantra "mā nas toke."

With water from the decoction of *aśvavā* plants, he offers parched grains (*lājaka*) with the verse beginning "sumitrā na"; with parched grains (*dhānā*) he offers them with the verse beginning "agna ā yāhi"; and with flowers he offers them with the verse beginning "puṣpāvatī".
One should also consecrate Maheśvara with the mantra "samudrajyeṣṭhā," with the mantra "brahmajajñāna," and with water mixed with turmeric and water mixed with barley flour.
With the *rakṣohaṇa* mantra and white mustard seeds, with the *śanno devī* mantra and water mixed with sesame,
with the *vāstoṣpate* mantra and rice-water, and indeed with the *ayana* mantra and dūrvā-grass water.

One should bathe [the deity] with lotus-water for the sake of prosperity using the *triṣṭubh* verse; with blue-lotus water using the verse beginning with "āśuḥ śiśāna-"; and with clay-water using the same [verse].

With the Śrīsūkta [one should bathe] with fragrant waters; with the Kadrudra hymn, with water containing fruits; with the Camaka [hymns], with water containing grains; and with the Puruṣasūkta, with water containing essences.

One should bathe the King of Waters with the first [mantra] using waters containing jewels; one should bathe this [deity] with ashes and water from wells using the *traiyambaka* mantra for Rudra. (326)

One should perform [the rite] with water from a spring using the *Kanikrada* mantra, with water from a mountain torrent using the *Īśāna* mantra, with water from a pond using the *Puruṣa* mantra, and with water from the ocean using the *Aghora* mantra.

[One should purify oneself] with the Vāmadeva hymn, with river waters, with waters from lakes using the Ajāta [mantra], with holy fords (tīrtha) using the "imaṃ me gaṅge" verse, and with cow dung using the "gandhadvārā" verse.

With water infused with medicinal herbs by means of the Rudra-mantra, with sprouts and water by means of the Svasti-mantra and others, with saffron-water by means of the Pavamāna-mantras, and with camphor by means of the Sāvitrī-mantra; || 329 ||

With water mixed with *kuśa* grass and reciting the hymn beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ," and with water from the five parts of a *bilva* fruit while reciting the mantra "yāsāṃ rājā," [he should perform the ritual].
One should sprinkle [the image] with cow's urine while reciting the mantra "yāsāṃ devi," and one should bathe it with water from sprouts while reciting "śivena mā cakṣuṣā. (331)
One should bathe [the image] with the waters of the [five] elements from the *Pavamāna* hymn,
followed by the *Suvarjana*, *Jātavedas*, and *Pavitra* sections, in their proper sequence.
One should bathe and rub [the image] with powders such as barley and black gram, and likewise with the waters of the "Haima" weapon-mantra, beginning with the hymn "ambhasy apāre."
Then, with water infused with rudrākṣa beads and reciting the hymn beginning with "taratsamandī," one should consecrate Mahādeva, alternating with offerings of flowers, incense, and water.
Beginning from the inner enclosure of the womb and proceeding outward to the final outer enclosure,
one should bathe Śiva with water-pots in sequence according to the directions and intermediate points.
Following the bathing with nine arrays for each individual covering, one should bathe [the deity] with cool water and flowers while reciting the Śivagāyatrī.

Having honored [the deity] with flowers and incense, one should bathe [the image] again and again; indeed, until the completion of the pitchers, one should bathe it according to the prescribed sequence.
One should perform the purification with cleansing substances as enjoined by Īśāna, [reciting the mantras] Brāhmī, Vaiṣṇavī, Raudrī, Vimalā, and Kṛtāñjali. (338)
Having combined rajanī, sahadevī, śirīṣa, sūryavartinī, sadābhadrā,
and the tips of kuśa grass, one should cleanse Śiva.

Then, having sprinkled [the image] with fifty blades of *darbha* grass while reciting the "śanna indra" hymn and others, one should bathe it with water and then perform the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*). || 340 ||

[He should worship] with [offerings] prepared from rice flour and other substances in golden vessels and so forth, in due order, as well as with the eight divine auspicious symbols and the weapons of the world-protectors.
A man should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for the Lord with flour-cakes, lamps, dūrvā grass, white mustard, lotuses, curd, and unbroken grains (akṣata), all properly arranged.
With songs, dances, and instrumental music—conchs, kāhala trumpets, and gomukha horns, along with timila drums, ānaka drums, kettledrums (bherīs), and others—resounding incessantly; 343.
Having performed the lustration ceremony with the resounding sounds of the Vedas and auspicious cries of "Victory! and so forth, one should then bathe [the deity] with the central pitcher.
Having consecrated [the image], one should then wipe it with a pure cloth; thereafter, with very fine, unwashed cloths made of wool or even cotton.

Having clothed [the deity] with the root mantra, one should then offer water for the feet (pādya) to the Lord; likewise, one should offer the respectful oblation (arghya) to the faces with the heart mantra, and the water for sipping (ācamana) with the eye mantra.
Having adorned [the deity] with ornaments of gold variegated with various gems, beginning with the crown and ending with the ornaments of the pedestal, according to what is beautiful; 347.
One should adorn [the deity] with a beautiful face and also offer water for rinsing the mouth with well-ground sandalwood mixed with camphor and cool water. 348.
One should smear [the image] on the left side with a fragrant paste mixed with saffron and agallochum, and one should also adorn it from head to foot with flowers and garlands.
One should fumigate Śambhu with a crest of incense consisting of black aloe-wood, camphor, and camphor-powder combined with sugar; and one should offer a lamp according to the ritual rule.
Then, having performed the *ārātrika* rite with lamps lit by means of camphor, incense, and other fragrant substances, one should lower it while reciting the *astra-mantra*.
Then, the food offering (naivedya), which is well-prepared and delicious,
should be made with one prastha of śāli rice grains, or half of that, or even half of that again, measured by jars.

The offerings should consist of the finest ingredients and the like, saturated with a generous amount of clarified butter; as well as milk-rice (pāyasa), and well-prepared rice mixed with curd and turmeric.
One should offer kṛsarānna, gulānna, and mudgānna, respectively, smeared with abundant clarified butter, before the faces beginning with Īśāna. (354)

Everywhere there was an abundance of curd, honey, clarified butter, and sugar-candy, along with excellent juices; it was rich in soups and garnished with side dishes of vegetables, as well as roots, fruits, and sweetmeats.
One should offer to Śarva water that is cool and fragrant—
water mixed with cloves, nutmeg, black pepper, camphor, and cardamom.
Having given water for washing the hands and likewise having offered water for sipping (ācamana),
it was accompanied by nutmeg, black pepper, camphor, and betel nut.
Then, having offered betel-leaf and having praised and bowed with devotion, he circumambulated Śiva and duly enclosed the fire.

One should join Śiva, who resides in the fire, with the one in the pitcher, and the one in the pitcher with the one in the heart; then, having dismissed the guardians of the door and the corners, one should feed the Guru and the image-protectors (mūrtipās).

[He should provide for] students and attendants, as well as Brahmins and those bearing sectarian marks (liṅgins), and also for the poor, the blind, the wretched, and other people seeking food. || 360 ||

Having gratified them with choice foods and clarified butter according to the sequence prescribed for the installation, one should satisfy them with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) as well as garments, ornaments, and other gifts. || 361 ||
Then, having gratified [the officiants] with cattle, villages, elephants, horses, and so forth, the patron, his mind serene,
together with the preceptor, shall have his feet, hands, and face washed.
Having sipped water for purification, entered within, and having bowed to and propitiated the Lord,
he should take water together with fragrant substances, dūrvā grass, and flowers in his hand.
One should offer the fruit of bathing, worship, giving, and so forth, in its entirety, to Śarva at his feet with this verse: [364]
Oṃ!
Free from stinginess regarding wealth, with devotion and according to my capacity, you have been bathed and honored, and whatever was to be given has been offered by me.
O Lord of Gods, you who are gracious along with Ambā, please accept all of this;
may it be the means for me to attain the fruit [of my actions]. (366)
p.
510) Thus one who desires enjoyment should offer [the rite], and one who desires liberation should do so likewise: "By Your grace, O Lord, may this action not be a cause of bondage for me. (367)
Thus one should offer the ritual action into the two lotus-feet of the Lord.
Thus has been declared this noble procedure for the ceremonial bathing (snāpanavidhi), established in the Śaiva Siddhānta, beginning with the hundred jars and ending with the Nandakumbha.

Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, the Chapter on Ablution (*snapanapaṭala*), in the *Kriyāpāda* of the *Siddhāntasāra*, within the *Śrīmadīśānaśivagurudevapaddhati*, which is a wish-fulfilling tree for the prayer of desired human goals for the illustrious Moon-crested Lord.
Now begins the fifty-first chapter. Now, the installation of the deities beginning with the Sun has indeed already been shown in brief within the installation of the Śiva-liṅga.
The ritual acts beginning with the plowing and ending with the festival that have been described here are equal [in all cases];
likewise, the sequence for the placement of the principles (tattva), the forms (mūrti), and so forth, is indeed the same everywhere.
Sūrya, Vighneśvara, Skanda, as well as Hara, Nārāyaṇa;
Durgā, Gaurī, Sarasvatī, Śāstā, Kālī, and the Mothers. || 3 ||
And Kṣetrapāla, either as an integral part of Śiva or separately, in these locations— all these are to be installed and worshipped individually.
Now, the installation and other rites for these [deities], categorized according to the distinctions of form, the lords of form, and the mantras,
are briefly described here as they truly are.
The mantras and the worship of the Sun have already been fully described.
In the ritual for its consecration, the primary image should be ten *tālas* in height.
But that which consists of painting and so forth, made of gold, base metals, gems, or stone, should be endowed with the measurements, proportions, and other characteristics prescribed for images.
For its consecration, as before, there are four archways (toraṇas) in the pavilion: Vibhūti, Vimala, Tāra, and Ārādhya in the east.
Pratyūṣa and Prabhāsa, Pradyota and Dyotana, Daṇḍin,
Piṅgala, Caṇḍa, and Tīvra are the gatekeepers. (9)
One should worship two jars at each of the eastern, southern, western, and northern gates;
the world-protectors, marked with their respective weapons, and their presiding deities, the banners, should be worshipped.
Then, from the scattering and dispersal [of the offerings] and from the rotation of the sun-vessel and the weapon-vessel,
one should take hold of the pavilion and worship the world-protectors residing within the vessels.
Having performed the purification of the form as before and the opening of the eyes,
one should then perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) in water with the root mantra and the limb-mantras.
After circumambulating the village clockwise, as before, one should bathe [the deity] in the meditation pavilion with seven sets of seven filled jars, as previously described.
Then, with the Aghamarṣaṇa Sūkta beginning with "Asatyena," and likewise with the hymns beginning with "Udyannadya" and the Pavamāna hymns in their proper order.
Then, one should perform the consecration with the limbs based on the Khaṣa-mantra, with the eight-syllabled Sāvitrī,
and with the ten Praṇavas of the Gāyatrī in its middle.
Having performed the sacrifice, one should cause the deity to enter the consecration pavilion; one should have the deity lie upon the bed as before and place the sleep-vessel (nidrākumbha) there.
In the northeast, one should place the Sūrya-kumbha and Astra-kumbhas, and the Deva-kumbhas in the four directions;
then one should install the principles (tattvas), beginning with the Self, up to the knees, throat, and head.

In the portions beginning with Brahmā, one should contemplate the Maṇḍala endowed with the qualities of the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, and Sāmaveda, as well as the Puruṣa and the rays, respectively, in the three divisions.
One should also arrange the twelve forms in three sections as follows:
earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, ego, and intellect. (19)
Nature, the individual soul, time, and the Supreme Self are his forms; likewise Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Mitra, Varuṇa, Aṃśa, and Bhaga. || 20 ||
Pūṣan, Vivasvat, Parjanya, Savitṛ, Indra, and Viṣṇu—these are the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās), and their powers (śaktis) are likewise twelve. || 21 ||
Dīptā, Sūkṣmā, Jayā, Bhadrā, Vibhūti, Vimalā, as well as Amoghā and Vidyutā— these are said to be the Sarvatomukhī [mudrās].
One should install those powers— Prabhā, Sandhyā, and Saṃjñā— with the Sāvitrī mantra, using the root-mantras of one's own limbs, Khaṣotka, and the forms together with their presiding deities.

Furthermore, the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās) should offer oblations into the sacrificial pits as before, using the Śaktis, along with fuel-sticks of Palāśa and Arka wood, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, sesame seeds, and unbroken rice.

Having offered oblations of one hundred times with clarified butter along with *siddhārtha* seeds and all types of grain, and having again offered oblations with the clarified butter from which drops have fallen, as well as with the waters from the *śānti*-pitcher; || 25 ||

Having sprinkled [the water] in three portions, the preceptor and the image-keepers (mūrtipās) should touch [themselves]; and having meditated upon Kriyāśakti on the pedestal, he should install her there.
And having performed the previously mentioned preliminary rites and consecrated them, one should perform the morning bath and other duties, and then enter the inner sanctum. || 27 ||

One should place the tortoise-stone (kūrmaśilā) upon the foundation; then, having worshipped it, one should install the five groups beginning with gems (ratna) according to the previously mentioned sequence and consecrate them with mantras.
Then, internally reciting the mantra beginning with "Oṃ, salutation to Vyāpinī," the Guru should invoke the Foundation Power (Ādhāraśakti) and worship her according to the prescribed rite.

One should place the pedestal, which consists of the power of action (kriyā-śakti), upon it; then, when the auspicious moment has arrived, the installer (sthāpaka), together with the guardians of the forms (mūrtipas), [should proceed].
Then,
meditating upon the form of the Sun as consisting of the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti) upon a pedestal [formed] by the power of action (kriyāśakti), one should install it with the Praṇava-mantra.
One should place the *haṃsa*—which has the root of the limbs and the *khaṣotka*—into that heart;
one should then consecrate it with the *gāyatrī* and *sāvitrī* mantras preceded by ten *praṇavas*.
Having stabilized the image by means of the eightfold binding (aṣṭabandha) and having washed it with waters,
one should consecrate it with the sleep-vessel (nidrākumbha), and also slightly with the water of pacification (śāntyudaka).

Then, having washed [the image] in sequence with the *arghya* and the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), followed by water and incense, and subsequently with the waters of the *kumbha* and *astra* mantras along with barley flour and other substances; || 34 ||
One should consecrate [the disciple] with the Veda-pitchers and also place the Śānti-pitcher; one should complete the remaining ritual as before with its own mantra. || 35 ||
Having performed the placement of the principles of the Self (ātmatattva) and so forth upon the image as previously prescribed,
there should be the seat of sovereignty (prabhutāsana), the pedestal (pīṭha), and [the powers] such as Vibhūti and Vimalā.
One should meditate upon the *prabodhinī* [power] in the center of the four feet of the pedestal;
having worshipped the powers beginning with *dīptā* within the mandala, one should worship the Sun as the Puruṣa. (37)
Having meditated and performed the placement of the root-mantra and its limbs, one should likewise perform the placement of the paths (adhvan):
the root, the limbs, *khaṣoṭka*, and the ten-starred [mantra].
The Gāyatrī and the Sāvitrī are declared to be the path of mantras for Ravi;
however, the words of the ten-praṇava Gāyatrī are equal in number to the principles (tattvas).
The path of his feet has been specified; the remaining paths are as before.
Having thus meditated upon that form, one should contemplate the *haṃsa* together with the *tāraka* within the heart. (40)

Having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa), one should worship the deity with offerings such as the arghya and other services. Then the preceptor (ācārya) should offer clarified butter into the fire within his own sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with these [mantras].
Then it is stable, pervasive, and likewise immeasurable; beyond that, it is beginningless awakening, eternal, and also unchanging.
With the mantra "nityatṛptaśca saptānte bhavasvāhā" joined [to the end], these are the mantras;
having offered clarified butter with these, one should then touch the deity.
One should offer clarified butter a thousand times, or half of that, or a hundred times,
with the mantras beginning with *aṅga*, *mūla*, *khaṣotkā*, and so forth, as well as with the *vyāhṛtis*.

Having offered the full oblation and worshipped with the weapons of the world-protectors and other items, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and bathe [the deity] as before, performing worship even unto the final offering (nivedya).
Having meditated upon the deity and requested His presence within that image through mantra, he should offer the bali-oblation to the spirits at night for three days, as previously described.
Having led [the body] away, on the fourth day he should offer oblations into the fires for him with the mantra of Sāvitrī and Gāyatrī separately one hundred and eight times each.

Having offered the *jayā* oblations and others with clarified butter (*ājya*), as well as the expiatory (*prāyaścitta*) oblations, he offers the final full-oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) from the fire, reciting "O bearer of oblations" (*havyavāha*) and so forth,
and then offers it with the *yājyā* verse beginning "O Agni, [thou who hast] well-sacrificed" (*sviṣṭam agne*). This is the extent of the procedure.
Having employed the fierce Tejacaṇḍa with the remains of offerings (nirmālya) in the domain of Īśa,
one should worship the three-eyed, tawny-eyed, red deity, who is clad in red garments and so forth.
One should worship the four-armed deity who holds a lotus and bestows boons and fearlessness; then, one should consecrate the deity with water-pots according to the prescribed method.

And having given the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to be bestowed according to the sequence previously mentioned, one should then perform the rite according to the daily injunctions, in accordance with one's means.
One should properly perform the worship with its ritual offerings at the three junctions of the day. || 52 ||
The Chapter on the Installation of the Sun:
In the daily festival of the Sun, however, Caṇḍa and Piṅgala are stationed at the door.
The eight planets beginning with Soma are located in the positions of Lokeśa in sequence;
likewise, the Mothers, Durgā, Tejas, and Caṇḍa are situated in the directions.
In front of the pavilion, Aruṇa should worship seven horses according to their names—the Gāyatrī, Uṣṇih, Anuṣṭubh, and so forth. || 54 ||

One should worship the Bṛhatī, Paṅkti, Triṣṭubh, and Jagatī meters in their proper order; one should worship the two intermediate [deities] as the gatekeepers of the gateway, and the two wings as white and black.
In the same manner, having placed offerings for those two who reside outside— the southern and northern solstices—
and having given them their *bali*, one stands outside the *balipīṭha*.
The preceptor should summon all the carrion-eaters and the hosts of the Sun— those who, desiring offerings, abide pervading the entire world.
"May all the attendants of the Sun accept this supreme offering.
Then, [one should offer] to the twelve zodiac signs in their respective places, proceeding clockwise. (58)
One should offer oblations to the months beginning with Meṣa (Aries), together with those [deities]:
to Madhu, Mādhava, Śukra, Śuci, and likewise Nabhas.
Then one should offer an oblation to Nabhasya, likewise to Iṣa, Ūrja, and Sahas; thereafter, to Sahasya, Tapas, and Tapasya.

Then, one should cast [offerings] for the eight Gaṇas in all eight directions around the pedestal of Bali (balipīṭha), using their respective names followed by the word "gaṇa" and ending with "namaḥ."
Then the Gandharvas and the hosts of Asuras, the Pitṛs and the hosts of Rākṣasas, as well as the Nāgas, the hosts of Maruts, and likewise the Yakṣas and the hosts of Bhūtas. || 62 ||
On the lotus petals are situated the hosts of sages; having honored them with their own names, one should offer a bali-oblation to them. (63)
The ritual for the perpetual festival.
During the great festival, however, one should raise the banner according to the path taught by Śiva, and having invoked the Gaṇas as before, [one should raise] a flag marked with a red horse.

And likewise, having first performed the rite of sowing the seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa), one should cause the festival to be celebrated for the deities stationed at the joints, according to the previous procedure and in the sequence beginning with the "excellent" (uttama) and so forth.

Having worshipped, as before, with the mantras for casting the offerings (bali) ending with those of the Sun’s attendants, and with the mantras beginning with "yebhūtādyaiḥ," one should cast the offering to them.
Having scattered the bali offering all around according to the procedure prescribed for the perpetual festival,
one should cast the bali outside the heap according to the specific ritual rule.
Outside [the enclosure] from Indra and the other world-protectors and their weapons, in the eastern direction (aindrī),
there are those hosts who hold thunderbolts in their hands and possess great strength.
With these and other directional mantras (diṅmantra), one should scatter the bali offering all around;
thereafter, as before, [one should offer] the bali to the Gaṇas stationed upon the bali-pedestal.
Having cast [the image] and bathed it as before, one should cause the inner deity to enter;
having performed the binding of the *kautuka* and so forth, and the pilgrimage (*tīrthayātrā*) as previously described. (70)
Having performed [the rites] according to rule with their own mantras, one should conclude with the ritual bathing.
Thus, the procedures from consecration to the festival as proclaimed here in the Sūryatantra are summarized;
all that is taught in the Bimba and other tantras is to be inferred in its entirety according to the path declared in the Śaiva scriptures.
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, on the Sūryatantra, in the Kriyāpāda of the Siddhāntasāra, the *Śrīmad-Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati*.
Now begins the fifty-second chapter.
Now, the image of Vighneśvara may also be made according to the five-tāla measurement. The mantras shall be exactly as previously stated, and the rite of consecration shall be like that of Śiva.
Indeed, the cycle of ritual actions prescribed for the installation of the Sun is for the most part exactly the same as that used in the installations of Vighneśa and others.
This specific distinction should be understood individually: the archways, the gatekeepers, the forms, the lords of the forms, and their powers. (3)
The mantras, the retinues, and the paths of both the *pada* and the *mantra* are as follows:
Supūrṇa, Pūrṇabhadra, Praśānta, and likewise Vijaya. (4)

The arches (toraṇas) should be in the east and other directions; the banners are said to be the weapons of the world-protectors (lokeśas). At the eastern gate stands Kuṇḍodara, and likewise Kumbhodara as well.
Vikaṭa and Vāmana are to be worshipped at the southern gate, while Jaya and Vijaya are to be worshipped at the western gate;
furthermore, Meghanāda and Mahodara are to be worshipped at the northern gate.

One should worship the door-keepers and the world-protectors residing within the jars; and having worshipped the jar of Gaṇeśa in the northeast and the weapon (astra), one should circumambulate those two.
One should worship the weapon of the goad (the weapon of Gaṇeśa) in the form of a woman,
having sequentially taken possession of the two pavilions for the preliminary consecration and the ritual bathing.
Then, having performed the purification of the hands and the opening of the eyes in the water, and having consecrated [the site],
one should circumambulate the city and other areas clockwise.

Having caused [the deity] to enter, one should snap the fingers, then cause [the deity] to lie down, and perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa). The five forms are Earth and the others, as well as mind, ego, and intellect.
The eight forms of Gaṇeśa, whose lords are the Vighneśas and others, are:
Vighna, Vināyaka, Vīra, Śūra, and likewise Hastimukha; then Ekadanta, Kṣipraprasāda, and Gaṇeśvara; and [the goddesses] Tīvrā, Jvālinī, and Nandā.
The bestower of enjoyments, she who can assume any form at will. || 12 ||
One should assign these Śaktis—Ugrā, Tejovatī, Sandhyā, Navamī, and Vighnanāśanī—to the three divisions of the forms beginning with Earth (Kṣmā). || 13 ||

One should place and worship the Kriyā-śakti at its side on that pedestal; furthermore, one should place the pitchers and the Astra-mantra on the altar in the northeast, and the deities of the forms (mūrtīśas) within the pitchers in the cardinal directions.
Having placed the sleep-pitcher upon the pillow, he offers oblations for these; then, having entered the inner sanctum, he should install the Śakti and the tortoise-stone.

Having installed the pedestal made of jewels and so forth, as well as the image endowed with form, one should [invoke] the all-pervading, subtle consciousness, which has that seed-syllable enclosed by the *haṃsa*.

One should place [the deity] brought from the lotus in the sky of one's own heart into that very heart-lotus; then, one should likewise place the mantra of that form, the limbs (aṅgas), and the mantras beginning with "gaṇānāṃ tvā. (17)
One should also project the *gāyatrī* of Gaṇeśa and the path of mantras (*mantrādhvan*):
"We know Vināyaka; we meditate on the elephant-faced one; may that Tusked One (Dantī) inspire us.
As for the words of the *Vighna-gāyatrī*, their path of words (*padādhvan*) is as before.

Having performed the meditation on the six paths (ṣaḍadhvabhāvanā) and having bathed [the deity] as before, one should worship it. As for those mantras of Vighneśvara which have been declared in the section on mantras: || 19 ||
Furthermore, the forms described in the Kalpas should be installed according to the rules by their respective devotees,
using the appropriate mantras, enclosures, and so forth.
The sacred seats (pīṭhas) named Śakti, Kūrma, and Ananta, as well as Dharma and the others,
are located in the lotuses of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa within the solar orb of the three qualities (guṇas).
The first enclosure is with one's own limbs, then with the powers (śaktis) beginning with Tīvrā; the second is also with the lords of the forms (mūrtipas), and the third is the fourth [enclosure].

Then, with the [deities] established in their own places, one should worship the fifth [group] with the World-Protectors (Lokeśas) and their weapons and so forth; at the end, [the mantra] should be [concluded] with "to the attendant of Vighna" (vighnapāriṣadāya), using the respective names.

One should assign the name of each of them, ending with "namaḥ," to their respective attendants; having thus worshipped the Lord of the Gaṇas, one should then proceed with the seven [verses] beginning with "sthirā."

Having offered the oblation, one should touch [the deity] as before; however, the expiation must be performed from the very beginning with the limbs [of the mantra], the Gaṇeśa-gāyatrī, and then with the verse beginning "gaṇānāṃ tvā. (25)

Having offered oblations in all the central and other fires with the mantras of Mūrti and Lokeśa, using sacrificial fuel (samidh) and other materials as before, one should conduct this for three days.
On the fourth day, as before, having performed the expiation with the Gāyatrī and the Jayā-mantras and so forth,
one should perform the ritual up to the final sprinkling (apariṣecana).
Having propitiated Gaṇacaṇḍa and withdrawn the fires into himself, he dismissed the lords of the pitcher-world, the gatekeepers, the arches, and the banners.
Having worshipped Gaṇeśa with a ritual bath and having bestowed sacrificial fees and other gifts,
one should scatter the bali offering at night and perform worship according to one's means.
Having resolved upon the daily worship (*nityapūjā*), the practitioner attains his desired goal.
This concludes the section on the installation of Gaṇeśa.
During the perpetual festival of Gaṇeśa, Kuṇḍodara and others serve as the gatekeepers.
Lokeśa and his vehicle, the mouse, as well as the Mothers, are situated in their respective directions; Bhṛṅgīśa is in the west, Vāyu, Tāra, and Caṇḍikā are in the north-west, and Nāga.

Bhallāṭa is in the south-east, Guha in the north-west, Aṅkuśī is traditionally placed in the northeast of Śrīdevī, and Gaṇacaṇḍa is also there; having worshipped these, one should scatter the bali offering.
Below the gateway (gopura), Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa are situated to the south and north; Gaṅgā and Yamunā are above; and Dvāraśrī is over the central gateway.
These deities are to be worshipped, and one should offer them an oblation (bali). Then, in the eight directions of the midday circuit, there are the lords of the Gaṇas.
Vajradanta, Gajāsya, Bhīma with the face of a buffalo, Meghanāda, Virūpākṣa, Vikaṭa, and Bahubhakṣyabhuk. (35)
These are the lords of the hosts of crores; having worshipped them, one should offer the bali-oblation to them.
Then, on the bali-altar, starting from the east, [one should worship] Gajavaktra, Vighneśa, and Gaṇanāyaka.
Caṇḍavikramakṛt, Vighnakara, Bhujagamekhala, Śūrpakarṇa, Nāgadanta, and then Rudravaktra. || 37 ||
And Gaṇasena is the tenth among them; one should offer an oblation upon his seat.
With the mantra "Oṃ namaḥ sarvavighnapārṣadebhyastatpārṣadebhyo namaḥ," one should cast all the remaining food, accompanied by water and flowers, upon the seat in the center.
The procedure for the daily festival is the same, and this [procedure] is the same for the great festival as well. || 38 ||
Furthermore, the rat should be worshipped on the banner with its own mantra:
"Oṃ mūṃ, obeisance to the rat.
Having invoked all the Gaṇas as before, one should scatter the bali offering.
Then, by the name of Gaṇeśapariṣad, there was the assembly of attendants; and outside, in the ten directions, were those beginning with Vajradanta.
Airāvata, Puṇḍarīka, Kumuda, Añjana, Vāmana, Puṣpadanta,
Sārvabhauma, and Supratīka, according to the sequence of the directions. (41)

One should worship them as before with their names beginning with "Tārā" and ending with "namaḥ. In the eastern direction, those who are the Gaṇas, holding vajras in their hands and possessing great strength— || 42 ||
With these and other mantras ending in "namaḥ," which sequentially terminate with the attendants of Vighna,
one should indeed scatter the bali offering at night with the Bhūtakrūra mantra.

One should perform the ritual bath at sacred fords as before, as well as the ceremonial bathing; however, the mantras for the bathing are those declared by Śiva, originating from his own primary limbs.
And with the Gāyatrī mantra and the hymn beginning with "gaṇānāṃ tvā," he should sprinkle the Lord of the Gaṇas from the central jar with the prescribed ritual services (upacāras).
The sacrificers and others obtain the fruit previously described.

Thus, having thoroughly examined the Gaṇeśatantra as it is stated in other tantras in brief, the rites beginning with installation and ending with the festival have been declared; however, they should be performed according to the Śaiva tradition.
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, the Gaṇeśatantra-paṭala, in the Kriyāpāda of the Siddhāntasāra, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva.
Now begins the fifty-third chapter.

Now, the ritual for the installation of the *skanda* and so forth is remembered as being the same as that of Śiva; however, those specific details therein which are enjoined by the *tantra* are here written down.
The image of Skanda is prescribed to be ten *tāla*s in height;
as before, it may be made by means of painting and other techniques, or likewise in stone or metal.
For him, [the image] may be made of clay or born of jewels, standing or seated; or for the six-faced one (Kārttikeya), it may be mounted upon a peacock and possess six faces.
One should have Sanatkumāra, Skanda, and the others made with a single face; they may be made with four arms or two arms, and they should indeed be made with only two eyes.
He has six faces, twelve arms, and twelve eyes, and is well-adorned; or he may have six arms or four hands, and stands mounted upon a peacock.
Holding in his right hands the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), a spear, an arrow, a vajra, and a goad, and likewise in the left hand bestowing the boon while touching the hip. (6)
The all-pervading Lord has twelve arms; starting from the lower left hand and moving upwards, he holds a staff, a javelin, a bow, a bell, and a noose.

The omnipresent six-faced one should be depicted with six arms, holding in his right hands the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya), a lotus, and a spear, and in [the others] a boon-granting gesture, a lance, and a thunderbolt.
Holding a lotus, a spear, and a citron in his right hands, and a noose in his left,
he has six faces or a single face, and possesses four arms.
If Guha is two-armed, he is endowed with a spear touching his hip and the gesture of granting boons; or he may hold a spear and a vajra, or else hold a staff and a spear.
The forms of Skanda should have serene faces and be red in color, adorned with red ornaments, and equipped with crowns, earrings, necklaces, and other finery. (11)
When only a single image is to be installed, it should be a single form; however, when many images are to be installed, six or twelve forms may be installed.
Varada, Yaśoda, Puṣṭida, and Śrīprada—these shall be the arches (toraṇas) in order starting from the east; the banners (dhvajas) are marked with the weapons of the world-protectors (lokeśas).
Vīrasena, Mahāsena, Bhadrasena, Suṣeṇaka, Cārusena the commander-in-chief, and after him Pūrṇasena. (14)
Citrasena and Kumbha, these two each, shall stand as gatekeepers in the east;
at every door, there shall also be jars of parched grain and jars of seeds and sprouts.
Having placed [the materials] by scattering them from the *kumbha* vessel, one should also worship with the *kumbhāstra*;
[the materials are] dūrvā grass, tips of kuśa grass, mung beans, rice, grains, and sesame seeds.

Siddhārtha and Tulasī are known as the scattering offerings (vikira) for Skanda. In the water-pot (kumbha), one should place Skanda seated upon a peacock, and in the cock (kukkuṭa), the weapon (astra), along with the vardhanī vessel.

Having performed the sacrifice as before, having circumambulated as before, and having taken possession of the pavilion as before, one should purify the source, perform the opening of the eyes, and the preliminary consecration with water.
Having performed the wandering of the village, the ceremonial bathing, and the laying to rest,
one should place the Kumāra-vessel, the Astra-vessel, and the six Mūrti-vessels upon the altar (vedi).
Having worshipped the sleep-pitcher upon the pillow, one should then perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana).
One should [worship] Brahmā and the others, endowed with the three qualities, within the portions of the principles (tattva) beginning with the Self. (20)
The five elements beginning with earth, along with the ego (ahaṅkāra), are the six forms of Guha;
likewise, Sanatkumāra, Skanda, Viśākha, and Ṣaṇmukha.
Naigameṣa and Hemacūḍa—these six are remembered as the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās). Devasenā, Devayānī, Ṣaṣṭhī, Vidyā, and Kukkuṭā [are the others].
And Vijayā—these are the six Śaktis of the Mūrtis in their respective order;
one should also install the Mūrtis, the Mūrtīśas, and the Śaktis within the three sections.

And in the center, in the six sacrificial pits, the Guru and the bearers of the forms should likewise offer oblations with the root-mantras, the limb-mantras, the form-mantras, and the Śaktis. || 24 ||
Once cooked, however, one should offer it separately a hundred times with the *skandagāyatrī* and the root-mantras (*mūlāṅga*).
The root-mantra has already been shown previously in the section on the extraction of mantras (*mantroddhāra*). (25)
Now, the limbs of the Gāyatrī are also described by that very same [method]: "Mahāsena" ending in the dative case, followed by the word "vidmahe. (26)
The word "Śaktihasta" ending in the dative case, the word "dhīmahi" with the word "tat," "naḥ" followed by "skanda," and then "codayāt" preceded by the syllable "Tāra" (Om). 27.
Then, by means of the Śaktis, the Mūrtis, and the twelve Mūrtis, Bāṇa, Śākha, Bhadrasena, and the army commander who was the son of Bhava [were established].
Subrahmaṇya, Kārttikeya, Guha, indeed Kukkuṭadhvaja, Mayūravāhana, and Gāṅgeya—after that [are the names]. 29.
Thus, the twelve forms are proclaimed as ending with "the General of the Divine Army. Their mantras should consist of their own names preceded by "Tārā" (Oṃ) and ending with "namaḥ" (namas).
One should always offer oblations with [mantras] ending in "svāhā" and always in the dative case;
[the sacrificial wood should be] from the mayūra, khadira, aśvattha, plākṣa, udumbara, and rauhiṇa trees.

The sacrificial fuel for the six fires should consist of Palāśa wood, as prescribed for the central fire; likewise, one should offer clarified butter, cooked rice, barley, rice, lentils, white mustard, and black mustard.
They should also offer peacock feathers as sacrificial fuel (samidh) everywhere in due order, with clarified butter dripping from the oblation,
and likewise with the water from the peace-pitcher (śāntikumbha).

The preceptor and the image-keepers should sprinkle [the site] in the various sections with the *skandagāyatrī* mantra; then, outside the pavilion, they should do so in the cardinal directions with the mantras of the deities who are the lords of the worlds.

They should offer oblations separately of fuel-sticks, clarified butter, sesame seeds, parched grain, and sacrificial porridge; likewise, in the southwest and the northwest, they should offer those produced from the *bilva* and *kārṣmari* trees.
One should offer one hundred and eight oblations of fuel sticks, weapons, and cooked rice (caru) into the fire;
then, having placed the Kriyā-śakti upon the pedestal to the left of the image (bera).
Having then given his consent, the Guru, having performed his daily rites at dawn, shall enter the inner sanctum and place the tortoise-stone upon the auspicious moment.
Having worshipped the foundational power (ādhāra-śakti) there, one should place the five groups beginning with jewels within it,
in the central pit as well as in the directions starting from the east.
One should place, in order from the center to the exterior, a golden elephant, a peacock, a spear, a thunderbolt, a cock, a lotus, mercury, and a ruby.
Likewise, one should place the Kriyā-śakti upon its pedestal;
then, having covered it with cloth and other materials, the preceptor goes outside.
Having entered the temple at the auspicious moment, the preceptor, accompanied by the bearers of the images, should install them firmly upon the pedestal with the *dhruva-ādi* and *aurādi* mantras.

Having meditated on the six-faced form as consisting of the power of knowledge and having performed its ritual placement (nyāsa), one should invoke the God into that form with these mantras in their proper sequence.
Oṃ, come, Skanda! May it be well with you, O Kumāra, born of Śiva! O Lord who has the peacock as your vehicle, [and] here, O you whose vehicle is the elephant! || 43 ||
O Subrahmaṇya! Salutations be unto you, O Kārttikeya! O Lord of the gods! O God, commander of the divine army!
O crusher of the lords of the asuras! || 44 ||
O wielder of the spear and vajra weapon! O bearer of the staff, the excellent goad, the discus, and the javelin! O All-pervading Lord, crusher of the lords of the asuras! || 45 ||
Having uttered "O God, I invoke you," at the end of which the root mantra along with its limbs is joined,
one [should draw forth] the supreme light in the form of the Cave from the lotus of one's own heart.

Having led [the breath] into the light situated in the center of the lotus of the sky, and having taken it even from there into the partless (niṣkala) state, one should then recite the root mantra and the *haṃsa*.

Having brought [the deity] through the path of the channels, one should place it within the heart-lotus of the image; then, having flooded the celestial lotus with waters of nectar, one should restore it to consciousness.
Having meditated upon the form within the heart-lotus of this [deity], one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the path of mantras;
that is traditionally taught as consisting of the root-mantra, the limb-mantras, the Gāyatrī, and the form-mantras.
The feet of the *skandagāyatrī* and the path of its feet are as before; [they are placed] in the heart, the mouth, likewise on the head, the navel, the secret place, and the two feet. (50)
One should properly install the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan) after clearly visualizing them in their correct order;
then, having bathed [the deity] with the Mūrti, Īśa, Nidrā, Kumbha, and Astra [mantras], one should worship.
It is as follows:

having bathed and performed the ritual of complete consecration (sakalīkṛtya), one should worship the obstacle and the door; having cast the weapon-mantra (astra) and entered within, one should place that [weapon] upon the threshold.
Having worshipped the Vāstu, Brahmā, and the seats, and having sat down with the limbs and forms [of the deity], one should perform the ritual integration (sakalīkaraṇa),
prepare the arghya offering, and carry out the fivefold purifications.
Wearing three sectarian marks (tripuṇḍra), a forehead mark (tilaka), and a crest made of flowers,
he [visualizes] those residing on the body of the peacock-throne known as Ādhāraśakti and Ananta.
One should worship Dharma and the others, as well as the lords of the mandalas such as the solar disc and those beginning with Ka, upon the filaments;
and one should worship the powers of the Vidyā in the center.
Vidyā, Śānti, Smṛti, Medhā, Prajñā, Kānti, Dyuti, Dhṛti, and Vyāpinī—these possess graceful forms and are situated in order starting from the east. (56)
One should worship the two goddesses Devasenā and Devayānī, who resemble pomegranate flowers, on the right and left [sides] with divine garments and other offerings. (57)
Having invoked in sequence the seat, the form of Skanda, the mantra-body, and then Guha,
one should perform the ritual unification (sakalīkaraṇa) with the limbs of the form and the powers.

One should worship with the ritual services beginning with the *arghya* and ending with the *nivedya*; the enclosure on the petals is formed by the limbs (*aṅgas*), while at the tips of the petals is the Form together with the lords of the forms (*mūrtipas*).
The third [mandala] should consist of the twelve forms on the edge of the pedestal;
the fourth by the door-keepers; and the fifth by the world-protectors (lokeśa) together with their weapons. || 60 ||
One should likewise worship the sixth enclosure with the fivefold offerings;
then, having offered oblations with the seven mantras beginning with "sthirā," one should touch Guha.
Having worshipped for three days as before and offered oblations into the fire,
on the fourth day, having performed worship, one should go to the abode of Dhūrtasena.
Having installed the omnipresent Lord, who holds a spear and a chisel in his hands, in the northeast corner— one who is red in color and adorned with red ornaments—
one should worship him with floral offerings from previous worship.

As for the expiation, having offered oblations with the mantras of the Mūla, Aṅga, and Mūrti, as well as the Śaktis, one should then offer sesame seeds and clarified butter separately with the Skanda-gāyatrī.
Having offered five hundred oblations with the Jaya and other mantras,
and having performed the expiatory rite and the Sviṣṭakṛt offering, one should withdraw the fires into one's heart.

Then, one should bathe [the deity] with a special ablution, or with any one of the [other] excellent types, using the mantras proclaimed by Śiva in their proper sequence, according to what is available.
Having performed the great worship, one should offer the bali-oblation to the spirits at night; and sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) should be given according to one's capacity, as before.
Having resolved to perform an uninterrupted daily worship by means of villages, fields, wealth, and so forth, the performer obtains the abundant fruit previously described. (68)
The Chapter on the Foundation of the Skanda Temple:
At the perpetual festival of Skanda, Vajradhara and Śaktidhara stand as gatekeepers in front;
then follow Vighneśvara and Viśveśvara, as well as Vīrasena and Suṣeṇa. (69)

And Vajrasena shall be the commander-in-chief; starting from the east in sequence, the world-protectors (lokeśas), ending with Skanda and his attendants, shall be stationed in their respective directions.
Having worshipped Mayūra in the pavilion, the Mothers in their own places, Vidhu at the bolt,
and Dhūrtasena in the northeast, one should offer the bali-oblation to them.
One should worship Agniketu and Sūryaketu at the gate of the gopura; then, having gone outside, one should stand before the balipīṭha.
Oṃ!
To those who, desiring the offering, abide pervading the entire world— * * * * * *
May all accept this supreme offering. || 73 ||
By this [mantra], however, one may also invoke all the hosts of Skandas; thereafter, one should invoke the lords of the hosts (gaṇeśvaras), such as Unmātha and others, for the outer circumambulation.
Having worshipped the presiding lords of the hosts of koṭis and koṭis, one should cast the bali offering for them:
Unmātha, Pramātha, Subhāsa, Bhāsvara, and Maṇi. || 75 ||
Sumaṇi, as well as Jyotis, Jvālājihva, and the eighth;
then one should offer oblation upon the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha) from these ten forms.
Parigha, Vikaṭa, Bhīma, Utkrośa, Vajra, Valkala, Daṇḍahasta, Vardhana, Kumuda, and likewise Nandana. (77)
Then Skandasena is the tenth [deity] in the center of the lotus seat; this procedure for the daily festival (nityotsava) is the same as that for the great festival (mahotsava).

The specific detail is stated therein: one should worship the peacock upon the banner with "Oṃ, obeisance to the Peacock; obeisance to the vehicle of Skanda. Then the Guru should invoke all the hosts of Skanda as previously described.
Oṃ!
Those beings who are the leaders of Skanda’s army and the lords of Skanda’s retinue—may they be satisfied, may they attain joy; salutations again and again to them and to those [goddesses]. 80.
Having thus invoked the hosts of Skanda in the eight directions beginning with the east,
there shall be thirty-two lords of the Gaṇas, consisting of millions upon millions of Gaṇeśas.
Then Kumuda, Kundara, Ḍambara, Aḍambara, Vakra, Anuvakra, Sumukha, and Suvrata are situated in the direction of Agni (the southeast). 82.
Satyasandha, Suprabha, Śubhakarmā, and Lāṅgalin are in the south; then in the southwest are Kāla, Bala, Atibala, and Alasa. (83)
Suvarcas and Ativarcas, as well as Kāñcana and Atighana, are located in the west; furthermore, Meghamālin and Sthira are in the northwest.
The fourth is exceedingly firm and lofty, and is fond of guests; in the north is Meghanāda, characterized by conciliation, subversion, and war. (85)
In the northeast are Puṣpadanta, Śaṅkukarṇa, Jaya, and Mahājaya— these four lords of hosts of many millions of attendants. (86)
Immediately after these, and following their respective assemblies,
one should offer the bali-oblation ending with "svāhā" at the conclusion of the section for Skanda’s attendants.

At the conclusion of the designated day, however, preceded by the commencement of the auspicious thread ceremony (kautuka), one should undertake the pilgrimage to sacred sites (tīrthayātrā) after having invited [the preceptor] as before. || 88 ||
Oṃ!
O Lord, O Ruler of the Gods! You must undertake a pilgrimage tomorrow;
you should grant permission for the commencement of the *pratisarā* rite there. (89)
Having thus addressed the god Guha according to the rites for Śiva’s festivals, and having performed a pilgrimage to sacred sites with his own mantras, he then returned.

Having caused the Six-faced One to enter within after the special worship, and having offered the bali-oblation to the spirits at night, [one should proceed] with the bathing of the principal deity and the others.
One should bathe [the deity] according to one's capacity with the mantras prescribed for the Śaiva ablution;
then, one should duly perform the great worship (mahāpūjā) according to the rules.
Lord Śiva himself has stated that one obtains the previously mentioned fruit:
"Thus, the Ṣaḍāsya-tantra, from the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) up to the festival (utsava), has been correctly described;
one should understand it according to the Śaiva [tradition] as seen in the primary Bṛhattantras."
Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, the Skanda-tantra, in the Kriyāpāda of the Upper Section of the Siddhāntasāra, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva.
Now begins the fifty-fourth chapter.

The installation and other rites of Haranārāyaṇa are now declared. The mantra consists of *vaṃ* ending with a bindu (*vaṃ*), followed by Brahmā (*bha*), then Agni (*ra*), and the fifth vowel (*u*). This final [vowel] is long.

The fire-mantra (agnibīja) is with the long vowel, as is the wind-mantra (vāyubīja) and the letter *ta* joined with the long vowel; this ten-syllable mantra ends with *namaḥ*, preceded by the *tāra*, *śakti*, and *ravibīja*. || 2 ||
Its meter is considered to be Atijagatī, consisting of thirteen syllables; its seer is Brahmā, and its deity is Lord Hari himself. (3)

One should form the seed-syllable of Śakti with long vowels, joined with the name and the [appropriate] caste-suffix; by means of that, one should fashion the six limbs beginning with the heart, ending with the weapon.

Having placed those [mantras] on the fingers according to the sequence taught by Śiva, starting from the base, one should then place the pervasive [mantra] and the [mantras of the] heart and so forth, each in its own respective location, in due order.
First, the syllable *tāram* (Om), and then *vidmahe* for Śaṅkara; immediately after that, *nārāyaṇāya*, and at its end, the word *dhīmahe*; and then the word *naḥ*. (6)
And then the Puruṣa-sūkta should be recited, ending with the word "prehi"; likewise, the Gāyatrī of Hari-Nārāyaṇa is appropriate for the sacrifice.

Having first joined the seed-syllables of Śakti, Śrī, and Kāma to the beginning of the root mantra, and having placed "namaḥ" at the end for [the deity] who is the self of all beings— this is the mantra for worship.
One should place the Brahmās, beginning with Īśa, from the head down to the feet; likewise, one should place Harārdha in their respective locations, and Vāsudeva elsewhere.
One should place Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha, and Keśava respectively upon the head, the face, the heart, the private parts, and the feet of Hari. These constitute half [of the deity].

The wheel of ritual action (kriyācakra) taught in the Śaiva tradition is for the most part the same here as well; however, the specific details regarding the consecration pavilion (adhivāsanamaṇḍapa) are now being stated.
The archways starting from the east should be worshipped with the names of Śiva and Viṣṇu;
on the southern half of the archway are Śānti, Bhūti, Bala, and Ārogya.
Suśobhana, Subhadra, Supūrṇa, and Pūrṇa—
these should be worshipped by their own names on the left side of the archways (toraṇas).
At each door, however, stand four gatekeepers stationed in jars: in the east are Nandīśa and Pūrṇa, and Mahākāla and Puṣkara.
To the south are Bhṛṅgīśa and Nandana, as well as Vighneśa and Nandana; to the west are Vṛṣa, Vīrasena, Ṣaṇmukha, and Suṣeṇaka.
One should worship Durgā, Sambhava, Udarka, Caṇḍa, and Prabhava, preceded by Vikira and Kṣepa, in the water-pot (kumbha) for Hari and Harihara.
Having worshipped and taken possession of the trident and the discus along with the *vardhanī* vessel,
one should enter the pavilion and divide the fire of the central pit into nine parts as before.
The preceptor and the image-keepers should perform oblations with the previously mentioned substances and their own root-mantra components;
having performed the satiation of the mantra, they should carry out the purification of the syllables (ākāra-śodhana).
The opening of the eyes, the dwelling in water, as well as the circumambulation of the village, the ceremonial bath, and likewise the resting in the pavilion as before; (19)
On the sacrificial altar, one should worship the jars, the weapons, the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas), and the eight forms (Aṣṭamūrtis).
It is as follows:
[one worships] the earth together with Ananta, the water joined with Sūkṣma, and Śivottama.
Then, having worshipped in this manner according to the sequence declared by Śiva: Sāgni, Ekākṣavāyu, Kha, Śikhaṇḍin,
Śrīkaṇṭha conjoined with Manas, Trīmūrti conjoined with Buddhi,
and Ekarudra conjoined with Ahaṅkāra.
Then one should place the pitchers, beginning with the [pitcher of] the principles (tattva). || 22 ||

One should know the three principles beginning with the Self (ātman) as extending up to the knees, the throat, and the head; likewise, the lords of the principles beginning with Brahmā, the forms beginning with earth, and the Sun.
One should install the twelve forms in their respective portions: Soma, the sacrificer, mind, ego, intellect, and primordial nature (prakṛti). || 24 ||
[He worshipped] Śarva and the others, the lords of the eight forms, as well as Vāsudeva and the others; [he worshipped] Vidyeśvarī, Śivā, Sūkṣmā, Śāṅkarī, and Harivallabhā.
Vaiṣṇavī, Mahālakṣmī, Kṣamā, and likewise Nārāyaṇī—
these indeed are the general powers (śaktis) of Hari and Nārāyaṇa.
One should likewise install the nine powers beginning with Vāmā and those beginning with Vimalā: Vimalā, Utkarṣaṇī, Jñānā, Kriyā, and Yogā. (27)

Satyā, Pṛthvī, and likewise Īśānā—the ninth is thus remembered. Having thus performed the placement (nyāsa), worshipped, and meditated upon the omnipresent Lord in His manifest form (sakala), [one should proceed]. || 28 ||
Likewise, having placed the power of action (kriyā-śakti) upon the seat, one should worship it; and right there, one should also sacrifice to the eight powers beginning with Dhārikā.

Having thus offered oblations in the nine sacrificial pits with the principles (tattvas), the lords of the principles (tattveśvaras), and so forth, as well as with the root-mantra, the limb-mantras, and the Gāyatrī, according to the sequence taught by Śiva; || 30 ||

Having performed the satiation with mantras, one should pour [the water] into the peace-pitchers (śāntikumbha). The preceptor (ācārya) and the guardians of the images (mūrtipāḥ) should touch them in succession three times.
All materials, mantras, rituals, and so forth, are to be understood by the preceptors here as being entirely equal to those prescribed for the installation of Śiva. (32)
p.

529) Then, having entered within at the auspicious moment (lagna), one should install the tortoise-stone (kūrmaśilā) as before. And upon that [stone], one should worship the sustaining power (dhāriṇī-śakti) along with the principles (tattva), the lords of the principles (tattveśvara), and so forth. || 33 ||

And having arranged the five groups beginning with the jewels above that as before, one should place the pedestal (pīṭha) and the Power of Action (kriyāśakti) situated therein along with the [other] powers (śaktis). || 34 ||
Having established the Lord, the all-pervading one whose nature is the power of knowledge, at the eastern gate,
one should invoke His form with the root mantra and contemplate Him as having a body composed of mantra.

In that very same way, the stainless light within his own heart-lotus— consisting of the syllable *haṃsa* encased by the three previously mentioned seed-syllables— is [to be drawn] from the lotus of one's own heart.
Having led the consciousness of the sky-lotus [the deity] to the lotus of the heart of the image,
one should then wash and bathe it with the waters from the altar-vessel and the weapon-mantra.
Then, one should assign the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan) using the eight jars beginning with Ananta,
[accompanied] by one's own root-mantra and its limbs, one's own Gāyatrī, the Brahma-mantras, and the Praṇava and so forth.
The path of mantra is indicated by the names beginning with Vāsudeva, joined with "namo bhagavate" and ending in the dative case, as well as by means of words. (39)
The path of the *gāyatrī* consists of its quarters (*pada*), while the remaining paths are as before;
then, having offered oblations with the *sthirā* and other mantras and having touched [the deity], one should worship.

One should proceed with the ritual services (*upacāra*) in their proper sequence, beginning with the seat (*āsana*) and so forth, as follows: having worshipped the Lord of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*) and the Guru, and having performed the ritual of personification (*sakalīkaraṇa*) upon one's own body; // 41 //
One should offer the general arghya to Vighna and Sarasvatī on the upper lintel and the two sides of the door,
and to Gaṅgā, Yamunā, and Śrī in the middle.
One should worship Nandīśa and Caṇḍa as the two door-keepers stationed at the upper part of the door;
and one should worship Mahākāla and Pracaṇḍa on the right side of the door.
Having entered within and deposited the weapon, one should discharge the Nārāca weapon;
then one should worship Vāstveśa, Vedhas, and likewise Anantāsana in the center.

Then, having performed the fivefold purification, adorned with a tilaka mark and a flower crown, and having offered the arghya with water, milk, kuśa grass, and unbroken rice grains while reciting the root mantra and its ancillary mantras; || 45 ||
One should worship with barley, sandalwood, white mustard seeds, and even flowers;
having sprinkled oneself and one's materials and so forth with that [water], one is protected by the enclosure of the *astra* mantra. (46)
The foundational power (ādhāra-śakti), the tortoise (kūrma), and likewise the seat of Ananta;
dharma and the others, as well as adharma and the others, māyā, vidyā, and the three qualities (guṇatraya). || 47 ||

From the reflection of the sun and other luminaries pervading the vessel and so forth, there arises an eight-petalled lotus; on each pair of filaments are the Śaktis, Vāmā and the others, as well as Vimalā and the rest.

"Oṃ, salutation to Vāmā and Vimalā"—thus [one should worship] on the filaments and other parts of the eastern petal, proceeding in order from the east, and in the center [worship] Manonmanī for the sake of grace; likewise, upon its pericarp, one should [visualize] her form, whose body consists of the Vidyā and the Mantra. (49)

Having performed the sacrifice as before from the heart-lotus, [one should perform] the invocation (āvāhana), the installation (sthāpana), the presence (sānnidhya), and the descent [of the deity] (sannipātana) which is of the nature of Śiva, the light of Brahman.

One should perform the consecration with the *prarocanā* and *amṛtīkaraṇa*, as well as the veiling (*avaguṇṭhana*), having performed the ritual integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*) in due order by means of the root-mantra and its limbs along with the *gāyatrī*.
One should meditate upon the omnipresent Lord Haranārāyaṇa, who has four arms:
a trident and an axe in his right hands, and a conch and a discus in his left hands.
Or he may be depicted bearing a skull, a trident, a lotus, and the Sudarśana discus;
on his left side, a tiger skin, and wearing yellow garments. (53)
He was adorned with necklaces made of many half-snakes as their ornaments,
and he wore earrings shaped like sea-monsters upon his beautiful face.
The Lord, wearing a crown of matted hair and the crescent moon as his crest-jewel,
adorned with bilva leaves, blue lotuses, red lotuses, and garlands of tulasī.
Adorned with various serpent-jewels, finger-rings, bracelets,
and armlets, and decorated with a single cool gem shining upon his half-blue throat.
With a waist-thread and foot-ornaments bound with gold from the Sahya mountains, shining with ashes as body-paste, and anointed with yellow sandalwood; 57.
The Lord, whose form was both fierce and beautiful, a treasury of all splendor and majesty,
was resplendent with Pārvatī and Śrī stationed at his right and left sides.
In this manner, one should worship Hara and Hari in succession with ritual offerings, along with their limbs (*aṅga*),
powers (*śakti*), the lords of the eight forms (*aṣṭamūrtīśa*), and the gatekeepers (*dvārapālaka*). (59)

Then, having worshipped the fivefold enclosure with the previously mentioned world-protectors (lokeśas), and having thus fully honored Hara and Hari, he should offer oblations of sacrificial fuel (samidh) and other materials into the fire.

And on the second day they should offer oblations with the Tryambaka mantra, and on the third day with the "Viṣṇornuka" hymn and others, as well as with the root-mantra and its ancillaries, in due order.

On the fourth day, having performed the expiation (prāyaścitta) by offering oblations with the Aghora-weapon mantra, using Sudarśana, Palāśa wood fuel-sticks, and clarified butter in the proper sequence; 62.
Having propitiated Caṇḍasena as before with the Jayā and other oblations,
he likewise performed the expiatory rites, offered the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), and the sviṣṭakṛt offering.
Having deposited the fires within the lotus of one's own heart and having dismissed them,
[one likewise dismisses] the deities residing in the archways, banners, world-protectors, gateways, and water-pots.
Then one should bathe [the deity] with one hundred and eight jars, having worshipped him with special care and having bestowed sacrificial fees and other gifts.

Having offered the bali-oblation to the spirits at night for the sake of accomplishing daily worship and other rites, and having made a formal resolve with devotion according to one's means, one obtains the fruit as desired.
The Chapter on the Installation of Śaṅkara-Nārāyaṇa:
In the daily festival (nityotsava), Nandīśa and Caṇḍa are at the eastern gate; Mahākāla, Pracaṇḍa, Bhṛṅgī, and Vighna are at the southern [gate].

In the west, [he should offer] to Vṛṣabha and Ananta; and in the north, to Caṇḍasena. He should cast the bali offering to the world-protectors in their respective directions with their own respective mantras.
In this regard, the distinction is as follows:
"Homage to Indra, lord of the gods, together with his weapons, vehicles, and retinue, and to the attendants of Śaṅkara and Nārāyaṇa; homage to those attendants. Thus it is said.
In the daily festival, one should scatter the bali offering in all directions with mantras containing the words "attendants of Śaṅkara-Nārāyaṇa. In the great festival,
however, one should do so with [mantras] such as "for the destruction of the pride of the Daityas," and [the mantra beginning] "those beings who dwell in front."
With these and other mantras proclaimed for the great festivals of Śiva, such as "O Blessed Śaṅkaranārāyaṇa," one should offer the oblation (bali) there.
Having worshipped the bull, the half-Garuda, and the one stationed in the pavilion, one should cast the oblation.
Gaṇeśa, Vīrabhadra, the Mothers, and Śāstṛ as well. || 69 ||
One should worship Durgā, Soma, and Caṇḍasena in their respective directions;
having offered them with [the gestures of] the spear, the discus, the boon-granting gesture, and the protection gesture, one should cast the sacrificial offering (bali). || 70 ||
Having worshipped Mṛgāsya, Pāñcajanya, Tīkṣṇanetra, and Sudarśana at the four gates of the city, one should offer them an oblation.
Standing to the east of the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha), one should invoke the Gaṇas with this [mantra]:
"Oṃ!
May all the attendants (pārṣadas) of Śaṅkara and those of Viṣṇu come here. (72)
Remaining there, pervading the entire world, may they accept this supreme offering; then [offerings] to Nandīśa and the others, as well as to Kumuda and the others.
In each of the two mandalas, one should offer oblations in every direction as follows:
Nandīśa, Mahākāla, Bhūtanātha, and Mahīdhara. (74)
Parvateśa, Guheśa, Kālapāśaka, Kapālī, Kumuda, Kumudākṣa, Puṇḍarīka, and Vāmana. (75)

"Śaṅkukarṇa, Śaṅkunetra, Sumukha, and Supratiṣṭhita—Oṃ, salutation to Nandīśa and Kumuda, the attendants (pārṣada) of Śaṅkara and Nārāyaṇa. Thus, one should scatter the offering (bali) in the eastern direction; likewise, one should scatter the offering in the directions beginning with the southeast (āgneyī).
Then, however, on the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha), [offerings] were made to Bhūtidā and the others. || 76 ||
To the one who bears the conch, the discus, and likewise the mace; to the one who bears the Śārṅga bow, the lotus, the mallet, the noose, and likewise the goad. || 77 ||

Above the *kumuda* [petal], one should offer the oblation (*bali*) upon the pericarp of the pedestal-lotus with the mantra "Salutation to Nandakī," followed by "to Hari, Hara, and the others," and "to the Army" (*senāya*). || 78 ||
Here too, as before, one should offer oblations in the cardinal directions with two [verses] each:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Bhūti and Dakṛi, the attendants of Śaṅkara and Nārāyaṇa," and so forth, using dual forms of words.
This is the procedure for the daily festival, which is the same as that for the great festival.
The specific detail is stated: on a cloth, one should draw Garuḍa in the form of half a bull; he should be worshipped by his own name, and thereafter one should scatter an offering.
On the third necklace, by the mantras, there are various lords of beings—those of Śaṅkara, Vaiṣṇava, and others—according to their own names and in the order of the directions.
There should be twenty Śaivas and fifty Vaiṣṇavas in the various directions. They are as follows:
Mahākāla, Vidhātṛ, Vajrapāṇi, and Kratu-prabhu. (82)
He is skillful, like Śatakratu, immeasurable, and heroic; he is eternal, possesses the brilliance of lightning, holds a trident in his hand, and has three eyes. || 83 ||
The lamp of his own limbs, the destroyer of darkness, the creator of the universe, and he of vast prowess; Māndhātṛ, the one of great heroism, the eternal union, and the one who bestows grace. (84)
Utkūṭa, Prakaṭa, Unmukha, Dvimukha, Hari;
Aśvagrīva, Aśvavadana, Aśvajihva, and Aśvalocana. || 85 ||
Keśava, Vāmana, Nara, and Nāraka; Mandara, Mandadṛṣṭi, Kanda, and Kandukalocana. || 86 ||
Paṭahākṣa, Viśālākṣa, Kṣāmaka, and likewise Kṣamaka; Pāṇḍara, Pāṇḍupṛṣṭha, Durdina, and likewise Sudina. || 87 ||
Vāmadeva, Mahādeva, Mohana, Madhusūdana, Kalana, Kālana, Bhāvana, and the Blessed Lord Bhava. || 88 ||
Hanumān, Bhāgadheya, Bhāskara, and likewise Bhāsura; Viśveśa, Viśvasena, Viṣvaksena, and Visāraṇa. || 89 ||
Vistāra, Vistara, Vidaṇḍin, Daṇḍa, Kāmuka, Akāmuka, Kāmahṛt, and Kāmanāśana. || 90 ||
There are seventy hosts belonging to Haranārāyaṇa in the east: Agni, Agnisamāna, Jvālāmālin, and Viśvabhuk. (91)
The sacrificial fire is embodied, all-pervading, tawny, with red eyes; he is fierce, smoke-colored, with a red body, possessing seven flames, and the universal medicine. || 92 ||
Then Sutapā, Vegavān, Bhasmacchanna, Marutsakha, Rudraṇa, Yogapriya, Dāruja, Āgneya, and likewise Nidhana. || 93 ||
Agnijihva, Hutāśa, Agnirūpa, Agniketana, Agnivarṇa, Agni, Agnyāsya, Mahāsena, Mahodara, Mahānāsa, Karāla, Kālajihva, and Vivartaka. (94) p. 534)
Maṇḍūra, Maṇḍūka, Kākāsya, Deva, and likewise Devalaka. || 95 ||
Śamaka and Camaka, Śaṅku and Śaṅkuśravas, Mārīca, Droṇamārīca, Mahiṣa, and Bhīṣaṇa; || 96 ||
Kumbhanāsa, Vināśa, Kumbhakarṇa, and then Kumbhaka; Visarī, Vikramī, Matsarī, and likewise Maskara. (97)
Sūkara and Sūkarāsya, Śaśa and likewise Śaśamukha; Siṃha and Siṃhamukha, as well as Nārasiṃha and Nara. || 98 ||
Kālahṛt, Kālasūtra, Sūtraka, Sūta, Vinālī, and Nālakarṇa—these seventy reside in the south-eastern direction. (99)
Yama, Vivasvat, Ghātā, Daityaghātī, Prajāntaka, Mṛtyu, Pretādhipa, Dharma, Kṛṣṇa, and Kṛṣṇākṣa. (100)
He is the eternal yogi, Time itself, the swift-acting one who consumes the departed; he is the one whose form is illusion, the end-maker, the truth, the lover of truth, and the friend.
Pitṛnātha, Kīnāśa, Dharma, Dharmarata, Dharmya, Dharmaja, Dhanvī, Praśraya, and Naya; || 102 ||
Kuṇaka, Kuṇivāha, Niḥśreya, Nīriṇa, Alasa, Niṣkopa, Niranukrośa, Kubja, and Pāṃsuvimardana. (103)
Āho, utāho, āhu, nirmala, nivaha, vaha, ekalavya, palala, ūhu, and likewise saṃrakṣaṇa. || 104 ||
Śaṅkhin, Cakrin, Dhanvin, Kaṅkaṭa, Kaṭuka, Viṭa, Vasudeva, Subhadra, Śārṅgin, and likewise Śārṅgadhara. (105)
Citrāṅgada, Citraratha, Ketumān, Ketuda, Kṣamī, Vallaka, Vallakīhasta, Dvirada, Vigraha, and Ambara. || 106 ||
Ārjama, Dundubhi, and Śveta—these are situated in the southern direction;
as well as Rākṣasa, Asura, Kravyād, Vīrahā, and Nirṛti. (107)
He was Tīkṣṇanetra, a Yātudhāna, a destroyer of sacrifices, a night-stalker; he was Mahāmūrti, the son of Kaikasī, cruel, and likewise possessed of a cruel form.
Dakṣa, Koṇapaka, Dhūmra, Dhūmrākṣa, and likewise Bhīṣaṇa;
Vīrūpākṣa, then Bhasmāṅga, Sukṛti, and likewise Vikṛti. (109)
Dāruṇa, Damana, Nairṛti, Prakṛti, Māṃsapa, Māṃsaka, Rākṣasa, and likewise Rakṣaka. || 110 ||
Pralamba, Lambaka, Niṣṭhura, Kharabhāṣaṇa, Vīrasena, Akṣarāśa, Prāṇada, and likewise Praṇava. || 111 ||
Kāmada, Vibhāṣin, Raktākṣa, Lohitākṣaka, Vidyutkeśa, Viśālākṣa, Raktajihva, and Vijihmaka. || 112 ||
He is both the imperishable and the perishable, the observer free from egoism;
