he is all-pervading, all-knowing, fair-complexioned, able to assume any form at will, and yet possessed of diverse forms. (113)
Vaikartana, Vikartana, Saṃplava, Sambhava, Vimada, Madana, Vāruṇa, and Vasu. || 114 ||
Nandakī and Nandaka, as well as Kapardin and Vṛṣabha, Śoṇa, Pinākī, and Varuṇa—these are stationed in the southwest (nair-ṛta). || 115 ||
Varuṇa, Śabala, Ambhodhi, Pracetas, Nimnagāpati, Yādonātha, Pāśapāṇi, Ānanda, Ambupati, and Śiva. (116)
Kapardin, the giver of life, Śveta, Śyāmanetra, Sanātana, Pratyaṅnivāsa, Jalada, Jīvana, and Nakravāhana. || 117 ||
Payodhinilaya, Vāruṇa, and likewise Vāraṇa; Kṣepaṇa, Kṣobhaṇa, Pāśī, Pāśadhara, and Guru. || 118 ||
Sannāha, Nāhana, Haṃsa, Nārada, Parvata, Ravi, Bhānumān, Vasumān, Bhadra, Vaikuṇṭha, Parama, Para. || 119 ||
Mahākarṇa, Vikarṇa, Vidrava, and likewise Pradrava;
Vānara, Tāraka, Śaśaka, Śākala, and Śala. || 120 ||
Cakrabhṛt, Śaṅkhabhṛt, Vajrī, Karṇī, Karṇa, and likewise Aṃśumān; Kurara, Kurava, Vajranābha, and Vināyaka. || 121 ||
Durgandha, Pūtigandha, Dakṣiṇa, Adakṣiṇa, Suhṛd, Virodha,
Rodhana, Rodha, Tārkṣya, and Garuḍa. (122)
Aṅgadī and Kaṅkaṇī—these constitute the seventy members of the Vāruṇī group.
Vāyu (the Wind), Gandhavaha, Sūkṣma, Sparśana, and Prabhañjana; || 123 ||
Prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna; nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya. || 124 ||
Dhvajapāṇi, Pavana, Śvasana, Māruta, Anila, Vidvān, Marut, Māruta, Vāta, Vahnisakha, and Hari. (125)
Alarka, Vartaka, Kaṅka, Mārgaṇa, Praṅkaṇa, Bala, Abala, Baladhī, Vīra, Dvidhīra, and Rodhaka as well. (126)
Savidhi, Suvidhi, Saṅgara, and likewise Vikaṭa; Mālī, Mānī, Sudhī, as well as Samartha, Sāhasa, and Dhara. (127)
Kukuṭa, Kuṭaka, Gandha, Gandhavaha, Saktaga, Asaktaga, Rāgī, Secana, and Svanas.
Medicine, the healer, the living being, the sick person, disease, fortune, the happy one; the cause, the instrument, the agent, the dependent on another, the strong, and the weak. (129)
Thus these seven groups are situated in the northwestern direction; [there dwell] Rayimān, the lord of Yakṣas, Soma, Māṇibhadra, and Guhyaka. || 130 ||
Celī, Mālī, Kubera, Jambhala, Śibikuṇḍalī, the Lord of Kinnaras, Ailavila, Dhanada, and Dhanādhipa. || 131 ||
Likewise, Rājarāja, Śrīda, Jyeṣṭha, Mālādhara, Dhana, Uttarāśānivāsa, and then Ekakuṇḍala. (132)
Soma, Somakala, Saumya, Somavid, Somavardhana; Sudhā, Sudhātā, Bhaṅgīra, Surāṣṭra, Kāṣṭhali, and Kali. || 133 ||

He possesses time, he is the wheel of time, the deadly *kālakūṭa* poison, and the fever of time; he is the nectar, the lord of nectar, the water, the one adorned with armlets, the absolute, and the powerful.
Viṣṇu, Kṛṣṇa, Piśaṅgī, Rekhā, Lekheśvara the supreme,
Nalaka, Śunaka, Krātha, Śyena, Śyenamukha, and Aruṇa. (135)
Mārjāra, valgu, akṣī, gulma, kaṇavaka, kaṇa, śeba, viśeṣa, viśleṣa, kardama, and pūtivigraha. || 136 ||
Sāmba, Saṃvatsara, Sambhuvegin, Vegadhara, and Amara—
these Gaṇas residing in the northern quarter are remembered as the attendants of Hara and Harī.
Īśāna, Īśvara, Śambhu, the trident-handed, the three-eyed; the one without beginning or end, the Sustainer, Kapila, the tawny-eyed. (138)
Rudra, lord of the hosts of Rudras, the sustainer of the universe, sky-clad, blue-throated, with matted hair, bull-vehicled, and having the bull as his banner. || 139 ||
Hara, Śarva, Viśvabhuj, Īśa, Vyāpin, Triśūladhṛk, Vīra, Bharga, Vaśin, Śambhu, Vivāsas, Vyasana, and Budha. (140)
He is the tree, the earth, the one devoted to forbearance, the bird, the bird Vaṭa;
he is the friend of Brahman, the knower of Brahman, the Brahman, Mārīca, and Haripiṅgala. || 141 ||
The knower of the Vedas, the friend of those who know the Vedas, the one belonging to Brahman, and the means for attaining Brahman;
the wise one, the one of right vision, the eightfold self, Śaṅkara, and likewise Śāṅkara. || 142 ||

The discipliner, the one with blossoming hair, the eloquent speaker, the disciplined soul, the performer of disciplined deeds, the single-eyed, the all-consuming, the all-encompassing, the dispeller of sorrow, and the shaker of the lamp. || 143 ||
Govinda, Gopati, Goptṛ, Sarvabhāgin, Sanātana, Daṇḍin, Muṇḍin, and Śikhaṇḍin—these are the seventy Gaṇas in the northeast. (144)

Having thus offered the bali-oblation to these [deities], one should cast the bali on the bali-pīṭha; then, having caused the deity to enter within and having bathed, one should also worship as before.
At the conclusion of the festival, having performed the principal ablution as before, he should lower the banner as previously described and dismiss all the Gaṇas.
One should bathe [the image] according to one's means and worship it with special offerings;
immediately thereafter, one should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor and the others.
One should bestow upon supplicants that which is to be given, according to what is appropriate,
having observed what has been declared in the great *Bṛhat-tantra* known as the *Devodbhava*.

From the installation ceremony until the conclusion of the festival—thus has the *Haraharitantra* been correctly explained in brief; all the ritual actions herein should be inferred in accordance with the Śaiva tradition. (148–1/2)
Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, the Śaṅkaranārāyaṇatantra-paṭala, in the Kriyāpāda of the Upper Section of the Siddhāntasāra, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva.
Now begins the fifty-fifth chapter.
Next, the installation of Durgā and other rites as enjoined by the Tantras are described;
for the cycle of rituals prescribed in the Śaiva tradition is for the most part identical here as well.
The extraction of the root-mantra of Durgā and other mantras is also described:
the Tāra (Oṃ), the Śakti-bīja (Hrīṃ), and the third letter of the fifth [varga] (Pha). Thus, the nine-syllabled mantra of Durgā is formed. (2)

The fifth vowel joined with the staff (daṇḍī), followed by that same [vowel] devoid of its bindu; the letter ending in kha (khānta) with the long vowel of the syllable sa (sadīrgha), and the wind (marut) possessing the twelfth vowel. 3.
The nine-syllable mantra of Durgā consists of "namaḥ," the seed-syllable of Śakti,
and the sound (nāda) joined with fire (ra), combined with the long vowels and the [six limbs] beginning with the heart.
In the fourth [verse], the six limbs joined with the birth-mantras are derived from the weapon-mantra; however, for the worship, that Gāyatrī begins with the two *śakti* and *tāra* mantras.
One should know the word *tāram* (the syllable Om), followed by the word *Kātyāyanī* in the dative case (*kātyāyanyai*), and then the phrase *vidmahe*;
after the words *kanyākumāryai*, the word *dhīmahi* should follow. (6)
At the end of those two words, one should utter "durgāyai" and "pra". For this is the Durgā-gāyatrī; with it, one should worship Śivā.
Then follows the verse beginning with "jātavedase," and after that, the verse beginning with "tām agnivarṇām"; and thereafter, the verse beginning with "agne tvam viśvāni. (8)
The Ṛg verse beginning with "pṛtanājita" is the fifth [mantra] of Durgā; thus has been described the path of mantras for Durgā as enjoined in the Tantra.
She may have four arms, eight arms, or sixteen arms; she may be seated upon a lion throne or standing atop a buffalo. (10)
Durgā should be installed in times of fear and other such crises, seated upon a lion;
Durgā has four arms, holding the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, as well as a conch and a discus.
When she has eight arms, she holds a threatening gesture (tarjanī), a bow, a shield, and a conch in her left hands, while holding a trident, an arrow, a sword, and a discus in her right hands.
She holds a skull, a goad, a mace, a *śataghnī*, two spears, and a bow; likewise, she carries a shield and a conch in her left hands, and in her right [hands]... 13.
When she has sixteen arms, she should hold in her first set of lower hands a trident, a noose, fire, a vajra, a lance, an arrow, and a sword, as well as a discus.
The image, measured according to the female proportion, should be ten tālas in height at the waist; in the pavilion, archways should be constructed as before, made from milky trees.
In the four directions beginning with the east, Yajñeśa, Prabhākara, Maṅgala,
and Subhadra should be installed in sequence by means of the Vedas and other [mantras].
Within each gateway were two banners, as well as their respective deities: Kundā, Kumudā, Vidyunmālā, and Bhīṣaṇā. (17)
Kaluṣī, Ghoṣaṇī, Karālī, and likewise Vikṛti—these should be worshipped upon their banners; one should mark them with symbols such as the conch and so forth.
White, reddish, black, dark-green, smoky-grey, yellow, and variegated; furthermore, at each door, two messengers of mixed colors stand in succession.
Kālī, Karālī, Virajā, Mandarā, Vindhyavāsinī, Suprabhā, Siṃhavaktrā, and the eighth is Daityamardanī.

One should worship all those [deities], adorned and holding swords and shields, as residing within the pitcher; then, by scattering the *vikira* offerings, one should worship Śivā, seated upon a lion, within the pitcher.
Having worshipped the weapon (astra) and performed the purification of the form within the *vardhanī* vessel,
one should perform the release of the eye, the immersion in water, and the circumambulation of the village as previously described.

(540) The ceremonial bathing for the purpose of consecration, the act of placing the deity upon the bed in the pavilion, and on the altar, the worship of the eight vessels— the central jar, the weapon-jar, the one called the sleep-jar, and the six image-jars. (23)

Then, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the divisions of the principles beginning with the Self (ātman), such as Brahmā and the rest; likewise, the eight forms beginning with Earth (kṣmā), and the lords of those forms beginning with Dhārikā.
One should place Dhārikā, Dīptimatī, Ugrā, Jyotsnā, Cit, and Balotkaṭā; and Dhātrī and Vibhu—the wise one—upon the pedestal (pīṭha) in the form of the ritual action (kriyā). || 25 ||

As before, when the fire has been divided among the nine sacrificial pits by the mantra-expert, one should invoke Durgā with her root-mantra and limb-mantras, and sequentially with the principles of the self (ātmatattva) and so forth.

Having offered oblations as before, the image-consecrators together with the preceptor should touch [the image]; then, at an auspicious moment, the Guru should perform the installation (pratiṣṭhā) when the planetary positions are favorable.

Within the womb at the seventh step, one should install the images of Brahmā and the others upon their respective pedestals; however, the image of Durgā should be installed like that of Śiva, whether it be made of stone, precious gems, or iron.

Likewise, having installed an image of Durgā made of clay for a rite dedicated to the gods, or one made of wood for a rite dedicated to humans, or one depicted as a painting on a wall, one should perform the permanent worship.
Upon the tortoise-stone at the base, one should install the power known as the Support (Ādhāra-śakti),
and likewise place the five groups beginning with jewels upon the pedestal.

One should place the power of action (kriyā-śakti) in the center of the pedestal and the physical form (bera) upon the pedestal; within that form, one should place the embodiment consisting of knowledge (jñāna-ātmikā mūrti) and the seed-syllable *haṃsa* in its heart.
Having raised up from the hollow of the lotus of one's own heart the Kundalinī, who has emerged [from there],
one should awaken the power consisting of consciousness situated within the enclosure of the *haṃsa*.
The wise practitioner, reciting that mantra up to the partless (niṣkala) state, should join the seed-syllable of Śakti upward into the lotus of the void by means of the term "Brahmanāḍī."
Therefore, pronouncing the supreme Śākta light ending with the Niṣkala, one should bring it forth and place it within the lotus of the heart of the image using a handful of flowers.

Having thus invoked [the deity], established [him], and dissolved [him] from the root, having caused him to be present, rendered him nectar, and performed the encircling and the proclamation; || 35 ||
The Gāyatrī, its own root-limbs, and likewise the five Durgāṇavas constitute the path of mantras (mantrādhvan).
The path of words (padādhvan) is considered to consist of the words of the five Durgās. (36)
One should meditate there upon all those remaining paths as before; then, having washed them with water from the image-vessel and the water of the weapon-mantra (astravāri). || 37 ||
Having consecrated [the deity] as before, one should worship with the arghya and other offerings.
For instance:
having bathed and washed one's hands and feet, one should then worship Vighneśa.

Then, having performed the purification of the self and having consecrated his body with the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, he should hold the general water-offering (sāmānyārghya) at the door, as well as Jaya and Vijayā.
One should worship Gaṅgā, Yamunā, and Dvāraśrī above;
having driven away the terrestrial obstacles and others by means of striking with the heels and other such methods. (40)
Having entered within and deposited the weapon, one should discharge the iron arrow (nārāca-astra);
outside, however, there is a rampart of weapons and a covering with armor.
Having established Vāstveśa and Brahmā in the center, one should worship them upon their respective seats; then, having sat down and performed the fivefold purification with the special arghya water.
Having applied a tilaka on the forehead and adorned the head with flowers, one should then offer [homage] to Prakṛti in the center, and then to Vajrāsana.
Thus, having worshipped the golden lion-throne ending with "namaḥ," as well as Āryā, Pralayā, and Mahāpralayakā; 44.

One should worship Sṛṣṭi and the feet beginning with Agni in the cardinal directions; then, one should worship the Unmanifest (Avyakta), Niyati, Kāla, and Kalā in the directions starting from the East (Indra) in sequence.
By means of the three qualities (guṇas), one should visualize the bulb, the stalk, the lotus, and the orbs of the sun, moon, and fire,
along with the petals, filaments, and pericarp pervaded by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara.
[One should worship] Prabhā, Māyā, Jayā, Sūkṣmā, Viśuddhā, and Nandinī,
as well as Suprabhā and Vijayā, in the cardinal directions and in the center, [the latter] bestowing all perfections.

One should worship in sequence with well-proclaimed names beginning with long vowels and ending in *namaḥ*, [at the tips of the filaments] and in the center; thereafter, one should worship the form of Durgā and her body of power (*śaktideha*) by means of the root mantra. (48)
Having invoked the heart-mantra and so forth, one should then [invoke] the Goddess from the heart-lotus,
[she who is] nourished by the consciousness that is the nectar-stream of the lotus of the sky. (49)
The preceptor, having invoked [the deity] into the image using the seed-syllable mentioned at the end of the *niṣkala* [mantra],
performs the rites beginning with installation up to the consecration with nectar (*amṛtīkaraṇa*), exactly as before.
Having performed [the rites] as described and having meditated upon her with the Gāyatrī of that [deity] and the [mantras] for the heart and other limbs,
one should worship Śivā with the offerings of water for the hands (arghya) and so forth, according to the previous procedure.
For the sake of enjoyment, one should place the limbs (aṅgas) upon the limbs [of the deity], the weapon (astra) in the corners, and in the four directions;
furthermore, on the edge of the pedestal outside the lotus, one should place the weapons beginning with the conch (śaṅkha) in due order.

Having first joined the eight-syllable mantra ending with the *bindu*, one should perform worship up to the offering of food (*naivedya*); thereafter, in the cardinal directions, one should worship with the mantras of the deities who are the lords of the worlds.
Having offered on the second day sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, cooked rice, sesame seeds, parched grain, rice grains, white mustard, and milk-rice, each separately; || 54 ||
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the root mantra and a tenth part with the limb-mantras, on the third day he should offer clarified butter with the five Durgā mantras.
In the fourth [quarter], one should worship Nirmālyadhāriṇī in the northeast; likewise, one should place the world-protectors, the lion, and the Mothers in their respective directions.
Having worshipped the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha) and the deities situated there,
one should bathe [the image] with one hundred and eight [verses], as before.
One should perform the consecration with those various Vedic mantras prescribed for the Śiva-bath, with the Gāyatrī, with the five Durgā-mantras, and with the Madhyama-mantra.

Having offered the bali-oblation to the spirits at night and having bestowed sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), one should also resolve upon the necessary resources for the accomplishment of the daily worship and other rites.
The agent, however, obtains the fruit previously mentioned both in this world and in the next;
[this applies] to those [mantras] dedicated to Durgā beginning with the *triṣṭubh* meter, or to those such as Vanadurgā.
If they establish [the image] in this manner according to the respective prescriptions and worship it, having accomplished the Durgā-mantras as described in the previous manual; || 61 ||
p.
543) They attain, without effort, those various accomplishments (siddhi) proclaimed in their respective kalpas.
[End of] the Section on the Installation of Durgā.
In the perpetual festival of Durgā, however, there are female door-keepers at the eastern and other gates.
Jayā, Vijayā, Raudrī, Bhīṣaṇī, Śūlinī, Prabhā, Aparājitā, and Jayantī— these maidens carry canes and swords.
Having cast the bali-offering to those guardians of the world (lokapālas) each in their respective domain, one should likewise offer it to Durgā’s attendants, applying this everywhere as appropriate.
In the pavilion for Siṃha, one should offer the bali with the mantra: "To you, the Great Lion, whose weapons are diamond claws and fangs, HŪṂ SVĀHĀ, NAMAS. || 65 ||
One should likewise cast an offering to Vighneśa, the Vīramātṛs, Śāstṛ, Skanda, and Indu in their respective directions, and cast the bali offering to Siṃhikā.
Siṃhikā is the bearer of the floral remains (nirmālya);
furthermore, Hrādinī and Mādinī are at the gate and inside the gateway (gopura), respectively.
And to Kātyāyanī and Caṇḍā at the outer gate of the city;
then, standing before the pedestal, one should utter this mantra: || 68 ||
Oṃ!
To all those attendants of Durgā who move about pervading the entire world, desiring the sacrificial offering— may they accept this presented bali.
Then, in the directions of the second necklace, there are eight goddesses beginning with Kālikā: Kālī, Karālī, Virajā, Mandarā, and Vindhyavāsinī.
Suprabhā and Siṃhavaktrā, the eighth, who crushes the Daityas; having scattered an offering to them, one should then deposit it upon the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha).
Brahmaghoṣā, Sughoṣā, and the maiden Varavarṇinī; Āryā, Hemavarṇā, and Kṛttikā, the bestower of fearlessness. (72)

The eight [goddesses] beginning with Prāgā are situated in the directions, while Brāhmī resides upon the kumuda; Durgāsenā is in the center of the seat, and one should offer an oblation (bali) to her.
This procedure for the daily festival shall be the same as that for the great festival; however, the specific detail is that a lion should be depicted on the banner and worshipped with mantras.
Likewise, on the third enclosure, eight maidens are stationed in each direction; they are led by a thousand commanders. (75)
Saumyā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Nandā, Kundā, Kumudā, Dyuti, and Vidyunmālā are in the east; then in the southeast is Mahābalā. (76)
Balā, Subalā, Vālā, Abalā, Bhīṣaṇā, Rati, Kaluṣā, Ghoṣaṇī, Nandanī, and Smṛti are located in the southern direction. || 77 ||
Yuddhapriyā, Devasiddhapūjitā, Vikṛti, Kṛti—these seven, and the eighth on this [day], Mahāsuravimardanī. (78)
Then there are Vikarālī, Pālinī, Śūlakātyāyanī, Mahāyogeśvarī, Gaurī, Caṇḍā, Caṇḍī, and Khaḍginī. || 79 ||
Then, in the south-west and the west, there are Hrādinī, Kṣemakārikā, Āryā, Bhadrā, Bhadrakālī, Vāruṇī, and Amṛtāmbikā. (80)
Then Kṣemyā, Vedagarbhā, Anantā, Sarvaniṣkalā, Śānti, Bhairavī, Prāṇā, and Cetanā reside in the sphere of Vāyu. (81)
Ṛddhi, Lakṣmī, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Kīrti, Ghaṇeśvarī,
Adbhutā, and Madā— these eight are the presiding goddesses in the northern direction.
Śruti, Smṛti, as well as Nīti, Bhīmā, and Brahmacāriṇī; Nīlāmbarā, Śūlinī, and Sarasvatī shall be the eighth. (83)
Standing in the northeast quarter, one should scatter the bali offering for all of these; outside of them, in the various directions, one should offer bali to the Gaṇas as before.

With the previously mentioned mantras in their proper order, beginning with "Those hosts in the eastern direction who have thunderbolts in their hands and possess great strength," one should scatter the bali offering.
Whatever ritual action has been prescribed for the festival of Śiva should be performed here as well; however, there may be some difference here regarding the mantras and the deities. (86)

Having made the formal resolve (saṅkalpa) as before, one should perform the ritual bath at a sacred ford (tīrthasnāna); specifically in the month of Caitra under the asterism Citrā, and in Vaiśākha under the asterism Viśākhā.
In the month of Āṣāḍha under the asterism Pūrvaphalgunī, in Śrāvaṇa under Kṛttikā, on the Mahānavamī in autumn, and on the full moon day of Kārttika; || 88 ||

In the month of Puṣya, during the asterism of Puṣya, and also in the month of Phālguna, during the asterism of Uttarā-phālgunī, a festival should then be performed by men for the satisfaction of Durgā. (89)
For virtuous people who have thus installed Durgā and worship her with devotion, all desired fruits—both seen and unseen—shall become easily attainable. (90)

Thus, this Daurga Tantra, which was spoken by the God for the sake of purification, is remembered in brief; indeed, all the rites beginning with consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) and ending with the festival (*utsava*), have been declared here in accordance with the Śaiva tradition. (91)
Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, on the Durgā Tantra, in the section on ritual practice (kriyāpāda) of the Upper Part of the *Siddhāntasāra*, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva.
Now begins the fifty-sixth chapter.
Now, the installation (pratiṣṭhā) and other rites for Gaurī are correctly described in brief.
Her root-bīja, previously designated as Śakti, has already been shown.
The syllable *tāra* (oṃ), the seed-syllable of Śakti (hrīṃ), the end of *kha* (ha) joined with the vowel *au*, followed by the subtle fire (*sa*), then the word *rudra* and the word *dayite*. || 2 ||

The wind (ya) joined with the end of twelve (au), and the end of space (ha) together with the eleventh vowel (ī)—this is the eleventh syllable. The fire (ra) situated in the letter va, joined with the first of the eighth [group] (u) and with the subtle (i). || 3 ||
This seventeen-syllable mantra ends with "huṃ phaṭ" and the word "agnipriyā";
its syllables are assigned [powers] by the numbers two, seven, five, four, two, and two, according to their respective classes.

The first [syllable] consists of the letter *ṣa* with a long vowel and the sound *nāda*; the six limbs [are formed] from the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*). Then, the third letter of the eighth [group], conjoined with the fifth vowel. (5)
The fourth letter from the sixth group [ṇa], the two syllables "gāyai," the words "vidmahe" and "kāma," and "mālinyai" and "dhīmahi. (6)
At the end of that [word], Gaurī should be placed, and at the very end, one should utter the word "prakāraḥ. This is indeed the Gaurīgāyatrī; its application is in worship and other such rites.
The image of Gaurī should be ten tālas in height; she has four arms, bestows boons, and holds a noose, a goad, and displays the gesture of fearlessness.
She has full and lofty breasts, is radiant with a dark blue braided hair and crown, possesses three eyes, has a smiling face,
and is adorned with jeweled earrings.
Her necklaces and strings of pearls shimmered upon her neck, while her waist was bound with a girdle;
golden armlets gleamed, and her fingers were encircled by rings set with radiant jewels. (10)
Resplendent in garments of silken cloth shimmering with a golden girdle,
her lotus-feet were adorned with anklets that gleamed with the rays of jeweled nails.
The image of Gaurī shall be of such a form as Manonmanī, the abode of all qualities of loveliness, beauty, and tenderness.

Constructed from stone, metal, and other materials, according to the prescribed measurements for women in their respective order, one should install Śivā within the aforementioned temple according to the path taught by Śiva.
Whatever specific detail differs from what was previously stated, I shall now describe each of those here:
the consecration pavilion (adhivāsana-maṇḍapa) should be provided with sixteen pillars.
The four inner pillars are Dharma and the others, and the suns are on the outside;
likewise Bhadra, Vijaya, Vijṛmbha, and Lohita. (15)
The deities beginning with Jayā are to be known as being located at the eastern gateway and the pitchers at the doors; Jayā, Vijayā, Ajitā, and Aparājitā are situated in the east.
Nityā, Vilāsinī, Śauṇḍī, and Aghorā are in the directions starting from the south; likewise Kundā, Kumudā, Vidyunmālā, and Vibhūṣaṇā. (17)
One should worship Kaluṣā, Ghoṣaṇī, Karālī, and Vikṛtā— the two messenger-deities (dūtīs) for each of the two upper banners— in due order when [the sun] has entered the pitcher (kumbha).

Following the scattering of grains during the *puṇyāha* rite, one should worship as before the *kumbha-astra* (the jar-weapon); Gaurī mounted upon a bull in the jar, and the Weapon [deity] situated on a lion in the *vardhanī*.

She has the form of a woman with four arms, holding a trident, an axe, and displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; she has full, elevated breasts, is dark-complexioned, adorned, and possesses three eyes. (20)
Wearing a tightly bound loincloth, he was fierce and the terrifier of all asuras; with tawny hair standing erect, adorned with various serpents, he was both gentle and terrifying.
After thus wandering for the sake of her worship in the form of Umā,
she divided the Śaiva fire situated in the central pit into nine parts.

Having cast [the materials] into the nine pits as before, the preceptor and the image-keepers, having invoked Gaurī into his heart-lotus, should perform the oblation with the root mantra and the limb-mantras.

Having performed the purification of the form and the opening of the eyes as before, one should likewise carry out the ritual immersion in water, the wandering through the village, and the ceremonial bathing. (24)
Then, in the pavilion, upon the altar, on a bed spread with fivefold coverings,
having laid the Goddess— who is composed of the five elements— he should worship her.
Then, one should place the jar and weapon [deities] covered with red and yellow garments;
one should install the jar of Gaurī in the position of the head, and the jar of Nidrā as well.
On all sides, within the image-pots, one should place Brahmā and the other four [deities] together with Vāmā and the rest,
as well as Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, and Sarasvatī.
One should install the power of action (kriyā-śakti) upon the pedestal and the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) upon the image;
furthermore, one should install the principles (tattvas) and the lords of the principles (tattveśvaras) in their proper sequence across the three divisions.

Having offered oblations separately and in sequence to the forms beginning with Earth and to their presiding deities beginning with Dhārikā as previously described, the preceptor and the guardians of the forms should touch them.
Then, at the auspicious moment in the morning, one should place the tortoise-stone as before,
along with the five groups beginning with gems, and then the pedestal according to its own root-mantra.

One should place the image upon a pedestal; then, having projected its conscious essence from the heart-lotus and the seed-syllable of its power from the water-pot, one should perform the ritual bathing.

By means of Rudra, the Pavamāna hymns, and also with [the mantra] beginning with "Gaurī," and then by the Mūla-mantra, the Aṅga-mantras, and the Gāyatrī, the path of Mantra (mantrādhvan) is constituted through its constituent parts.
The path of the feet (padādhvan) should be as before, and the remaining paths likewise;
then, [one should worship] her who has been consecrated by the jar-form known as Pradhānanidrā.
One should worship the Supreme Goddess with the *arghya* and other offerings as before.
It is as follows:
having bathed, washed one's feet, sipped water (*ācamana*), and performed the ritual of self-protection (*sakalīkṛta*).
Having worshipped Vighna and the Guru, the Guru, holding the general arghya vessel, [proceeds] while Jayā and Vijayā stand at the door, staff in hand upon the ground.
The Gaṅgā and Yamunā are above, and Dvāraśrī is over the central gate; having worshipped them, discharged his iron arrows, entered, and deposited his weapons, [he stood there]. (36)
Having worshipped the site, the Brahmā-seat, and so forth, and having performed the five purifications,
one who has offered the *arghya* water completed with the root and limb mantras, and who bears a forehead mark (*tilaka*) and a flower crest (*puṣpaśekhara*), [should proceed]. || 37 ||

One should meditate upon the Tortoise below, the supporting Śakti, and that Śakti-seat (śaktyāsana) upon the pedestal; then, having visualized the golden lion-throne (siṃhāsana), one should likewise visualize its legs as Dharma and the other virtues.
The lotus with its stalk and bulb arises from *sattva* and so forth, while the syllables *sū*, *r*, *i*, *m*, *b*, *o*, and *k* and so forth are placed upon the petals;
thereafter, the Śaktis beginning with Vāmā are situated at the tips of the filaments.
Manonmanī herself is directly Gaurī-Śivā in the center; one should [visualize] her form, whose body is mantra, as the power of consciousness (cicchakti) from the lotus of one's own heart. (40)

One should place [the deity] residing at the end of the twelve [fingers] into the heart-lotus as before; likewise, one should perform the installation (sthāpana), the presence (sānnidhya), the confinement (sannirodha), and the invitation (prarocana).

One should perform the rite of immortalization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) and the veiling (*avakuṇṭhana*) with the *hṛdaya* and other [limbs]. Then, one should place the Brahma-mantras and the [mantras] beginning with Īśāna upon the mouth, heart, teeth, and feet respectively.
One should place the five Śaktis— Hṛllekhā, Gaganā, Raktā,
Karālikā, and Mahocchuṣmā— within the letters beginning with 'ka'.
Then one should place Brahmā and the other four at the feet and so forth, Sarasvatī in the heart, and Gāyatrī as well as Sāvitrī upon the breasts. (44)
One should duly worship Śivā with the offerings beginning with *arghya* in due order;
having worshipped the enclosure of the limbs (*aṅgāvṛti*) upon the petals, one should worship the eight female messengers (*dūtī*) on the outside.
Anaṅgarūpā, Anaṅgamadanā, Madanāturā, likewise Pavanavegā, and then Bhuvanapālikā. (46)

She may be entirely cool, the embodiment of the pain of love, and the girdle of the bodiless god; having worshipped her with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should also worship the door-keepers, Jayā and the others.
One should worship Indra and the other world-protectors in the front pavilion, Vṛṣabha, Vīra, Vighna, the Mothers, Śāstṛ, Skanda, and Niśākara.

One should place the goddess named Subhagā, who holds the remains of offerings (nirmālya), in the northeast; and having established her upon the altar of oblations (balipīṭha), one performs the fire-offering (juhoti) to the guardians of the quarters.

Then, on the second day, one should perform [the oblation] with the root-mantra and its ancillaries, with the Gāyatrī, and with the eight substances beginning with fuel-sticks (samidh)— one hundred times with the root-mantra and a tenth part for the ancillaries. || 50 ||

And on the third day, with the Gāyatrī mantra repeated a hundred times, and also with the hymn beginning "Gaurī mimāya," one should perform the rite with sesame and clarified butter using the Aghora-weapon and the Śiva-weapon mantras.
Having offered oblations with the Pāśupata weapon and performed expiatory rites such as the Jaya-homa and others, on the fourth day,
having worshipped the goddess Nirmālyadhāriṇī as previously described, [one should proceed].
Having withdrawn the fires into himself, he should bathe with hundreds of jars;
and having given sacrificial fees at night, he should offer the bali-oblation to the spirits.
One should scatter flowers for the sake of daily worship and also provide the necessary offerings; the performer attains all the fruit described for the installation of Śiva.
The invocation [mudrā], the installation, the harsh, the agitating, as well as the deluding, the liquefying, the attracting, and the bringing into proximity. (55)
The *vandanī* and the *mahāmudrā*, along with the *gaurīmudrā*, are remembered as the ten; the *añjali* is the full-blossomed [mudrā], which is turned upward to the limit of the twelve.

The mudrā brought from the heart of the formless one is known as the Āvāhanī (invocation); that same mudrā, when turned downwards and performed without flowers, is known as the Sthāpanī (establishment).
The *niṣṭhurā* [mudrā] is formed from two hands with fists clenched and the thumbs raised;
the two hands are joined facing each other with the index fingers extended.

From the joining of the middle fingers and the thumbs, it becomes the *kṣobhaṇī* (agitating) and *prarocanī* (enticing) [mudrās]. With the palms joined and the thumbs and index fingers extended, [it is the *prasāraṇī*]. (59)
The *mohanī* [mudrā] is traditionally taught as the joining together of the little, ring, and middle fingers;
one should perform the *amṛtīkaraṇa* (the rite of making nectar) for the Goddess by means of the *mohinī*.
In the same way, having extended the two index fingers of the joined hands,
[the mudrā] formed by the union of the middle fingers and the thumbs bestows the bliss of melting.
That same [mudrā], when the well-joined hands have the tips of the curved index fingers joined, becomes the *karṣaṇī*;
with it, one should contemplate the Goddess as being gracious.
That same [mudrā], when the middle and index fingers press down upon the two thumbs, is the Sannidhānakarī mudrā; by means of it, one should effect the presence [of the deity].
With the two hands joined in the hollow of the palms like lotus buds, this is the mudrā called Vandanī;
it should be employed for acts such as salutation.
Having bound the two ring fingers below the two index fingers of both hands, with the palms facing upward, the middle and little fingers [are joined]. 65.
With the two sides joined at the tips, they should be held straight and extended;
then one should touch the two tips of the thumbs to the roots of the little fingers.
This tenth Mahāmudrā of Gaurī bestows all accomplishments. This concludes the section on the consecration of Gaurī.
In the perpetual festival of Gaurī, the Goddess should be fashioned from gold or other materials. (67)

Having invoked the Gaurī-weapon-mantra situated within the Amātrā and having worshipped it, one should carry it forward; [then worship] the gatekeepers beginning with Jayā, the world-protectors (lokeśas), and Vṛṣa.
One should offer the bali-oblation to all the attendants of Gaurī,
as well as to the Vīras, Vighneśa, the Mothers, Śāstṛ, Skanda, and the Moon.
Having offered a bali-oblation to Subhagā at the two sides of the gateway, and having also offered one to Triśūlinī and Khaḍginī,
he should depart from the gateway.
Standing at the edge of the seat, he should address the Gaṇas with this mantra:
"Those who, pervading the entire world, move about desiring offerings. (71)
"May all the attendants of Gaurī accept this offered bali-offering. Then, for the second circuit, there should be eight leaders of the Gaṇas.
Karālī, Vikarālī, Ugrā, Vāṇī, Śacī, Mohanī,
Māyā, and Mahālakṣmī as the eighth.
Then one should offer oblations to these [goddesses] situated in the eight directions of the offering-altar: Ṛddhi, Smṛti, Dhṛti, Śraddhā, Medhā, Kānti, Mati, and Śruti.
The noble Kumudakā is on the seat, and Gaurīsenā is in the center;
one should respectfully scatter an offering for them with their respective names, ending each with "namaḥ. (75)
This procedure for the daily festival (nityotsava) shall be identical to that of the great festival (mahotsava).
The bull known as Gaurī’s vehicle is to be worshipped and shall serve as the banner (dhvaja). (76)
The invocation of Gaṇeśa and the other deities is prescribed as before for the festival of Gaurī;

however, there is this distinction: having scattered the bali offering in each direction within the maṇḍala for those spirits who are ever-present, one should [scatter it] outside of that in each direction for Gaurī and the other goddesses.
One should scatter an offering to the twelve thousand leaders of the assembly;
they are ninety-six in number,
as follows:
Vidyā, Prajñā, Sinīvālī, Kuhū, Hrī, and Puṣṭi. || 77 ||
Rudravīryā, Prabhā, Nandā, Poṣaṇī, Śubhadā, and Kṣamā—these are in the east; then in the southeast are Kālarātrī and Kapardinī. (78)
Bhadrakālī, Vikṛti, Daṇḍinī, Kapālinī, Musuṇṭhinī, Indukhaṇḍā, and then Nisumbhamathinī.
Śikhaṇḍinī, Indrāṇī, and Rudrāṇī are likewise established; as are Nārī, Nārāyaṇī, Bhadrā, and she who forms half the body of Śaṅkara.
Viśālākṣī and Samṛddhi are on the right. || 81 ||
She is intellect, growth, the sacrificial offering (svadhā), the exclamation (svāhā), she who is known as illusion (māyā),
the supporter of wealth, the sustainer of the three worlds, the earth, the great one, and the sovereign of the thirty gods.
And Aruṇā—these twelve Nāyikās are situated in the southwest; as well as Surucā, Bahurūpā, Skandasenā, and Vāruṇī. (83)
Amalā, Vimalā, Khyāti, Prakṛti, Vikṛti, Sthiti, Sṛṣṭi, and Sandhyā—these twelve Nāyikās reside in the western quarter. (84)
She is Saṃhṛti, Jaganmātā, Satī, and Haṃsinī; she is Devamātā, Vajriṇī, Mardanī, and Bhagavatī as well. || 85 ||
Padmāsanā, Devakī, Trimukhī, and Caturmukhī— the principal attendants of Gaurī— these twelve are stationed in the northwest.
She has seven faces and eight mouths, she is the crusher of gods and asuras;
she has hanging lips and long hair, and her hair stands erect while her belly is large.
Rekhā, Śaśarekhā, Viśvarūpā, Kṛśodarī, and Dhanadā—these twelve heroines are situated in the north (Kubera’s direction). Surarakṣaṇikā [is also among them]. 88.
The noble Vāgīśī, [the goddess] of vows, Vajravegā, Vāyuvegā, and Maheśvarī. || 89 ||
Aiśānī, Jvalinī, and Śāṅkarī are the names of these leaders;
these twelve attendants of Gaurī are stationed in the northeast.
These [goddesses], each surrounded by thousands of assemblies,
are the causes for the destruction, creation, maintenance, and grace of the world.
The preceptor, moreover, should devotedly offer an oblation to all of these with white rice, boiled grains, and milk-rice (pāyasa), saturated with ghee and honey.
Then, one should perform the ritual bath at the sacred ford (tīrtha) according to the path taught by Śiva,
and worship with particular care using the root mantras and the Vedic ancillary mantras.
And one should bathe [the deity] with thousands of jars and so forth, according to the prescribed procedure. Śivagaurī and Ekagaurī are recorded as being of two types:
Sthiragaurī and Dvidhā.
She who is established as the wife of Śiva himself, residing near his fixed liṅga,
is indeed known as Śivagaurī.
If that Gaurī were established as Ekagaurī by the gods, the sages, or even by humans, without a fixed liṅga; || 96 ||
A great festival for Śiva and Gaurī separately is not recommended; however, during a festival of Śiva, her procession together with Maheśa is praised. (97)

The worship of Śiva and Gaurī should be performed according to the prescribed rules, concluding with a perpetual festival; however, for Gaurī alone, a great festival should be conducted independently and separately.
Having thus installed Gaurī with devotion according to their means, those who perform the daily worship according to the rules, concluding with a festival, [attain the highest state]. 99.
It is not possible to describe their merit even in hundreds of ages,
for whatever is most cherished in the world, whether its fruit be seen or unseen, is of great value.
Those who act with devotion obtain all of that without effort.
Thus has this Tantra, which is both charming and like a beautiful reflection, been succinctly proclaimed here by Gaurī.

And having observed the Bhānutantra, all the various ritual procedures here— such as the rites of installation (pratiṣṭhā) and so forth— are to be inferred in accordance with the Śaiva teachings already mentioned.
Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, the Gaurītantra, in the Kriyāpāda of the Uparibhāga of the Siddhāntasāra, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva.
Now begins the fifty-seventh chapter.
Next, the installation of Sarasvatī as enjoined by the Tantra is described. [The mantra consists of] Tāra (Oṃ), Nāda, and Bindu; preceded by that [Tāra], it is conjoined with the final vowel.
The word *vada* is repeated [as *vadavada*], followed by the word *vāgvādinī*; this [phrase] ends with *marutsakhapriyā*. Indeed, in the *jagatī* meter, the *vāṅmanu* consists of six syllables. (2)
For the twice-born, [the mantra] beginning with *tārā* (om) is prescribed; for others, it is remembered as being without [such a prefix].
However, for those who maintain the sacred fire (*sāgni*), it is the sound *nāda* preceded by *tārā*, joined respectively with the long vowels.
And with the words "Ṛgveda" and so forth, the term "Dharmaśāstra," and the term "Purāṇa," combined respectively with six mantra-words in sequence. (4)

One should arrange the limbs ending with the weapon-mantra, each joined with its own seed-syllable; and [the mantra] "Vāgīśvarī" followed by the dative case-ending, conjoined with the word "vidmahe. (5)
At the end of the word *vāgvādinī*, the word *dhīmahi* should follow; then *tannaḥ sarasvatī* and *pracodayāt* are joined [to complete the verse]. (6)
Tārā and the others [are fashioned] from Sarasvatī; Gāyatrī bestows all accomplishments. She is described as having a middle measurement of ten tālas, being made according to the female proportion.
There should be an image of Sarasvatī, white in color and four-armed,
holding a book and a pen in her left hands, and also bearing a water-pot.
Likewise, she holds a book in her right hand, positioned both below and above;
she is as white as a conch, a kunda flower, or the moon, and she is adorned with matted hair and a crescent moon as her crest-ornament.
She has three eyes, wears white garments, and is adorned with garlands and perfumes; her high, full, and swelling breasts are radiant with a captivating necklace. (10)
Her lotus-face is exceedingly serene, she is adorned with all ornaments, seated upon a lotus throne, and graced with fresh youth. (11)
In the consecration of Vāgīśvarī, the ritual should follow the path declared by Śiva; the specific detail is that she should be installed at the southern gate, facing southward.
She should be worshipped facing north in the consecration pavilion; [the four guardians are] Puṣkara, Pūrṇabhadra, Ānanda, and likewise Nandana.
Likewise, there are two banners on each of the arches starting from the east in due order:
on the eastern [arch] is that of Indra, marked with a thunderbolt, and on the southern, that of Yama, marked with a staff.
Then there is the one belonging to Varuṇa, marked with a noose, and the one belonging to Kubera, marked with a mace; [these are] Medhā, Prajñā, Prabhā, Vidyā, Dhī, Dhṛti, Smṛti, and Buddhi. || 15 ||
The female messengers (dūtīs) stationed at the door-pitchers are to be worshipped by their respective names;
likewise, the four [deities] beginning with Ṛgveda and the others are to be worshipped on the central pillars in the directions starting from the southeast (āgneya).
Outside the Veda are the pillars of the Sun: phonetics, ritual, etymology, prosody, astronomy, the recitation of the Sūtras, Mīmāṃsā, and the extensive Nyāya. || 17 ||
The Dharmaśāstra, the Purāṇa, and the Daṇḍanīti are, in due order, the canopy consisting of knowledge; the ground itself, however, is the earth. (18)
In all cases, one should worship with names beginning with "Tārā" and ending with "namaḥ," using their well-proclaimed appellations.

Then, following the scattering of the auspicious day (puṇyāha) grains, there is the worship of the jar and the weapon-mantra. Within the jar resides Vāṇī seated upon a swan; that weapon-mantra rests upon a crane.
Clad in red garments, red in color, with six arms and three eyes, she has a feminine form and is adorned; in her left hands she holds the gesture of granting boons, a book, and a noose.

In the south, she holds the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), a pen (*lekhanī*), and a goad (*aṅkuśa*). As before, in the nine sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*s), the fire is divided into the central and other sections. || 21 ||
Having deposited [the fire] and invoked Vāgīśī, the Guru should perform the oblation in the central [fire] with the root mantra and the limb-mantras;
meanwhile, the bearers of the forms should offer oblations in the various directions with the mantras of the Yogamūrti and the other forms.
p.

555) Also with the Gāyatrī and with the mantras of the Lords of the World (lokeśa), in due order [he should offer] sacrificial fuel-sticks, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge, parched grain, rice, white mustard seeds, and black mustard seeds. || 23 ||
They should each separately offer one hundred and eight oblations of sesame seeds;
as before, they should perform the purification of the form and the opening of the eyes.

One should perform the ritual immersion in water, the procession through the village, and likewise the ceremonial bathing; then, one should worship the forms of Sarasvatī within the eight jars of knowledge.
Yogā, Satyā, Vimalā, Jñānā, Buddhi, Kriyā, as well as Medhā and Śraddhā—all of them held water-pots and books. || 26 ||

Those who hold rosaries and pens, who are white and dressed in white garments and so forth, [should be placed] then in three parts of the image (bera), extending from the knees to the neck and up to the head.
One should sequentially assign the Lords of the Principles, beginning with Ātman, such as Brahmā and the others;
and upon them, the eight forms beginning with Earth, along with their powers (śaktis) beginning with Dhārikā.
The wise one should place the Śakti called Kriyā upon the pedestal of the Goddess’s body; and having offered oblations repeatedly with her mantras, they should touch it as before.

Then, having performed his morning bath along with the image-bearers and having completed the ritual of the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), the Guru should install the [deity] named Kūrma in the auspicious moment at the Liṅga.
One should place the five groups beginning with jewels and the pedestal upon it as before; and upon the pedestal, one should install the image and make it very firm by means of the binding rite.
Having washed [the image] and offered some oblation, one should install the Vidyā-form (vidyātanu).

One should install the Speech-form (vāṇīmūrti) residing in the pitcher from the root-mantra into the lotus of the heart. Then, one should install the root-mantra, the limbs (aṅgas), the Gāyatrī, and the syllables mentioned in the Mātṛkā.
The syllables have been stated, meaning the Name, Power, Vāgbhava, and Ānī; the path of mantras is by means of the words alone, and the path of words is as before.
Then, having filled his cupped hands with flowers, he himself meditated from Kuṇḍalinī onwards upon the subtle [Paśyantī], the Madhyamā, and also the Vaikharī speech.
Having raised that speech, which resembles a streak of lightning,
upwards and having joined it at the *dvādaśānta*, one should augment it with consciousness.

Having caused [the deity] to transfer well into the handful of flowers while uttering the syllable *haṃ* with a *pluta* (protracted) accent, one should bring her through the *brahmanāḍī* and place her within the lotus of the heart of the [divine] form.

Having performed the rites of installation (sthāpana), complete cessation (sannirodha), pleasing (rocana), veiling (avakuṇṭhana), and the transformation into nectar (amṛtīkaraṇa) with the limbs [of the mantra], and having offered the respectful oblation (arghya); || 37 ||

Having performed the meditation on the six paths (ṣaḍadhvabhāvanā) and having consecrated [the deity] with the eight jars of knowledge (vidyākumbha), as well as with the sleep-mantra and the weapon-mantra, one should worship him in due order with the arghya-offering and other rites.
As follows: having bathed, worshipped Gaṇeśa, and performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa upon his body, he should worship the two door-keepers, Vighna and Kṣetrapati, with the general arghya offering.
Having cast the Gaṅgā and Yamunā as before, and likewise Dvāralakṣmī above, and having cast the Astra-mantra, he enters within and places it upon the threshold.

Having worshipped the Vāstu deity, Brahmā, the seat, and so forth, and being well-seated, he should offer the arghya water; then, having performed the five purifications, he, adorned with a tilaka mark and a flower crown, [proceeds].
One should visualize the Earth as the foundational power (ādhāraśakti) in the form of a lion-throne,
with its legs— the Kṛta, Tretā, and other ages— shaped like lions and extending toward the intermediate directions.
Rajas, tamas, and sattva are the bulb, the stalk, and the lotus;
and the presiding deities of the spheres beginning with the sun—Brahmā and the others—are located in the coverings and so forth. (43)
One should worship Meru in its pericarp, the mountains on the twelve petals, one in each of the cardinal directions, and those called filaments in the intermediate corners.
On the eastern petal is Mount Mandara, on the southern Gandhamādana, Vipula on the western petal,
and Supārśva on the northern leaf.
One should worship Himavat, Hemakūṭa, Niṣadha, Mālyavat, as well as Kailāsa, Nīla, Śveta, and Śṛṅgin. || 46 ||

Having invoked the Goddess, whose body is speech and whose form is knowledge, according to the previously mentioned path, and having performed the rites of installation and so forth with the root mantra and its limbs; || 47 ||

One should worship in sequence with the ritual services beginning with the *arghya* and ending with the *nivedya*; having worshipped the limbs (*aṅga*) upon the filaments, one should then worship the twelve powers (*śakti*).
One should worship Ṛddhi, Rati, Prīti, and Śānti, situated on the petals of the directions; and likewise, one should worship two pairs of Yogās, beginning with Satya, in each pair of corner-petals.
The two, the Moon and the Sun, shine above, one to the south and one to the north; Brahmā is to the right of the Goddess, Viṣṇu to her left, and Śiva is in front.
In the western [quarter], one should worship these sages depicted on the walls;
two each, beginning with Medhā and Prajñā, are stationed at the four doors as door-keepers.
He should place the world-protectors in their respective directions, Haṃsa in the pavilion of the face, Vīra, Vighna, the Mothers, Śāstṛ, and Caṇḍikā as well.
One should install Soma and Kṣetrapāla in their respective directions; having established the altar for offerings (balipīṭha), one should worship them on the first day.

On the second day, [he should worship] with his own root-mantras and the mantras of the limbs, as well as those of the deities of the forms and the world-protectors; on the third day, with the *vyāhṛtis*, the *gāyatrī*, and the *jaya* mantras and others.
Then, having performed oblations with expiatory rites on the fourth day, one should bathe her as before and worship Mati, who wears the remains of the previous offerings.

Having offered the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and the sviṣṭakṛt oblation as well, one should unite the fires within the lotus of one's own heart, or at the dvādaśānta; then one should bathe [the deity] with more than a hundred [mantras].
Then, having worshipped with special offerings and given the fees for the preceptor and others, one should offer the bali-oblation to the spirits at night and perform the daily worship.
As previously stated, the performer enjoys the fruit according to his wealth. This concludes the section on the installation of Sarasvatī.
In the perpetual festival of Sarasvatī, Medhā and the others are the female door-keepers.
Having scattered the bali offering to those world-protectors as before, there is this distinction here:
"Homage to Sarasvatī’s attendants; homage to her attendants."
One should offer oblations using the names of the respective world-protectors;
[one should offer] to the swan, the vehicle of Sarasvatī, in the front pavilion.
One should offer the bali-oblation to Vighna, Vīrabhadra, the Mothers, and Śāstṛ; as well as to Caṇḍika, Indu, Kṣetrapa, and Mātṛ.

For the sake of ritual action and for inspired intuition, one should deposit [the offerings] at the gate of the city-gate (gopura). Then, having reached the front of the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha), one should invite the Gaṇas. (61)
May the attendants of Sarasvatī, who move about pervading the entire world in their desire for offerings, accept this presented oblation.
Thus [it is said].
Then, in the eight directions of the second enclosure, one should likewise offer oblations to the elephants of the quarters (diggajas) who reside there, using their respective names. 63.
Airāvata, Puṇḍarīka, Kumuda, Añjana, Vāmana, Puṣpadanta, Sārvabhauma, and Supratīka as the eighth. || 64 ||
Then, on the bali-altar, one should offer the bali-oblation to the ten Viśvedevas:
Kratu, Daśa, Suvastavya, Kāma, and Dhvani. (65)
While performing [the rite], those situated in the eight directions of the pedestal are indeed accompanied by the Kumudas; one should offer the bali-oblation to them in the center.
"Salutation to Rocamāna of Sarasvatīsenā"—with this, one should place [the deity] Rocamāna in the center above the pedestal (*pīṭha*).
[This is for] the daily festival, the offering (*bali*), etc. || 67 ||
The bhūtas are the attendants at the front. || 68 ||
One should offer the bali-oblation with [mantras] beginning with "To the Blessed Sarasvatī," and likewise on the third garland,
to the Gaṇas stationed in the eight directions.
Namely: the Vasus, the two Aśvins, the Rudras, the Pitṛs, and the hosts of Ādityas; then Tārkṣya, the Seven Sages and others, and the Lords of Creatures (Prajāpatis). || 70 ||
And they are—Dhara, Dhruva, Soma, Āpa, Anila, Anala, Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa; these are the eight Vasus who go before. (71)
The two Aśvins, Nāsatya and Dasra, are established in the south-eastern quarter;
then follow Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Virūpākṣa, and Raivata.
Pinākin, Īśvara, Sthāṇu, Kapālin, Tryambaka, Bahurūpa, and Bhava— these are the eleven Rudras in their respective order. (73)
These are situated on the right:
Soma accompanied by the Pitṛs, likewise Yama, the lord of the host of Pitṛs, Agni accompanied by Aṅgiras, and the seventh, Kavyavāhana. (74)
The Pitṛs, those called Pitāmahas, and likewise the Prapitāmahas—these ten are known as the Pitṛs who abide in the domain of Nirṛti. (75)
Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Mitra, Varuṇa, and Bhaga; Indra, Vivasvat, Pūṣan, and Parjanya is remembered as the tenth. || 76 ||
Tvaṣṭṛ and Viṣṇu—these are the twelve Ādityas in the water;
as well as Tārkṣya, Ariṣṭanemi, Garuḍa, and Aruṇa.
Aruṇi, Krathana, Krātha, Suparṇa, Gautama, Bharadvāja, Viśvāmitra, and Kaśyapa are the seven Maruts. || 78 ||
Jamadagni, as well as Atri, Vasiṣṭha, and Arundhatī, along with Dhruva and Śiṃśumāra—these are situated in the north. || 79 ||
Bhṛgu, Dakṣa, Marīci, Aṅgiras, Pulaha, Kratu, Pulastya, Atri, and Vasiṣṭha—these stand as the lords of progeny. || 80 ||
This refers to the [deity] Aiśa.
Then, on the fourth garland are the Gandharvas and the hosts of Apsarases, as well as the Siddhas, Sādhyas, Nāgas, and the hosts of Vidyādharas. (81)

The Yakṣas, along with the Rākṣasas and Daityas, are stationed respectively in the eight directions; one should offer the bali-oblation to them using their names beginning with "Tārā" and ending with "namaḥ."

Then, with mantras beginning with "In the eastern direction, the hosts with thunderbolts in their hands, possessed of great strength," one should scatter the offering (bali) in all ten directions as well.
At the end of the designated day, having dismissed the attendants as before, he should then perform a pilgrimage to a sacred ford and worship Gīr with special rites.
Then, having brought down the banner and bathed it with a thousand jars and other vessels according to the prescribed rites, he worshipped it.
Having given the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) and the items to be bestowed according to the rule as before, one obtains the previously mentioned fruit through the grace of Vāgīśvarī. (86)

Thus has been declared that which is sung in the *Bṛhattantra* and seen in the *Bimba*, known as the *Devodbhava*; this *Tantra* of Vāgīśvarī should be inferred here in its entirety according to the principles of the Śaiva [tradition]. (87)
Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, the Vāgīśvarī Tantra, in the Kriyāpāda of the Upper Section of the Siddhāntasāra, the *Śrīmadīśānaśivagurudevapaddhati*.

Now begins the fifty-eighth chapter. Next, the installation and other rites of the Teacher (the Buddha), as enjoined by the Tantra, are described. Furthermore, the mantras, both at the beginning and at the end, are adorned with the ninth vowel.
Accompanied by the Bindu and Nāda, the word "namaḥ" should then follow; then the first letter of the sixth [vowel], along with its long form, fire (ra), wind (ya), and the word "goptre. || 2 ||

This is the root mantra, beginning with Tāra and consisting of eleven syllables (rudrārṇa). It consists of Tāra, followed by the fourth letter of the sixth [varga], which is long, accompanied by Anusvāra and Nāda. (3)

The mantra for its worship consists of the words "Bhūtādhipataye" ending with "Namaḥ. Then, according to the scripture, [the mantra continues] with "Revantāya," followed by "Goptre" and likewise "Prabhave. (4)

For the Dīptṛ and the Praśāstṛ as well, these six [mantras], beginning with the Praṇava, ending with "namaḥ," and joined with their respective Jāti-mantras, constitute the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) in due order. || 5 ||
The weapon-mantras for the sword, the dagger, the bow, and the arrow, beginning with *huṃ phaṭ* and ending with *namaḥ*, should be applied in their respective order.
To his left is the goddess Prabhā, and to his right is his son Satyaka;
then Skanda, Gajānana, Śāmba, and likewise Madhuka.
Seated outside the pedestal are those mantras with their respective names: Goptṛ, Piṅgalākṣa, Vīrasena, and Śāmbhava.
The three-eyed one, the wielder of the trident, Dakṣa, and likewise the eighth, Bhīmarūpa—
these are the eight forms of the Teacher, endowed with earth and the other elements.

Their mantras consist of their own names ending with "Tārā" and "Namaḥ. The Noble One (Ārya), the Teacher (Śāstā), the one near the cave (Guhasannas), the General (Senānī), and the beloved of spirits (Bhūtavallabha). || 10 ||
Born of Rudra, possessed of Rudra, full of desire, the granter of boons, and honored by the world; he has blue horses, white elephants, a dark complexion, and is anointed with yellow unguents. (11)
Wearing a red garland, heroic, illusory, beloved by the assembly of Mothers, clothed in black, lord of the Gaṇas, sword in hand, and bearing a bow. || 12 ||
Sahajāya, Janāveśa, Sādhu, Saṃsārarakṣaka, Madhumān, and Śambara—these are indeed the twenty-eight names in the Citta [Kalpa]. 13.

The mantras of Bhūtanātha consist of the syllables preceded by *tāra* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*; they are concluded with *namaḥ* during recitation and worship, and joined with *svāhā* during the fire-oblation (*homa*).
Indeed, by means of these twenty-eight names, which possess the power of great festivals, the lords of the Bhūtasenās are to be employed in the exterior. || 15 ||
"Bhūtanātha" ending with the dative case (bhūtanāthāya) is joined with the word "vidmahe"; likewise, "bhavaputra" is placed at its end, followed by "dhīmahi" and "tannaḥ" as well. (16)
"O Teacher, please inspire me; this is the Gāyatrī preceded by the Tāra.
This concludes the section on the extraction of mantras.
One should have the image of the Teacher fashioned with a measurement of ten *tāla*s for the little finger. (17)
Endowed with the prescribed proportions and other attributes, with a gentle countenance and four arms,
he is seated comfortably upon a magnificent lion-throne lotus, with his left foot [extended].
With his right leg hanging down, he stands treading upon a lotus; possessing four arms, he holds an arrow, a razor-edged dagger, a bow, and a sword.
His limbs were beautiful with fresh youth, his hair was dark and curly, his large eyes were as broad as lotuses, and his face resembled the full moon. (20)
His crown was radiant with a net of jewels, his earrings were made of highly polished gems,
his limbs were beautiful with charming necklaces, and he wore a girdle bound around his waist.
Adorned with jeweled rings, bracelets, and beautiful armlets,
he shone with a girdle and a radiant red garment, and wore lovely anklets.
He held a firmly gripped sword, was dark-complexioned with a delicate form, wore red ornaments, had well-set shoulders, possessed a divine appearance, and was enchanting. || 23 ||
And [he saw] Prabhā, nine *tāla* units in height, adorned with a divine form, seated on his right with her lotus-feet hanging down. (24)
[One should visualize] Satyaka, who resembles an eight-year-old child and measures eight *tālas* in height, holding a blue lotus in his hand and leaning toward the left side of the Teacher. (25)
Standing on the right side of the Teacher, having a divine form and adorned; having thus prepared the images, one should then perform the consecration.
As before, in the consecration pavilion provided with sixteen pillars, there are Kṣurikeśa,
Khaḍgeśa, Dhanveśa, and Śareśvara.
First, the four archways (toraṇas) are to be worshipped, as well as the eight banners:
those of Indra, Agni, Yama, Nairṛta, and Varuṇa. || 28 ||
Then one should worship all those marked with their respective weapons— the Vāyavya, Kaubera, and Aiśāna— with offerings such as the arghya, ending with prostrations, using their individual names.
Vīrabāhu, Mahāvīrya, Vidyujjihva, Vilāsina, Tīkṣṇa, Tīkṣṇanetra, Kākākṣa, and Bhavodbhava. || 30 ||
One should worship these two pitchers placed at each of the gates in succession;
then, following the scattering of the auspicious water (puṇyāha), one should worship the pitcher-weapon.
The Lord of Beings (Bhūtanātha) is mounted upon a horse; the Weapon (Astra) is in the pitcher;
the one with the sword-weapon (Kṣurikāstra) is in the form of a woman, adorned with red ornaments, and three-eyed.
Having worshipped him whose fierce loincloth is bound and whose tawny hair stands erect and blazing,
one should [proceed] upwards from that point of rotation toward the fires placed in nine sacrificial pits.

Following the invocation and the fire-oblation of the root-limbs and the forms of the Teacher, one should perform the purification of the form and likewise the opening of the eyes, as previously described. (34)

One should perform the ritual immersion in water, the procession through the village, and the ceremonial bathing, as well as the placement on the altar-bed as previously described, according to the path taught in the Śaiva scriptures. (35)

Then follows the worship of the Kumbha-weapon, Nidrā, the Eightfold Form (Aṣṭamūrti), Kumbha, and so forth; for the eight previously mentioned forms, beginning with Goptra, are the embodiments of the Teacher (Śāstṛ).
As before, having separately installed in sequence the mantras of the three principles (tattva) and their lords,
then [one installs] Goptr and the others, joined with Earth and the rest, as well as the forms of the Guru.
Having offered oblations with these very [mantras] as before, having emanated [the deity], and having worshipped [her],
one should place the power called Jñāna-śakti in the image (bere) and the power consisting of action (kriyātmikā-śakti) on the pedestal (pīṭha).
Having installed Dhārikā and the others and worshipped them according to the prescribed rite, the Guru, having performed his morning ablutions, then proceeds together with the image-bearers.
Having performed his daily rites and entered the inner sanctum at the auspicious moment, he should place the tortoise-stone (kūrmaśilā) upon the human plane (mānuṣapada) as previously described.
One should place the five groups beginning with jewels upon the pedestal; having installed the image, one should place the pitchers and the root-mantra in its heart.
Having thus engaged the image and its mantra-body, one should then wash them;
[one should contemplate] the light rising from the *ādhāra* [cakra] through the *suṣumṇā* and residing in the heart-lotus.
Having led it upward from the *bindu* to the ether (*vyoman*) together with the lotus and the moon, it is transferred into the handful of flowers, augmented by *nāda* and *bindu*.

Reciting the mantra ending with the *pluta* vowel, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) within the heart-lotus of the form; having performed the rites of installation (*sthāpana*) and so forth with the limbs [of the mantra], one should [proceed] with sleep, the form, and the water from the jar.

Having consecrated [the disciple] with his own root-mantra and limbs, one should contemplate the six paths; this path of mantra (mantrādhvan) is proclaimed for him by means of the root-mantra, its limbs, and his own Gāyatrī. || 45 ||
One should delineate the path of words by means of these very words; then, having contemplated the remaining paths as before, one should perform worship. That is to say:
having bathed and performed the ritual of self-protection (*sakalīkaraṇa*), one should worship the obstacle and the door.
One should worship two door-keepers on both sides, holding a razor and a sword in their hands.
One should worship the Yakṣa, the Vidyādhara, and the Door-Goddess (Dvāraśrī) above; then, having cast the weapon-mantra (astra), one should enter within and place it upon the threshold (dehalī).
Having worshipped the Vāstu, Brahmā, and the seats with the root mantra and its ancillaries,
one should offer the arghya water using perfumes, flowers, kuśa grass, milk, sesame seeds, white mustard, and unbroken grains.

The *arghya* for the Lord of Beings (Śiva) should consist of sesame seeds, flowers, unbroken rice, and water; likewise, sandalwood, turmeric, and water constitute the *pādya*, as do the lotus and sandalwood.
One should offer the *lavaṅka*, water, and the rinsing (*ācāma*) entirely with the heart-mantra.
Having performed the five purifications, one should move the protective enclosure of the weapon-mantra (*astraprākāra*) outside. (51)
The *tilaka* with its crest-flower is the *śaktipīṭha* whose nature is the Earth;
[it is offered] to the one who possesses the abundant lion-throne and who consists of all powers.
Having honored the feet [of the Lord] with the word "namaḥ," one should worship Dharmā and the others in the form of lions,
as well as Tamas, Sattva, and Rajas, Padma, and Śakti— these eight located at the tips of the petals.
One should worship Goptrī, Piṅgalākṣī, Vīrasenā, Śāmbhavī, Trinetrā, Śūlinī, Dakṣā, and Bhīmarūpā.
On the left [he should place] the ninth light, and likewise Satyaka on the right; then, having conceived the form as the body of the mantra, he should invoke the All-pervading Lord.

One should worship [the deity]—which has arisen from the support (ādhāra), consists of pure consciousness, and is merely light like that previously described—by means of invocation, installation, and so forth, up to the offering of food (naivedya). || 56 ||
Furthermore, one should place the attendants upon the filaments with one's own limbs, on the tips of the petals with the eight Śaktis, and outside the pedestal with Vighna and the others.
Having stationed two [deities] outside with swords and daggers in their hands, one should likewise place the world-protectors in their respective directions, and the horse in the front pavilion.
One should place Vīra, Vighna, the Seven Mothers, and Soma in their respective directions;
having also placed the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha), they should offer oblations with the names of the world-protectors (lokapālas).

On the second day as well, one should perform [the rite] in sequence with the previously mentioned sacrificial fuel (samidh), clarified butter (ājya), and so forth, using the root mantra and its limbs, the Gāyatrī, and the mantras known as the Mūrti-śaktis and the Aṣṭakas.
On the third day, they should offer oblations twenty-eight times with sacrificial fuel and other materials,
and one hundred and eight times with the *hetimantras*.
Having offered oblations with the Jayā and other mantras, and then performed expiatory offerings (prāyaścitta), the preceptor, on the fourth day, unites the fires within himself.
One should place and worship Ghoṣavanta, the bearer of the floral remains (nirmālya), in the northeast;
one should bathe the Lord with eighty-one jars according to the prescribed method.

Having given the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) as before and having cast the offering to the spirits (bhūtabali) at night, one should make a formal resolve regarding one's wealth and other resources for the sake of accomplishing the daily worship and so forth. (64)
The performer attains his desires through the arising of both visible and invisible fruits.
This concludes the section on the installation of the Lord of Beings (Bhūtanātha).
During the daily festival, the two gatekeepers shall carry a dagger and a sword. 65.
One should scatter the bali offering to Lokeśas and their mounts, the horses;
then to the attendants of the Teacher, ending with those of his retinue.
Having respectfully offered the bali-oblation up to the one named Lokeśa, one should offer the bali to the horse with the mantras: "Oṃ, homage to the mount of the Teacher; Oṃ, homage to the horse."
Then [offerings] to Vīra, Vighneśa, and the Mothers, and to Soma and Ghoṣavatī. || 67 ||
One should place [the image] of Tīkṣṇa, who has piercing eyes, at the gate of the city-gate; standing before the sacrificial pedestal, one should address the Gaṇas with this [mantra].
Oṃ!
May all the hosts of Śāmba and the others, who exceed [in number] by tens of millions upon tens of millions, with minds well-pleased, accept this bali offering. 69.
Then, in the eight directions starting from the east, are situated the forms beginning with Goptṛ; namely, Goptṛ, Piṅgalākṣa, Vīrasena, and Śāmbhava.

The third-eyed one, the wielder of the trident, Dakṣa, and likewise the eighth of fearsome form—to them a sacrificial offering (bali) should be cast; furthermore, offerings are placed in the eight directions around the pedestal of the sacrifice (balipīṭha).

Vīrabāhu, Mahāvīrya, Vidyujjihva, Vilāsavan, Sutīkṣṇa, Tīkṣṇadaṃṣṭra, Tārākṣa, Bhavodbhava, and the one known as Bhūteśa—these reside in Kumudaka; one should offer an oblation to them. It would be thus.
But Bhūtanāthasena is in the lotus center of the seat. || 73 ||
To him, an offering (bali) should be cast with the name preceded by "Tāra" and ending with "Namaḥ. This is the procedure for the daily festival, which is the same as that for the great festival.
The specific details are now described: a horse should be drawn on the banner and it must indeed be worshipped;
one should also invoke the Gaṇas with mantras containing the names of the Teacher (the Buddha).
At the conclusion of the offering of the bali to Lokeśa,
[one recites] with the verses beginning: *oṃ śāsturbhagavato ye bhūtāḥ purassadaḥ*, and so forth.
One should offer the bali-oblation to all [of them].
Likewise, for the third circuit, there are twenty-eight forms.

One should offer oblations to those who stand as the leaders of the Teacher’s own retinue; the Noble Teacher is situated near the cave, and the General is stationed in the direction of Indra (the east).
Bhūtavallabha, Rudratejas, and Rūpavān—these three are situated in the direction of Agni (the southeast); then there is Kāmī and Varaprada.
Lokārcita and Nīla—these four are stationed in the south;
Śyāmī, who possesses a white elephant and has yellow unguents, is in the southwest (Nairṛta).
Wearing a red garland, the hero, the master of illusion, beloved by the host of Mothers; then in the west and the northwest is Kālavāsas, the leader of the Gaṇas.
These three have swords in their hands; likewise, in the north is the bow-wielder Sahajāya, Janāveśa, and Sādhu—these are stationed there.
Likewise, Saṃsārarakṣaka, Madhumān, and Śambhara—these three lords of the Bhūtasena hosts are stationed in the northeastern quarter. (82)
Having scattered the bali offering to these, one should also scatter it outside in the eight directions:
"Om, those hosts in the eastern direction who have thunderbolts in their hands and possess great strength... (83)
By means of these [procedures] in sequence, as before, one obtains the previously mentioned fruit.

Thus has been told this Tantra of the Lord of Beings (Bhūtanātha), which was also declared in the *Devodbhava* [Tantra] concerning the image; having observed all of that, from the installation (*sthāpana*) up to the festival (*utsava*).
This should be understood by those of pure intellect in accordance with the Śaiva ritual procedures. || 84½ ||

Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, on the Tantras of the Teacher, in the section on Ritual Practice (Kriyāpāda) of the Upper Portion (Uparibhāga) of the *Siddhāntasāra*, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva.
p.
567) Now begins the fifty-ninth chapter.
Next, the installation of the Mothers and other rites are written down, starting from the bright fortnight.
That which has indeed been proclaimed in the Svacchanda and other [tantras], as well as in the Mātṛtantras; || 1 ||
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, and Cāmuṇḍī is remembered as the seventh. || 2 ||
Seated to their right and left were Vīrabhadra and Vighnarāja;
[the mantras consist of] the letters beginning with 'ya' and ending with 'ha', joined with the vowels of the Śakvarī meter.
The eight seed-syllables ending with the bindu, followed by the letter *kha*, then *lambodara*, then the *tāra* (om), the seed-syllable, the word *namaḥ*, and then *bhagavatī*. (4)
The name of the Fully Awakened One should also follow the mantra of his mother and so forth;
following that, the mantras are here written down individually in their proper sequence. (5)

"O you who bear the circles of the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas, and the *kūrca* grass-bundle! Salutations, salutations!"—this is the mantra of Brahmāṇī. "O Goddess! O wielder of the axe! O you of white form! O Maheśvarī!
Salutations, salutations!"—this is for Māheśvarī. "O wielder of the spear! [Salutations, salutations!]—this is for Kaumārī.

O you who ride upon a peacock! O you whose banner is a cock! O you of saffron hue! O Kaumārī! Salutations, salutations to Kaumārī! O you who bear the conch and discus! O you who ride upon Garuḍa! O Vaiṣṇavī!
Salutations, salutations to Vaiṣṇavī! O you who bear the plow and the mace!
O fanged one! O you who ride upon a boar! O lion-vehicled one! O Vārāhī!
Homage, homage to Vārāhī! O wielder of the thunderbolt! O elephant-vehicled one! O dark-complexioned one! Homage, homage to Indrāṇī! O skull-wielder! O you whose color is like blue water!
"O bearer of the hungry ghosts! O you who utter 'huṃ'! Homage, homage to Cāmuṇḍī!

[The mantra consists of] the *tāra* (oṃ) of Vīrabhadra, his own seed-syllable, and Lakulīśvara; then the word 'puruṣa' ending in the dative case, followed by 'to the bearer of the thread of the fortnight and fire'."
The three words "to Dhruva," "to the Lord," and "to the one whose form is Yoga"; then first "to the Pervasive One" (Vyāpine), and after that the word "Vīrabhadra."

The mantra of Vīrabhadra is known to consist of [the name] ending in the dative case and joined with "namaḥ"; it should begin with the Praṇava (Oṃ) and its own seed-syllable, followed by the word "Vighneśvara. (8)
The word *gaṇādhipati* and then the term *hastivaktra*; all these, ending in the dative case as *gaṇapataye*, followed by *namaḥ*, constitute the mantra. (9)
The root mantra of Gaṇapati.
568) These mantras are prescribed in sequence for the consecration of multiple images; however, for a single image, [the mantra is] the Tāra.
And the sound "ca" is joined with the sixth vowel. || 10 ||
The seed-syllable accompanied by the *bindu* and *nāda*, followed by "namo bhagavati," and then:

"O Three-eyed One! O Kālī! O You of dark complexion! O Eight-armed One! O Wielder of the Trident and Skull! O You who ride upon a corpse! O You whose mouth is filled with the fat and blood of heroes! O Cāmuṇḍī! Salutations, salutations!"
Thus: their respective seed-syllables are joined with the long vowels in sequence. (11)
One should arrange the six limbs ending with the weapon-mantra for all mantras: the swan, the bull, the peacock, Garuḍa, the lion, and the elephant. 12.

The ghost (preta) belongs to the Seven Mothers; the bull and the rat belong to Vīra and Vighna respectively. These are the vehicles and banners of Brāhmī and the others, in their respective order. (13)
The broom, the trident, the spear, the discus, the plow, the thunderbolt, the skull-cup, the rosary, and the goad— these are also the nine weapons.

"Having said, 'We know her who is the source of vehicles and the like, and who is called the weapon; we meditate upon her who is the hand; may she, whose name is auspicious, impel us toward that. (15)

Thus, in this sequence, there are indeed Gāyatrīs for Brāhmī and the others: "Tāraṃ bījaṃ ca lakulī īśvarāya atha vidmahe" (The seed-syllable Tāra and Lakulī; we know [the mantra] for Īśvarā). || 16 ||
"To the wearer of the rosary," "we meditate upon that," and "Vīrabhadra" as a form—thus "may he impel" is joined [to these]. (17)
The Gāyatrī of Vīrabhadra:
Oṃ is the seed-syllable; then "Ekadanta," ending in the dative case, we know; then "Hastivaktra," ending in the dative case, we meditate upon; and likewise "tanno" (that to us). (18)
Then, at the end, "May Gaṇapati impel [us]"—thus they were impelled.
This is the Gāyatrī of Vighneśvara. The extraction of the mantra is as follows:
Their forms, arms, faces, eyes, and weapons resembled those of their respective deities. || 19 ||
Their forms are female and their attire is similar; they are known to have images consisting of only six [limbs]. However, in the case of many images, Cāmuṇḍā is black in color and four-armed.
With high breasts, her three round, tawny eyes fixed upon them; she holds a skull and a noose in her left hands, and a trident and a sword in her right. (21)
