Or she may bear a hand-drum (ḍamaruka), with blazing tawny hair, adorned with snake-earrings, armlets, bracelets, and a girdle around her waist. 22.
Adorned with various necklaces, pendants, waist-bands, and ornaments for the feet;
her face radiant with fangs, she is arrayed in red garlands, perfumes, garments, and the like.
Even in the case of a single image (ekabera), it is said that its form should possess a fierce symmetry;
it has the luster of a terrifying dark cloud, with round, tawny, three eyes.
Her hair, rising upwards, was tawny like the crest of a blazing fire; her face was formidable with protruding fangs, and her breasts were high, full, and rounded. || 25 ||
She wears a red bodice, with black serpents bound around her breasts; she has a slender waist, well-nourished limbs, is divine, and is adorned with various snakes.
On her left is the serpent-earring, and here on the other is the earring made from the ear of a corpse-child;
she wears a garland of the heads of various warriors, terrifying with its network of small bells.
With her left hands she holds a skull-bowl, a shield, a bell, and a snake-noose; with her right hands, she likewise holds a trident, a sword, a vetāla, and a sounding ḍamaru drum.
Bearing eight arms, the formidable goddess stands with one foot firmly placed upon a throne of a corpse and a lion,
while the other is drawn up and tucked beneath her.
With her left foot extended, she tramples upon a wooden beam, while being surrounded by hosts of *bhūtas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, and others,
including *śākinīs* and *ḍākinīs*.
Surrounded by yoginīs, with a form that is heroic, fierce, and formidable—such indeed is the image of Cāmuṇḍā, fashioned from stone or other materials. (31)
The body of Vīrabhadra should be like that of Dakṣiṇāmūrti; the image of Gaṇeśa should also possess the characteristics previously described.

The celestial vehicle (vimāna) should have its entrance on the east or the north and be elongated horizontally; this is likewise approved even in the case of a single-liṅga (ekabera) shrine for the Mothers.
Having fashioned the celestial chariot (*vimāna*) and the image (*bera*), one should then perform the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*).
Having constructed the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) prescribed for the preliminary ritual (*adhivāsana*), it should measure sixteen cubits.
Having adorned it with canopies and other ornaments, one should set up the gate-arches;
these arches are named Pramoda, Nyagbhaya, Śānti, and Śubhada. (35)
Their deities, in order, are Kumbhī, Nikumbhī, Vajrabhīṣaṇā, and Maṅgiṇī; furthermore, those residing in the door-pitchers (dvārakumbha) are at the bases of these [deities].
Then there are Dūtikā, Pālinī, Daṇḍinī, Bhavahastakā, Pāśinī, Vāruṇī, Śaṅkhinī, and Padminī. || 37 ||
And the banners were marked with the signs of a swan, a bull, a peacock, a hawk, a lion, a lordly vulture, a ghost, a bull, and a mouse.
Whether there are many openings or only one, the banner should bear the mark of a Piśāca;
then, through the scattering of auspicious offerings (puṇyāha-vikiras), one should worship the pitcher and the weapon.

One should worship Cāmuṇḍā, whose form is mounted upon a Piśāca, in the Kumbha; and in the Vardhanī, one should worship the black Astrarāja, who is seated on a lion and is terrifying in the form of a woman.
One should worship that [deity] whose head is marked with a trident and who holds a skull and a sword in his hands;
then, following its circumambulation, one should proceed as before in the nine sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).
Having divided the fire and established Cāmuṇḍā in the central pit,
one should worship and offer oblations to Brahmāṇī and the others in the pits starting from the east.
With their respective mantras, one should offer sacrificial fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, sesame seeds,
mustard seeds, white mustard seeds, and parched grain flour in due order.

The sacrificial fuel (samidh) for the rites beginning with the Brāhmī consists of wood from the Palāśa and Plakṣa trees; likewise, it may be from Udumbara, Bilva, Karañja, or Indrataru trees. || 44 ||

Then there are the red and white vaṭa trees, and the pippala trees in sequence—these nine; in the absence of whichever sacrificial fuel sticks [are prescribed], those made from palāśa should be taken there.
Having offered ghee one hundred times each with the respective mantras and sacrificial fuel sticks (samidh),
he should perform the purification of the form and the rite of opening the eyes.
Then, one should perform the ritual immersion in water and the wandering through the village; having prepared the altar as before with rice and grains of śāli rice.
Having prepared separate beds from the center up to the northeast, there should be a single-stripped bed,
and a five-limbed one in the middle of the altar.
One should cause Cāmuṇḍī to lie down in the center, and Brāhmī and the others in order starting from the east;
having placed one jar for each of the images [of the deities] and so forth in the north. (49)
One should place the respective mounts and weapons made of gold upon them; then, one should install Cāmuṇḍā and the others in the jars according to the sequence starting from the center.
One should worship Vīrabhadra in the northern pitcher and Vināyaka in the northeast pitcher,
adorning them as before with covers, tufts of grass, cloths, and other ornaments.

Having anointed [the deity] with *gāyatrī* verses, one should worship with perfumes and other offerings. Then, outside the altar, one should place eight jars for the retinue in the various directions.
Having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa) and invocation (āvāhana), one should worship the Śaktis beginning with Aindrī in due order: Aindrī, Āgneyī, Yāmyā, Nairṛtī, and likewise Vāruṇī.
The goddess of the northwest, that of the north, and the eighth is remembered as that of the northeast;
they all have four arms and three eyes, with tridents and nooses held in their upper hands. (54)
With both hands joined in *añjali* and possessing colors equal to those of the guardians of the directions, one should place another purified jar upon the *balipīṭha* for the purpose of consecration.
In that jar, one should visualize Ugrasenā, who is dark-complexioned, with a face formidable with fangs,
holding a sword in her right hand and touching her own hip with her left.
Then, having invoked the two-armed, formidable goddess adorned [with ornaments], one should worship her,
as well as the principles beginning with the Self (ātmatattva) along with their presiding deities, and the forms (mūrti) along with the lords of those forms (mūrtīśvara).
One should place Dhārikā and the others in the three sections, starting from the knees and so forth, as before;
likewise, the principles (tattvas), the lords of the principles, Earth and the others, and Śarva and the others, in their respective order.

One should place the limbs and secondary parts sequentially upon the bodies of Vīra and Vighneśa. Having offered oblations as before with their respective mantras, the Guru and likewise the bearers of the forms [should do so].

They should touch [the image] at three points and sprinkle it with water from the jars; one should meditate upon the Jñāna-śakti in the body and the Kriyā-śakti on the pedestal, as previously described.
One should perform worship up to the offering of food (naivedya), or one may offer oblations into the fires of Indra and the other deities with the mantra "brahmajajñānam" and another [mantra].
From the *traiyambaka* [mantra], likewise from the *kumāra*, then from the *yatteyam* and so forth;
from the *idaṃ viṣṇu* and so forth, from the *svasti na indra* and so forth, and likewise from the *īśa*. (62)

With the mantra "gaṇānāṃ tvā" and others, one should offer clarified butter (ājya) and sacrificial cakes (caru) and so forth, each according to its own root-mantra; this should be done in the same way for a multi-liṅga shrine, but for a single-liṅga shrine, it is as previously described.
Having placed eight jars all around Cāmuṇḍī, one should also [place] Bhavānī,
Śarvāṇī, Ugrā, and Pāśupatī within them.
One should install and worship Śāṅkarī, Śaśinī, Bhīmā, and Rudrāṇī;
and having invoked Cāmuṇḍā in the central pit, they should likewise offer oblations.

In the same manner, one should offer oblations in the cardinal directions with the *puruṣa*, *aghora*, *vāma*, and *sadyojāta* mantras, and in the corners with the limbs (*aṅga*) of the Gāyatrī, in due order.
And he offers a bean-cake as a substitute for goat-flesh;
likewise [he performs expiation] upon sneezing, spitting, and so forth, as well as upon the breaking of silence.

Having sipped water, one should offer clarified butter with the Vyāhṛtis in their proper sequence; having offered the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should perform the Sviṣṭakṛt rite and scatter the bali offering to the spirits.
One should cast the bali offering mixed with sesame, rice, jaggery, clarified butter, curd, red rice, and a substitute for meat. (69)
In the east, however, the Kṣetrapāla, Piśācas, Pitṛs, and Rākṣasas,
as well as Nāgas, Asuras, Yakṣas, and Gandharvas are stationed.
To the beings in the upward direction and those dwelling below on the earth and in the waters—
one should scatter the bali offering to them with their respective names followed by the word "namaḥ."
Then one should feed seven maidens, another Brāhmaṇa,
and likewise other Brāhmaṇas and ascetics (liṅgins) with milk-rice, clarified butter, and other offerings.
And those women who are devoted to their mothers, he should feed them along with his other devotees;
likewise, having kept a vigil at night with dancing, singing, and other such performances.
Having bathed in the morning and completed the twilight rituals (saṃdhyā) together with those who bear the [divine] forms, the preceptor,
after worshipping the icons, should worship either the entire set of icons or a single icon.

In the inner sanctum (garbhageha), which is the domain of the Piśācas, once the Puṇyāha rite has been recited, one should place either a single pedestal (pīṭha) or multiple pedestals upon the tortoise-stone (kūrmaśilā).
One should deposit the five groups beginning with jewels, as well as vehicles and weapons made of gold, into their respective pits along with their corresponding seed-syllables. (76)
Then, when the auspicious moment had arrived, she was purified with water from the Saraṇyū river,
accompanied by auspicious sprouts, lamps, and the like, as well as instrumental music and song.
Then, having placed the images upon the chariot to the accompaniment of Vedic chants, and having placed ghee, dūrvā grass, unbroken rice, curd, and flowers upon their heads; 78.

Having circumambulated [the shrine] clockwise, one should cause [the deity] to enter the inner sanctum; at the auspicious moment, one should install the images in their proper order with the mantras of their respective seed-syllables.

From east to west, the [lines] beginning with Brāhmī and the others should be established along a single thread; facing north, they should be positioned at intervals of two finger-breadths from one another.
To the north of the two side-lines of Brahmāṇī and Cāmuṇḍī,
Vīrabhadra and likewise Vighnādhipa are to be installed in the east and west respectively.
Vīrabhadra should face westward, and Vināyaka should face eastward; however, in the case of a single image, it should be in the center, facing either east or north.
Then, having washed the images and placed their respective seed-syllables (*bīja*) within the lotuses of their hearts, one should bathe them with their respective ritual jars.
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the path of mantras (mantrādhvan) with their respective mantras and their own gāyatrī;
the path of words (padādhvan) with their respective words, and the remaining paths as previously described.
Then the Guru [visualizes] the Supreme Power (parā śakti), which has emerged from the Kuṇḍalinī at his own root-lotus,
subtle in form and resembling a streak of lightning.
Having led it upward through the path of the channels to the heart, the bindu, and the end of the twelve,
one should cause it to be drenched by the essence of the nectar of the digit of the moon within the lotus of that space.

Having brought that [seed-syllable] into unity with the power of pure consciousness (cinmātra), while reciting the seed-syllable situated in the middle of the encapsulated *haṃsa* and adorned with the vowel at the end of the *nāda*, [he should perform the rite]. (87)
[She who is] well-transferred into the handful of flowers—beyond qualities, incomparable, to be known through the Vedas, and stainless. (88)

Having brought [the deity] through the path of the channels, one should place it in the heart-lotus of the Goddess; then follows the installation (sthāpana), the presence (sānnidhya), the confinement (sannirodha), and the veiling (avakuṇṭhana).
One should perform the rite of consecration with the *prarocanā* and the *amṛtikāra* using that *gāyatrī*. Then,
one should place the eightfold retinue (*parivāra*) all around the temple.
Having consecrated her with jars associated with Indra and the other deities, one should install that Ugrasenī,
who resides in the jar, upon the sacrificial pedestal following the ritual ablution.
Having placed and established [the deity] in the center, one should then worship according to the prescribed rule.
For instance:
having bathed, performed the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā), and consecrated one's own body through the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa... || 92 ||

Having fully worshipped Vighnarāja (Gaṇeśa), and then holding the general *arghya* water in his hand, he should sprinkle the doors with the *pāvamānī* verses and with the water from the *arghya* using the *astra-mantra*.
Having opened the door-panels, one should worship the gatekeepers; specifically, one should worship the Rakṣohaṇa and Valagahana at the eastern gate.
Sumukha, Kāladaṇḍa, Atithi, Mudita, Sakala,
and Śuktikarṇa are remembered as the gatekeepers of the southern and other directions.
One should worship these—named after the eastern and other directions, as well as Pramodanī, Abhayā, Śānti, and Śubhakarī—by their respective names. (96)
Karālī, Kāmukā, Subhagā, and Dāhanī; Gaganā, Hlādanī, and Kauberī Viṣphuliṅginī. (97)
One should worship Virūpākṣī and the others in pairs at the eastern and other doors; having cast the nārāca weapon inside and entered within, one should then deposit the weapon.
Having worshipped the Vāstu and the Brahmāsana, and being well-seated, one should offer the Arghya;
then, having performed the five purifications, adorned with a tilaka and a flower-garland. (99)

Then, upon the lotus of the seat of Paretāsana, one should worship the foundational power (ādhāraśakti), as well as the three qualities (guṇatraya) together with the solar and other disks and their presiding deities.
The Yoginīs, beginning with Sundarī, reside on the tips of the lotus petals starting from the east: Sundarī, Śākhinī, Viṣakaṇṭhī, and Vasundharā. (101)
Yoginī, Amṛtapūrvā, Ghātakī, and thereafter Vetālī and Mātṛsenā—these are to be worshipped by their own names. (102)

Then, having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the form whose body is mantra, one should thereafter invoke the supreme Goddess, the Power (*śakti*), as before, through the root-mantra and its limbs, by means of the rites of installation (*sthāpana*) and so forth. (103)
Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, one should worship [the deities] individually with clarified butter and other offerings;
whether in a multi-linga shrine or a single-linga shrine, one should worship Cāmuṇḍā in this manner.
One should also worship with these nine previously mentioned mantras: [the colors] yellow, variegated, red, yellow, blue, and the color of a parrot.
A garment that is excessively red, white, or red is approved for the Brahma and other [deities]; likewise are Śrīkaṇṭha, saffron, Yakṣakardama, and the Granthi [incense].
Black agallochum, tamāla, musk, sandalwood, and red sandalwood are prescribed in sequence for the [mantras] beginning with Brāhmī. (107)
Regarding "fragrances":
the palāśa, kārkī, kumuda, tulasī, and kadamba; as well as the mallikā, japā, blue lotus (nīlotpala), and karavīraka. || 108 ||
These indeed are the nine desired flowers for the [deities] beginning with Brāhmī: white [flower], black [flower], agallochum, honey, clarified butter, resin of the Sarja tree, and incense.
Śrīkaṇṭha, Indu, and Uśīra, as well as incense materials in their proper order; then milk-rice, curd-rice, mung-bean rice, and rice with jaggery.
Food made with black gram, kṛsara rice, red food, pure food, and fruit-food— these nine offerings are to be presented to the goddesses beginning with Brāhmī, in their respective order.
Having thus worshipped and offered the final service with the prescribed offerings, one should worship Caṇḍasenā in the northeast corner with the remains of the floral garlands (nirmālya).
Having likewise offered oblations into the fires or into the fire itself, as prescribed by those [authorities] in due order,
with their own root-mantras and ancillary mantras, with the Gāyatrī, and with the Vedic (śrauta) mantras enjoined [for the purpose].

Having offered oblations in sequence with the *jaya* mantras and others, as well as with clarified butter for the expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*), and having also offered the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) and the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation, one should dissolve the fire into the lotus of one's own heart.
Having directed the deities stationed at the archways and other locations,
one should dismiss them with the prescribed eighty-one jars, nine being assigned to each.

Then, one should bathe [the deity] with many images, or with all of them if it is a single image; and at night, having given the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor and others, one should scatter the bali offering.
Having given the gifts to the Brahmins, to those bearing sectarian marks (liṅgin), and to others as well—
especially after having bestowed them upon those who are devoted to their mothers and upon the mothers themselves— 117.
One should cause that food and other offerings to be given to everyone without restriction;
for the sake of accomplishing the daily worship and so forth, one should provide wealth according to one's means. (118)
Having formed the resolve, the performer obtains the desired fruit, both seen and unseen. This concludes the section on the installation of the Mothers.
Regarding the daily festival (nityotsava), however, it should be performed by the Mothers or by the Mother in an auspicious amulet-thread (vāmaka). 119.

In the morning, the liṅga may be made of gold or other materials on one side; at midday, it should consist of flowers; and in the evening, the liṅga should likewise be made of unbroken grains (akṣata).

When that vessel has many compartments and lotuses are fashioned here upon the petals, Cāmuṇḍā should be placed in the pericarp, while Brāhmī and the others are in the eastern petal and the subsequent ones.
Having invoked and worshipped it with its seed-syllables, and having had it mounted by attendants,
it should be provided with a strong frame and endowed with the splendor of parasols and other regalia.
Adorned with the sounds of conchs, kettledrums, and the like, as well as the music and songs of women, the yogi should offer the inner oblation to the yoginīs in all eight directions.
Then one should offer the bali-oblation to those headed by Sundarī and Karālī, and likewise to the door-keepers beginning with Rakṣohaṇa.

One should offer [the oblation] in the abodes of the world-protectors, starting from Indra and the others in the eight directions, or in front of their vehicles, or even to the vehicles themselves. 125.
Then, having cast [the offering] to Caṇḍasenā and reached the city gate, he went outside after making an oblation to Kumbhinī and Nikumbhinī.
In front of the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha), he should address the Gaṇas with the mantra: "Those Mothers and their attendants who stand pervading the entire world... (127)
And also the yoginīs, the śākinīs, the pretas, the kaṭapūtanas, the ḍākinīs, the piśācas, the vetālas, and likewise the pramathas. || 128 ||
Those who dwell in the netherworld, on the earth, and in the sky— may they,
with well-pleased minds, accept this offering. 129.
Thus,
one should scatter the bali offering to the groups mentioned in the eight directions: to the Yoginīs in the east, and likewise to the Śākinīs in the southeast.
Likewise, [offerings] for the pretas are in the south, and for the pūtanās in the southwest; for the ḍākinīs in the west, and for the piśācas in the northwest. (131)
Having scattered the offering (bali) for the Vetālas in the north and for the Bhūtas in the northeast,
one should then approach the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha).
Having meditated upon Ugrasenā together with her attendants and worshipped her by her own name, one should offer a bali-oblation of all the remaining food to her upon the pedestal.

Having wandered about as before and entered within with a concentrated mind, he should worship the Goddess residing in the *liṅga*, reciting either the full set of mantras or a single mantra alone. || 134 ||
One should assign the Mothers, or the Mother, to their respective principal images (*mūlabera*). This concludes the section on the authority for the daily festival (*nityotsava*).
Now, the Great Peace (*mahāśānti*), which brings welfare to the country and the king, is described. (135)
For the pacification of diseases, calamities, epidemics, and portents,
[one should perform this] during the months of Māgha, Phālguna, Caitra, Vaiśākha, and Jyeṣṭha.
It is ordained for the months of Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa, Proṣṭhapada, and Aśvayuja, as well as for Kārttika,
Mārgaśīrṣa, and Puṣya.

Whether in the dark fortnight or the bright fortnight, during the seven days beginning from the second and ending with the eighth lunar day, when the asterism is favorable for the kingdom and other such matters. (138)
And that [rite] ending on Saturday, the day of Bhauma (Mars), is prescribed as the Mahāśānti;
the names of those days are given by means of the names beginning with Brāhmī.

Peace is said to be excellent, middling, or inferior according to whether it takes seventy-three, seventy-two, or seventy-one days; this applies to a city, a kingdom, a village, a forest, or even a mountain. (140)
Wherever the presence of the Mother [Mātrkā] may be, there one should perform the rite of pacification (*śānti*).
Having determined the pacification—whether it be the most excellent or otherwise—and having performed the offering of sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) as previously described, [one should proceed]. (141)
One should raise a banner upon it and paint a Piśācī on the cloth—her hair standing erect, her eyes wide open, and her body devoid of flesh, consisting only of bone. (142)
She has a long nose, pendulous lips, two arms, and a long neck;
she holds a skull and a vetāla, and likewise possesses a distorted face. || 143 ||
She has a short belly, hands, and feet; her breasts resemble cow horns;
she wears a strung garland of tinkling bells and is adorned with various serpents.
When there is only one *bera*, it should be thus; but when there are many *beras*, then one should draw the *piśācī* and the other eight vehicles surrounding her.
On the roof of a palace, in the assembly hall, in the middle of a village, or at a crossroads,
there should be an auspicious mudrā-maṇḍapa measuring ten cubits in size.

In the center of that, there should be a square pedestal like that of the offering altar (balipīṭha). Then, in the cardinal directions and also at the junctions of the village, city, and so forth, in due order— || 147 ||
One should prepare well-smeared mandalas for the purpose of the bali offering;
then, with the sounds of musical instruments and other such things, and with auspicious performances such as song and dance. (148)

One should cast the bali-offering, accompanied by the trident-weapon and the journey, into the cardinal directions; it should consist of śāli-rice with curd and clarified butter, saturated with a substitute for meat.
One should offer the bali-oblation, consisting of red perfumes and flowers, with their respective mantras; to Brahmā in the center and to the world-protectors in the cardinal directions as before.
At the forefronts of all temples, at village gates and assembly halls, at crossroads, at shrines, and at the residences of chief kings. || 151 ||
In stables for cattle, elephants, and horses, at principal trees and rivers, at wells, groves, ponds, in forests, and in cremation grounds; || 152 ||

And at other locations containing hidden treasures, one should sprinkle water and scatter the bali offering; one should likewise scatter it at the three junctions of the day immediately after the presentation of the bali.
Having entered the pavilion, one should place the weapon-mantra (astra) upon the pedestal as before; one should worship it there and then set forth the procession of the Goddess.
With the Narayana musical instrument, with songs, dances, and other auspicious performances,
with the sounds of conchs, kettledrums, and the like, and with canopies, parasols, and fly-whisks; (155)
It was adorned with beautiful courtesans wearing ornaments, and by well-bathed, heroic warriors, decorated and holding swords in their hands. || 156 ||
Frequented by other people as well with the clamor of their voices, one should slaughter flour-effigies every night and offer them.
In the morning and evening, a Pāraśava skilled in the art of dance and hand gestures should perform a charming musical dance in that pavilion in the presence of the weapon.
Just as it is prescribed for the great festival of Śiva during the lowering of the banner,
one should likewise offer the silent oblation at midnight every night.
Then, on the night of the sixth day, one should bind the sacrificial cord upon the great victim:
for a Brahmin it is a deer, and for a king it is an elephant.
For a Vaiśya, a buffalo is the great animal; for others, even a goat may serve as such. However, in the absence of all these, a buffalo may indeed be the sacrificial animal.
On the seventh day, in the afternoon, having slaughtered the secondary animal (upapaśu), which is a goat,
and having adorned it while tied to the sacrificial post, he should then immolate the great animal (mahāpaśu).
Then one should offer that blood to the Mothers or to one’s own mother;
with food mixed with that blood and meat, one should cast the bali-oblation in the cardinal directions.
Then, on the eighth day, as before, preceded by a festival of powder (cūrṇotsava),
one should conclude the pilgrimage according to the prescribed rites for a Śaiva festival.
Then, having dismissed the Gaṇas as before, one should also lower the banner;
one should bathe it with eighty-one jars as before and also worship it.
Having given the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) that are to be bestowed, the performer attains the fruit;
likewise on Sundays, in the evening, according to the previously mentioned method. || 166 ||
By performing the Bali-yātrā, one shall obtain all desired objects; [this should be done] on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, as well as on Tuesdays and Sundays.
For the attainment of all desires, one should perform offerings and worship.
Thus, indeed, the Mātṛtantra, including its installation rites and so forth, has been declared to be completely pure. (p. 580)
This should be performed correctly, in accordance with the Śaiva tradition as prescribed, concluding with worship and a great rite of pacification (mahāśānti). || 168 ||
Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Mātṛtantras," in the Kriyāpāda of the *Siddhāntasāra*, which is the *Śrīmad-Īśānaśivagurudeva-paddhati*.
Now begins the sixtieth chapter.
Hereafter, the installation and other rites of Kṣetrapāla are declared;
one should assemble the ritual procedures here as well, in accordance with what has been taught for Śiva.
The final syllable, endowed with the vowel *u* and adorned with the *bindu* and *nāda*, should be preceded by the *tāra*;
thereafter comes the word "Kṣetrapāla. (2)

This nine-syllable root mantra (mūlamantra) consists of [the deity's name] ending in the fourth case and followed by "namaḥ. For the fire-oblation (homa), it should end with the wife of Agni (svāhā). The seed-syllable (bīja) is joined with the long vowels.
The six limbs ending with the weapon-mantra are joined with the *jāti* suffixes in their proper sequence; his *mālāmantra* also consists of the *tāra*, the *śakti*, and the eighth [syllable].
The sixth vowel with fire (ra) is Daṇḍin; Ra and Mu follow.
With the eleventh vowel (au), the final [syllable] is joined with the fifth [consonant] and fire (ra).
Then, "pāla-mahāśabdau," followed by "bala" and two "kapila"s; at the end, one should utter the word "jvālāmukha" while radiant with a mass of matted locks. (6)
And accept this worship of perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and offerings; after the word "Bhairava," there should then be the word "rūpeṇa. (7)
The word *taru*, the word *muru*, the word *khaḥ*, and the words *phaṭ*;
at the end of the word *aṭṭahāsa*, there is also the phrase *ḍāmarādhipa*. (8)
The mantra beginning with the fifth vowel (Ū) and ending with "svāhā" is thus declared; one should perform worship with this, for recitation and other rites will grant success.
Now, the bali-mantra for that very [deity], beginning with Tārā, is also being told: "Ehi," the syllable "dhū," and three times "turu vajra hana. (10)
And having uttered the word "vinā," ending with a repetition (vīpsā), followed by the words "mahārava," then the words "kṣetrapāla," and saying "gṛhṇa gṛhṇa" with the wife of Agni (svāhā), || 11 ||
The mantra for the bali offering:
first the Praṇava (Tāra), then the Śakti, followed by Vaṭuka in the dative case.
The rescue from calamity is as before; then, moreover, there is a pair of Kurus. (12)
The word *vaṭuka* ending in the dative case, followed by the seed-syllable of Śakti, constitutes that mantra;
this twenty-two-syllabled mantra bestows the attainment of desired goals through recitation and other practices. (13)
One should have the Kṣetrapāla fashioned with a height of ten *tālas* for the youngest [size]; he should be the color of collyrium, with wide-open eyes and hair standing erect and blazing.
A youth of immense body, clad in red garments yet naked, with a fierce face and prominent fangs, adorned with various shimmering ornaments. || 15 ||
His waist was bound with a girdle of golden bells and tinkling chains,
and his lotus-feet were adorned with jingling golden anklets.
One should have [the image] fashioned with a straight, elongated, and steady form, seated upon a golden pedestal-lotus, having four arms, eight hands, or even two arms.
Holding a skull-bowl, a trident, a noose, and a hand-drum in his hands, one should likewise represent him as four-armed, bearing these [attributes] both downward and upward.
He bears a trident, a sword, and a khaṭvāṅga staff, as well as a ḍamaruka drum;
furthermore, in his right hands he holds a skull-cup, a bell, and a bow with an arrow.
The eight-armed [deity] should be fashioned, characterized by the previously described marks; he holds a skull and a mace in his left and right hands, respectively, or he may have two arms.
He appeared like an eight-year-old child, with dark, curly hair,
adorned with locks of hair, his lotus-face graced by the clear sprouts of his fangs.
Furthermore, this Lord Vaṭuka, the guardian of the sacred field (kṣetrādhipa), is red in color;
or, as stated by others:
he bears hanging matted locks like clouds, has three eyes, and possesses the luster of a mountain of blue collyrium.

I ever worship that all-pervading Kṣetrapāla, who holds a mace and a skull-bowl in his pair of arms, resplendent with red garlands, perfumes, and ornaments; who is formidable with the mingling sounds of the jingling bells on his waist-girdle and the *jhāṅkāra* resonance; and who wears a variegated serpent as an earring. 22.
The consecration pavilion should have sixteen pillars, as before. || 23 ||
Śama, Vibhūmi, Subala, and Āroga are the archways (toraṇas) in sequence;
likewise are Heruka, Tripurāntaka, Agni, and Vetāla. (24)
Agnijihva, Karāla, and Ekadaṃṣṭra as the seventh, and Bhīmarūpa as the eighth—one should worship these in the pitchers at the doors. (25)
Then, preceded by the scattering of auspicious offerings (puṇyāha-vikirāḥ), the eight Sārameya-dhvajas should be worshipped under the names beginning with Aindra and Āgneya.

In the water-pot (kumbha) is the Lord of the Field (Kṣetrapati), described as having a dark horse for his mount; in the vardhanī vessel is that same deity with a trident weapon, in female form, accompanied by a dog.
Having performed that sacrifice, thereafter, in the fire placed within the central pit,
one should invoke the Guardian of the Field (kṣetrapa) as before and offer oblations of sacrificial fuel (samidh) and other materials.
One should perform the purification of the form, as well as the casting of the gaze; likewise, the ocean-garment, the wandering through the village, and the entry. (29)

In the pavilion, one should perform the worship of the bed upon the altar, as well as the worship of the primary pitcher (mūlakumbha) and the weapon-mantras; then, one should install the sleep-pitcher (nidrākumbha) and the pitchers for the deities of the directions (mūrtighaṭas).
Anala, Agnikeśa, Kāla, Ghaṇṭārava, Mahākrodha, Piṅgalākṣa, and the seventh, Piśitāśana. || 31 ||

One should worship these eight, beginning with Ūrdhvakeśa, located within the pitchers by their respective names; likewise, one should worship the principles (tattvas) beginning with the Self, the lords of those principles, and the forms (mūrtis) beginning with Earth.
One should place Mūrtīśāna, Sitāṅga, and the others in the three sections: Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodha, and Unmatta.
Kapālī, Bhīṣaṇa, and Saṃhāra are the eight guardians of the forms (mūrtipās). These are followed by the word "Bhairava," joined with the dative case ending and the word "namaḥ. (34)
One should place [the mantras] at the joints of the knees, the throat, and the head, in each respective section;
having offered ghee with their respective mantras, one should touch [the body] and sprinkle it with the *kumbhaka* breath-retentions.
One should assign the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti) to the body and worship the power of action (kriyā) on the pedestal;
having passed the night with dancing, singing, and other arts, when the sun has risen, [one should proceed].

Having bathed and performed the twilight prayers and other rites, one should place the tortoise-stone (kūrmaśilā) at the auspicious moment; then, upon that stone, in the human region (mānuṣapada), one should place the groups [of deities] and the gems and so forth.
One should install the pedestal and the image upon the pedestal with the root mantra; having made them firm and washed them, one should place the seed-syllable from the water-pot into its heart.
Having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa) and consecration (abhiṣeka), and having likewise established the seat and the form,
one should then project the mantra-body from within the lotus of one's own heart.
Having led the consciousness through the path of the channels, and from there the *bindu* as well,
together with the light of the power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*) residing in the moon of the lotus at the end of the twelve (*dvādaśānta*).
Having placed [the deity] within a handful of flowers and brought it back as before, one should effect its unification with the heart by means of the mantra situated in the center of the lotus.
The path of mantra (mantrādhvan) consists of its own root-mantras and limbs; the path of words (padādhvan) is said to consist of their constituent words.
One should contemplate and then deposit the remaining paths in their proper sequence, as previously described.

Thereafter, having consecrated [the deity] with jars containing the forms of sleep according to the prescribed rite, one should worship [him] with the offerings of water for honor (arghya) and water for refreshment (arghya), using the mantras of one's own limbs and the root mantra, according to the previously mentioned method.
Namely:

having bathed and worshipped Vighneśa, with his body rendered invulnerable through the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, he should [worship] the Trident-bearer and the Skull-bearer at the entrance with the general water-offering (sāmānyārghya).
Having worshipped the Goddess of the Door (Dvāraśrī) and cast his weapons upward, he enters within;
then, having deposited his weapon at the threshold, he performs the worship of the Vāstu-Brahmāsana.

Having performed the protection ritual with the weapon-mantra as before, one should sit down and offer the *arghya*; then, having performed the five purifications, one should wear the *tilaka* and a crest of flowers.

One should worship Śakti and the Earth as the pedestal upon the lotus of the qualities such as Sattva; then, one should worship the eight Śaktis surrounding [the deity] Tryakṣa with the names of his forms.
Having worshipped [the deity] with the *arghya* and other offerings and having invoked the God as before,
one should worship the *hṛdaya* and other limbs in the fires beginning with the southeast, and the *netra* in front.

Having placed the weapon-mantra in the directions and in the center, and having worshipped it as before with offerings beginning with the *arghya* and ending with the *naivedya*, one should also perform oblations with the root-mantra and its limbs.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations beginning with "kṣetrasya paṭa," one should then install the attendants, placing Kapālin at the door.
And one should [worship] the eight forms of the Trident-bearer (Śūlin), who reside respectively in the abodes of the world-protectors (lokeśa),
possessing forms identical to those world-protectors, beginning with Anala and Agnicara.
O Agni, the dog is your vehicle;
*oṃ*, salutation to Sārameya.
Having also installed Vīra and Vighneśvara, as well as the Mothers and the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha) here in the fire, [one should proceed].
One should offer fuel sticks and other substances with the mantra beginning "kṣetrasya patiḥ" and so forth; then, on the second day, one should worship Kṣetracaṇḍa as before.

Having performed the ritual placement in the northeast, one should worship that Vaṭuka with the remains of the previous offerings; likewise, one should place the gentle and the fierce deities at the gate of the gopura.
Having installed the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha), one should offer clarified butter with the root-mantras and the [mantras of the] tips;
then, as before, with the Jayā and other mantras, and with the expiatory offerings and the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).

Having performed the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation, one should divide the fire and unite it with oneself; then, as before, one should dismiss the banners and cause the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and other gifts to be given.

The practitioner should perform the ritual of dissolution for the sake of accomplishing the daily worship and other rites; then, having passed three nights, he should proceed with the ritual application using water-pots.
One should consecrate him with one hundred and eight [verses] as before; having thus installed the Lord of the Field (Kṣetreśa), there arises the attainment of both visible and invisible fruits.
One obtains enjoyments, prosperity, victory, and sons as is appropriate. This concludes the section on the installation of the Kṣetrapāla.
In the daily festival (nityotsava) for the Lord of the Field (Kṣetrapati), an offering of food is prescribed in the morning. 59.
A liṅga made of flour [should be used] at midday, and a liṅga of flowers at the beginning of the night;
the festival image, as before, may be made of gold or any other [precious material]. (60)

One should arrange a procession for the offering (bali) with instrumental music, song, dance, and so forth, as well as with splendors such as umbrellas; then [one should place] the two door-keepers, Śūlika and Pālina.
In this regard, four [deities] in the four directions, terrifying in their seated posture, resembling Kṛṣṇa, dark-complexioned, holding bows and arrows in their hands, are to be worshipped. (62)

The mountain-dwelling king [Śiva] was honored with the arghya and other offerings by the Great-Souled One; likewise were Anala and the others, as well as the vehicle, Vīrabhadra, and the lords of the Gaṇas.

One should offer a bali-oblation to the Mothers, Kṣetra, and Caṇḍa who reside there; at the gateway of the city (gopura), one should offer a bali-oblation to both the gentle and the fierce deities. (64)
Having gone outside and stood before the pedestal, he should address the Gaṇas: "Those who, desiring the offering, remain pervading the entire world... (65)
"May all the hosts of field-protectors accept this offered bali.
Then, in the eight directions, the previously mentioned Heruka and others are stationed in sequence. (66)
Having offered the bali-oblation to them in sequence all around the seat (pīṭha), one should stand [there],
with the sixteen lords of beings (bhūteśas) and Kṣetrasena in the center.
Then there is Aparājita, Apavatsa, and Indra-mūrti; likewise Īśāna, Ugra with upraised arms, Ṛṣabha, and Ṛbhava. (68)
Surrounding the pedestal (pīṭha) and extending upwards from there, these [deities] reside upon lotus petals:
Asambhava, then Anūjanman, and after that Ekadaṃṣṭra.
Airāvata, Oghabala, Auṣadheśa, Janaprabha, Asambhava, Kṣetrapāla, and Sena are the names of the middle [group]. (70)
This same procedure applies equally to the daily festival and the great festival;
the distinction is that one should worship after hoisting a banner marked with the dog (Sārameya).
Oṃ, homage to Sārameya. Oṃ, homage to Kukkura. Oṃ, homage to the vehicle of Kṣetrapāla.
Thus, after the offering of the bali-oblation to the forms located at the positions of the World-Protectors (lokeśa), [one recites]: Oṃ, in the east...
Those beings who are the attendants standing before the protector of the field (kṣetrapāla).
With these and other mantras as before, one should cast the bali offering in those respective directions.
Then, on the third enclosure, outside the perimeter of Heruka and the others—
One should offer bali to those four who stand in each direction: Kambalī, Khara, Gandhapriya, and Ghaṇṭārava.
He whose form is the syllable Ṅa, who is fierce (Caṇḍa), who moves according to his own will, who wears matted locks;
who resounds with the sound of Ḷa, who strikes the sound of Ña, and who likewise consists of the syllable Ṭha. || 75 ||
Ḍāmara, Ḍhaṅkṛti, and likewise Ṇamaya, who is conscious of the principles (tattva); then Mūrti, Dantura, Dhanapāla, and Nandaka. (76)
Parāntaka, Phaṭkārī, Barbaro, Bhavanandana, Mahābala the lord of Yakṣas, and likewise the Rākṣasa Lambana. || 77 ||
Vanarakṣa, Śumbha, Ṣaḍbhuja, and Sadasaspati—having offered oblations to these in the upward direction as well as downward. (78)

Then Haraṣeṇa stands as the one to be worshipped, followed by the night-stalker (Kṣaṇadācara); all of them are [to be addressed] with their own names beginning with Tārā and ending in the dative case. || 79 ||
There should be salutation and worship, as well as the offering of bali; all these possess great strength, being lords of the field and protectors of the field. (80)
When worshipped, they grant all desires, even when offered individually; and outside of these, in the cardinal directions, in the same sequence as before. (81)
With mantras such as "Those hosts in the eastern direction who hold thunderbolts in their hands and possess great strength," one should scatter the bali offering as previously described.
Then, at the end of the designated day, having performed the formal vow (saṃkalpa) for the pilgrimage as before and having completed it, he should bathe [the image] according to his means.
Having dismissed all the Gaṇas and the deities of the junction as before, and having given the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) and abundant food and drink, [he should proceed]. (84)
All that is desired by oneself, whether its fruit be visible or invisible, is said to be "distinguished.

Thus, having examined the *Kṣetrapāla-tantra* according to the tradition—including the rites of installation and so forth up to the festival—in brief, this has been sung here; it is to be inferred accordingly.
And everything is in accordance with the Śaiva tradition. || 85½ ||
Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, the Kṣetrapālatantra-paṭala, in the Kriyāpāda of the Upper Section of the Siddhāntasāra, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva.

Now begins the sixty-first chapter. Furthermore, when the medicinal herbs have ripened, in the months of Śrāvaṇa, Aśvayuja, Pauṣa, or Phālguna, the offering of fresh oblations (navanaivedya) is prescribed.
On a lunar mansion presided over by the respective deity, the king who establishes a village,
preceded by the ritual sowing of seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa), should act under favorable constellations and astrological ascendants.
For the purpose of plowing, preceded by a ceremonial procession with weapons from an auspicious moment,
the Guru [should proceed] while the laborers, having bathed, are accompanied by the sounds of musical instruments, songs, and the like.
Together with those wearing white garments and holding sacrificial grass (darbha) in their hands, and accompanied by a witness, one should circumambulate the field and offer an oblation of curd-rice.
Having offered the sacrificial strainer (lavitra) with a blade to Soma, to the plants, to the Earth, and to the Guardian of the Field,
he should face either the east or the north.
Having first harvested the rice and other grains, one should subsequently gather a handful of mung beans, black gram, and so forth.
Then, laborers shall carry loads of medicinal herbs, fruits, and vegetables, as well as sugarcane roots and other such items.
One should perform the circumambulation of the village and so forth with the sounds of songs and other music; having brought [the image] inside the temple, they recite the Svasti-sūkta.

The twice-born should recite the Śakuna-sūkta and scatter flowers and unbroken grains (akṣata) over it; however, this should be done only after a svastika and a lotus have been fashioned with flour in the pavilion.
Having placed a pitcher made of gold or one of the other [metals] in its center and having filled it with water,
Soma, the lord of medicinal herbs, is to be worshipped therein.
In that [place] which has been thoroughly adorned on all sides with auspicious sprouts, lamps, and so forth,
one should place a heap of grain and worship according to the prescribed rite.
One should worship the goddess Śrī, known as Suprabhā, the sovereign of all medicinal herbs; then, in a well-smeared and beautifully adorned storehouse, one should proceed.
One should perform the gathering of grain when Jupiter is in Jāmitra, during the rising of Saturn or its navāṃśa,
and when the moon is in Udvela or in the sign of Varuṇa (Cancer).
Then, having decorated the temple and other structures with rice grains and ears of grain, along with bilva leaves, aśvattha sprouts, and indravallī creepers tied together.
He saw the mortar, the pestle, the winnowing basket, the prastha-measure, and so forth,
as well as well-husked rice being prepared by well-adorned women.

Having washed and consecrated the food offering (*naivedya*) according to the procedure for cooked sacrificial rice (*caru*), and having likewise washed nine white unbroken grains (*akṣata*) with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), [one should offer them]. (16)
At the arrival of an auspicious moment, [he should offer] rice mixed with cow's milk and honey, consecrated with the root-mantras and the [other] limbs, as well as fresh sacrificial porridge (caru).
First, one should offer [the oblation] to the Sun and Vighneśa, and then present it to the deity;
furthermore, one should perform the fire-sacrifice (homa) with clarified butter for the retinue deities in the fire.

One hundred and eight oblations should be offered with the root mantra, and a tenth part of that for the forms and the limbs; likewise, offerings should be made with rice and fresh grain to the medicinal herbs by their respective names.
Having offered oblations to Soma and Suprabhā, he offers the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti);
he should then give the remaining rice grains to the king and others in due order.
Then one should offer the *bhūtabali* to the teacher, to the disciples, to the Brahmins, to those who seek, to those bearing sectarian marks (*liṅgin*), and to the attendants.
The Chapter on Fresh Offerings:
On the full moon day of Kārttika, and especially under the Kṛttikā nakṣatra,
one should perform the festival of lights for Śambhu and for the other enemies of the Asuras.
Likewise, on the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight of Āśvayuja,
as well as in Phālguna under the asterism Uttaraphalgunī, and during the two equinoxes and the two solstices, [the rite] is prescribed.
One should perform it in the month of Pauṣa under the Puṣya asterism, or in Caitra under Citrā— the deity of which is Indra-Agni— or in Vaiśākha, or even on days of great festivals.
Having performed the rite of offering sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) seven or five days prior,
one should place beautiful, straight lamp-stands on all sides, together with their bases.
Having raised [the pillars] outside the neck of the temple to a height equal to it, positioned at intervals of two or three cubits, and having fixed their tops [with capitals] upon them; || 26 ||
One should drive stakes into those [spaces], twelve finger-breadths apart, which are provided with upward-covering and bound by bamboo and its derivatives.

[One should calculate] those [mandalas] measured by three, five, eight, eleven, eleven, and seven [units], as well as the primary and secondary [mandalas] and so forth, by means of the hanging series of inner lamps. 28.
There should be as many tiers of lamp-rows in due order; however, at the location of the banner, there should be a principal lamp-tree, elevated like a banner. (29)
Having raised it from its base to its tip, one should cause rows of lamps to be made;
in its corners starting from the southeast (vahni), with a distance of seven hand-spans between each.
Having constructed a set of four altars adorned with archways and other ornaments, and having prepared sacrificial pits upon them,
one should perform the Puṇyāha ceremony.

On the preceding day, at night, before the deity, on a sacrificial mound of sand or in a fire consecrated by the five purificatory rites, [one should offer] fuel-sticks of *palāśa* wood and clarified butter.

One should offer milk and sacrificial porridge (caru) in sequence with the root-mantras and the limb-mantras of the Brahmā-mantra; then, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the Gāyatrī, one should proceed to the northeast of the fire.
Upon the lotus on the rice-field altar, one should place nine shallow bowls; filled separately with a *prastha* measure of clarified butter and provided with wicks, one should light them.

Having worshipped that [deity] in the fire with the Heart-mantra and the nine powers beginning with Vāmā, and having offered oblations for victory and other purposes, he performs the expiatory oblations.
After performing the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, one should subsequently tie the protective amulet (*kautuka*) on the lamp-tree,
preceded by the sounds of singing, dancing, and musical instruments.
Having completed the daily morning rites, one should then worship Śiva with special offerings. Then, there should be three, two, or one large earthen vessel (mahāśarāva) consecrated by Śiva.
Having placed the best [wick] and so forth upon the top of the lamp-tree, one should fill it with either ghee or oil, and then insert the wick into it. || 38 ||
Having prepared [the altar] with new cloths of ten, eight, or six palas, of the finest quality and so forth,
one should then divide the fire on the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) among the corners, the pavilion, and the fire-pits (kuṇḍa).
Having placed [the offerings] in the fires and other [sacrificial sites], beginning with Brahmā and ending with Īśvara,
[he offers] fuel-sticks of palāśa, vaṭa, śamī, and arka, as well as clarified butter and sacrificial porridge (caru).
Having offered oblations at the foot of the lamp-tree, one should worship Sadāśiva; having adorned the base of the lamp-tree with garments and other offerings. (41)
p.

590) That rite of lighting lamps should be performed with the sounds of musical instruments, songs, and so forth. Then, having offered the oblation to Śiva, the Guru, having received permission, [proceeds]. || 42 ||
Having unified the previously ignited lamps of power (śakti) in sequence,
one should lead them from their state in the vessel of Manonmanī down to the base of the tree of light.
Having bathed, wearing white garments, pure and well-attired, the attendant,
taking a spear and a lamp, should ascend the lamp-tree.
One should join the lamp of power (*śaktidīpa*) with the great wick situated at its tip;
then, starting from that point, one should arrange all those rows of lamps on every side. (45)
They should cause lamps provided with abundant, smooth wicks to be lit, as if in an instant,
upon all the parts of the temple and in the dwellings of the attendants.
And having lit lamps filled with abundant oil in the pavilions and the sal trees,
they worshipped them with auspicious songs, musical instruments, and other such ceremonies.
One should conduct the preliminary procession of the festival image as before;
having performed a circumambulation outside the temple of all the lamps.
While the lamps are indeed blazing, having caused the Lord of Gods to enter within three or five times, one should then cast the offering for the spirits (bhūtabali).
Having acted in this manner for one night, or three nights, or five nights,
up to seven nights, during festivals ranging from the lowest and most inferior to the highest.
Every day, one should perform a special worship during the daytime, as well as the procession and the circumambulation of the village and so forth, just as before.
Then, at the conclusion of the pilgrimage, having performed the ritual bathing according to the prescribed rules,
one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and also provide food and other provisions without restriction.
Likewise, those men who behold the Festival of Lights with devotion,
having obtained enjoyments in this world, go to heaven, free from all affliction.
Even if one were to have thousands upon thousands of mouths here, a lifespan equal to that of Brahmā, and the eloquence of Bṛhaspati; (54)
Even so, it is impossible to describe the fruit of a single lamp; how then could one be capable of describing the fruit of lamps during the Festival of Lights and the like? (55)
Thus, in the Tantras, the procedure for the ninefold food offering (navanaivedya) has been shown exactly as enjoined; likewise,
the ritual of the lamps beginning with Kṛttikā is approved for Śiva and all the celestial beings.

Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, concerning the nine types of food offerings, the Kṛttikās, and the lamps, in the section on ritual action (kriyāpāda) of the second part of the *Siddhāntasāra*, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva.
Now begins the sixty-second chapter.
The funeral rites for all those who have passed away— whether they be practitioners, preceptors, or twice-born initiates— are now described.

Or, for one who is about to die or has already died, one should whisper into the right ear the mantras beginning with "āyuṣaḥ prāṇam," reciting them in sequence, each tied together with the root mantra.
Having offered the clarified butter with the verse "pareyivāṃsam" into the fire consecrated by him, the disciple, or else the wife or the son, should loosen his hair and bathe him.
Having placed gold in the mouth and covered it with new garments— up to the point of reciting "idaṃ tvā vastreṇa"—
and having tied [the offerings] between the two thumbs with a blade of darbha grass, [one offers] ghee, curd, unbroken rice, and sesame seeds.
One should lead a water-pot and gold in front, saying "May Pūṣan [lead]";
[and one should carry] a new, very sturdy palanquin constructed from bamboo, wood, and other materials.
Having covered it with red garments, adorned with banners, garlands, and other ornaments,
encircled by a wreath of *darbha* grass, and having placed upon it a well-spread [seat], || 6 ||
Here, the disciples and others, having bathed, wearing their sacred threads over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītins), all clad in single wet garments and reciting mantras, shall carry the weapons.
Another person, taking a blazing fire in a vessel,
should go ahead toward the exterior of the village or similar place, at a distance from it but near a river or other such body of water.
Having lowered the palanquin onto the path at one-third of its length,
and having strewn it all around with *darbha* grass, may they protect you from the left according to the mantra.
May his sons and others also circumambulate him with the right hand first and the left hand behind; may they drive away misfortune from us with their own splendor and cause it to perish. (10)
Furthermore, if the gentle carriers should stop while looking at the life-force being led away,
one should restrain them and lead it back again.
Having lowered the corpse onto a litter upon pure ground,
one should dig a funeral pyre extending from south to north, leaving a space for the eight Vasus on the earth.
Having made a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) to the south, measuring two cubits in width and four cubits in length, sloping toward the north,
square-shaped, and provided with a single girdle.
With that clay, one should prepare a square sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in the northwest;
it should be one cubit in size, six parts in height, well-smeared, and there should be three such mounds.

Then his son or his disciple, having bathed and performed the purificatory rites appropriate for the occasion, should proceed clockwise around the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) while remaining with the minister.
Seated facing north, having fixed his body in the posture of withdrawal (saṃhāra), he should perform the ritual of self-protection (sakalīkaraṇa) and empower himself with the weapon-mantra (astra).
Having sprinkled all of that with water, one should place the Pāśupata weapon there upon the vardhanī vessel on top of the scattered offerings within the northeastern mandala of the altar.
Having constructed the secondary compartments upon the funeral pyre using five squares,
one should place the elements beginning with earth (pṛthvī) in their midst, specifically within the central pentad of squares belonging to the element of earth.
Thereafter, one should worship Brahmā; then, in four separate compartments, those of Wind, Protector (Rakṣas), Fire, and the Wielder of the Trident (Śūlin), along with Water and Fire. 19.

Having worshipped Viṣṇu and the other four [deities] in their respective chambers, and having worshipped the world-protectors (lokapālas) and their weapons in the four directions in reverse order; || 20 ||
On the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila), however, one should worship Dharmā, Vāmā, and the others in reverse order; having scattered ashes mixed with sesame seeds upon it, one should worship Śiva.
Having offered oblations into that fire in the pit along with Śiva, he offers the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti);
[he then offers] wooden stakes with their tips downward, wrapped with red thread.

One should place [the materials] counter-clockwise with the Astra-mantra in the southeast corner and the other directions; then, having filled the pit with fuel, one should fill it with kuśa grass, flowers, sesame seeds, and unbroken rice grains.

Having scattered [the obstacles] with the *vikīryāstra* mantra and worshipped [the deity], one who is clothed in inverted garments should establish [the image], purified with earth, cow dung, and water, and also with ashes. (24)
Having covered [the corpse] with new garments and seated it near the sacrificial pit, one should [perform the rite] upon that body purified by concentration (dhāraṇā) using the Saṃhāriṇī mudrā.
One should unite that consciousness with its name followed by "namaḥ"; having ascertained its body of knowledge (vidyādeha), [one should place it] in its head, heart, navel, and private parts.

Thereafter, one should assign the digits (kalās) beginning with the past (atītā), and then the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva). Having assigned Śakti and Śiva, one should then [proceed] for the sake of the abiding of consciousness (caitanya).

Having offered a hundred oblations of clarified butter with the root mantra, and having sequentially assigned the kalās beginning with Nivṛtti to the fire, one should worship it, performing the invocation of Śiva and the other deities.

One should perform the striking, the separation, the extraction of consciousness, and so forth, as well as the purification by bathing that ends with birth, eligibility, and experience, and the final expiation. (29)
Concealment, the severing of bonds, crushing, the making of a circle, the body,
the causal material cause, and likewise the transfer of authority.
Having performed the union of consciousness with Śiva and completed the ritual acts,
he should place him upon the funeral pyre with his head facing south, and cover him with fuel.

One should have his wife lie down [with him] as "this woman" while he is accompanied by his wife; having cast gold at the doors, one should [protect] him with the mantras beginning with "Agnim" and so forth.
One should kindle [the fire] with the very fire situated in the saṃsṛṣṭi-kuṇḍa; when the fire blazes, one should cause the full oblation to fall upon his head with this [mantra]. || 33 ||
Oṃ!
O Agni, you who are the southern portion, accept this great oblation, purified by mantra and offered by Śāvya, which has been brought forth by Time itself. 34.
Thus:

"May he not harm him with fire, etc."—having recited this preceded by [the appropriate ritual action], one should also mutter the six verses beginning with "The sun is your eye" (*sūryas te cakṣuḥ*). || 35 ||
The Hotṛ priest, having offered nine oblations with clarified butter along this path, casts the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and the water-jar (*karkarī*) face-downward into the fire.
Whirling it counter-clockwise near the shoulder of one who possesses outflows (āsrava), and having sprinkled [the area] with its water, he,
having bathed, should deposit it back in its original place. || 37 ||
When the body has been reduced to ashes, without looking back, one should go and bathe with the *dhātāpunaḥ* mantras; then, having bathed, one should sit upon a bank strewn with *kuśa* grass.
Placing the left knee on the ground, one should offer a handful of water with the words "This is for you,
[Name]," using these three mantras in succession.
Oṃ hāṃ, O pure self, become the Lord; svāhā! Oṃ hāṃ, O pure self, become Sadāśiva; svāhā! Oṃ hāṃ, O pure self, become peaceful; svāhā!
They should perform the water-rites there with the names of the mantras ending in "iti";
then, having bathed and worshipped the Sun with the hymn beginning with "ud vayaṃ tamasaspari," [they should proceed].
On dry ground smeared with [cow-dung] and strewn with darbha grass, one should offer the bali-oblation by means of one's own name;
this applies to the preparer as well as the disciples, sons, wife, and others. (41)
They should observe a fast and sleep on the ground at night; their impurity lasts for ten days, during which they should eat only once a day and only by day.
Having avoided anointing the body, as well as the use of cosmetics, betel, and the like, and having refrained from riding in vehicles and similar activities, if one should touch this guru; 43.
One becomes pure merely by bathing; those such as a carrier [of the corpse] become pure after three days; and mothers, fathers, brothers, sons, and so forth, after ten days.
The disciples as well shall be purified merely by bathing, as shall other people, on the fourth or fifth day, or on the ninth and eleventh days.
The śrāddha that is being offered is called the *navaśrāddha*; all of his kinsmen should perform worship and other rites for its sake. (46)
Then, on the third day, for the purpose of collecting the bones, one should fill a water-jar with milk and water and place the bones therein.
Therefore, one should either bury it in sacred fords such as the Gaṅgā or cast it away;
for one who seeks liberation, no concern for funeral rites exists here in this world.
If one who desired worldly enjoyment dies, his consecration (saṃskāra) and post-mortem rites (ūrdhvakriyā) are prescribed; [these are performed] for ten days, increasing by one each day. (49)

Water mixed with sesame seeds should be offered using the root-mantra of that [deceased]; then, having performed the śrāddha rites during the period of the intermediate daśās, one should do so on the eleventh day.
Having smeared himself [with ashes], bathed within the monastery, and prepared the rice, he should select a single distinguished Brāhmaṇa who is knowledgeable in the Śiva-āstra.
Having resolved, "For the sake of the sign," and having performed the washing of the feet and other preliminaries, he should seat [the recipient] facing north upon *darbha* grass and worship him.
On a sacrificial mound or in a worldly fire that has been spread around in the reverse manner,
one should place cakes, condiments, cooked food, and other offerings outside the enclosing sticks (paridhi).

Having performed the rites ending with the *praṇītā* water, one should place *kuśa* grass with their tips pointing south within a circular mandala of fire to the south, and upon them, one should set down the vessel.

Having filled that [vessel] with water and placed a tuft of grass (kūrca) inside, one should perform the taking of the *svadhā* offering, beginning with the mantra: "O deceased one, come hither" (*āma āgacchatu preta*). || 55 ||
One should say to Antaka: "I accept this *svadhā* for you, the deceased. If a woman is the cause [of the offering], one should utter the words ending with the feminine gender. (56)

But everywhere, [the mantras] beginning with "for the departed" (*yathāpreta*) and so forth, as well as "Thou art sesame, Soma is thy deity" (*tilo 'si somadevatyaḥ*) and "O honeyed wind" (*madhuvātā*), [should be recited]. || 57 ||
Then one should add honey; first, having purified it with all the fingers, one should extract whatever portion belongs to the splendor of Soma.

Having placed [the vessel] inside a pit protected from venomous snakes and other dangers, and having touched it while reciting "śanno devī" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.7.6) and "vīrabhīṣṭaye," he should worship it and cover it with *kuśa* grass.

Facing south, he should cause that [deceased] to be invoked by the twice-born with the mantra beginning "Come, O Preta," while reciting the words "granting wealth and nourishment in me" into this [offering].
"In this Ekoddiṣṭa Śrāddha, let a moment be granted to the deceased. Having said this, he should touch the right hand of the recipient with both hands holding Darbha grass.
"May I perform the *kṣaṇa* [rite]; Oṃ, let it be so," he should say; then one should say, "May you obtain this," and he too should say, "May I obtain it. (62)
Then, having placed water and the *svadhā* [offering] into his hand along with *darbha* grass, he should lift it up and offer it to the deceased while saying, "Svadhā namaḥ. (63)
Then one should worship him with water; thereafter, one should scatter sand and sesame seeds, reciting "Apo hi ṣṭhā," for protection on all sides.
Having sprinkled the vessel for eating with the first [verse] beginning with "udīrṭām," the mantra used therein should be in the singular number; for a woman, it should end in the feminine suffix.

Thereafter, when told, "I shall take it out and offer it into the fire," he should say, "Let it be taken out as you wish; let it be offered into the fire as you wish. Then, having performed the rites up to the mouth of the fire (agnimukha), having uncovered the cooked offerings and so forth, having sprinkled them with water while reciting the Astra-mantra, and having illuminated them with *darbha* grass and offered clarified butter over them (*abhighāra*).
Having scattered sesame seeds over them and sprinkled water, he then offers clarified butter into the fire with the *vyāhṛtis*.
Having spread a base of ghee in the ladle, taking portions from the entire [oblation] once each,
and having poured clarified butter over them, he draws out embers mixed with ash to the south [of the fire]— if he is initiated— or simply to the south— and offers [the oblation] upon them.
"Oblation to this deceased one and to Yama, Svāhā! To Agni Kavyavāhana Sviṣṭakṛt, Svadhā!
Adoration to the Auspicious One, Svāhā!"—this is the Sviṣṭakṛt oblation.
Having likewise offered with the Vyāhṛtis, let him sprinkle water around.
Without incense, lamps, [conch] sounds, or prostrations,

having fed a Brahmin with food consisting largely of pure rice-cakes, milk-rice, curd, milk, and fruit— regarding it as an auspicious omen— one should, from the remnants of what he has eaten, [place them] to the south of the fire upon southward-pointed [grass].

Upon *darbha* grass, one should offer a rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) soaked in sesame, honey, and clarified butter with this [mantra]: "Om! May this food be a cow of plenty (*kāmadugha*), free from blindness, inexhaustible, fragrant, and fulfilling all desires.
May it attend upon you—ageless, eternally pure, milking forth the *svadhā* offering for the sake of the immortals."

"May it satisfy [the deceased]; may the piṇḍa reach such-and-such a departed one. One should sprinkle water containing nourishment and food with that which is called *svadhā*. To him who has had his hands sprinkled, one should then give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Whatever may be useful to him—such as houses, fields, wealth, and so forth, as well as ornaments and the like—all that having bestowed upon this person, [one should give it]. (67)
Having thrown a ball of rice into a river, or having bathed, one should perform the rite for an auspicious day;
then, having given that food and other provisions without restriction, one should fast oneself.
Having performed the rites, the performer shall fast for three days at the conclusion of the ekoddiṣṭa, as well as after one year;
on the following day, he may eat.
Having thus performed the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite along with the offering of water and food,
one should continue to give [these offerings] every day according to the procedure for the *ekoddiṣṭa*. (70)

Likewise, one should offer the monthly *śrāddha* on the anniversary of the month, and similarly the three-fortnightly *śrāddha* at the end of three fortnights; likewise, one should offer the monthly *śrāddha* as well as the funeral rice-balls (*piṇḍas*). (71)
Then, for one less than six months and likewise for one less than a year,
[one should perform] twelve monthly Śrāddhas and sixteen Piṇḍas.
It is traditionally taught that the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite should be performed at the end of one year;
having made the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) for it on the preceding day, one should select distinguished twice-born brahmins.
On another day, having bathed and prepared cooked rice along with cakes, side dishes, and so forth,
he should serve it to pure, bathed Brahmins in the manner of preparing a *caru* oblation.
Having prepared two sacrificial altars (sthaṇḍila) with cow-dung and water on the south and north,
one should place one's own fire on the south and likewise a common worldly fire on the north.
Having taken [the offerings] for the sake of the Viśvedevas and having invited two Brāhmaṇas facing east,
he should perform the washing of their feet and other rites, and then seat them facing east.
Having performed the *kṣaṇa* rite, he should then pour water over the darbha grass held in their hands;
having prepared the *arghya* with barley and water, and recollecting the nectar (*sudhā*), he should cast it [into the fire].

"Viśvebhyo devebhyaḥ svadhā namaḥ svāhā. Following that, having selected a suitable twice-born man for the purpose of the rite as before, three twice-born men [are assigned] to the father, the grandfather, and his father.
If it is a woman, she should be given to a maternal uncle; in that case, there should be three twice-born men for each such maternal uncle.
All of them must be endowed with noble lineage, Vedic learning, and proper conduct, and be devoted to Śiva.
Having honored them and divided all that food and other offerings into two parts,
he should place that portion intended for the gods into a vessel and sprinkle it with water.

Then, with those two [fingers], excluding the nails and the thumbs, he should show [the offering] to the Viśvedevas with the words "To the Viśvedevas," ending with "svāhā," while shifting the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvīta).
In the same manner, having performed the *nivāpa* and so forth, he should scatter sesame seeds along with sand,
reciting the verse "udīratām avaraḥ" while pronouncing the names of the ancestors.
p.
598) Having sprinkled the locations as before, one should then place the vessels separately upon *darbha* grass with tips pointing south, to the south of the worldly fire (*laukikāgni*). || 83 ||

One should set aside all cooked food toward the north and perform the rite of circumambulation with fire; then, when the vessels have been prepared, one should offer the *svadhā* oblation to the ancestors and others in due order.
Having performed [the preliminary rites] as before, he should cast sesame seeds while reciting "tilo 'si" and so forth; then [he recites] "madhu vātā" and "madhu somasya tviṣiḥ āditaḥ. (85)
Having ground [the ingredients] and cast away the venomous snakes as previously instructed, [he should say]:
"O raw [grains], come from the east, preceded by the names of the ancestors and others. (86)
Having uttered "svadhā" and consecrated it with the mantra "śanno devīḥ," he should touch [the food];
then, having honored those twice-born ones and covered them with *darbha* grass, their feet should be washed. 87.
Having seated all of them— those for the sake of the ancestors and others on the south, and those for the sake of the deceased on the north— upon seats of darbha grass, facing north.

Having been told "I shall perform [the rite] in the fire as before," and having been answered "So be it," [he performs the rites] from the Paridhāna [offering] in the south, up to the end of the Agnimukha, without piercing the fire.
With the *sruva* ladle, he offers clarified butter in five portions while reciting these mantras:
"Those which arise in the east," etc., is the first; "I have hidden myself behind the mountains," etc., is the second; "I have hidden myself behind the seasons," etc., is the third.
The fourth [offering] begins with "yan me mātā" and so forth; the fifth begins with "yad vastapyādam" and so forth.
Having divided the cake into eight parts, one offers them in portions beginning with "somāya" and so forth. || 90 ||

O Agni, carrier of the *kavyas*, accompanied by the Aṅgirases for our protection— having offered three oblations of the three-part [sacrificial materials] and having taken up the ladle (*sruc*) from there— 91.
One should offer oblations of cooked rice, barley gruel, and the remnants of the clarified butter from the fire-sacrifice, stirring them with a ladle,
preceded by the libations to the ancestors.
Then, for Agni Kavyavāhana, [he offers] in the eastern part of the southern half.

Having performed the ritual actions ending with the sprinkling and the throwing [of the grass], having touched [the vessel] with the formula "The earth is your vessel," and having sprinkled water around the northern fire, he spreads a base of ghee in the ladle.
Having cut off portions from all [the substances] once each and having sprinkled them with clarified butter,
one should remove embers mixed with ash to the south and, upon them, offer: *oṃ pretāyāmuṣmai yamāya ca svāhā | agnaye kavyavāhanāya sviṣṭakṛte svadhā namaḥ*.
One should offer the oblation with "svāhā. Having sprinkled water around in the same manner, one should take the prepared food and other offerings for the Viśvedevas as before.

Having placed [the food] into the two vessels, touched it while reciting "The earth is your vessel," and having caused the food to touch the tips of the ring fingers and thumbs with the mantra beginning "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," [he places it] into the hands of the ancestors and others who have been invited, which hold *pavitra* grass.
As before, having poured pure water with the *svadhā* names into those vessels,

having touched the food and other offerings therein, and having given them water for rinsing the mouth in their hands, he should likewise contemplate that the Immortal is established in the vital breath (*prāṇa*) of the recipient.

He himself recites in sequence the mantras for the oblations to the vital breaths (*prāṇāhuti*), beginning with "I offer" (*juhomīti*). They, in turn, should offer [the oblations] into their respective mouths. He himself causes the proclamation of the *abhiśrāvaṇa* verses, such as "Make ready thy vigor" (*kṛṇuṣva pājaḥ*), verse by verse, in the manner of the *rākṣoghna* (demon-slaying) rites.
He mutters the *Ṛgveda* hymns beginning with *dahāśasa*, the *prācīsūkta*, the *triṇāciketa*, the *trisuparṇa*, and the *īśāna*.
Then, when they have finished eating, showing them the *mekalana* food (?), he should ask, "Are you satisfied? (*tṛptā stha*)?
They should say, "We are satisfied. He then scatters that food, along with water, upon the ground while circumambulating it clockwise, with this [mantra]:
"Those in my family who were consumed by fire, those who died untimely deaths, and those not consumed by fire—by what is given on the earth..."
"May they be satisfied; being satisfied, may they go to the supreme goal.

Then, having gratified the ancestors and others with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and garments, and having raised them up in due order, he should subsequently seek permission regarding the remaining food and other items for the specific purpose.
Having offered oblations into the northern fire with the *vyāhṛtis* and performed the remaining rites, he should dismiss that fire; then,

having poured the water from the vessel of the deceased into the *svadhā*-vessels of the ancestors and others in due order, he should join them together with the three verses beginning with "The honeyed winds for the righteous one" (*madhu vātā ṛtāyate*) and the two verses beginning with "Unite [with us]" (*saṅgacchadhvam*).
To the south of the fire, having strewn *darbha* grass from the right side,
he offers the rice balls (*piṇḍas*) with the mantras for the libation to the ancestors (*pitṛtarpaṇa*), honors them, covers them with *darbha* grass,
and then joins the rice ball of the deceased (*preta-piṇḍa*) into the rice balls of the ancestors in three ways; the mantra is the same.

With the two verses beginning with *saptitih* and *samānī va ākūtiḥ*, he should unify the rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) for the father and the others; then, with the two verses beginning with *atha ye samānāḥ* and *ye sajātāḥ*, he should pay homage to them.
