By that means, he unifies the waters from the *svadhā*-vessels.

He sprinkles water around the *piṇḍas*. Then, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*), having performed the oblations beginning with the *jaya* offerings and ending with the expiation (*prāyaścitta*), and having completed the ritual up to the granting of the boon to the cow (*āghenu-varapradāna*), he dismisses the ancestors and the deities.
Having received permission from the gateway, he [distributes the remains] to the twice-born, to those bearing sectarian marks (*liṅgin*), and to those who are needy.
Having given food, drink, and sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to his own kinsmen without restriction, with the intention of dedicating them to Śiva,
he should perform the worship of Śiva for their sake. If he is capable, he should install a liṅga for that purpose and arrange for its worship and other rites according to his means.
And having associated the deceased with the desired enjoyments of heaven and so forth,
he himself also attains the pleasures of this world and the next.
This concludes the section on the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite.
Likewise, on that same day every year, [one should perform the rite] for one's mother and father, as well as for one's brother, maternal uncle, teacher, and other kinsmen.
One should perform the annual Śrāddha, dedicating it to those various [ancestors] according to one's capacity.
Now, the procedure for the Aṣṭakā-Śrāddha is described here with full concentration.
And it is said in the Purāṇas and other texts:
"The thirteenth and fifteenth days of the dark fortnight of the month of Nabhasya, and [the same] in Māgha."
"In the eclipse of the moon and the sun, in the three Aṣṭakās, and also in the two solstices"—
this reading is seen in the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"In the eclipses of the moon and the sun, in the three Aṣṭakās, and in the two solstices."
A self-restrained man should also offer water mixed with sesame seeds here to the ancestors;
that water and food offered there provides satisfaction for ten thousand years to the men born in his lineage.
Thus it is said. Furthermore:
"On all new moon days, on the thirteenth and eighth days of the lunar fortnights, especially during the dark fortnight, and on the *vyatīpāta* and *kṣaya* [yogas]."
On the equinox, on the fifth lunar day, upon the arrival of new grain and the like,
when visiting sacred fields or pilgrimage sites, and when a Vedic scholar has come to one's home.
Or, having seen one's ancestors in a dream, one should perform the *śrāddha* with devotion,
[inviting] the best of the twice-born who are endowed with noble lineage, good character, sacred learning, and right conduct.

O twice-born ones, on the previous day, at night, those who are pure should especially select Śiva-devotees for the task of cooking the sacrificial oblation (caru) upon the hearths, according to the prescribed method.
Having bathed and wearing white garments, they should prepare that oblation; for a śrāddha, all grains—both cultivated and wild—are recommended.
Having excluded those grains that grow in cultivated fields, as well as chickpeas, kodrava, shriveled grains, millet,
and especially flat beans.
Among fruits, the *kakubha*, *abdhamala*, and *ambuka* are well-known; likewise, the *bimba* and *trāpuṣa* [are known], and among roots, the *laśuna*.
One should also avoid onions, radishes, and various leafy vegetables; for salt, asafoetida, and black pepper must be avoided at a śrāddha.
Spices, oil-cakes, and oil for anointing—these are recommended, except when used as an ointment; likewise, milk, curd, and clarified butter from cows are excellent, as are those from buffaloes.
Goat and sheep meat are middling, while curdled milk and sour gruel are low; these should be avoided.
(The Viśvedevas and the twice-born are pleased.

One should properly feed those who have arrived— those who are pleasant-faced, firm in their vows, purified by ritual bathing, and especially learned in the Vedas— preceded by the washing of their feet and other rites.
Regarding this, there is a traditional teaching (smṛti):
"Three things are purifying at a śrāddha: a daughter's son, a kutapa blanket, and sesame seeds; and three things they praise here: purity, freedom from anger, and lack of haste."
When the sun has become weak in the eighth part of the day, that is the time called Kutapa; what is given to the ancestors during that time becomes inexhaustible.
Satisfaction for one month is attained through milk; satisfaction for one year, however, through milk-rice (pāyasa).
Through honey, clarified butter, and milk-rice, satisfaction shall last for twelve years.

Regarding the ancestors: the forenoon, the two twilights, the Nandā tithis, the fourteenth day, the days of Venus, Mercury, and Jupiter, and the birth asterism of the performer [are to be avoided] at the [appropriate] times.

Then, having smeared a square mandala one cubit in extent with cow-dung in the courtyard, and having spread darbha grass with its tips pointing eastward along with barley and unbroken grains (akṣata),
one should offer water for the feet (pādya) with barley to an even number of Brahmins upon that [mandala], regarding them with the thought that they are the Viśvedevas.
Having given [water] and washed their feet with earth and water, and having had them sip water (ācamana),
he should lead them inside and seat them facing east upon seats provided with *darbha* grass. Thereafter, to the west,
upon a circular mandala marked with *darbha* grass whose tips point south, [he should seat] the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather in uneven numbers.

Having first offered water for the *arghya* oblation mixed with sesame seeds, he should lead the twice-born— who have washed their feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*)— inside; then, seating them facing north upon seats of *darbha* grass, he should further seat them on a mandala to the south of the *pitṛ*-mandala, which is prepared with *darbha* grass whose tips point toward the south, accompanied by sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).

For the mother, paternal grandmother, and paternal great-grandmother, as before, having caused the Brahmins— who have performed the purification of their feet— to enter there, immediately thereafter [one should offer] for the maternal grandfather,
maternal great-grandfather, and maternal great-great-grandfather, together with their wives.

Having seated the Brahmins as before and having invited them with the mantra beginning "āyantu pitaraḥ," he should offer the *svadhā* to the ancestors (fathers and so on), the maternal ancestors (mothers and so on), and the maternal grandfathers (maternal grandfathers and so on) into three vessels using the mantras as before, and [ward off obstacles] with the weapon-mantra beginning "apahatā asurāḥ."

Having scattered sesame seeds mixed with sand and, while they hold *darbha* grass in their hands, having separately offered pure water and *svadhā*-water to them in sequence according to the previous mantras,
and having worshipped the ancestors in reverse order, [he offers] the sacrificial food (*caru*) and other items consecrated as before.

One should offer oblations for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. The specific difference, however, is that after the offering of the rice-cakes (*apūpa*), one should recite the fifteen-verse hymn beginning with "This very [light] first shone forth" (*iyameva sāyāt prathamā vyaucchat*) and the single verse "for the sacrifice" (*yuṣṭaye*), as well as the monthly [oblation] for the year, with the mantra: *oṃ agnaye kavyavāhanāya*.

One should offer oblations with "Svadhā namas śivāya svāhā," and so forth, to Soma who consists of the ancestors, to Yama, to Aryaman, to Aṅgiras, and to the Agniṣvāttas, the Barhiṣads, the Somapas, and the Ūṣmapas. [The offering of] clarified butter— [with its tip facing eastward]...
p.
602) Having placed a portion of that remaining food individually into the vessels of the ancestors and others, he spreads clarified butter over it with sesame seeds. Then—
Having divided the food— abounding in rice, milk-rice, ghee, molasses, cakes, and fruits— into three portions, he first offers one portion to the gods; then,
having sprinkled it with water and consecrated it with mantras by means of a man, he places sesame seeds upon the food intended for the ancestors and others.

Having scattered [the oblation] with the *aghora* mantra and sprinkled it around with the *vāmadeva* mantra, one should lead the hand of the recipient— which is not turned upward— clockwise around the oblation with one's own hand turned upward; then, with the tip of that respective thumb, one should offer the oblation to Viṣṇu with the mantra beginning "idaṃ viṣṇu."
Saying "Protect [this]," having touched the foods and taken water in his own hand, he should offer the food with the formula:
"In this *śrāddha*, this food given and yet to be given to the Viśvedevas until satisfaction—all that is not mine; it is for immortality (*amṛta*). Thus is the eating.
The person should offer [the water] with the mantra, "Thou art the under-layer of nectar" (*amṛtopastaraṇam asi*). For the ancestors and others, it is exactly the same.

However, the specific difference is that one should touch [the vessel] with the words, "O Viṣṇu, protect the *kavya*," and with the formula beginning, "In this *śrāddha*, for the ancestors," and so forth. For the ancestors and others as well, the consumption of water is as before.
He should give them. And they should drink that water as before.

The sacrificer himself recites the mantras for the oblations to the vital breaths, such as "I offer the nectar seated in the prāṇa," and so forth; and they themselves should offer those oblations. Following that—
With the left hand placed between the knees and touching the vessel, and likewise with the right hand, they should eat in silence as they please;
the patron (*yajamāna*), facing north, should [recite] the *Īśāna-sampuṭa* and the *rakṣoghnas*.

While reciting the verses beginning with *kṛṇuṣva pājaḥ* and those beginning with *prācī*, as well as the *Trināciketa* and *Trisuparṇa* hymns, he should remain standing [as if performing the Jyeṣṭhasāman].
At that time, if a guest should arrive, he should honor him with the thought that he is the Lord himself.

One should feed the remaining [guests]. Then, when they are satisfied, one should take food with a ladle and show it to everyone, saying, "Are you satisfied? and they should reply, "We are satisfied. One should then scatter that food on the ground, [reciting]: "Those born in our family who have been consumed by fire, and those who have not been consumed by fire..."

Having scattered [the food] as before with the words, "May they be satisfied by what is given on my ground; being satisfied, may they go to the supreme state," and so forth, he should also give a handful [of water] with the mantra, "Thou art the covering of nectar" (*amṛtāpidhānam asi*).
Having drunk that and performed the rinsing of their hands, they should sit in the same manner within that very mandala.

Having scattered *darbha* grass with the right hand and sesame seeds with the left, and taking portions of the remnants of the meal mixed with sesame, clarified butter, curd, and honey, he should offer them to the ancestors and others with the mantras beginning with "This for you, O Father" (*etat te pitaḥ*) and ending with the root mantra, using the Īśa, Puruṣa, and Aghora mantras respectively. It is as follows: "This for you..."

"Obeisance and *svadhā* to your fathers, to those who were your maternal grandfathers, to those who were your teachers, to those who were your preceptors, to those who were your friends, to those who were your kinsmen, to those who were your ministers, to those who were your pupils, and to their wives; and to them and to those women, *svadhā* and obeisance. This is for you, O grandfather.

And so on. Likewise, with the words "Thus, O great-grandfathers," and so forth; and similarly, having offered three *piṇḍas* each to the maternal grandfather and the others, as well as to the paternal grandmother and the others, one should then place the remnants of the food upon the *darbha* grass on the ground.

Having scattered [the grains] here, he wipes with a small amount: "To those by whom fallen embryos are consumed, partaking of blood—to them, their own kin, be *svadhā* and homage; may they be satisfied and rejoice!
Those that are raw, those that are cooked, and those that are spoiled which fall upon us."

To them, who are born of themselves, be our own *svadhā* and obeisance; may they be satisfied and may they rejoice. Those children and those women who are unknown and fall upon us—[to them be this offering].

To them, who are self-born, [be] *svadhā* and obeisance; may they be satisfied and rejoice. Then, with the two verses beginning "Those who are equal" (*ye samānā*) and "Those who are kinsmen" (*ye sajātāḥ*), he should perform the ritual three times counter-clockwise (*apradakṣiṇam*) using his left hand, and [continue] with the verse beginning "Carrying strength" (*ūrjaṃ vahantīḥ*).

Having sprinkled water around the base [of the vessels] and having given the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consisting of clothing, ornaments, gold, and so forth, one should turn the *svadhā* vessel face upwards. Then, having caused the twice-born to rise by grasping their hands with the *puruṣasūkta* and the verse beginning with "vāje-vāje," etc., [one should proceed].

Having circumambulated [the fire], the patron bows down. And those Brahmins should pronounce blessings with the words "saṃpitaraḥ" and so forth. When asked by the patron, "What shall be done with the remnants of the food?", they should respond with the word "iṣṭaiḥ" (as desired).
Having said, "Let it be enjoyed together," he should depart. He should follow them as far as the door.

Then, having offered twenty-four rice-balls with the mantras for the libation to the ancestors (*pitṛtarpaṇa*), excluding the word *svāhā*, and having sprinkled water around them as before with the mantra "ūrjaṃ vahantīḥ," [he should proceed].

Having performed the rite beginning with the *jaya* offerings and ending with the expiation (*prāyaścitta*), and having bestowed the gift of a cow as a boon, he should release the fire after completing the actions up to the sprinkling of the *praṇītā* water. Thereafter, the wife who desires a son consumes the middle *piṇḍa* with the mantra beginning, "O Fathers, take this... and so forth. Then...

Having fed other Brahmins as well, and eating the remnants of the offering for the ancestors together with his sons, friends, servants, and others, he attains all desires pertaining both to this world and the next.
Thus has been declared this procedure for the final rites (antyēṣṭi), as well as the separate rules for the *navaśrāddha*.
With sixteen [offerings]; then, having determined the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* and the *aṣṭakā* rites according to the procedure as declared in the Tantras.
Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, on the funeral rites (antyeṣṭi), in the Kriyāpāda of the Upper Section of the Siddhāntasāra, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva.

Now begins the sixty-third chapter. For the pacification of errors such as omissions or slips, and for those [errors] that are extraordinary, the expiation for both regular and occasional rites is now proclaimed.
When the number of people performing the purification of the discarded offerings (nirmālya) is reduced to three, two, or one,
one should respectively bathe and worship [the deity] with the minor ablutions (kaniṣṭha-snāna).
If the remains of offerings (nirmālya) remain upon the head of the Liṅga during the twilight hours,
it destroys the divine presence and causes the loss of the King’s power.
If there is a deficiency in incense, there will be poverty; if there is a deficiency in flowers, there is the loss of prosperity.
Worship that is devoid of incense and lamps bestows disease and suffering.

If the food offering (*naivedya*) is deficient, there will be famine; if the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) is neglected, there will be fear of drought in the kingdom; and if the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) is cut off, there will be the destruction of the subjects. (5)
If there is a cessation of the daily festival, there will always be fear of an enemy army; if the great festival is interrupted, there will be the destruction of both the king and the performer.
Therefore, a wise person should not omit any ritual service;
for through such performance, prosperity increases.
Even if one falls away from worship in this life due to negligence or obstacles, [the merit remains].
Having performed worship doubled for each [of the previous rites], one should recite the Aghora mantra a hundred times;
for if the sacrifice to the bull is omitted, the destruction of the cows will surely occur.
For the pacification of that [evil omen], the worship of a bull should be performed twice as much;
for if the festival is held without a banner, the king will suffer affliction from his enemies. || 9 ||

Or, upon the breaking of that banner, a plague increases in the kingdom; for its pacification, however, one should perform an oblation in the fire within the northeastern sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) using the mantra of Vṛṣabha.

Having offered oblations with the eight [mantras] beginning with *samit*, one should worship both the bull and Śiva. This means that once again, having raised the banner, one should proceed with the festival. If it is devoid of the auspicious sprouts (*maṅgalāṅkura*), there will be misfortune for kings and others.

Having offered oblations with the *Tiyambaka* and other mantras, one should worship Śiva with special rites; for if the binding of the protective thread (*kautuka*) is omitted, the protection of the kingdom perishes.

There, having offered oblations of clarified butter with the Traiyambaka mantra and performed the sacrifice, one should arrange that festival of powder for the sake of pacifying disease that occurs in the kingdom. (13)
Having performed oblations here with the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra, one should worship Śiva with special rites. If there is no pilgrimage, the kingdom will suffer from a lack of water. (14)
Having offered clarified butter with the Saṃhitā mantras, one should set out on the pilgrimage;
for if the lowering of the flag is omitted, the fierce wind will cause affliction.
Having performed the propitiatory rite as before and having worshipped Śiva, one should lower [the image];
for there is no dismissal of the Gaṇas who have been invited for the festival.
To pacify disturbances within the kingdom, one should worship Śiva and offer the Jaya-bali; then, having scattered offerings to all the Gaṇas and honored them, one should dismiss them. || 17 ||

(605) However, during a perpetual festival or even a great festival, if the *liṅga* or the image (*bera*) should fall from a vehicle or similar object, it causes the destruction of the king, the kingdom, and so forth. (18)
As for the expiation, one should place the deity there in every respect,
enclose it with a curtain, and smear that spot with plaster.
Having bathed and performed the rite for a holy day (puṇyāha), one should then prepare another image made of food;
having fashioned that as well, one should worship it right there according to the prescribed ritual.
Then, having consecrated him with the *navaka* [mantra], and having offered rice cooked with *śāli*, ghee, and milk-porridge (*pāyasa*),
one should establish the fire here in the east, after performing the ritual of naming (*nāmānta-saṃskṛta*).
One should offer clarified butter, sacrificial porridge, fuel-sticks, honey, milk, and parched grain with white mustard seeds, using the Gāyatrī mantra beginning with Īśa and ending with Sadyojāta.

Having offered sesame seeds, [offerings with] the Astra-mantra, the Mūla-mantra, and rice, each one hundred times, and then likewise with the mantras beginning with Ādhāra-śakti and those of the lords of the directions (digīśvara), || 23 ||
In whichever direction that *liṅga* has fallen due to the failure of its protective mantra,
one should offer a hundred oblations of sesame and clarified butter, as well as the *jayādi* expiation.
Having performed the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, one should give the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) prescribed for the guardians of the directions:
a golden elephant, gold, and queens together with buffaloes.
A golden goat, as well as a necklace of gold combined with copper, milch cows,
and silver are declared to be the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) in their respective order.
One should resume the procession and scatter the remaining offerings as a bali-oblation; however, if the image has fallen or been broken, the [penance] prescribed there shall be fourfold.
There should be an expiation, a sacrificial fee, and food that is not restricted; having installed another image, one should carry out the remainder of the festival procession.
One should perform the great bathing rite (mahāsnāna) at the primary liṅga, according to the gravity of the duration of the interruption in worship. || 29 ||
One should perform an expiation consisting of worship twice as extensive as that [period], and having offered fire oblations and a sacrificial fee,
one should proceed with the worship.
If the worship is interrupted for up to twelve days, an expiation is prescribed;
however, in the case of a human-made *liṅga*, one should subsequently have it re-consecrated.
Having performed the ritual sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa) once again for the liṅgas of the Ṛṣis and the Self-Existent One (Svayaṃbhū),
one should worship them after bathing them simply by means of the rite of restoring the dilapidated (jīrṇoddhāra). || 32 ||

In the event of the breaking of the Śiva-pot or the weapon-vessel, one should predict the death of the performer; having offered oblations there by the hundreds with clarified butter and other substances accompanied by the Saṃhitā mantras, [one should perform the rite].

One should worship the *tila* (sesame) and *ājya* (clarified butter) with the *astra-mantra*, and there, one should worship [the deities] in the *kumbha* and the *astra*; once they have been worshipped, [one proceeds] for the purpose of the ritual bath (*snāna*) in the primary jar (*kalaśa*) or in all the jars.
Or, if [the vessels] have been broken, one should fill others and worship them likewise;
having offered a hundred oblations of clarified butter with the Astra-mantra, one should pour the remaining ghee into those [new vessels].

In that same manner, having performed the recitation for that duration, one should give gold as an offering for the sake of pacification, whether [the image] is in the temple, in the courtyard, or if it has died or been wounded by blood.

Or if it has been sprinkled with urine, excrement, and so forth; or by a woman in her courses, a woman who has recently given birth, and the like; or by Caṇḍālas, jackals, vultures, owls, and donkeys. (37)
When he has entered [the womb] and when she has given birth, the expiation is declared: there, having dug that respective ground to a depth of two cubits all around, || 38 ||
Having extracted that clay and discarded it, one should burn it with a fire of cow-dung;
then, having cast away those ashes, one should fill [the vessel] with cow's urine.

One should gradually fill [the pit] with the water from the sacred footprint of a Brahmin, with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and with earth trodden upon by cows, using eight types of earth.
Having constructed a water-shed or a pavilion, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas there;
and when the fire has been consecrated and Śiva has been invoked in the crescent-shaped sacrificial pit (ardhendu-kuṇḍa) to the south.
Audumbara wood, Apāmārga fuel-sticks, ghee, cooked rice (caru), and white mustard seeds— one should offer eight thousand of each respectively.
Having offered oblations with the Īśāna and Brahma mantras, one should again [offer] rice, sesame, barley, mung beans,
sweet dūrvā grass, and milk-rice (pāyasa-caru) in sequence.
One should again offer oblations with the Brahma-mantras, the Mūla-mantra, and the Gāyatrī; and one offers with all the ritual substances at a tenth part of the quantity used for the limbs (aṅgas).
Having given food and other offerings without restriction, one should cast the bali offering at night;
having also bathed [the deity] with the supreme and other ablutions, he is then dismissed according to the prescribed rule. (45)
Having bestowed the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) that are to be given, one should perform the worship;
[this applies] when the Liṅga has been touched by heretics, Caṇḍālas, dogs, or those practicing malevolent spells.
Having performed all the previously mentioned rites, such as the movement of the cows, accompanied by mantras, and having then fashioned a chest made from the wood of a sacrificial tree; || 47 ||
Having fashioned it with its lower boundary well-formed, perfectly round like a sphere, and having placed it firmly and without gaps upon the *liṅga*, making it as high as a palm tree; 48.
For three days each, in sequence, one should perform the cleansing with cow-products individually and collectively,
as well as with decoctions, the eight types of earth, and fragrant water from sacred fords.
With the two Vyomavyāpis, the Astra-mantra, the Brahmaprāsāda, the Tārakas, the Mṛtyuñjaya, the root-mantras with their limbs, the Rudras, and the Pavamānas; || 50 ||
Then, having completed the filling rite, they should perform the recitation for twenty-one days, or fourteen, or seven,
according to the gravity of the defects.
Or, if [the image] falls down or dies, having sprinkled it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and performed the rite of declaring an auspicious day (puṇyāhavācana), || 52 ||
Just as before, one should offer oblations to Agni Apsumat with the previously mentioned mantras and other rites;
the abundance of oblations and the dignity of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should also be inferred according to the gravity of the situation.
Likewise, upon touching a woman in her menses, one offers to Agni Aśuci.
If, during the consecration or installation,
the ritual is not yet completed and the patron or the preceptor remains present in the form of an image, [the following applies].

There too, after the invocation for merit (*puṇyāha*) with the *gavya* vessel, one should perform the sacrifice with the three verses beginning with "tvaṃ no agne" and with the *saṃhitā-mantras*, as before.

Having performed the fire-oblation and given gifts such as cows and gold, one should proceed with the ritual; food and other provisions should be offered to the Brahmins and others without restriction.

In the fourth case, prior to the ritual bathing, if the gateway or the banner is broken, or if the prescribed fire-oblations and other rites are interrupted, one should perform the remedy there as well according to the stated method.
At the conclusion of the oblations of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and so forth, one should perform the placement (*vinyāsa*) of each respective [deity] and worship them;
this constitutes a minor expiation (*alpaprāyaścitta*).
Then, [he should look for] an anthill or honey among the palace pendants.
Or a red maiden may be born, or vultures, owls, and francolins; or they may enter the inner chamber, or a thunderbolt may fall upon the celestial chariot.
Even in that case, one should effect the pacification of the previously mentioned defects; likewise, when portents have arisen, such as the appearance of comets and the like. (60)

During an earthquake, when the quarters of the sky are ablaze, during a fierce wind or a conflagration, when trees fall without being blown by the wind, or when the bow of Indra appears at night; || 61 ||
Then, regarding other extraordinary occurrences, in order to pacify those defects, one should first perform the weapon-sacrifice (astrayāga) and worship Śiva with special rites.
For example—
having constructed a pavilion as before in the east, the northeast, or the north,
and having adorned it with the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha), preceded by the scattering of parched grain (vikira). || 63 ||
Having circumambulated from the sacrifice of the pitcher-weapon (kumbhāstra) and having fashioned a *bhadra* on the altar,
one should [worship] with the six limbs and the root-mantra, along with the [six] limbs, according to their respective colors in due order.
Likewise, having consecrated his body with the ritual applications (sakalīkṛta) using [mantras] joined with the birth-syllables (jāti),
and having worshipped the obstacle-remover (Vighna) and filled the arghya vessel, he should apply the forehead mark (tilaka) and wear a flower crown.
Above the seat of Śakti and Anantāsana, [he sits] upon the lotuses of the qualities such as Dharma;

possessing the brilliance of the sun at the end of an aeon, he has ten arms, five fierce faces with fangs, and is formidable with tawny beard and matted hair; he has three eyes and is adorned with a garland of severed heads.
Bearing an axe, a shield, a skull, a bow, serpents, a trident, a sword, fire, an arrow,
and a hand-drum (ḍamaruka), adorned with snakes, wearing a garment of tiger-skin, and clad in red—
having thus meditated upon [the deity], one should perform the ritual identification (sakalīkaraṇa) with the root mantra and its limbs and then worship.

Then, with offerings such as *arghya* and other enjoyments, one should worship the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvaras*) upon the coverings starting from the southeast, and the ten world-protectors (*lokapālas*) outside of them in their respective directions.
One should duly honor their respective scriptures on both sides;
likewise, having cleansed [the area] with fuel-sticks of *khadira* wood in the fire of the triangular sacrificial pit (*trikoṇakuṇḍa*), [one should proceed].
With milk, bark, ground ashes, Lakṣmī, the goddess, dūrvā grass, ākrānti, and eleven lotuses. (69)
With *śakravallī*, *sadābhadra*, *musali*, and *madhupāhvaya*; with *rocanā*, *agaru*, *karpūra*, *māṃsī*, *kuṅkuma*, and *candana*.
One should also apply a paste made from ground uśīra, uru, and kuṣṭha; then, having washed it with water from a sacred ford, one should rub it with bilva leaves.

One should perform the worship without mantras as before in the consecration pavilion; [one should bathe the deity] on the bed with water from a golden pitcher filled with gold, jewels, and other substances.

Having performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) as before with the three-part reality (tribhāgatattva), the primary forms (mūrti), and so forth, one should invoke Śiva into that [liṅga] using the root mantra and its limbs, and worship Him during the auspicious moment (lagnaka).
One should join Śiva, who resides in the pitcher, to the liṅga and perform the consecration; having worshipped him as before with the primary ablutions and other rites. (74)
One should consecrate the Lord through rebirth as before and perform the worship;
this is the atonement for a great fault.
Now, when the linga is perspiring, salivating, or afflicted by smoke and heat: || 75 ||
If it has been touched by uninitiated Brahmins and others, or by those bearing other sectarian marks (liṅgin), then as before,
[the image] in its wooden casket should be cleansed with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) individually and in sequence.
Having caused the immersion with all [the ingredients] for six days, and having rubbed [the body] with earth and sandalwood paste and so forth, he should then bathe [the deity].

Having performed the meditations on the six paths (adhvan), beginning with the three-fold reality (tattva), the form (mūrti), and so forth, and having duly worshipped Sadāśiva with offerings such as arghya; || 78 ||
One should perform the consecration by means of any one of the ablutions, ranging from one hundred and eight down to twenty-five, as appropriate.
Having performed the great worship and the fire-ritual according to the previous procedure,
one should scatter the bali offering to the spirits and give food and sacrificial fees.
One should carry out the festival and other rites during the worship as before;
when the fire into which Śiva has been invoked is extinguished, one should proceed in due order as previously described. (81)

Having performed the *āghāra* oblation, he offers clarified butter with the mantra beginning "tvanno agne," and again eight thousand oblations of fuel-sticks, sesame seeds, and rice-porridge from the *astra-mantra* starting with "kṛṣṇa."
One should perform the rites beginning with the Jaya-homa and ending with the expiation (niṣkṛti) exactly as before;

whether the fire has not yet been invoked for Śiva or the invocation for Śiva has already been withdrawn, once the fire has become extinguished, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations for each [deity] using the previously mentioned mantras and substances.

One should give gold as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to those who bear the form of the Guru and others. If the fires of Śiva should be touched by the fire of Śiva, [then they are indeed] the fires of Śiva. || 83 ||
One offers oblations with the preceding mantras and others in sequence for Agni Vivici;
for the mixing of either a common fire or a divine fire, one offers for Agni Śuci.

This means that one should offer oblations with the mantras of the previous substances. Furthermore, if the fire is touched by a corpse, a woman in childbirth, a Śūdra, or others, or if it comes into contact with impure substances through negligence, or if a living being [enters] it, one should perform a thousand-fold recitation.

Then one should offer oblations of fuel-sticks (samidh) with clarified butter, milk-rice (pāyasa), sesame seeds, white mustard (siddhārtha), sacrificial porridge (caru), and dūrvā grass— one hundred of each—
with the root mantra and its limbs (aṅga-mantras) in ten parts, and once each for the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas) and the weapons (astras).
Having offered oblations in that manner, one should present a bali-offering with red rice at night.

One should scatter [the offerings] according to the prescribed path, accompanied by auspicious acts such as dance and song; having thus performed the sacrifice of the weapon (astrayāga), one should worship Śiva with special rites.
Therein shall be universal peace; likewise, there shall be auspiciousness everywhere. This concludes the section on the weapon-sacrifice (astrayāga).
Thus indeed is the expiation for all the deities, each individually. (89)
One should effect purification and the pacification of defects by means of the respective independent [tantras],
as well as with the sacrificial fuel and other materials prescribed in those very independent tantras.
One should perform oblations for the sake of pacifying defects and worship each respective weapon-mantra; having performed the ritual bathing as before, prosperity increases. (91)
And through this delimitation, the presence of each respective deity arises for the sake of pacifying defects and for the attainment of desired objects. (91)
And one should scatter the *jayābali* offering; its procedure is also described:
either when the sun is situated in its northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*), or when some calamity has occurred. (92)
On the eighth and fourteenth days of both the bright and dark fortnights, as well as on the day of Ārdrā,
one should perform the great worship of Śambhu.
Having cleansed it with the five products of the cow as well as the five nectars, [one should perform this] three times or four times a day, which is eightfold more than the daily [rite]. || 94 ||
Adorned with fire-rituals and accompanied by vocal music, instrumental music, song, and dance, [the festival] was celebrated at night with rice cooked from one *prastha* of raw grain.
But when the *bhūtakrūra* has been recited, one should scatter the offering (*bali*) to the spirits with all the *bali*-mantras proclaimed for great festivals, in their proper sequence.
Śuddhodana respectfully offered an oblation to the gods, to the spirits, and to the hosts of elemental beings who had arisen for the great festival.
He should scatter food and feed the Brāhmaṇas as well as those bearing sectarian marks; he should also give delicious food to others without restraint.
At the conclusion of that, one should consecrate the Lord with a ritual bath; for this indeed brings about all peace and bestows sons, trees, wealth, and victory. (99)

It destroys the afflictions caused by calamities, planetary influences, spirits, ghosts, and elemental beings; it increases longevity and prosperity, and therefore it should be performed by men for their own welfare. (100)
The procedure for expiation (prāyaścitta), which is prescribed in the Śaiva Tantras both as a regular obligation and for the pacification of occasional faults; the quelling of portents (utpāta);
and the worship of the Weapon-mantra (astra-pūjā) along with the Jaya-bali offering, which destroys the afflictions of all the misfortunes of men.
He is celebrated as Vijayaśrīvardhana. || 101 ||
Thus ends the sixty-third chapter, concerning expiations and related matters, in the Kriyāpāda of the Uparibhāga of the Siddhāntasāra, the *Śrīmadīśānaśivagurudevapaddhati*.
p. 612) Now begins the sixty-fourth chapter.
I shall describe, in due order, the procedure for the restoration of ruined *liṅgas* and temples when they have become fragmented.
When it is burst, split, moved, fallen, or carried away. || 1 ||
When the human linga is burnt, decayed, mutilated, pregnant, wounded, displaced, or—due to ignorance—is either too large or too small; || 2 ||
Or when a linga established for the sake of food is afflicted by a river or the ocean, the mantras abandon that linga, and the deity as well, quite evidently. (3)
Once abandoned by the mantras and by the Lord, it becomes like a mere stone;
yet even so, piśācas and brahmarākṣasas take refuge in that liṅga here on earth.
If it is corrupted by the aforementioned defects, the seat (pīṭha) must clearly be abandoned;
for these same defects apply equally even in the case of the Sakala [mantra]. || 5 ||
These same defects apply equally to the images of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and other deities; therefore, such [images] should be abandoned.

There, outside the main temple (mūlālaya), one should construct the temple for the child-deity (bālālaya) to the south, or to the east or north; it should be made at three-fifths of the distance from the base.

The Bālālaya [temple] is prescribed with nine divisions (navāṃśa) for five parts, three parts, or two parts; however, the Mūla [temple] should have its western door facing toward the southwest or the northwest.
Having likewise decorated a pavilion in front of that [shrine] as before, one should, according to the prescribed injunctions, prepare a bed upon the central altar therein.
Having fashioned a very beautiful wooden liṅga together with its pedestal from the primary types of wood known as Nandā, using proportions of three, five, and three parts respectively; || 10 ||

Following the recitation of the *puṇyāha* and the casting of the *vikira* grains, and after the circumambulation with the water-pot and the weapon (*kumbhāstra*), preceded by the worship of the archways, the gates, the world-protectors (*lokeśa*), and the jars.
Having placed the jars of the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśa) all around the bed,
one should then place upon the bed a jar made of gold or any other [precious metal].
In that [vessel] filled with water from sacred fords and joined with gold, gems, and other [substances],
one should [place] the root-mantra, the limb-mantras, the Brahma-mantras, and likewise the two Vyomavyāpi mantras.
One should place the Gāyatrī, the Sāvitrī, and the two weapon-mantras; and having touched them, one should worship them as before and perform the recitation (japa) of them.
One should lead the pitcher to the inner sanctum amidst the sounding of conchs, drums, and other instruments;
one should perform the *yātrā-homa* (procession oblation) with the root mantras and their limbs to the east of the sanctum. || 15 ||
Having sprinkled the linga and other objects with water from the pitcher, he should then proclaim the command of Śiva:
"O you, by whatever being this wicked linga has been inhabited! (16)
Let him quickly abandon this and go to his desired place, where the Lord, as before, is joined by the Vidyās and the Vidyēśvaras. (17)
"May Sadāśiva, together with the Goddess and his attendants, be ever present.
Having spoken thus and offered the arghya water, one should dismiss the Piśācas and other spirits from this place. (18)
The word "Vyāpakeśvara," ending in the dative case and preceded by "Namaḥ" and "Tārā" (Oṃ), [is used];
one's own six limbs [are assigned] with their respective seed-syllables. || 19 ||

Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa upon himself, he should meditate on Śiva as pervading that [liṅga] within the temple of the liṅga and other such places, and then make a request with this mantra: || 20 ||
Oṃ!
O Blessed One! Since this limb is wicked and brings about defects, may there be peace for all through its removal, O Lord of the Pervader! (21)
"O Śaṅkara, preside over me as I proceed with its extraction! Having been thus commanded by the Lord with the words "So be it," he should perform the propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma).
One should offer milk, clarified butter, honey, and tips of dūrvā grass one hundred times with the recitation of the mantra;
however, for the purpose of causing the linga to tremble, one should offer clarified butter one thousand times.
Having performed the re-installation with the root mantra ten times and with its auxiliary parts,
he then offers a hundred oblations of milk-rice (kṣaireyī), followed by those of the Pāśupata weapon.
Having consecrated each of the thousand portions, beginning with those of Brahmā, separately with the waters from the *śānti*-vessel, one should touch each respective portion.

Having performed the recitation according to the number of oblations and having offered the *arghya* in reverse order, one should perform the re-consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) again after as much time as is possible for it.
Having determined that limit, the Guru should slowly inform him of it, [using] the Praṇava at the beginning,
along with the restrained Mūla-mantra, the Aṅga-mantras, and likewise the Brahma-mantras.

But in reverse order, having meditated upon that pervasive Lord— the pervader who resides within the *liṅga* and other supports, pervading them like space and situated within the thread— one should unite him with the jar.
Having invoked the mantras belonging to the portions starting with Brahmā, as well as the root mantra, into that pitcher by means of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan),
one should worship them in sequence with the arghya and other offerings.
Having wrapped [the jar] with a cloth and offered the *arghya* water,
the Guru himself should lift up the jar and proceed, carrying it on his head, performing a circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇya*).

Having led [the disciple] into the pavilion, he should place him upon the bed as before; and as previously described, he performs oblations with the Brahma-mantras in the cardinal directions and with the Aṅga-mantras in the intermediate corners.
The meditation on the three sections should be performed as before for the wooden liṅga.
At dawn, when the auspicious moment has arrived, the wooden liṅga together with its pedestal should be placed in the Bālā temple.
Having established the mantras residing in the pitcher and having joined the deity [to them], one should consecrate [the image] while it remains there and thus address Śiva: || 33 ||
Oṃ!
O Śaṅkara! As long as the Liṅga has not been fully completed and consecrated in the root-abode, so long do you remain present in this wooden Liṅga. 34.

Therefore, you must go to that very place; be gracious to me on account of this sign. Having meditated upon the mantras of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan) within that [liṅga] according to the sequence of emanation (sṛṣṭikrama), [proceed].
Having worshipped with the arghya and other offerings as before, and having performed the fire-oblation for three days as previously described,
one should perform the ceremonial bath on the fourth day using the *navaka* [mantra].
One should carry out the rites such as the daily worship and festivals there; and when Caṇḍeśvara is present, one should dismiss Caṇḍa and cast him into the waters.
Then, having dug with a golden spade and with a weapon, the preceptor, if the pedestal is found to be free from defects, should lift it up and place it elsewhere.

He alone should protect and worship [the deity], since he is the Lord who is worshipped in the temple of the child; having bound the wicked linga with a golden cord and yoked it to a bull, [he should cast it out].
Having placed it upon a cart, one should cast it into waters that are not deep;
such is the rule for a stone linga, but if it is made of wood, [it should be burned] with the fire of Śiva.
If a gem or an earthen object is heated by fire with a *daheda* mantra, and it remains unaltered in color and undamaged, one should install that very same object once again.
Having again prepared that very iron [image] with its proper characteristics as before,
one should install it, worship it, and furthermore construct a new temple.
Furthermore, having consecrated according to the prescribed method new images made of clay, lime, and so forth, one should worship them by applying colors and other ornaments. || 43 ||
When the pedestal itself is corrupted, one should abandon it and, having consecrated another according to the previous procedure, join it to the primary liṅga. || 44 ||

Once the primary liṅga has been completed, having performed the preliminary rites such as the consecration (adhivāsana) in the foremost pavilion of the deity as before, one should install it in the inner sanctum (garbhamandira).

Having placed the deity residing in the child-liṅga into the water-jar as before, one should then join it to the primary liṅga once it has been installed, according to the previous procedure. || 46 ||
If the temple itself has become dilapidated, then its restoration is now described; having collected all the mantras of the temple in their proper sequence, [one should proceed]. (47)

Having joined [the deity] to the sword according to the very sequence previously described, one should worship it; and when the temple has been successfully completed, one should [worship] its mantras in the same manner as before.

Having taken a sword and joined it [with the ritual substances], and having sprinkled [the image] with consecrated water, one should bathe Śiva; the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the restoration of a dilapidated shrine is ten times that of the initial installation.

One should give to those who bear the form [of the deity], and even more than that to the preceptor; likewise to the Brahmins, to those bearing the linga, to the carpenters, and to those who are seekers.

In that same manner, one should give abundant gifts to the laborers and others; or rather, the fruit [obtained] when the Liṅga has been installed is the same as the fruit from the construction of a temple.

Therefore, when the restoration of a ruined [shrine] is performed, one obtains twice that fruit. Thus, for the sake of embodied beings in this world to attain worldly enjoyment and liberation through distinguished dharma,
[this work is composed] by means of the meanings of the universal scriptures manifested from the lotus-like mouth of Śambhu, whose body is knowledge.

The divine teacher, the wise one, declared that entire first section on ritual action— the wheel of rites beginning with the daily (nitya) ceremonies, including their procedures, as they appear in reality, from the regular observances up to the restoration of ruined temples— this he called the Kriyāpāda.
Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, on the Restoration of Dilapidated Temples, in the Kriyāpāda of the Uparibhāga of the Siddhāntasāra, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva.
The Kriyāpāda is completed. Śrī.
The *Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati*, composed by the venerable *Īśānaśivagurudevamiśra*.
(The Fourth Part: Yoga)
Now begins the first chapter.
Now, liberation shall be fully accomplished for the embodied soul through perfect knowledge; knowledge arises from dispassion, and dispassion arises from one's own nature.
"Self-nature" (svabhāva) is the definition of the essential character of saṃsāra;
saṃsāra, however, consists of the notion of a self regarding the body and the sense of "mine" regarding objects. (2)

The body also should be known as twofold, through the distinction of the gross and the subtle; likewise, the elements such as earth and the rest serve as the substrates for the sense organs, such as hearing. (3)
The organs of action, such as speech and the rest; likewise wind, bile, and phlegm; and the skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, semen, and the channels. (4)
In the mūlādhāra, in the kuṇḍalinī, and at the navel, heart, throat, and head,
there are lotuses with four, six, eight, ten, twelve, and sixteen petals respectively.
The gross body is joined [to the subtle], while the subtle consists of the "eightfold city" (puryaṣṭaka):
the five objects beginning with sound, the mind, the intellect, and the ego.
The two bodies, however, consist of the adhyātma (the internal self), the adhibhūta (the elemental), and the adhidaivata (the divine).
For example: the ears and so forth, as well as speech and so forth, are indeed the distinct adhyātma elements. (7)
Sound and the rest, as well as speech and the rest, are held to be the objective domains (adhibhūta). Likewise, space, wind, fire, water, earth, and light; || 8 ||
Indra, Viṣṇu, Mitra, and Prajeśa are the presiding deities;
as for the internal self (adhyātma), it consists of that triad: mind, intellect, and ego.

That which is to be thought of (*mantavya*) and that which is to be understood (*boddhavya*), as well as the ego-sense (*māna*), constitute the *adhibhūta*. The Moon, the individual soul (*jīva*), and Viriñca are, in sequence, the *adhidaivas*. (10)
That which consists of the three qualities is Prakṛti, as is Puruṣa; likewise, all the principles beginning with Rāga and Vidyā and ending with Māyā [are included]. (11)
Impurity, action, and illusion are all its instigators; likewise, there are the three states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep. (12)
Desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and envy—these six waves are known as the pervaders within the ocean of delusion that is to be pervaded. (13)
Such is this body, resembling an unbaked earthen pot, which is utterly transitory and superimposed with the six modifications beginning with birth.
Lacking independence, entering and even departing [from the body], and even wandering through the cycle of existence under the power of karma, the self indeed roams about unperceived. 15.
Likewise, these bodies are of five kinds, both mental and physical:
those born from a womb, those born from an egg, those born from sweat, and those born from sprouting. (16)
In that regard, the bodies of gods and others are mental and not born from a womb;
indeed, the bodies of humans and animals are born from a womb.
The bodies of reptiles, snakes, and winged birds are born from eggs; furthermore, there are bodies born from a womb and those born from eggs that move about in water. (18)
Worms are said to be born from sweat, and stationary beings are considered to be born by sprouting; all are subject to their own karma, coming into being and ceasing to be.

In the terrible ocean of worldly existence, which has birth and death for its waters, is agitated by the fish of pleasure and pain, is turbid with grief, delusion, and the like, and is bottomless; (20)
Emerging and sinking, all embodied beings are bound by the sole fetters of merit and demerit within the realms of heaven, earth, hell, and so forth. (21)
In this body, which is a cage of bones, marrow, sinews, and excrement, urine, pus, flesh, and blood, and is merely covered by skin—whence can beauty be remembered? (22)
In this skeleton-essence, a receptacle for urine, phlegm, and impurities, covered by flesh, hair, nails, sinews, blood, and skin; (23)
If anyone takes pleasure in the body, he will take pleasure even in hell;
or rather, it is because of the ignorant that this is spoken of here as a perception of happiness within the body. (24)

Even the pleasures of the senses, such as sound and the rest, are devoid of essence according to the method of positive and negative concomitance, just like the songs sung by the intoxicated or the ravings of the insane. (25)

And they are seen playing instruments, just as madmen act out transformations; likewise, the happiness of gold [is perceived] through the contact of one limiting adjunct with another limiting adjunct. (26)
Just as there is pleasure from the discharge of pus, urine, and so forth from a wound, or the pleasure of itching and scratching in eczema, pleasure in sexual intercourse is similar to that. (27)

The pleasure of the visual faculty that arises from beholding dancers, beautiful women, and the like—dance does not lose even the slightest bit of its quality because it is the behavior of one who is intoxicated. (28)

Upon seeing [a woman] with beautiful eyes, a fine nose, a lovely face, and beautiful teeth, and so forth—who among the skin, bones, flesh, and other [elements] could be considered truly charming? (29)

Regarding palatable objects, the satisfaction resulting from the cessation of hunger and thirst due to the fickleness of the gustatory faculty is merely the removal of suffering; it is not true happiness. (30)
If the suffering of sleep were happiness, just as there is pleasure in sleeping, then that would be designated as the bliss of the Self upon the withdrawal of the senses. (31)
Even regarding fragrant scents that must be sought with effort, it is observed that they can be obtained easily and with pleasure in forests and similar places.
And what happiness can there be for him during residence in the womb, at birth, or in childhood? He is like one who is not independent, like a bird constrained by others. (33)
In youth, for an embodied being whose mind is overwhelmed by passion and other afflictions due to union with the undesired and separation from the desired, how can there be any happiness? (34)
In old age, for one who is incapable yet still desires to perceive sense objects, whose functioning of the senses has been exhausted by afflictions such as disease and passion; (35)
How could there be happiness for one who is being tormented? Or for one who is about to die? The suffering of one who is dying would not be matched even by that in hell.
Then, [he saw] the suffering of evildoers as they go to the world of Yama—those falling, those who have fallen, and those about to fall, by the sight of which [they suffer]. (37)
For the suffering in the hells is well known; therefore, it is not mentioned here. If one were to perform only meritorious deeds, one would possess a divine body and so forth in heaven. (38)
Even when divine enjoyments such as celestial palaces have been presented to them, they see the splendor of others—though it be slight—as radiant and superior to their own. (39)
Afflicted, he experiences sense-objects while bearing misery in his mind;
and even more so when he beholds the downfall of those whose merit has been exhausted.
The kind of suffering that exists within the heart cannot be described;
for even if there were happiness in kingship and such things, it would belong only to one who is already tormented by the sufferings of the twilight hours and the like. (41)
How can there be happiness for one who has fear even from his own sons?
On this point, Parāśara says:
"To whatever extent a living being forms relationships that are dear to the mind, to that same extent..."
Pikes of grief are driven deep into the heart.

"Whatever is in the house remains in the mind wherever one may dwell; its destruction, burning, or theft belongs to that very thing alone"—so it is recited in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa. Where, then, is there happiness for those who possess property, given the fear of loss, decay, and the like?
Thus it is said:
"From whatever one turns away, from that one becomes happy; for by turning away from everything,"
He does not experience even the slightest suffering.
Thus it is said: nevertheless, a living being, tormented day and night by craving,
never attains freedom from thirst for the acquisition of wealth and other such things.
And so it has been said:
"The hair of one who grows old decays; the teeth of one who grows old decay;
the eyes and ears also decay; but craving alone remains free from affliction."
Whatever rice, barley, gold, cattle, and women there are upon the earth, they are not enough for even one person; therefore, one should cast that craving far away.
Therefore, there is no need for ritual action, nor for progeny, nor for wealth;
for it is only through renunciation that immortality can be attained by the wise. (42)
Therefore, among virtue, wealth, and pleasure, liberation alone is superior, because the three aims are unstable and also difficult to achieve. (43)
Enough, enough with excessive prolixity; let us follow the subject at hand.
Having thus understood that saṃsāra is essence-less, the supreme path to liberation—the yoga with its constituent limbs—should be accomplished by the wise man through detachment from it. (44)

And that perfect yoga is to be attained through renunciation (saṃnyāsa), and not otherwise; renunciation does not consist merely in shaving the head, nor even in the taking up of the staff and other such emblems.
The wearing of saffron robes and so forth, the shaving of the head, the carrying of the staff, and whatever else of this kind has been prescribed for the body, is not for the embodied soul. (46)
How can an embodied being attain liberation merely by changing the dress of this inert body, which possesses the nature of a jar, a wall, or similar objects? (47)
For this very reason, the body possesses neither agency nor the state of being an enjoyer; rather, it is the agent of the body's actions, which are to be refined by those seeking their fruits.
For this very reason, renunciation (sannyāsa) must be the abandonment of actions performed for desire; the wise know that the relinquishing of desire-driven actions is renunciation. (49)

For he who has indeed always desisted from the pursuit of worldly objects, sons, and wealth, as well as from [the duties] pertaining to his own caste and stage of life, and likewise from his own [sectarian] tradition; || 50 ||
However, the performance of prescribed duties without regard for their fruits, with the intention of dedicating them to the Lord, is held to be renunciation (nyāsa). || 51 ||
One who merely has a shaven head is neither a true ascetic nor a renunciant; he should be known as a perpetual renunciant who neither hates nor desires. 52.
Whether he be a student, a householder, a forest-dweller, or an ascetic; whether clothed in bark, wearing matted hair, carrying two staffs, or shaven-headed—53.

Either naked, or wearing white garments, or else clad in saffron robes, having performed the renunciation of ritual action (karmasaṃnyāsa), he takes refuge in yoga with its constituent limbs (sāṅgayoga). || 54 ||
Having obtained the grace of Śiva, the yogi shall attain liberation; for,
having realized that this saṃsāra is indeed essence-less, he does so through dispassion and through the grace of Śambhu.
Having attained yoga through the instruction of a guru, the yogi reaches liberation before long.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Definition of Yoga," in the section on Yoga within the Upper Part of the *Siddhāntasāra*, which is the *Śrīmad-Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati*.
Now begins the second chapter.
Now, yoga should be understood as that which bestows the liberation of the qualities and sovereign powers; Patañjali, however, has defined yoga as the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind. (1)

The root *yuj* refers to meditative absorption (*samādhi*) between the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*); this union is designated as *yoga*. Thus spoke the great sage. (2)
For the mind is indeed the cause of bondage and liberation for all beings; having rendered the mind free from its fluctuations, one should merge one's own self into the Supreme Self.
"Having united with the Supreme Self through yoga, one becomes liberated; this is intended as the primary yoga. Thus it is said.
When the mind, having correctly reached Śiva, remains steady and does not waver, that state in which the nature of Śiva is manifested is held to be the yoga of liberation (kaivalya). || 3 ||
And that [knowledge] shines forth through the avoidance of defects such as passion; and those [defects], passion and the rest, perish through the practice of the limbs of yoga.
Those who know them indeed declare that there are eight limbs of yoga,
namely:
the restraints (yamas), the observances (niyamas), likewise the postures (āsanas), and the controls of breath (prāṇasaṃyamas).
Withdrawal, concentrations, meditations, and absorptions; the restraints (yamas) shall be of five kinds, and the observances (niyamas) likewise fivefold.
There are five postures, while breath-control (prāṇāyāma) is of many kinds; withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra) is fivefold, and concentration (dhāraṇā) is recorded as being manifold.
Meditations are of many kinds; alternatively, concentration is of one kind or three kinds. Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness [are the five yamas]. (8)
Those Yamas are of five kinds, for their individual subdivisions indeed exist;
here in this world, the injury to living beings is threefold by way of mind, speech, and action.

They declare non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) to be abstention from those [actions] in all circumstances. Truth (*satya*) is the speaking of things as they are, provided it is beneficial to all beings; [for when truth causes harm to others, it is not truth]. (10)
The wise know that even truth which causes suffering to others is indeed untruth; whereas that which is beneficial to living beings, even if it be untrue, is truly truth. (11)
When truth would cause pain to others, one should then resort to silence;
likewise regarding the dwellings and other properties of others, whether they are currently occupied or abandoned.

The non-appropriation of things belonging to others—whether they be blades of grass cast aside, or anything else—by means of action, mind, or speech, is remembered as the supreme form of non-stealing. 13.
They say that celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is the restraint of the senses;
therein, however, it is specifically the withdrawal from the object of the genitals. (14)
However,
they know that supreme celibacy (*brahmacarya*) consists in turning away from sexual union with women through the absence of looking, touching, longing, imagining, speaking, and so forth. (15)
And even there, for householders, because they do not transgress with women other than their own wives,
approaching them only when they have bathed after their menses is considered the highest form of celibacy.
Because one perceives the faults of acquisition, loss, preservation, and injury, the primary form of non-possessiveness (*aparigraha*) consists in the non-appropriation of objects. (17)
This has been prescribed for monks; for others, it is remembered differently: whether one is a celibate student, a householder, a forest-dweller, or a silent sage. (18)
But for one who has a family, non-acceptance (aparigraha) consists in desisting from improper gifts for the sake of nourishing his teachers and others. || 19 ||
Thus are the Yamas.
The observances (niyamas) are purity, contentment, self-study, austerity, and likewise worship of the Lord; these five are further divided. (20)
Purity, however, should be understood as the cleansing of the actions of mind, speech, and body. That which consists in not thinking of improper deeds is mental purity. (21)
Mental [impurity] is purified by speech, while bodily impurity is cleansed with earth and water; this is the washing away of stains and the purification of the internal organ.

The non-performance of evil deeds by those engaged in ritual action is considered purity, provided it is achieved without contradicting the duties pertaining to one's caste, stage of life, and so forth. (23)
Contentment is said to be the satisfaction derived from one's livelihood through wealth, grain, and so forth;
it consists of not grieving over what has passed and being free from longing for things yet to come. (24)

Non-attachment toward present circumstances is proclaimed as contentment; likewise, the absence of pride upon the arrival of joy and the state of being free from sorrow in the face of occasions for grief. (25)
Equanimity toward all things is also called contentment; likewise, there is the practice of the Praṇava and also of the Upaniṣads. (26)
Furthermore, for yogis, even the recitation of one's own respective mantra, when performed without attachment to its fruits, is designated as *svādhyāya*; thus, it is of three kinds.
And so they have said:
"From Vedic study one should proceed to yoga; from yoga, one should proceed to Vedic study within the self.
Through the perfection of both Vedic study and yoga, the Supreme Self is revealed."
Both that Brahman of Sound and the Supreme Brahman are to be known; one who is proficient in the Brahman of Sound attains the Supreme Brahman.
Thus:
"The emaciation of the body by means of eating once a day, fasting, and so forth, as well as by the Kṛcchra, Cāndrāyaṇa, and other such penances—that is declared to be austerity (tapas). (28)
In that regard, neither fasting nor overeating is desired;
the ascetic who eats at the time prescribed by his vow shall partake in yoga.
And so the Blessed One said: "Yoga is not for him who eats too much, nor for him who does not eat at all;
it is not for him who is habitually addicted to sleep, nor for him who is ever awake, O Arjuna!"
For one who is moderate in diet and conduct, disciplined in actions, and regulated in sleep and wakefulness,
yoga becomes the destroyer of suffering.
Thus,
the worship of Śambhu which is impelled by internal and external substances such as fragrances and so forth in due order— that is the worship of Īśvara.
Even there, without aiming for a fruit, the worship of the beloved deity through action and even through the mind, performed with devotion and according to one's capacity; 31.
The worship of the Lord is praised for the sake of yogis' accomplishment of yoga; Yājñavalkya and Vasiṣṭha were great sages and masters of yoga.
They have here declared the separate restraints and observances, which are of ten kinds: non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, compassion, and uprightness; || 33 ||

Forbearance, fortitude, moderation in diet, and purity—these are the restraints (yamas) and so forth; austerity, contentment, faith in the scriptures, charity, and worship of the Lord [are the observances (niyamas)]. || 34 ||
Listening to the established doctrine, modesty, and intelligence; muttering [mantras] and offering oblations—these are the observances (*niyamas*).
Thus [end] the observances.
The postures (āsanas) have also been described in many ways in the previous manual. || 35 ||
For them, only five are prescribed as truly bringing about the accomplishment of yoga: the Svastika, that which is named Padma, the Bhadra, and likewise the Yogāsana. (36)
And as for Gomukha, their characteristics are described separately:
having sat upon a seat and pressed the big toes together within the space between the knees,
with the middle, neck, and front of the body held straight, one assumes the Svastika posture.
Established. || 37 ||
Having placed the tips of both feet upon the root of the pair of thighs as before, one sits in the posture known as Padma; when it is done in the reverse manner, it is called Bhadra.
Having placed the right foot upon the thigh and the left foot upon the right thigh, if one sits well-settled as before, they call that the desired yoga posture. (39)
Having firmly grasped the left calf and foot at the ankle,
with the buttocks resting upon it, and with the right knee placed above, that yogi is indeed established in the cow-faced posture (gomukhāsana).
Seated Postures (Āsanas)
The retention of the vital breath within the body is declared to be *prāṇāyāma*. (41)
And that [prāṇāyāma] is said to be of many kinds by those proficient in the Yoga scriptures;
these three are inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka). || 42 ||
Of the breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), however, the other limbs follow in sequence;
that which possesses three limbs is called *tryaṅga*, excluding the inhalation (*pūraka*).
One should fill the air into the abdomen through the left nostril;
that is to be known as *pūraka* (inhalation), measured by the prescribed number of *udghāta* (upward thrusts). || 44 ||
Or else, from the restraint of the wind alone once it has been filled, when one remains like a completely full pitcher, that is known as *kumbhaka*. (45)
The gradual release of the air that has been filled through the nostril other than the left is taught as *recaka*.

In that regard, the common *pūraka* (inhalation) is considered to consist of sixteen *mātrās*; the *kumbhaka* (retention) should consist of sixty *mātrās*, and it is traditionally taught to contain five *uddhātas*.

The exhalation (recaka) consisting of the extraction of even [units] shall consist of twenty-four measures; this breath control (prāṇāyāma) is indeed mild, while the middling [breath control] shall be double that.

The three-fold [prāṇāyāma] is to be known as superior through the practice of sequential training; those breath-restraints are remembered as being both "without seed" (agarbha) and "with seed" (sagarbha). || 49 ||
Breath-control (prāṇāyāma) accompanied by internal mantra-recitation is known as "with seed" (sagarbha);
those which are devoid of internal recitation are remembered as "without seed" (agarbha).
Of the breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), that which is "with seed" (sagarbha) is said to be superior to the "seedless" (agarbha).
For example:
having performed the retention (kumbhaka) of the vital air within the belly, one should mentally recite one's own respective mantra. (51)

One should perform *prāṇāyāma* with seed-syllables (*sagarbha*), with the mind fixed upon that; if one's own mantra consists of a single syllable, its recitation (*japa*) should be two hundred times. || 52 ||
Having clearly visualized the thirty phonemes in their proper sequence through the progressive expansion of each syllable,
one with extended breath should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma).
p.

626) Therein, breath-control (prāṇāyāma) should be performed—augmented by the respective meditations—from the eight-syllable mantra up to the primordial nature (prakṛti), through the successive omission of one syllable at a time. || 54 ||
Therein, having understood the body, the channels (*nāḍīs*), and the wind situated therein, and having performed their purification, one should then practice *prāṇāyāma*. It is as follows:
the body measures ninety-six finger-breadths (*aṅgulas*) according to its own fingers; upwards...
The vital breath (prāṇa) extends twelve finger-breadths beyond the body. || 56 ||
Two finger-breadths above the penis is declared to be the center of the body; that is the Mūlādhāra, which is triangular for gods and others, as well as for human beings.

For animals and the like, however, it is in the heart; for those born from eggs, it is circular; and for quadrupeds, it is in the middle of the chest, while for those born from eggs, it is in the middle of the belly. (58)
For human beings, nine finger-breadths above the root is the navel-cavity;
above that is the navel-wheel, which is well-established with twelve spokes.
Below the navel, in the place called the *kanda*, resides the Kuṇḍalinī, eight-fold and circular, coiled like a sleeping serpent and four finger-breadths in width.
Seventy-two thousand channels emerge from its center;
among them, there are twenty-eight principal channels.
Among those, ten are indeed preeminent, beginning with Iḍā; even among them, three are [most] so:
Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumnā, as well as Gāndhārī and Hastijihvikā. (62)
Suyaśā, Alambuṣā, Pūṣā, Kuhū, and Śaṅkhinī—among these, Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumnā are remembered as the most excellent. (63)
Among these, the one called Suṣumṇā is remembered as the supreme Brahma-nāḍī.
Thus ends the group of ten channels.
Then Vimalā, Ghoṣaṇī, Pṛthvī, and thereafter Āpyāyanī are considered [the stages]. || 64 ||
Tejovatī, Vāyavī, Gaganā, Rodhanī, Rasāvāhā, Mṛdvaṅgī, Snaṃsanī, and also Marśanī. || 65 ||

The channels (nāḍīs) are designated in sequence as eighteen: Śabdavahā, Sparśavahā, Dūrṇā, Surūpā, Rasadhāraṇī, and Sarvagā. (66) Now, there are indeed five beginning with Prāṇa, and also five beginning with Nāga; [of these] Prāṇa... p. 627) ...is [the first].
From the seat located in the heart-lotus, there is the abiding in the heart. || 67 ||
Residing in the chest, it performs exhalation, inhalation, coughing, and so forth; since it constantly effects movement, it is proclaimed as *prāṇa*. (68)

The apāna [wind] governs the downward flow of urine, feces, and so forth; the vyāna resides in the joints of the hands and other limbs, and its function consists of relinquishing and grasping; therefore, it is known as vyāna. (69)
The udāna breath, however, situated from the navel up to the head, leads [the breath] upwards;
the movement of the limbs, eyes, and so forth is recorded as the function of the udāna. (70)
The *samāna* wind, however, pervades the entire body and resides in the joints; the winds beginning with *nāga* are situated in the skin, blood, flesh, fat, and bones. (71)
They are located, respectively, on the forehead, the chest, the conch-shell (the throat), the shoulder, and the navel.
Now, as for their colors:
they possess the splendor of the blue lotus, the indragopa insect, cow’s milk, lightning, the sun, and the moon. (72)
Resembling a furnace, split collyrium, the sun, a stone, or safflower, the activity of the *prāṇa* is said to extend from the digestion of food to its end.
The activity of the *samāna* is traditionally taught as nourishment and so forth; whereas that of the *udāna* begins with belching and so forth.
The opening of the eyes and so forth of the Nāga and the Kūrma [postures]. || 74 ||
The action of sneezing belongs to Kṛkara; yawning and so forth arise from Devadatta; and speaking and so forth belong to Dhanañjaya, who does not release the dead. (75)
But the Suṣumnā stands like a thread through the center of the body;
having reached the crown of the Bindu, it has emerged through the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). || 76 ||
The Iḍā and the Piṅgalā are on her left and right respectively; they are situated within the Suṣumnā, having issued from the left and right vital breaths (prāṇas).
From the back of the iḍā, however, the gāndhārī emerges from the left eye;
and the hastijihvā emerges from the tip of the big toe of the left foot.
Suyaśā emerges from the tip of the big toe of the right foot;
Alambuṣā, however, emerges from below the navel, reaching as far as the root of the anus.
Pūṣā, however, emerges from the back of Piṅgalā and exits through the right ear;
the ten channels beginning with Vimalā emerge from the tips of the hands. (80)
Kuhū, however, has emerged from the right eye of Piṅgalā;
Sarasvatī likewise has gone to the Viśvodara and reached the penis.
Moreover, all the channels are provided with internal cavities, and they are all filled with blood,
like lotus fibers.
The division of those branches and sub-branches is recorded as being manifold;
they are known as "hairs" (roma) that extend from the body, their tips protruding outward.
The beard grows from the mouth, and the hair emerges from the head; there are three and a half crores of hairs on the body. (84)
In the bodies of womb-born animals, the veins and body hairs are recorded as being threefold; in birds, however, they are half of that, and again half of that, in number.

The restriction of veins, hair, and so forth does not exist among insects and other such species; likewise, it is not observed even among stationary beings—all of them are considered living creatures. (86)

Having thus understood the channels, one should practice breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). Likewise, the restraints (*yama*), the observances (*niyama*), the postures (*āsana*), as well as the vital breaths and the network of channels (*nāḍicakra*)— these are declared to be the external limbs of yoga.
These, having been understood according to the instruction, are to be practiced. || 87 ||

Thus ends the second chapter, concerning the definition of yoga and related topics, in the Yoga Section (Yogapāda) of the Upper Part (Uparibhāga) of the *Siddhāntasāra*, which is the *Śrīmad-Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati*.
Now begins the third chapter.

Then, one desiring to know yoga, having approached a guru who is a knower of yoga, and having propitiated and fully satisfied him through service, the offering of wealth, and other such means; || 1 ||
Therefore, having understood the yoga and having given the teacher’s fee, and being permitted by the teacher, one should go to a delightful place. (2)
p.
629) A field of merit, a riverbank, a sacred ford, a forest, a mountain peak, and so forth; there, in a hermitage or a monastery, where roots, fruits, and water are abundant. (3)
Whether in a village, a temple, or even in his own delightful home, the yogi—pure in soul, free from attachment, and having conquered the senses—[should practice]. (4)
Performing the duties prescribed for one's own caste and stage of life, with regulated diet and conduct, and with regulated sleep and wakefulness; || 5 ||
Peaceful, bathing at the three sessions of the day, seeing all things with equanimity,
he sits upon a seat covered with cotton, down, and other materials, provided with an upper cloth.
Seated properly on a pure and well-conquered seat, he should then pay homage to the Teacher, the Guru, and thereafter to the two Śivas.
With body, head, and neck held straight, having performed the internal sacrifice within the heart, the wise man should practice yoga neither too hurriedly nor too slowly.

Now, those five knots which were shown in the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) are situated, respectively, in the heart, the throat, the palate, the space between the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). || 9 ||
Having pierced those [channels] with the upward-moving breath (ūrdhvavāyu) and released them through the right nostril,
one should then fill the interior of the abdomen with air through the left nostril.
That should be known as *pūraka* (inhalation), the procedure consisting of sixteen measures (*mātrā*). One should restrain its outward flow; that is remembered as *kumbhaka* (retention). || 11 ||
That exhalation (recaka) should last for about sixty [counts] due to his exhaling; having closed the left nostril, he should exhale through the right one alone. (12)
That, however, is designated as exhalation (recaka); their measurement is now declared: in inhalation (pūraka), by sixteen measures, one should meditate on the four-faced [Brahmā] in the navel-lotus.
