One should hold the form of the letter A, devoid of qualities, established in samādhi, and four-armed; during the kumbhaka, one should maintain it for sixty-four mātrās.
One should meditate upon Vāsudeva, whose form is the syllable *U*, who has the luster of a conch shell,
who holds a conch and a discus, who is gentle, established in samādhi, and possesses four arms, within the lotus of the heart.

One should retain the breath by means of the śakti as long as possible while recollecting the Diademed One (Kṛṣṇa); meanwhile, one should meditate upon Rudra, whose form is the syllable *makāra*, within the lotus between the eyebrows.
White in color, established in meditative absorption, with four arms and three eyes;
holding a deer and an axe, gentle, with the moon upon his crest and matted hair. (17)
One should exhale through the right [nostril] for twelve measures; then, having filled the air from the *praṇava* up to the space between the eyebrows.
Having restrained the self within the self in that seed-syllable consisting of a point, one should mentally recite the syllable *oṃ*, which exceeds the three measures, as a form of austerity.

This is the means for mastering the vital breath (prāṇa), which bestows both visible and invisible fruits; these five types of breath control (prāṇāyāma) are performed according to the method described in the Bhūtaśuddhi.
There are also three [practices] beginning with drying (śoṣaṇa); one should perform these either together or separately.
By drawing in the air during the two twilights and drinking it, one becomes eloquent. (21)
Indeed, his diseases perish either month by month or gradually over several months. Then, being deaf, he should place his self in the head and fill it with air.
Having closed all the openings [of the body] and being drenched by the nectar of the moon in the sky, one should release the breath through the two ears; thus one is freed from deafness. (23)

One should hold [the breath] at the sides or at the navel to alleviate the pain of abdominal tumors (gulma); wherever there is pain in the body, one should direct the vital air (māruta) to that very spot.

Having raised [the breath] through the regulation of the vital force (prāṇāyāma), one dispels each respective disease; then, having drawn up the apāna, one should employ it in the seat of fire (the navel). || 25 ||
And one should restrain the six sense-faculties; then the resonance (nāda) proceeds.
From the navel up to the head, the resonance proceeds like the sound of a lute.
Having heard that [instruction], he causes the Suṣumṇā to ascend; by means of the Brahma-randhra, his vital breath then departs through that [channel] according to his will. (27)
Residing within the lotus of the heart, the vital breath (prāṇa), uttering the sound "haṃsa," constantly generates exhalation throughout the day and night according to its count.
Sixty breaths are known as one *prāṇa*, and six *prāṇas* are known as one *ghaṭikā*.
Sixty *ghaṭikās* are known as a human day and night (*ahorātra*). (29)
The cessation of inhalation and exhalation proceeds from breath control (prāṇāyāma). Then, having meditated upon the four-faced one in the navel-lotus within the abdomen— || 30 ||
One should fill the interior with the wind by means of the *iḍā* [nāḍī] while in the form of the syllable *A*; having performed the retention (*kumbhaka*) as before,
one should mentally recite the *praṇava*.
Having made it firm and having withdrawn it, one should exhale through the right [nostril];
or else, [one should meditate on] the four-armed Vāsudeva residing in the lotus of the heart.
He holds a conch and a discus, is gentle, white in color, and wears a crown;
he has four arms, stands in a noble posture, and his body consists of the syllable *U*.
Recalling [the mantra] and mentally chanting the *tāra*, having performed the inhalation (*pūraka*), retention (*kumbhaka*), and exhalation (*recaka*) as before,
this indeed constitutes the Vaiṣṇava breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
Between his two eyebrows, within the lotus, he meditated upon the three-eyed Rudra, whose body consisted of the syllable *Makāra* and who was white with ashes as his bodily unguent.

One should mutter the Praṇava as before over the well-seated four-armed [deity]; this restraint of breath (prāṇāyāma), performed with inhalation and the other stages as previously described, is the Raudra [type]. || 36 ||

Meditating upon Īśvara, who is seated on a lotus in the Bindu-sthāna, possessing eight arms and four faces, and endowed with the previously described form and attributes, one should mentally recite the Tāra mantra. (37)
This breath control (prāṇāyāma), consisting of inhalation and the other stages as before, is of the nature of Īśvara;
likewise, one should meditate upon the Lord Sadāśiva in the lotus of the head.

Reciting the *tāra* (om) with the intellect as before, and having restrained the breath as previously described, this restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇasaṃyama*), when performed according to the instruction, shall be the remover of all defects. (39)
These five types of breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), when conjoined with the Lord of Causes, destroy all taints and defects; they are all accomplishers of every goal.
Indeed, there are five types of breath control (prāṇāyāma) that bring about the perfection of yoga;
these are practiced either in the center of the heart-lotus, or in the moon, or in the lotus of the sky.

[He resides] within the eight-petaled lotus of the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka), which is covered by the petals of the eight [faculties] and endowed with the coverings of its own respective limbs, together with the forms of the Lords of the Principles (tattva) and the Lords of the Principles who preside over the spheres (maṇḍala) beginning with the Sun.
Whichever deity a person is devoted to, he should, while recollecting that deity therein, mutter its respective mantra with his intellect,
following the sequence of inhalation (pūraka) and the rest.
By practicing the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇāyāma), one shall attain perfection in yoga; or else, by beholding the stainless light within the lotus of the heart and other centers.

Meditating with the intellect upon the auspicious mass of consciousness (ciddhana), which is free from the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of causes such as Brahmā, or reciting the Praṇava consisting of pure consciousness (cinmātra-praṇava) along with its three morae (trimātra); (45)
One should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma); before long, one attains perfection by meditating on the Śakti as she has emerged from the Kuṇḍalinī at the root-lotus (mūlābja).
Then indeed, she [visualizes] herself as having an upward-pointing body resembling a streak of lightning, like a lotus in the sky, being drenched by the outpourings of supreme nectar. 47.
Having returned again and again to the root-lotus,
she ascends through the *suṣumnā*, raining down a stream of nectar.

Meditating on the supreme, subtle power (śakti), or indeed on the *praṇava* which is pure consciousness, the knower of yoga, having restrained his vital breaths with his intellect as before, should recite [the mantra]. (49)
One attains the perfection of yoga before long; there is no doubt about this. Or else, [one may recite] that which begins with the *praṇava* and is preceded by the seven *vyāhṛtis*. (50)
Reciting the Gāyatrī together with its Śiras three times mentally, one should meditate upon the Supreme Self in the heart, or in the ether, or indeed upon Sāvitrī or the Sun itself.

Meditating by the previously mentioned method, following the sequence of inhalation (pūraka) and so forth, the yogi who practices the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇāyāma) shall attain perfection. || 52 ||
Furthermore, by means of six, twelve, and likewise sixteen [repetitions] in succession,
one may destroy here the sins born of mind, speech, and action.
Furthermore, by performing breath control (prāṇāyāma) twice or even thrice as many times—
as much as one hundred and eight— one may destroy even the sin of killing an embryo.
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya and Vasiṣṭha state:
"Even for the slayer of a learned Brāhmaṇa (bhrūṇahan), performed daily, it purifies [the sinner] within a month;
after three seasons, it purifies him from the sin committed in another birth; and after a year, he becomes all-knowing in this world."
One is even born as a knower of Brahman; furthermore, the *kumbhaka* breathings give rise to perspiration, trembling, and rising.
They are classified as inferior, middling, and superior, and their results are likewise;
by practicing breath control (prāṇāyāma) in successive stages, the vital winds (vāyus) are conquered.
p. 533) Without knowledge [of the breath], it is not possible [to control] inhalation, exhalation, and so forth;

likewise, without the *pūraka* (inhalation), and indeed without the *recaka* (exhalation), one who has mastered the vital air (*anila*) may remain for a very long time through *kumbhaka* (retention) alone. Furthermore, one shall attain a speed of movement equal to that of the mind.
And one perceives objects even from afar.
In twelve years, one becomes a Khechara, free from old age and grey hair; by twice that number of years, one becomes long-lived.
He sees and even converses with sages, gandharvas, gods, and others; then, after twice as many years, he attains the powers such as aṇimā.
The Section on Breath Control (Prāṇāyāma). The forceful withdrawal of the senses as they run toward their respective objects is called pratyāhāra (withdrawal). 55.
The wise know that the mental performance within the heart of beneficial actions, such as those prescribed for daily rites and so forth, without external ritual procedure, is called *pratyāhāra*.
Alternatively, some indeed call "pratyāhāra" (withdrawal) the bringing of the vital air under one's own control by drawing it into and placing it within the eighteen locations. (57)
Those various locations:
the two big toes, the ankles, the shanks, the knees, the thighs, and the genitals; then the waist, the *kanda*, the navel, the heart, and the chest. (58)
The pit of the throat, the palate, the nose, the eyes, the space between the eyebrows, and the crown of the head—these eighteen [sites] are reached sequentially from one place to the next. (59)
The wise have declared that the withdrawal of the breath after having drawn it in is called *pratyāhāra*;
by this, there shall be the pacification of diseases as well as the increase of lifespan. (60)

The Section on Pratyāhāra: For the yogin who has been purified by the five [restraints] beginning with yama, the stabilization of the intellect within the Self is declared to be dhāraṇā (concentration). 61.
The intellect (buddhi), together with the vital breath (marut), resides in a specific location within the body;
[one should contemplate] the lords of the causes (*kāraṇeśvarān*).

Having recollected the intellect (buddhi) right there, according to the path described for the purification of the elements beginning with the knees, from its own seed-syllable, as being devoid of any other supporting cognition; || 64 ||
Having established [the mind] together with the vital breath through the five fixations (dhāraṇās), each consisting of three [units], one becomes... 65.
Having joined Brahmā and the other lords of the causes with their respective causes—
through the differentiation of the syllables of the *praṇava* and by means of the syllables of the mandala beginning with earth (kṣiti)— [one should proceed].

Having united one's own self, which consists of that [consciousness], with the partless Śiva—who abides at the limit of the twelve finger-breadths (dvādaśānta) and is a mass of consciousness—one should [realize] Him as all-pervading and all-knowing. (67)
The Chapter on Concentration (Dhāraṇā).
Now, meditation (dhyāna) is said to be twofold: with parts (sakala) and likewise without parts (niṣkala). Meditation with form is "with parts," while that which is formless is "without parts. (69)

One should perform the recollection of the form of the desired deity within the heart and other centers, through various distinctions such as having four arms, being white in color, possessing two or three eyes, or having one face.

The meditation with form has been taught; now the formless is being described. [It is practiced] either in the heart-lotus, or between the eyebrows, or in the *bindu* located at the end of the twelve.
One should meditate upon the supreme *liṅga*-light, the size of a thumb,
shaped like a *kadamba* bud, illuminating the ends of the quarters with its radiance.
Therefore, the light, resembling the awn of wild rice, having emerged upward through the *suṣumnā*,
has attained oneness with Śiva who resides at the *dvādaśānta*.
With a steady mind, one should meditate on the light, blazing with crests of flame, emerging from the pores of the skin and sweat, pervading and encompassing the entire universe. (74)
But this is considered the supreme among meditations, and this is regarded as the highest yoga. Thus, with his self disciplined by truth, the yogi is shaken free from all bonds.

Having attained the sovereign powers such as *aṇimā* and the rest, he remains unamazed; untouched by the six waves [of physical and mental states], he is yet devoid of qualities such as friendliness (*maitrī*). (76)
Endowed with forgiveness, self-restraint, and tranquility, and compassionate toward all living beings, he cuts through the bonds consisting of the qualities and attains supreme nirvāṇa.
Meditation (dhyāna) is held to extend for twelve [cycles] of the dhāraṇās; from meditation, concentration (samādhi) clearly arises with a duration of twelve [cycles]. || 78 ||
The Chapter on Meditation:
Samādhi is the state of equality between the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman). Likewise, Brahman, called Śiva, is the supreme light, perfectly pure. (79)
It is a single mass of consciousness, peaceful, the cause of all causes, liberated from the three states, and beyond the sixfold modifications of being. (80)
It is the benefactor of all, all-pervading, eternal, and stainless;
it is [unaffected] by the great elements beginning with space, nor by objects such as sound. (81)

[He is distinct] even from the ten organs, the mind, the intellect, the ego, and the [three] qualities; as well as from the vital breaths and so forth, from primordial nature (prakṛti), and from the two that precede [it], namely ignorance (avidyā).
It is devoid of niyati, kalā, kāla, and māyā; yet it is the cause of all things through its proximity to Īśvara, vidyā, and śakti.
It is the eternal illuminator of the end of sound (nāda), the sole cause of the fivefold cosmic acts, without beginning or end, supreme and subtle; that which is "I am He" is indeed "I am He. (84)
The perfect fixing of the mind upon Śiva is traditionally known as samādhi; it occurs when the mind attains a state of equilibrium through the perception of equality everywhere. (85)
That which is free from defects such as passion, indifferent toward what is to be abandoned or acquired, and perpetually established in Śiva, is remembered as the supreme samādhi. (86)

In this body, there is the realization of non-self, and regarding objects, there is the realization of their lack of inherent existence; for one who has abandoned the three types of craving by relinquishing ritual action, sons, and wealth.
Through the renunciation of all undertakings and the avoidance of all attachments, one should cultivate the realization of oneness with Śiva, the all-pervading pure consciousness. 88.
p.
636) Continuous, uninterrupted concentration is the liberation from the noose.
[Whether] smelling, remaining silent, speaking, lying down, or even sitting...
Whether one is watching with eyes open or standing with eyes closed. || 90 ||
Whether one is awake or sleeping, or even while perceiving dreams, when the mind remains unmoving even as one walks, it is established in samādhi.

Through the withdrawal of the instruments [of action], there is non-manifestation even toward sense objects; that is to be known as the supreme yoga, and one who possesses it is called a lord of yogis. (92)
The supernatural powers, such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest, are the intermediate fruits of yoga;
indeed, these eight qualities of sovereignty become obstacles to yoga.
One should not take pleasure in those [other] yogas; for liberation is the fruit of yoga, therefore one should take pleasure in that. 94.
Thus, this yoga with its constituent limbs has been clearly demonstrated here in brief, having been recollected from the Yoga-shastras through the grace of Shiva. (95)

Through the application of knowledge and action, made clear and beautiful by the discernment of animals and other beings, the eightfold qualities of sovereignty are likewise easily attained; thus Īśānaśiva, the preceptor of the gods, has proclaimed the path of the Siddhānta for those seeking the highest good and ultimate liberation. (96)
Thus ends the third chapter, beginning with breath control (prāṇāyāma), in the Yoga Section of the Upper Part of the *Siddhāntasāra*, the *Śrīmad-Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati*.
The Yoga Section is completed.
And thus ends this *Siddhāntasārapaddhati*, the work of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva.
